Five London bars made the list, including The Connaught Bar, which dropped from its No. 1 ranking for two consecutive years, to No. 8 in 2022. London’s Tayēr + Elementary, which awards ceremony host Mark Sansom said is “one of the most original bars on the planet,” held onto its No. 2 spot from 2021. Europe dominated with more top bars than any other region. The list is the result of votes from 650 bartenders and bar owners, drinks writers and cocktail experts. More big winners New York rebounded from a less dazzling showing than usual in 2021 to become the city with the most highly ranked bars on the 2022 list. New York is home to six top 50 bars, including Double Chicken Please at No. 6 and Katana Kitten at No. 9. Double Chicken Please won the Highest New Entry award for its strong debut. Sansom, who is content director of The World’s 50 Best Bars, told CNN Travel the bar has “an almost Michelin-grade kitchen,” one example of a growing emphasis on food programs at the world’s leading bars. In Singapore, No. 33 Manhattan also does “seriously, seriously elevated bar food,” Sansom said. Mexico City is another North American cocktail capital with four bars in the top 50, including No. 4 Licorería Limantour, winner of the Best Bar in North America award. Cartagena’s Alquímico is the Best Bar in South America at No.10. There are three bars in Buenos Aires on the list as well as one in Lima. In Asia, Singapore, Bangkok and Hong Kong all had two bars in the top 50. At No. 12, Jigger & Pony in Singapore won the Best Bar in Asia award. Dubai had three bars in the top 50, including including No. 38 Zuma, the Best Bar in the Middle East and Africa winner for the third year in a row. In India, New Delhi’s Sidecar jumped 21 places to No. 26. The Best Bar in Australasia is Maybe Sammy in Sydney at No. 29. The world’s best bars for 2022 1. Paradiso, Barcelona (Winner: Best Bar in Europe) 2. Tayēr + Elementary, London 3. Sips, Barcelona (Winner: Highest Climber) 4. Licorería Limantour, Mexico City (Winner: Best Bar in North America, Legend of the List) 5. Little Red Door, Paris (Winner: Sustainable Bar Award) 6. Double Chicken Please, New York (Winner: Highest New Entry) 7. Two Schmucks, Barcelona 8. The Connaught Bar, London 9. Katana Kitten, New York 10. Alquímico, Cartegena (Winner: Best Bar in South America) 11. Handshake Speakeasy, Mexico City 12. Jigger & Pony, Singapore (Winner: Best Bar in Asia) 13. Hanky-Panky, Mexico City (Winner: Art of Hospitality) 14. Bangkok Social Club, Bangkok (Winner: Best New Opening) 15. Salmon Guru, Madrid 16. Drink Kong, Rome 17. Coa, Hong Kong 18. Florería Atlántico, Buenos Aires 19. The Clumsies, Athens 20. Baba au Rum, Athens 21. Cafe La Trova, Miami 22. Attaboy, New York 23. Satan’s Whiskers, London 24. Tropic City, Bangkok 25. Kumiko, Chicago For the full list of the top 50, visit the World’s 50 Best Bars site. What visitors will find in bars right now With barhopping curbed by the pandemic, customers are more likely to linger in one place, Sansom said, and bars are offering more live entertainment in addition to upping their food programs to keep guests occupied for hours. And the lines between food and drink are blurring. “The techniques and flavors associated with cooking and gastronomy are emerging in drinks and cocktail craft,” Sansom said, citing New York’s Double Chicken Please again. The bar’s Back Room menu features an array of food-inspired cocktails – from Waldorf Salad (whisky-based with apple, celery, ginger ale and walnut bitters) to Japanese Cold Noodle (rum-based with pineapple, cucumber, coconut, lime and sesame oil). Two Schmucks in Barcelona is also leaning on flavors associated with food. “Its Curry Colada is one of the best cocktails I think I’ve ever drunk,” Sansom said. Tools such as the centrifuge that made their way from science labs to restaurant kitchens in the past few decades have also appeared in craft cocktail bars in the past decade, he said. And custom glassware that sometimes inspires the drink rather than the other way around is increasingly important at many bars, including at world’s best bar Paradiso. After the past couple of years, great hospitality is more important than ever, Sansom said. “Post-pandemic, bars are a lot more aware of the value of each individual customer and making them feel wanted, safe, secure as they go into those environments.” CNN’s Maureen O’Hare contributed to this report. Top image: Paradiso in Barcelona is the No. 1 bar on the World’s 50 Best Bars list in 2022 and the Best Bar in Europe winner.

item.title: Asia Pacific set to lose title as the world's largest travel region
item.description:
Source: CNN Travel Score: 4.09
Editor’s Note: Sign up for Unlocking the World, CNN Travel’s weekly newsletter. Get news about destinations opening, inspiration for future adventures, plus the latest in aviation, food and drink, where to stay and other travel developments. Asia Pacific is home to some of the world’s most beloved travel destinations, from the natural beauty of Bali to the urban buzz of Singapore. These dreamy vacation hotspots – teamed with the region’s business power – secured Asia Pacific the title of world’s largest travel region for much of the past decade. But with destinations like China and Japan comparatively slow to drop Covid entry restrictions, air travel in Asia Pacific remains low compared to the region’s pre-pandemic levels. And a new report from international travel industry analysts the Centre for Aviation (CAPA) predicts Asia Pacific will no longer be the world’s largest travel region by the end of 2022, ceding the title to Europe. Where once Asian Pacific air traffic accounted for more than a third of all global passenger journeys, aviation in the region remains down by 45% compared to pre-pandemic levels, according to CAPA. Meanwhile, CAPA suggests European air travel has recovered to roughly 85% of pre-pandemic levels, even accounting for the continued impact of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Slow recovery In 2019, 3.38 billion passengers transited through Asia Pacific airports. In contrast, CAPA reports that current predictions from ACI Asia-Pacific – an industry organization that represents airports in the region – suggest 1.84 billion passengers will have passed through Asia Pacific travel hubs by the end of 2022. A key factor in this slow recovery is China’s “zero-Covid” border policy and Japan’s slow relaxation of travel restrictions, at least according to ACI Asia-Pacific and CAPA. Japan is set to officially reopen to tourists on October 11. “What happens there has an outsized impact on the rest of the region,” says CAPA of China and Japan, pointing out they’re two of the region’s top travel markets. CAPA reports that most travel in Asia Pacific destinations remains at 50% or more below 2019 levels, with only a couple of exceptions, such as India, which is only 11% below its 2019 figure. Domestic travel in Asia Pacific is recovering faster than international travel, notes CAPA – domestic travel within China, for example, is only down 5.4% compared to 2019 levels. All in all, CAPA predicts Asia Pacific won’t see a full return to pre-pandemic travel figures until the end of 2023 or early 2024. “Even then, recovery is dependent on countries opening their borders and ending lingering travel restrictions, as well as the wider economic and epidemiological situations,” reads the report. CAPA is arguing for “harmonization of international travel rules” and “political commitments towards openness and freedom of movement” as well as a continued vaccination drive, to aid travel recovery. Top photo of the Great Wall of China courtesy Powerstock/Adobe Stock

item.title: The Saint-Tropez Scene May Seem Impenetrable—Here Are Our 10 Unwritten Rules for Making the Most of It
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 6.39
Brigitte Bardot may be gone, but the mythology she unwittingly created in Roger Vadim's 1956 And God Created Woman still defines how the world imagines Saint-Tropez: a world of sun-kissed shores, seduction, and carefree abandon. But that enchantment began long before the beach clubs and celebrity sightings. Back in 1892, French artist Paul Signac dropped anchor here, encouraging friends such as Henri Matisse and André Derain to follow. And in the 1920s, weary of Paris, the writer Colette settled near Plage des Salins, finding joy in picking figs and lemons from her garden, dancing at open-air balls with young sailors—and eventually declaring she'd found paradise. Today's cast of characters is more likely to include billionaires, influencers, and a new generation chasing the White Lotus fantasy. Yet Saint-Tropez remains stubbornly itself, with social rituals and unspoken conventions that aren't always obvious at first. Knowing them won't just help you avoid the occasional faux pas; they'll help you navigate the village like a pro. Know thy beach club With some 27 private beach clubs spread across the three-mile sweep of Pampelonne, choosing the right place by the sea can be a conundrum. Some come for the high-octane DJs at Shellona or the all-day revelry of Nikki Beach; others swear by the legendary glamour of Le Club 55 or the festive energy of Casa Amor. For a bohemian spirit, there's Indie Beach or Cabane Bambou. Byblos Beach is for languorous lunches; La Réserve à la Plage for understated chic; Loulou Ramatuelle for Parisians-en-vacances chic; and Jardin Tropézina for White Lotus buzz. The trick isn't booking the hottest beach club—it's finding the one that suits your mood. Peak-season reservations are often made weeks in advance, so don't leave booking until the last minute—even the best hotel concierge won't always be able to guarantee you a table at Le Club 55. And if you're more interested in swimming than napkin waving, skip the clubs entirely and join the locals who plant an umbrella in the sand, unpack a cooler, and spend a couple of hours by the water. Dress well, change often Saint-Tropez has always welcomed a touch of fashion bravado. Cowboy boots, micro-minis, oversized hats, and platform sandals have all had their moments, but one thing never changes—Saint-Tropez is not a one-outfit kind of place, even for the most committed minimalist. Pack accordingly: men and women alike should expect to change clothes at least three times a day. A linen shirt or light cover-up is de rigueur as soon as you sit down for lunch at a beach club, and nobody parades around the port or the village in a bikini or bare-chested. Like a growing number of French seaside resorts, it's not only frowned upon; you can be fined. Come early evening, people head back to their hotel or villa to shower and change into finer clothing for the next round: dinner, and for some, a party that rages until dawn. Win them over A little local know-how can make all the difference. "The first thing you do when you arrive at a beach club is tip your waiter, not afterward," says one French property developer who grew up in the south of France and now lives in Miami. "That way they'll take care of you from the start.” For a group, he suggests around 100€. “Also, it's very rude to ask waiters their names." However tempting it may be to call out, "Xavier! Another tequila espresso martini!"—resist the urge. A discreet s'il vous plaît is much more in keeping with French dining etiquette. Don't broadcast The loudest person in the room is rarely the most interesting. Whether you're lingering over coffee and croissants, lounging by the hotel pool or sipping an apéro at Sénéquier, nobody needs to hear your Zoom call, who invited you aboard their yacht yesterday, or exactly how much your latest business deal raked in. In a village where money is often splashed around, talking about it remains distinctly un-French. Lunch will be long, so leave time for it The shimmering midday heat has a way of slowing everything down. Seek out a shady table, whether by the sea, beneath pine and tamarisk trees, or on a village terrace. This is lunch à la Provençale; expect a multi-course meal with pauses between courses (no, the service isn't slow). Bread, olive oil, and rosé arrive early. It's prime time for people-watching and catching up with friends. Take a seat Strolling through the village clutching an oversized water bottle, a takeaway iced latte, or a pastry is a dead giveaway that you're a tourist. Trying to eat an oozy tarte tropézienne while window-shopping is perhaps the greatest red flag. "There's no rush here—it's not like you're on your way to a meeting," says Emilia Jedamska, director of St Tropez House. Find a café and pull up a chair instead. The unofficial cappuccino cut-off comes at 11 a.m., at which point the French switch to espresso. As for eating on the move, the one exception is ice cream. From Barbarac to Cyril Lignac's new boutique on the port, a cone is a perfectly acceptable portable indulgence while gawking at the superyachts. Two wheels are the ultimate transport If you've ever fantasized about zipping around on a Vespa, now's your chance. Scooters, e-bikes, and even Mini Mokes make it easy to beat the traffic and explore beyond Pampelonne, from the quieter beaches of Les Salins and Les Graniers to the crystal-clear coves of L'Escalet. After dark, though, the rules change somewhat: you'll want your hotel to whisk you into town via chauffeur-driven Bentley or Rolls-Royce as part of the evening theater. Look beyond labels In a village you can cross on foot in little more than 15 minutes, around 230 international flagships and independent boutiques make shopping an essential way to get to know the place. But don't stop at the designer labels. Alongside the familiar brands are hidden galleries, locally made resortwear, and the town’s long-established sandal makers. This isn't department-store shopping. These are small, independently owned boutiques where shopkeepers expect a greeting when you arrive—and an au revoir when you leave, even if you haven't bought a thing. Take your time, but resist the urge to rifle through every rack, inspect every handbag, or try on 30 pairs of sunglasses. Where to stay in Saint-Tropez Don't over-schedule It's tempting to try to tick off every hotspot and fill every hour with concierge-planned itineraries and reservations. However, the regulars who've been coming to Saint-Tropez for years know that some of the best moments happen in between by just seeing where the day takes them. Just don't let it be aboard a stranger's Wajer—not every invitation is as glamorous as it first appears. One group of young women I know accepted an invitation aboard a yacht after drinks at a beach club, only to find themselves trapped aboard a drug-fueled party they wanted no part of. They ended up calling a friend anchored nearby, who hurried over in his tender to rescue them. "There are two kinds of visitors," says Chantelle Oriani, founder of Oriani. "There's the flashy, 'I want to be seen' crowd and then the people who know. They stay somewhere low-key or take their yachts to discover quiet ports and aren't interested in what everyone else is doing. They might drop into a big party at Shellona one afternoon with their private security, have an absolutely wild time, and then disappear. The next day they're hiking the coastal path around Gigaro, having lunch somewhere like Chez Camille, or stopping at a vineyard for a sundowner." There's more than the myth The village that Brigitte Bardot helped put on the map—a sun-drenched, hedonistic playground of beach clubs, superyachts, and late-night parties—is only one chapter in the year. Come September, the harbor fills with the gleaming classic yachts and modern racing boats of Les Voiles de Saint-Tropez, one of the Mediterranean's most prestigious sailing regattas. By late October, the annual Grande Braderie transforms the village into an open-air shopping event as boutiques roll racks of end-of-season merchandise onto the sidewalks at deep discounts. Return then, and you'll discover a very different Saint-Tropez.

item.title: NYC’s Best Bars, From Haute Hotel Lobbies to Intimate Listening Rooms
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.86
Ask 10 New Yorkers to name their favorite bar, and you’re likely to hear at least as many answers—few debates are more heated than which bar is the best in New York City. That’s because, on any given night, a thousand versions of New York are unfolding at once: Artsy types are listening to a jazz trio in Bed-Stuy, while across the river, a group of friends is deciding which bottle of Pet Nat to split in Chinatown. A couple is ordering their second round of date night martinis at a swanky cocktail bar in the West Village, while Japanese whisky cocktails are poured over hand-chipped ice in Greenpoint. There’s a compelling case to be made that NYC is the best bar city in the world—a place where a million people could be having entirely different nights, but still feel the same connective electric hum. With a list of bars at least as long as the Empire State Building is tall, narrowing the options down is no small task. That’s why we scoured the city for you to find its most exciting destination for drinks right now. Below, our favorite bars in New York City. Read our complete New York City travel guide here, which includes: - The Best Restaurants in NYC - The Best Sushi in NYC - The Best Steakhouses in NYC - The Best Jewish Food in NYC How we choose the best bars in New York City Every bar on this list has been selected independently by Condé Nast Traveler editors and reviewed by a local contributor who has visited that business. Our editors consider both high-end and affordable options and weigh stand-out drinks, dishes, location, and service—as well as inclusivity and sustainability credentials. We update this list as new restaurants open and existing ones evolve. Additional reporting by Devra Ferst. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Chinatown, Manhattan Annie Shi, the former beverage director of King and Jupiter, spent two years hunting for the right space before landing this 28-seat wine bar on Doyers Street, Chinatown's short, curved, and colorful pedestrian-only stretch. It's Shi's first solo venture and a deeply personal one, named for her late sister, Hannah, whose Chinese name was Lei. The wine list is 350 bottles deep and ranges from Burgundy and Champagne to Portugal, Greece, and China. Ask their knowledgeable staff for help picking a bottle to pair with hot and cold dishes from their curated menu, which features farmer’s market ingredients and inventive Chinese cuisine and can certainly be made into a full dinner. Cherry-toned mahogany tables, rush-woven chairs, and domed sconces give the room a warm glow at night. Reservations open 14 days out at 9 a.m., but walk-ins are welcome nightly, so arrive on the early side unless you’re prepared to wait. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Two Bridges, Manhattan Named for a sotol-and-osha-root drink from northern Mexico, this buzzy new bar in Two Bridges is proof that a Michelin star doesn’t have to mean a stuffy bar program. Instead, the team behind Corima and its Park Slope tortilleria, Vato, wanted a casual, late-night hang for friends, and that’s exactly the energy at this walk-in-only, two-story spot. Here, beverage director Edward Hardebeck keeps things loose but skilled: multiple Michelada options from the surefire classic to a fruity mango option, a sotol margarita cut with Granny Smith apple and cilantro, an Irish twist on a caraijllo with whiskey from the Emerald Isle, as well as Guinness. It’s open until 2 a.m. on weekends, two hours later than its usual 12 a.m., making it one of those rare bars that works just as well on a weekday after work as it does for your Saturday nightcap. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Financial District, Manhattan Located a whopping 64 floors up 70 Pine Street, Overstory can be found via its own dedicated elevator in an Art Deco tower, and just one floor above neighboring two-Michelin-starred Saga, a seasonally focused restaurant with a tasting menu. Patrons are not playing—they're here for serious cocktails and great ambiance. Here, a curated bar program delivers cool boozy concoctions like the Easy Money, featuring vodka, coconut, yuzu, lime leaf, and soda; the Velvet Green with sotol, green tea, Sauvignon Blanc, grass, and lime; and the aptly named In the Clouds, featuring whiskey, Earl Grey, vanilla, Champagne, and clarified milk. Brought to you by the Crown Shy team, the service at Overstory is almost unparalleled, with a keen eye for detail. Needless to say, the views from Overstory are almost as worth a visit as their cocktails, providing patrons with a unique bird’s-eye view of the Big Apple. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Greenwich Village, Manhattan Almost a century after this Greenwich Village watering hole was established in 1915, Dante snagged new owners and quickly became a global cocktail destination. The MacDougal Street original maintains a stylish vibe that conjures its famous regulars—Patti Smith, Hemingway, Anaïs Nin—of yore. There are aperitivi and Bellinis, obscure Amari and bitters, and a 15-cocktail-long "Negroni Sessions" menu that's available for $10 each between 3:00 and 5:00 p.m. daily. Dante's footprint also continues to grow. A second outpost, Dante West Village, opened in 2020 with a focus on spritzes and martinis. The team has since added Dante Accademia, which hosts mixology classes and guest residencies, and Dante Aperitivo, an all-day seafood-and-aperitivo spot on Bank Street. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: West Village, Manhattan Few bars anywhere have climbed ranks as fast as this West Village-based multi-concept cocktail destination. After winning Best New U.S. Cocktail Bar at the 2025 Spirited Awards, Sip & Guzzle jumped to the coveted number one spot on North America's 50 Best Bars list in 2026, with three more Spirited Awards nominations to follow. Globe-trotting drinks innovators Shingo Gokan (Angel Share, SG Club Tokyo) and Steve Schneider (Employee's Only) only debuted it in January 2024. Downstairs, Gokan helms Sip, the sleek subterranean bar with a rotating cast of inventive cocktails that includes Doctor Green, a tequila cocktail cut with a vibrant mix of green apple, tomatillo, and a shiso horseradish blend, and a melon and gyokuro-infused Negroni in the Shade. Street-level Guzzle pours highballs and classics like the Yuzu Mugirita and Spicy Paloma. Impress a date by ordering their Wagyu sando, served in a golden takeout box at Sip, and don’t forget to cap your experience with their entirely addictive Hokkaido Milk Soft Serve. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Upper East Side, Manhattan At Bemelmans, Ludwig Bemelman's illustrations—you might remember them from the Madeline books—adorn the walls. In one panel, a bunny smokes a cigar in Central Park; in another, a man hands a boy a clutch of balloons. This is a bar where gawking is permissible. It's the final boss of hotel bars, tucked as it is inside The Carlyle. The cocktails here very much depend on who’s making them: an Old Fashioned might be a bit watery, a whiskey sour too tart. But often a dirty gin Martini is just perfectly executed. Everything is expensive—it’s clear why you’re here—so take the edge off that sensation by digging into the free, hearty snacks that float your way. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Midtown Manhattan It’s no surprise that a dedicated cocktail bar by the founders of Cote, the highly revered Korean steakhouse, would be gorgeous. One could never have guessed, though, that it would be tucked inside the Philip Johnson-designed 550 Madison, and feature three distinct bars occupying one soaring, 60-foot atrium. Bar Chimera’s unofficial mascot, a Norfolk pine tree, stands over 20 feet tall in the midst of a convivial wine bar up front, a mirrored martini bar staffed by white-jacketed bartenders, and a whiskey library where bottles climb nearly to the ceiling. We’re partial to the martini bar, where guests can watch their glasses get flash-chilled with liquid nitrogen, the resulting smoke then tossed back into the air with a flourish. Every martini is made with specifically filtered and re-mineralized ice, with a choose-your-own-adventure option of a base spirit and garnish, as well as inventive options like the citrusy, herbaceous Evergreen Alaska, featuring Fords Gin, Komasa Tangerine Gin, Yellow Chartreuse, and Thai basil. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Harlem, Manhattan Slip through the unmarked door after ringing a doorbell to enter this Harlem cocktail sanctuary, and you’re immediately transported back to the jazz era. The vibe here is dark and moody, and the space being so tiny makes it feel very intimate. Stylish and low-key, with a mix of local creatives grabbing a drink after a show at the nearby Apollo Theatre and couples on a romantic date, make up the crowd here. The cocktail program here leans avant garde, with each menu entry reading as a chapter in a book, and incorporating housemade infusions, rare spirits, and herbal elements. Some cocktails even incorporate spirits from their own microdistillery, Atheras Spirits, in Industry City. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Bushwick, Brooklyn A T-rex skull as decor, dino nuggets on the menu, and a (delicious) Negroni made with ants and crickets: welcome to Bushwick’s strangest, most delightful new bar. Co-founder Misha Chavez credits a lifelong love of nature and a childhood spent glued to documentaries for the concept, which is separated into a cafe-style “Gift Shop” up front and a more serious cocktail bar in the back. To enter, walk through the gift shop and then down the “Exhibition Hall” featuring cases of natural curiosities (crystals, fossils, and the like) pulled from the team’s own collections, and enter a space both moody and playful. Dim lighting sets the scene for a Permanent Collection of cocktails such as the Insectarium with honey gin, fig, black ants, wormwood, and crickets, and Birds of the World, a crushable highball which lead bartender Bobbi Adler built based on seeds and fruits birds actually love to eat, such as sunflower, guava, and pineapple. We’ll be returning regularly for their limited-time special exhibits, the first of which, of course, centers around dinosaurs. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Gramercy, Manhattan In early 2022, Takuma Wantanabe, the Tokyo-born head bartender of cult cocktail den Angel's Share, opened this intimate spot in an 1800s townhouse. The elegant space has three floors of carefully crafted cocktails, including a lower-level private event venue. Martiny's pours intricate, often cerebral drinks with top-shelf ingredients and prices to match. One standout is the Caprese cocktail, a refreshing combination of tomato water, whiskey, grapefruit juice, basil, and milk that pours crystal-clear. No matter how busy the bar, the staff is unfailingly attentive. Want to sit alone with a fancy drink and stare blankly into your phone or the middle distance? They'll give you your space. Curious about a bottle of rare Japanese whisky or the makings of one of the more complicated cocktails? A bartender will gladly share the details. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Harlem, Manhattan This cozy wine bar and restaurant sits on a Central Harlem corner next to its sibling bottle shop, Pompette, a neighborhood favorite since 2015. The space has exposed brick walls, a slim bar, and fresh flowers on every table, making it equally popular among well-dressed locals, second dates, and wine geeks. In addition to beer and cocktails, the bar pours nearly 100 wines by the glass and bottle, and the list is organized not by region or grape, but rather by reds, whites, sparkling, orange, and "Black AF," or an array of Black-owned wine labels including New York City's own B.Stuyvesant. Expect to fall in love with your drinking companion, a well-priced glass of pet-nat, or both before you leave. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Lower East Side, Manhattan Named North America’s best bar in 2023, Double Chicken Please houses two distinct concepts in one snug space on an industrial-looking stretch of Manhattan’s Lower East Side. The walk-in-only front bar is modeled after the neighborhood’s early-20th-century soda shops and serves draft cocktails, called “taptails," as well as the excellent titular fried chicken sandwiches. Seats in the more formal rear bar, The Coop, can be reserved up to six days in advance, and have access to a menu of pricier, made-to-order cocktails—many of which are inspired by savory dishes. The Japanese Cold Noodle is a fan favorite for a reason, made with Bacardi Superior, pineapple, coconut, lime, and sesame. The more formal food menu in back includes plates of chicken liver mousse and an array of fried chicken sandwiches, including one on an out-of-this-world spicy mochi donut. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Cobble Hill, Brooklyn The lights over the booths are intimate and old-timey, and the decades-old bar itself—note the quadruple-paneled mirror by the cash register—is stunning. Folks throw on their nice pair of jeans, or some good earrings, to come here. Co-owner Toby Cecchini (who, incidentally, invented the Cosmo at The Odeon many years ago) has a following, and his cocktails are known around the city, so it’s a bit of a see-and-be-seen along the bar. The menu sports a short list of slightly twisted classics—a martini made with junmai daiginjo sake, a gimlet with ginger-lime cordial, a white negroni sbagliato. Pick one off the menu or list a mix of flavors you like; you’ll end up happy either way, especially if you pair your drink with a burger. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Lower East Side, Manhattan A minimalist shelter from the storm of Lower East Side partiers, Bar Goto has sleek Japanese design, attentive service, excellent highballs and bar food. Kenta Goto, owner and barman, was once at the dearly departed Pegu Club, and has retained that famous bar’s warm service and exacting attention to detail. It shines in his highballs and the delicate coupe cocktails, such as one made with a rosy cherry blossom, sake, gin, and maraschino. The food here is not an afterthought. The okonomiyaki—that killer izakaya drinking standard of fried cabbage and kewpie mayo, dancing with bonito flakes and stuffed full of pork belly, rock shrimp, and squid that will transport you to Tokyo—is some of the best in town. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Seaport, Financial District, Manhattan Sometimes, the beverage program at hyped bars starts to rest on its laurels. This is not the case at Dead Rabbit, a tri-level Financial District destination which offers an impressive mix of classic and house cocktails, a devoted list of Irish Whiskey drinks, draft beers, and non-alcoholic creations. Food menus vary by floor, with some overlap. Try Irish-accented pub grub like Guinness-braised burgers and chicken pot pie in the lower-level taproom, and smoked salmon deviled eggs and lamb chops in the upstairs Parlor Room. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: NoMad, Manhattan It goes without saying that the city has its fair share of hotel bars, but Portrait Bar in the Fifth Avenue Hotel sets itself apart, thanks to an invitingly cozy atmosphere and a top tier cocktail list, among other superb attributes. Designed by Martin Brudnizki (the brain behind other handsome NYC spaces like Fouquet’s), the Flatiron-based space features dark wood paneling, red velvet seating, and, you guessed it: an array of portraits adorning the walls. Sidle up next to the fireplace to enjoy one of their internationally inspired beverages dreamt up by Bar Director Darryl Chan, from a rum and scotch clarified cocktail that nods to Cebu Island in the Philippines with notes of calamansi (a Southeast Asian citrus) and Bay Leaf, to a star anise and yuzu-infused take on a whiskey sour reminiscent of Kochi, Japan. A solid menu of Parlor Snacks—comté gougères, mini tuna tartare tacos, a fois gras tartine—seals the deal on Portrait Bar’s position as a perfect after-work, pre-dinner go-to, or perhaps a third date you really want to impress. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: East Village, Manhattan Unless you show up right when they open, you'll want to make a reservation, lest you end up on a very long wait list. Death & Co. cropped up on New Year’s Eve, 2007, and made one hell of a splash. The drinks were so precise, containing instant classics now mimicked nationwide (and now available nationwide, too), that it lured talent who have since opened their own famous bars. Look for riffs on classic cocktails like the Jungle Strut, which substitutes the traditional Jungle Bird’s rum, Campari, and pineapple juice for sotol, clairin, and watermelon. Things get much more esoteric than that, though, so flip through the huge book to see what you might want. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn Ain’t the band swingin’? That’s what you’ll be asking your friends during an experience at Bed-Stuy’s LunÀtico, in a mid-Atlantic accent (of course), right after suddenly donning a pair of tiny round sunglasses and a pageboy cap. They’ll be startled, but will have to reply with resounding sounds of agreement. A jazz club, cocktail bar, and restaurant, LunÀtico is the kind of place that makes you feel like you’ve stepped back in time. Maybe it's the artfully weathered walls (and ceiling), or maybe it's the lively, unpretentious undercurrent of energy that only grows with the coaxing of a saxophone, bass guitar, and bacanora fizz—a take on the classic gin fizz with bacanora (a Mexican agave spirit), honey, lemon, orange cream citrate, orange blossom water, and egg white. The space here is narrow and typically packed, and reservations don’t exist. Neither do cover fees, though they do suggest bringing a $10 cash donation for the band. If you want to guarantee yourself a spot, especially if you’re hungry for dinner and craving their roast chicken with a black pepper orange zest béchamel, plan on arriving on the early side. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Williamsburg, Brooklyn The little round marble bar and a whiff of New Orleanian dishabille catch your attention first. This Williamsburg standby is renowned for its cocktail program, oyster happy hour, and general Southern Gothic vibe. The light is made for Instagram, and you’ll see brunchers taking full advantage of it. Absinthe addicts, attention: This is your bar. There’s a whole separate menu devoted to absinthe cocktails, a real vintage drip in-house, and barkeeps who know what they’re doing with it all. Brews are mostly locally sourced and tasty, and the non-absinthe drinks shine, too. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Red Hook, Brooklyn There's something satisfying about drinking a bourbon cocktail a few feet from where its star ingredient was made. That's the pitch at Botanica, tucked inside the working Widow Jane Distillery on Conover Street, steps from the Red Hook waterfront. Exposed brick and warm, low light set the tone for a cocktail program built almost entirely around the house's own bourbon and rye. Order their simple yet impeccable 10-Year Bourbon Old Fashioned, which highlights what Widow Jane does best, and is sweetened with Demerara and finished with orange peel. Alternatively (or in tandem) work through a whiskey flight to taste the range by the ounce. Pro tip: Start your experience with a tour of the distillery before getting cozy at the bar. Not too cozy, though, that you miss a stroll along the waterfront for prime views of Lady Liberty. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Midtown Manhattan That a bar in the heart of Times Square is so tourist-free is one of many mysteries at Jimmy’s, a boxing memorabilia-saturated spot once dominated by the Midtown media set. In one snapshot, the late longtime owner and former boxing trainer Jimmy Glenn poses with Muhammad Ali. Especially if you have visiting out-of-towners in tow who, bless their hearts, really only want to see Times Square. It’s a way to sneak them a little bit of Real New York. Recently, Jimmy’s has been getting some pretty serious attention for an ongoing legal battle with its landlord over an attempted eviction. The judge has temporarily halted proceedings, meaning the bar is open as usual for now, but consider this extra incentive to stop by sooner rather than later. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Harlem, Manhattan In 2018, three HBCU (Historically Black Colleges and Universities) grads and craft beer lovers opened this cozy beer bar in a Harlem storefront with a twinkling backyard. Longtime neighborhood denizens, young professionals meeting for happy hours, and craft beer pilgrims from all five boroughs convene to drink from any of sixteen taps that offer everything from IPAs to pilsners to sours and beyond, with a focus on beers made by Black and POC brewers. There's also canned beers and ciders starting at $5 each, and a full bar for cocktails like the Uncle Nearest Old Fashioned, made with Uncle Nearest Tennessee Whiskey. The best menu items are the three bratwursts (one vegan), which are perfectly snappy and served on pretzel buns alongside handfuls of kettle chips. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Fort Greene, Brooklyn You’d be hard-pressed to find a Fort Greene local who doesn’t know about, and love, Rhodora. The cozy wine bar from the Oberon Group was opened in 2019 and quickly became somewhat of an institution in the leafy neighborhood. Its indoor and outdoor tables (especially coveted when the weather is good) are always bustling with groups catching up over bottles of all-natural, low-intervention wine from a list curated with an eye toward small-farm producers. Service at Rhodora is equally low-intervention: walk-in only and counter service. We also love that its rustic, welcoming atmosphere makes it equally as attractive to stop in for an impromptu glass or two in any season. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Gowanus, Brooklyn Gowanus's Threes Brewing is one of those rare New York City taprooms that can please almost everyone. There are booths, a stellar backyard, a large bar, and beers that will impress hops nerds as well as folks who simply want a glass of something cold on a hot summer day. As the name implies, it's a functioning brewery, and the menu shows off not only the house-made beers but a rotating cast of brews from producers like Allagash, Suarez Family Brewery, and Other Half, a Brooklyn favorite. Each is listed beside its flavor profile, and many come in a range of pour sizes. There’s a small list of wines and cocktails, too. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Lower East Side, Manhattan Reserve in advance to visit this swank Lower East Side cocktail lounge. Brought to you by the team behind Maison Premiere (another of our other favorite bars in NYC), there's a compulsory but complimentary coat check and dress-to-impress door policy, neither of which hampers the high spirits in the space. New York's bright young things fill the candlelit tables and banquettes and eight-person, U-shaped bar, requesting custom combinations off of the "Martini by Ratio" menu. The Cigarette Martini, made with Truman vodka and a juniper spirit from Copenhagen's Empirical, is among the most popular. Tigre also pours wine, spirits, and a tightly curated selection of retro and modern cocktails, with 1970s throwbacks like the Screwdriver alongside inventive drinks like the Mister Softee, named for the ice cream trucks that roam city streets in the summertime and made with Singhani, the Bolivian eau-de-vie. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Downtown Brooklyn Tucked into the second floor of a landmark Brooklyn building, above the swish Gage & Tollner dining room, this nautically themed bar feels simultaneously transportive and deeply grounded in New York cocktail culture. Stylish Brooklynites and quite a few who made the trek over from Manhattan fill the nooks and crannies of the dimly-lit space. Some are longtime friends and fans of co-owner St. John Frizell, who introduced the bar concept as a pop up at his now-shuttered Fort Defiance, a Red Hook cocktail institution. Sip the shiso-infused Special Daiquiri, an impressive array of tropical non-alcoholic concoctions, or find a friend to share the large-format Shattered Skull, a two-person affair made with Barbadian and Jamaican rums. There's also a short but smart selection of wine and beer. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Lower East Side, Brooklyn Inside the former Milk & Honey space where the modern cocktail revival began, the speakeasy vibe remains, and the bespoke cocktails served today would make Sasha Petraske proud. If there’s a beer or wine list at Attaboy, it’s irrelevant. Everyone has a cocktail in hand—a pricey one. This is a menu-free environment, so bring your inner cocktail nerd and any questions you might have. Sam Ross, founding co-owner, invented the Penicillin, and if you haven’t tried that combo of ginger, lemon, and Scotch before, let today be the day. As of December 2025, Attaboy has also doubled its famously tight footprint, expanding next door into the space once occupied by its short-lived sister bar, Good Guy's. Now guests can find a second, mirrored bar top that finally allows for a handful of reservations, along with the occasional pop-up and cocktail class. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Williamsburg, Brooklyn Hailed as New York City's first female- and veteran-operated brewery, TALEA is named for its owners, Tara Hankinson and LeAnn Darland. The two former homebrewers opened this 9,000-square-foot space in 2021 and now have three other taprooms across the city. Locals fill the tables at the airy Williamsburg flagship, meeting for birthday parties, afternoon hangs, or the chance to try one of the new drafts on the sours-heavy rotating tap list. TALEA is best known for its sour beers, like the pleasantly briny Watermelon Splash and Fan Fan Tart Deco, a sour IPA named for beloved Brooklyn bakery Fan Fan Donuts. There are also light lagers, pilsners, hazy IPAs, and non-alcoholic beers, as well as wine and cocktails from a full bar. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Red Hook, Brooklyn Since 1890, this unapologetically quirky institution has been serving drinks near Brooklyn's windswept Red Hook waterfront. It became Sunny's in the 1990s and has since cultivated a loyal community of people who self-identify as poets, teamsters, painters, or all of the above. Expect friendly banter among the locals and various performers who come to play live music every night except Mondays. While this isn't the place to go for an elaborate custom cocktail, the full bar serves skillfully-made Negronis, Manhattans, and other classics, as well as an array of craft and macro beers, natural wine, and non-alcoholic drinks. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: East Village, Manhattan This Mexican American cocktail destination on a busy corner of Manhattan's East Village always feels like a party. Its warm energy and creative drinks are hallmarks of co-owner Ignacio "Nacho" Jimenez, formerly of ground-breaking agave bar Ghost Donkey. Its tables and barstools are almost always packed with local loyalists, cocktail nerds, well-dressed people on second dates, and raucous groups whose happy hours inevitably turn into late nights. The free-wheeling drinks menu has a culinary bent and includes everything from a mezcal margarita and green mango martini to a large-format tepache cocktail made with shochu, yuzu, and chile de Arbol. Non-alcoholic drinks, like the guajillo-infused Chamoy y Soda, are similarly impressive, as is the bar food (Ensada-style fish tacos, potato flautas, and a crowd-pleasing birria grilled cheese to name a few.) - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: East Village, Manhattan The fancy cocktail bar format can quickly feel repetitive, but East Village’s Schmuck presents something a bit different. Rather than two tops galore and moody lighting, the space functions as a sort of cocktail house party—separated into two rooms referred to as The Living Room and The Kitchen Table. Groups are sat together, or stand in mingle-friendly areas while sipping cocktails and listening to the upbeat house music that blares from the speakers overhead. The design here feels eclectic and playful, like your coolest friend who lives in Williamsburg (even though Williamsburg isn’t cool anymore). Their cocktail elements are eyebrow-raising as well, with elements such as parmesan cheese in the clarified Strawberry & Cheese, and toasted oats that lend themself to a Muesli cocktail alongside bourbon, honey, and raspberry. Don’t be intimated, though, as the finished products are surprisingly approachable. Pair one or two with a dish from Schmuck’s curated menu of “Lobb Food,” from a satisfyingly cheesy white bean cacio e pepe to a puff pastry pizza. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Gramercy, Manhattan A Japanese-inspired jazz and cocktail bar in Gramercy Park from the team behind Martiny’s? The description alone is more than enough to sell it. Another selling point: its approachability. Firstly, walk-ins are encouraged, and the space itself feels distinctly lived-in despite having opened in summer 2024. Note that Midnight Blue charges a reduced cover fee of $10 to enjoy their nightly jazz performances (7 p.m., 8:45 p.m., 10:15 p.m.) on Tuesdays through Thursdays, with a $30 minimum spend per person. You have to hand over a Jackson per person on Fridays and Saturdays, along with a higher $50 minimum per person. Cabaret-style tables dot the area in front of the stage, but the bar is the place to be if you’re solo or with just one other person. Not only can you (kind of) still hear your companion, but you also get to chat with the skilled bartenders and witness them at work as they craft Toki highballs with a grapefruit twist, an Old Fashioned riff with osmanthus-infused Hibiki whisky, and a Wabi-Sabi sour featuring spicy wasabi and tart apple. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Lower East Side, Manhattan Part time swanky lobby bar, part time historic architectural marvel, Swan Room at Nine Orchard in the Lower East Side (a sub-area some now refer to as Dimes Square) is truly something to behold. Neo-Renaissance details, from vaulted ceilings featuring intricate crown moulding to walls clad in pink Tennessee marble, set the scene for a martini- and negroni-dominant cocktail menu that includes inventive riffs on the classics—an Evergreen Martini with Chartreuse and pickled kumquat, a mushroom gin “Umami” negroni with white soy, as well as a large format Martini Service that sets a group of 3-5 back $125. Martini and negroni haters need not despair, for Swan Room also offers a selection of signature cocktails, as well as a refreshingly extensive non-alcoholic menu. Those coming hungry can enjoy a Nine Orchard Burger or nosh on a selection of elegant small bites and desserts. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: East Village, Manhattan Any cocktail bar that markets itself as a “tropical hellscape” is immediate grounds for a visit, and the pure kitsch that is Paradise Lost fortunately delivers on that off-the-wall promise. The experience starts in East Village with a doorbell to ring, and quickly leads to a faux-foliage-filled madcap descent (figurative, not literal) into a tiki bar decked out head to toe in wood paneling and artfully placed trinkets. Cocktails here are split into three categories: The Ancients (tiki classics), New Acolytes (creative concoctions with spooky names), and Behemoths (scorpion bowls). For a cocktail with a show, try Lilith’s Bacchanal, a spicy sipper which combines rum with coconut gin, carrot, buzz button peppers, and the piece de resistance—a flaming lime on top. Besides the sneaky strength of the cocktails, heed this warning about the “press me” buttons in the bathroom stalls. All we will say is that those who are afraid of the dark (or glowing skulls) should pass on the offer. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Chelsea, Manhattan It's hard to imagine the elegant space that houses Lobby Bar as mere storage, but that is exactly what it functioned as until 2022, when an 11-year remodel of the historic Hotel Chelsea finally ended. Today, the multi-room cocktail bar and lounge is the perfect reflection of the timeless bohemian spirit of the Chelsea—filled with character, from the ketchup and mustard checkered tile in the solarium to vintage chandeliers and lamps, which illuminate an inlaid ceiling and velvet sofas in the bar room and beyond. There are no reservations here, so landing a seat is the first hurdle you’ll have to jump, with the second challenge presenting as what to order from their extensive (and expensive) cocktail list. They are perhaps best known for an 1884 Martini, which nods to the year the building was constructed, with gin, lemon, vetiver, and olive oil, but there are unique ingredients to be found across the board—like fig leaf and pecan in their Cowboy Mouth 3.0, or Oakmoss and a Rhubarb Amaro, which feature in a drink called Naked Lunch. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Greenpoint, Brooklyn For those not yet indoctrinated into the world of the listening bar, Eavesdrop might just be your gateway drug. The concept of a listening bar is far from new (it first took root in post-World War II Japan), the format of an intimate, vinyl record-spinning watering hole has been experiencing a modern revival in New York and beyond. At Eavesdrop in Greenpoint, they take their sound just as seriously as they take their cocktails, but that doesn’t mean a thumping bass or a raucous crowd. Instead, it’s more a blonde wood-filled place for audiophiles and high-minded imbibers to enjoy Japanese-inspired libations such as the Mr. Plum, with Hakuto Matsui gin, umeshu (Japanese plum liqueur), umeboshi (salted Japanese plums), ginger, honey and citrus, while a DJ spins R&B records in the background. Eavesdrop also has dinner, and it’s quite good, with fusion-style dishes that fortunately don’t feel gimmick-y. - Read Full ReviewNeighborhood: Midtown Manhahttan Le Bernardin sommelier extraordinaire Aldo Sohm opened this chic wine bar in 2014, and it maintains one of the best wine lists in Midtown Manhattan. A respite from the corporate-leaning restaurants on its surrounding blocks, the space has low-slung sofas, graphic art, and glittering pendant lamps. The effect is akin to drinking in a very elegant friend's living room. Expect a mix of wine professionals and deep-pocketed executives from nearby Midtown offices, many of whom can rattle of the names of preferred vintages and intricacies of vineyard classification systems like their own phone numbers. There are 40 wines by the glass and 200 bottles on offer at any given time, spanning $15 pours of approachable Southern Italian white wines and expense-account-worthy cult bottles of Burgundy.

item.title: The 15 Most Beautiful Airport Landings in the World, Ranked
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.59
Whether you’re a seasoned jetsetter or a first-time flier, few things compare to the bird's-eye vista that comes into focus during the most beautiful airport landings in the world. While the long-legged aisle-hoggers among us might not relate, travelers lucky enough to settle into the window seat on certain flight routes can look forward to quite the show ahead of touchdown. But which destinations are worth visiting for the landing alone? To uncover the most beautiful airport landings in the world, AllClear Travel Insurance analyzed 32 airports around the world known for the dazzling views ahead of the runway. One hundred participants were presented with a series of images showcasing the airport runways, and their visual engagement was measured using eye-tracking technology to determine the most captivating landings. The speed at which participants first focused on an image, and the average length of time participants spent looking at each image, were both recorded and turned into a score. Some of the high-scorers are frequent landing spots for Condé Nast Traveler editors. These include Madeira Airport, in joint third place with Pitkin County Airport, which is known as having one of the world’s most challenging approaches. As the plane descends, a lush landscape of verdant mountains that flow down into charming villages, beaches, and the crystal-clear waters beyond appears. Many travel editors are familiar with the landing at London City Airport, too, where the glittering city skyline shows itself like a mirage after high-altitude journeys. You’ll have to head down under for the most beautiful airport landing in the world, however – as Australia’s Lord Howe Island Airport claims the title, closely followed by New Zealand’s Queenstown Airport. See the complete list of bucket list landings below. The most beautiful airport landings in the world The score that follows each of the most beautiful airport landings in the world below represents the ‘eye-catching score’, calculated using the ‘average time spent looking’ in seconds and the ‘average time to first fixation’ in seconds. 1. Lord Howe Island Airport, Australia (score: 85) 2. Queenstown Airport, New Zealand (score: 79) 3. Madeira Airport, Portugal (score: 77) = Pitkin County Airport, United States of America (score: 77) 5. Rio de Janeiro-Santos Dumont Airport, Brazil (score: 76) = London City Airport, United Kingdom (score: 76) 7. Innsbruck Airport, Austria (score: 74) 8. Paro Airport, Bhutan (score: 72) 9. Juancho E. Yrausquin Airport, Caribbean Netherlands (score: 69) 10. Daniel K. Inouye International Airport, United States of America (score: 68) = Lukla Airport, Nepal (score: 68) 12. Seychelles International Airport, Seychelles (score: 65) = Telluride Regional Airport, United States of America (score: 65) = Nice Côte d'Azur Airport, France (score: 65) 15. Wellington International Airport, New Zealand (score: 60) = Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport, Canada (score: 60) This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: I Tested a Dozen of the Best Portable Chargers—These Are the Compact Power Banks That Stood Out
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.14
Portable chargers have become nearly as essential as the devices they’re meant to revive. Phones now hold our cameras, boarding passes, maps, hotel confirmations, currency converters, and translation apps, while laptops, tablets, earbuds, and smartwatches all need their share of power too. The problem is that shopping for a power bank can be oddly maddening: Many look nearly identical, carry different brand names, and make big claims that do not always hold up in real life. For this guide, I tested a dozen portable chargers over a month and a half of travel, draining them in real-world conditions to find the ones actually worth bringing along. I also stuck to models that meet standard carry-on battery limits, since airlines are paying closer attention to lithium-ion batteries and in-flight fire risks. The options below are fast, packable, and practical, with picks for every type of traveler and trip. How I tested: I tested 12 portable chargers from eight different brands over six weeks of near-constant travel, carrying them through Minnesota, Wisconsin, Southern Oregon, South Africa, Madagascar, and along an 11-day Danube river cruise from Bucharest to Budapest. I packed them in purses and carry-ons, and relied on them in airports and rental cars, on safari, and anytime I was roaming around a city on foot. Beyond my iPhone, I also plugged in my MacBook Air, AirPods, Apple Watch, Insta360 camera, and my four-year-old’s iPad. Between travels, I kept testing them at home on long daycare commutes and motorcycle rides, where GPS, music, and action-camera filming drain batteries especially fast. I compared how comfortable each charger was to carry and hold, how quickly it powered up my devices, how long it held a charge before the battery itself needed a battery, how fast it recharged, and whether its ports, cables, size, and weight makes sense for busy travel days. Best overall Best fast-charging power bank Best magnetic charger Best pocket-size charger Best eco-friendly charger Best for multiple devices Best for sharing power FAQ: Can I travel with a portable charger on the plane? Yes, but portable chargers should be packed in your carry-on, not your checked luggage. Most everyday power banks fall under the standard 100Wh limit and are allowed without special approval, but larger chargers between 101Wh and 160Wh require airline approval, and anything over 160Wh generally is not allowed on passenger flights. Damaged, swollen, or recalled batteries should not be packed at all. What does mAh mean? Milliamp hours, or mAh, are a measure of battery capacity. In general, the higher the mAh, the more power a portable charger can store—but that does not translate perfectly to full phone charges, since charging speed, cable type, battery efficiency, and the device you’re charging all play a role. A 5,000mAh charger may be enough for an emergency phone boost, while 10,000mAh to 20,000mAh models are better for long travel days or multiple devices. What brand makes the best portable charger? Anker and Belkin are my favorite brands overall, though the best portable charger depends on how you travel. Anker makes some of the most reliable, thoughtfully designed power banks I tested, while Belkin stands out for polished, user-friendly designs. I also found strong niche options from brands like iWalk, Nimble, and Iniu, especially for travelers who want something lightweight or more sustainable. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Where was 'Lady' filmed? A look inside the real-life home of the eccentric Lady Isabella
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.16
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Lady filmed? “I’m Lady Isabella, welcome to Ravenhyde Hall. Come on in, come and see where the magic happens…” These are some of the first words we hear from the leading lady of, well, Lady – director Samuel Abrahams’ new dark comedy centred around the life of a narcissistic, bizarre aristocrat. Sian Clifford (Fleabag, Ludwig) plays in the titular role in the film, which premiered at the BFI London Film Festival in October 2025, with Juliet Cowan, Laurie Kynaston and Olisa Odele claiming the supporting roles. The opening shots of Lady Isabella set the tone of the eccentricity to come. First, legs draped in vivid purple trousers lead down to shiny black loafers are shown to belong to a figure… lying face down on a grand staircase. Next, Lady Isabella is face down in a bush, her hands by her side, dressed in gardening gloves. Then, face down at a dining table. The life of an aristocrat must be hard, hey? As the crew Lady Isabella’s hired to film her life around the home wander around, the lead character’s idiosyncrasies unravel among dressed dining tables that stretch into the distance, kitchens fit for rustling up banquets and a jumble of taxidermy creations. Among the outrageous asides and outlandish happenings, there’s another star that steals the spotlight – the gorgeous country estate in which everything takes place. To film the hilarious mockumentary-style flick, Lady’s production team descended on Somerleyton Hall, a Grade II listed country house and estate in Suffolk, a 20-minute drive south of the popular seaside town of Great Yarmouth. Somerleyton Hall’s history stretches all the way back to the age of the Vikings, with records of a homestead on the land as the Nordic warriors settled along England’s east coasts. The first property to resemble what would eventually become a fantastical manor arrived in the Tudor era as the Lords of Somerleyton (who later moved to America fearing prosecution for their Catholicism following the accession of Elizabeth I). The land has seen myriad comings and goings since, as the Jacobeans, Victorians and Edwardians built on the foundations left by the generations that preceded them. The Somerleyton Hall visited by countless curious families and history buffs today is a Jacobean Manor house surrounded by thousands of acres of resplendent gardens. The property and garden is open on select days between spring and autumn, typically opening around the beginning of April and closing at the end of October.

item.title: 11 best places to see bioluminescence for awe-inspiring adventures
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.48
The best places to see bioluminescence around the world sit atop many travellers’ bucket lists. Whether it's through the pages of glossy magazines like ours, glittering on social media feeds or told through the tales our jet-setting loved ones share on their return from their latest adventure, this natural phenomenon is undeniably captivating. Perhaps it's jellyfish that twinkle at the harbour’s edge or plankton that creates scenes akin to starry skies as toes paddle in the ocean – either way, bioluminescence is a fascinating natural phenomenon that, once witnessed, is impossible to forget. However, it’s unlikely that you’ll see glittering, rippling waters by chance. Here, from the shores of Oaxaca in Mexico to Maldivian atolls via our very own British Isles, we reveal the best places to see bioluminescence in all its dazzling forms. Where can I see bioluminescence in the UK? Cornwall is one of the most famous places to spot sparkling seas during the summer months, particularly Grebe Beach and Pedn Vounder. Starry seas can also be seen in Wales, with frequent spots in locations including Dunraven Bay (Vale of Glamorgan) and Rhossili Bay (Gower). Is it safe to touch bioluminescent water? It is generally safe to touch and swim in bioluminescent waters, especially in destinations where the sparkling waters are featured as tourist attractions with boat trips and excursions. However, some bioluminescence results from harmful algal blooms that can cause skin rashes and severe illness if ingested. If in doubt, research the area you’re visiting thoroughly and speak to guides on organised trips. 1. The Maldives The picture-perfect islands of the Maldives are some of the best places to see bioluminescence around the world thanks to an abundance of plankton that illuminates the waves after sunset. While it’s possible to see the phenomenon on islands across the archipelago, one of the most famous spots of them all is on the quietest side of Vaadhoo Island, a minuscule island of the Raa Atoll known for its beachy corner nicknamed ‘Sea of Stars’. When to go: Between June and October How to get there: Domestic flight and boat transfer from Velana International Airport in Malé Where to stay: Vaadhoo Island lacks the honeymoon-esque stays you may associate with the Maldives – check into InterContinental Maldives Maamunagau Resort and appreciate the glowing waters meters from your beachside abode. 2. Mosquito Bay, Vieques, Puerto Rico You may not have heard of the picturesque island of Vieques. However, you’ve likely seen the nighttime spectacle that occurs on glossy pages and social media feeds. After sundown, Mosquito Bay becomes a glossy blue portal thanks to the bioluminescent dinoflagellate Pyrodinium bahamense, which glows blue when agitated. Glide through the waters on a clear-bottomed kayak with a local tour operator for a truly mesmerising experience. When to go: December to April (dry season) How to get there: Direct flight from San Juan (SJU) followed by a ferry to Vieques Where to stay: Go back to nature – albeit with the luxury trimmings – at the cosy Finca Victoria. 3. Luminous Lagoon, Jamaica Home to dinoflagellates aplenty, Jamaica’s Luminous Lagoon is one of the most incredible excursions on the island, and a memorable way to shake up the evening itinerary. Hop on a tour boat at sunset and, soon enough, the water’s epipelagic zone comes alive with a vibrant blue light. Watch as sealife darts under the boat’s hull, leaving phantasmagoric lines of light in their wake. Should you choose, some tours allow you to hop into the (surprisingly shallow) water and watch as splashes create incredible displays of light. When to go: December to April (dry season) How to get there: Drive from Sangster International Airport (MBJ) Where to stay: Kick back a 30-minute drive away from the spectacle with an indulgent all-inclusive stay at Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay. 4. Jervis Bay, New South Wales, Australia Considering the length of its coastline and the abundance of wildlife that lies offshore, there are surprisingly few places to spot notable displays of bioluminescence around Australia. That said, places do exist, with Jervis Bay in New South Wales being one of the most famous. As the noctiluca scintillans dinoflagellate species washes ashore, settle into the powdery sand and watch the water’s ripples create an effect akin to the Northern Lights on the shore. When to go: Summer; September to February How to get there: About a 2.5-hour drive south of Sydney Airport Where to stay: Escape the hustle and bustle of everyday life with a glamping trip like no other at Paperbark Camp. 5. Krabi, Thailand There are a few bays and coves in this popular region of Thailand that promise a watery light display on clear nights. Ao Nang Beach is one of the most famous and most accessible, with beachside hostels, restaurants and bars a stone’s throw from the shoreline offering places to hide out in ahead of nightfall. While no less famous, perhaps, Phra Nang Beach is another spot a little further along the coast for a peaceful, intimate bioluminescent session reachable by boat transfers from Ao Nang Beach. When to go: November to May How to get there: 20-minute drive from Krabi International Airport Where to stay: Phulay Bay, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve, is just a 40-minute drive from the glistening waters. Expect dazzling villas and pavilions, sprawling pools and access to dazzling beaches through the lush landscape. 6. Toyama Bay, Japan While many of the best places to see bioluminescence around the world are so due to an abundance of glowing plankton and algae, the story is a little quirkier in Japan’s Toyama Bay come spring. Here, the bioluminescent performance atop the otherwise pitch-black Japanese waters is caused by a considerably larger creature – the firefly squid. Join a fishing trip and watch as the organisms emit blue light from photophores, creating a wet and wild firework display as they are pulled from the icy depths. When to go: April - May How to get there: Hokuriku Shinkansen bullet train from Tokyo Where to stay: The DoubleTree by Hilton Toyama is a perfectly plush spot to rest in between city exploration and bay visits. 7. Oaxaca, Mexico One of the most popular places to visit for bioluminescence in Mexico is the Laguna de Manialtepec, a coastal lagoon about west of Puerto Escondido. As fish (and people braving the water for a dip) dart through the waters, the twinkling algae that call the lagoon home make the water turn fantastically phosphorescent. A little farther on, similar experiences are available at Lagunas de Chacahua. When to go: July to October (rainy season) How to get there: Fly to Oaxaca Xoxocotlan International Airport (OAX), typically via Mexico City from the UK Where to stay: You’re spoilt for choice along this stretch of Mexican coastline – see our guide to the best hotels in Oaxaca for all the inspiration you need. 8. Koh Rong, Cambodia By day, the Cambodian island of Koh Rong is a natural playground for families and couples who take to the water armed with snorkelling gear, looking down at the vibrant sea life below. By night, the waters beyond the powder-soft sands take on a life of their own, akin to a starry sky beyond the resorts and lush vegetation. While the bioluminescent plankton isn’t unique to Koh Rong – you can spot it on other Cambodian isles – the lack of light pollution around these shores makes nighttime beach strolls and boat excursions under the new moon unforgettable. When to go: November to May How to get there: Fly to Phnom Penh, then catch a bus to Sihanoukville port and catch a boat transfer to the island Where to stay: The Royal Sands Koh Rong is the plushest address on this gorgeous island. 9. Cornwall, UK (Grebe Beach and Pedn Vounder) The waters that surround the British Isles aren’t the first that come to mind when you think of the best places to see bioluminescence. However, come summer, the English Channel throws a few surprises upon Cornwall’s shores. Some of the most notable places to spot starry shores in this corner of the world include Grebe Beach, a hidden gem at the end of the Helford River. On balmy nights, the water can turn a luminescent blue with a splash. Elsewhere, in Penzance, the bioluminescent action is best observed at Pedn Vounder, where, a few times a year, the Channel puts on a display under the constellations. When to go: July and August How to get there: 5 - 6 hour drive from London; direct trains to Penzance or connecting trains onto Falmouth Where to stay: In Falmouth, The Greenbank Hotel, a charming waterside retreat, gets our vote. In Penzance, hang out with the cool crowd at Artist Residence Cornwall, where unique bedrooms are set within a storied 17th-century property. 10. Cat Ba Island, Vietnam The region around Vietnam’s Halong Bay has long been a hotspot for those seeking glowing waters. However, being one of the stops on most travellers’ bucket lists, crowds and light pollution from boats and cruise ships mean the starry displays are notably more striking in the quieter coves and bays. Enter Cat Ba Island’s Beaches, where splashes at sea equate to dazzling scenes. The natural wonder is best experienced on an overnight boat tour, as captains typically anchor in quiet spots under sparkling skies. When to go: June to October How to get there: Bus transfers from Noi Bai International Airport (HAN) in Hanoi Where to stay: Why not take over your own incredible villa while soaking up the island’s tranquil vibe from Valía Villa Cat Ba. 11. Waitomo Glowworm Caves, New Zealand Instead of a swimsuit, pair of flippers or a kayak, the bioluminescence hiding in one of New Zealand’s most recognisable natural wonders requires visitors to wear comfortable shoes and a warm jacket. The Waitomo Glowworm Caves have been a tourist attraction for more than 130 years, with travellers passing through the awe-inspiring caves in silence, watching as the Arachnocampa luminosa glowworm species – only found in this part of the world – show off their captivating colours. When to go: Year-round How to get there: About 120 miles south of Auckland Airport (AKL) Where to stay: Assuming you’re based in Hamilton, about an hour’s drive north of the caves, for a few days, check into The Narrows Landing Hotel.

item.title: Virgin Trains' cross-channel services have been given the green light – here's the latest
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.24
It's been more than 30 years since the first Eurostar whizzed through the Channel Tunnel, transporting travellers metres under the seabed between London, Paris and beyond into the continent. While there has been word on the rails that rivals have sought to end Eurostar’s monopoly over the tracks for many years, plans were yet to be given the green light – until now. On 13 August 2026, the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) rail regulator announced the approval of a new framework track access agreement between HS1 Limited (trading as London St. Pancras Highspeed) and VTE OPCO Limited (Virgin Trains). The agreement means Virgin Trains are permitted to run up to 20 new daily return services between London and Paris, Brussels or Amsterdam. Furthermore, the head-turning approval grants access to cross-border rail services between 1 October 2030 and 31 December 2040. Following the ORR's announcement, Martin Jones, deputy director, access and international, said, “This is an important next step in bringing competition and growth to the market for international rail services, and we welcome the progress Virgin Trains and London St Pancras High Speed have made. While there is still more work to do, we are supporting Virgin and the wider industry to grow international services.” However, with many years before passengers can consider an alternative to Eurostar, there are still several steps to take. Virgin Trains must procure rolling stock, secure access to other rail networks, and obtain safety approvals from ORR and the relevant EU authorities. Following the announcement of Virgin Trains’ bid to run competitor services last year and the ORR’s approval for the group to use Temple Mills International rail depot in East London, founder Sir Richard Branson said, “The ORR’s decision is the right one for consumers – it’s time to end this 30-year monopoly and bring some Virgin magic to the cross-Channel route. Virgin is no stranger to delivering award-winning rail services, and just as we have successfully challenged incumbents in air, cruise and rail, we’re ready to do it again. We’re going to shake up the cross-Channel route for good and give consumers the choice they deserve.”

item.title: What Do Sex and Gender Even Mean Now?
item.description:
Source: Conor Friedersdorf | The Atlantic Score: 5.42
In her first argument as a lawyer before the Supreme Court, Ruth Bader Ginsburg famously quoted the abolitionist Sarah Grimké, who said, “I ask no favor for my sex. All I ask of our brethren is that they take their feet off our necks.” At some point, however, Ginsburg was encouraged to use an alternative to the term sex. “I’m typing all these briefs and articles for you and the word sex, sex, sex is on every page,” her secretary at Columbia Law School told her. “Don’t you know that those nine men”—that era’s Supreme Court justices—“they hear that word, and their first association is not the way you want them to be thinking?” The secretary suggested substituting gender to “ward off distracting associations.” But sex and gender don’t mean the same thing. The two terms have never been stable. Still, I recall a time when, among educated people, sex was typically understood to refer to matters of biology, such as a person’s reproductive organs, and gender to refer to matters that are socially constructed, such as the norm of dressing little boys in blue pants and little girls in pink dresses. Today, there seems to be no standard usage. Parents throw gender-reveal parties to disclose the sex of their baby. President Trump said in his 2025 inaugural address, “It will henceforth be the official policy of the United States government that there are only two genders: male and female”—but “male” and “female” are sexes. A statute in California defines sex (in part) as follows: “‘Sex’ also includes, but is not limited to, a person’s gender. ‘Gender’ means sex, and includes a person’s gender identity and gender expression.” The confusion that results from this lost distinction causes problems in academia––see the recent kerfuffle in anthropology––as well as in medicine, law, public policy, and more. People mistake meanings and talk past one another about matters that are fraught even when definitions are clear. How did we get into this semantic mess? The concept of a “gender role” was introduced in a 1955 paper by the researcher John Money to signify “all those things that a person says or does to disclose himself or herself as having the status of boy or man, girl or woman.” He believed that people born with ambiguous or atypical genitals, whom he called “hermaphrodites or intersexes,” contributed to “this new meaning of gender.” Would such individuals operate in society as men or women? He thought that rearing would better predict a person’s “gender role” than biology. The term gender identity, first defined as “one’s sense of being a member of a particular sex,” dates back to at least the early 1960s. The psychoanalyst Robert Stoller wrote that “gender role is the overt behavior one displays in society, the role which he plays.” By the ’70s, feminists were the most prominent group to adopt gender and related terms, using them to differentiate biological differences between men and women from differences imposed by society. In the 1972 book Sex, Gender, and Society, the feminist sociologist Ann Oakley suggested that biology may play little or no role in determining gender identity (that is, one’s sense of being a member of a particular sex). If a biological predisposition to a male or female gender identity exists at all, she wrote, it “may be decisively and ineradicably overridden by cultural learning.” In the 1990 book Gender Trouble, Judith Butler challenged the common assumption that gender mirrors sex and is binary, arguing that “a gender cannot be said to follow from a sex in any one way.” Butler also argued that “perhaps this construct called ‘sex’ is as culturally constructed as gender,” and the supposed distinction between them “turns out to be no distinction at all.” In 1997, the sex researcher Milton Diamond and the psychiatrist Keith Sigmundson reached the conclusion that sex is a distinct and important category. The two revisited a case that Money had included in his research. “The penis of an XY individual was accidentally ablated”—that is to say, severely damaged or removed—“and he was subsequently raised as a female,” the authors recounted. “Initially this individual was described as developing into a normally functioning female.” Money had treated the case as confirmation that nurture reliably overrides nature. But the story later changed: When older, the patient rejected “this sex of rearing” and “switched at puberty to living as a male.” This mattered in part because, the authors explained, “the standard in instances of extensive penile damage to infants is to recommend rearing the male as a female.” They urged doctors to reconsider that practice. The importance of sex as a category was further affirmed in 2001 by a group of experts convened by the Institute of Medicine (since renamed the National Academy of Medicine). Recounting several public-health guidelines that excluded women of child-bearing age from clinical trials on the erroneous assumption that they “will not differ significantly in response to treatment in most situations,” the report noted: “Sex, that is, being male or female,” is “an important basic human variable that should be considered when designing, analyzing, and reporting findings from studies.” But the importance of sex as a category of study did not guarantee sex a stable place in scholarship, as the Harvard evolutionary biologist David Haig showed by documenting a dramatic decline in the term sex and a rise in gender in the titles of academic articles between 1945 and 2001. At first, feminist scholarship converged on socially constructed gender and biologically determined sex, Haig wrote, but “that distinction was difficult to maintain,” because “no term remained to refer to situations in which causation was unknown, disputed, or involved an interaction between biology and culture.” Soon gender spread to other disciplines, and eventually gender rather than sex began to appear even in scholarship on the physiology of animals. “Among the reasons that working scientists have given me for choosing gender rather than sex in biological contexts,” Haig wrote, “are desires to signal sympathy with feminist goals, to use a more academic term, or to avoid the connotation of copulation.” By the 2000s, yet another obstacle to mutual understanding arose: What people meant by gender was changing, not only in academic discourse, but in popular usage. For many of the early feminists, gender was a cage built by society.
