Given that these AirPods will essentially be capturing and processing visual data from your environment, a dedicated secure pairing process makes a lot of sense from a privacy standpoint. These two additions give us a clearer picture of how Apple is approaching both the usability and the security side of camera-equipped AirPods. With more details surfacing from the same macOS Tahoe 26.7 build, it looks like Apple is getting closer to making this feature official.

item.title: ChatGPT can now read your Apple Messages chats on Mac
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends Score: 4.48
ChatGPT is getting a little more comfortable inside the Mac, with its latest update adding an Apple Messages integration. The feature lets users bring conversations from Apple’s Messages app into ChatGPT, giving the assistant another source of context without requiring users to manually copy and paste entire conversations. Another app joins ChatGPT’s growing ecosystem The integration is part of a broader push to make ChatGPT more useful as a desktop assistant rather than simply a chatbot sitting in its own window. OpenAI has been expanding the Mac app’s ability to work with other applications and information, including its Computer History feature, which can reference selected activity from supported apps and websites. Messages is an especially interesting addition because conversations often contain information that users may want to act on later. Instead of digging through a long thread, users can bring that context into ChatGPT and ask it to summarize a conversation, pull out important details, or help work with information contained within it. OpenAI’s broader desktop strategy is clearly heading in this direction. Its current Mac app combines ChatGPT with Work and Codex, while connected apps and plugins are designed to let the assistant work with external tools and information rather than keeping everything inside a standalone chat. But this is where things get personal Giving ChatGPT access to Messages is considerably more sensitive than connecting something like Google Drive. Messages can contain private conversations, personal details, addresses, financial information, and other information that users probably don’t expect an AI assistant to see. That’s why the permissions and privacy controls matter here. Apple’s existing ChatGPT integration already makes clear that users control when information is sent to ChatGPT, with Siri asking permission before sending files. The Messages integration therefore feels like a small feature with much bigger implications. ChatGPT is slowly moving from an assistant users talk to into one that can understand more of what they’re already doing on their devices. That’s undeniably useful, but the more of a user’s digital life it can access, the more important it becomes to know exactly what ChatGPT can see, when it can see it, and where that information goes.

item.title: One-third of the web is showing signs of AI authorship, thanks to ChatGPT
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends Score: 4.47
The internet has been filling up with AI-generated content ever since ChatGPT arrived, but a new analysis from Pew Research Center puts just how widespread it has become into perspective. According to the study, roughly one-third of web pages published since ChatGPT’s launch show signs of AI authorship. The internet didn’t become AI overnight The important word here is “signs.” Pew’s research isn’t saying that one-third of every webpage on the internet was written entirely by an AI. Instead, it looked for indicators suggesting that AI played a role in producing the content. That’s an important distinction because modern online writing isn’t simply divided into human and machine. A writer might use AI to generate a first draft, rewrite sections, clean up grammar, expand an article, or produce an SEO-friendly version. The final page can therefore contain both human and machine contributions. The trend is nevertheless hard to ignore. ChatGPT launched publicly in November 2022, and the share of web content showing signs of AI authorship has climbed substantially since then. The findings add to earlier research suggesting that AI-generated or AI-assisted content has become a significant part of the web rather than a weird corner populated by obvious content farms. And this creates a rather strange internet There’s an interesting irony here. AI companies need enormous amounts of human-created material to train their models, while those same models are now helping produce more of the content that eventually gets published online. The internet is increasingly becoming a place where humans write for machines, machines write for humans, and machines may eventually train on what other machines wrote. There is also a big difference between how much AI content exists and how much people actually see. Earlier research from Graphite found AI-generated articles approaching half of newly published online articles, while its separate analysis found that human-written articles still dominate Google search results and AI citations. That means the web isn’t necessarily about to become an endless wall of AI slop. But Pew’s findings show that the old assumption that something published online was probably written by a person is becoming increasingly unreliable. The internet is still human, but AI is no longer just visiting. It’s starting to move in.

item.title: Why Is This Restaurant Emailing Me Like We’re Friends?
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 5.53
A version of this post originally appeared in Eater Today, which spotlights the freshest news and stories from across the food world every day. Subscribe now. Recently, after I wrote about the tedious nature of making reservations these days, several readers emailed me to express similar feelings and to share their own booking-related gripes. For many of them, these have culminated into the same interaction: Instead of dealing with the whole reservations-platforms rigamarole, they were going old-school for bookings, they told me, by building relationships with general managers and servers in hopes of getting a business card with some information that might offer an easier (or just more direct) in. It feels anachronistic, in our modern QR-code, app-for-everything moment, but these are the touchpoints we long for now: a real person, a direct line; the possibility of being seen as a diner with loyalty and even idiosyncrasies, whether it’s a habit of saying “thank you” slightly too much or a tendency to finish a glass of water with astonishing speed, rather than just another faceless name on the backend of a reservations platform. Of course, in our post-tech world, this kind of olive branch has also gone digital: Those gestures of goodwill and relationship building have been automated. Consider the New York City banchan destination Sunn’s. After I dined there, I found an email in my inbox two weeks later. “Hey ,” said the email. “I just want to say thanks for checking out Sunn’s,” it read. “Most importantly, I hope you had a nice time, if not, definitely let me know!” The email offered me a discount code for wine delivery from Parcelle (a partner in Sunn’s), and then it dangled a more appealing carrot: the tantalizing promise of exclusivity. We have a text line, the email explained: “If you’re ever unable to find the table you need on Resy, shoot us a text.” (The restaurant is, proving my previous point, now on OpenTable.) It was not the rote, clinical, immediate “restaurant wants your feedback” follow-up that I expect after I dine at a Resy joint, but something with the illusion of being more personal. It was signed “Grant from Parcelle Wine.” As with any listserve blast, the errant space tipped me off that it was not, in fact, actually personalized but automated; still, it seemed more considered. Readers telling me about their reservations gripes mentioned receiving similar emails, sometimes including personalized links for booking. “N/naka sent me [an] email [like that] after I’d dined there twice, but there was a gap of at least a couple years between the last time I went and [when I received] the email,” one reader in Los Angeles said. A Michelin-starred restaurant, it’s “famous for keeping careful track of all their diners so I wasn’t totally surprised,” the reader added. They’d gotten a similar one after dining at the more casual yet once very in-demand Pijja Palace. After dining at Tanta, the Peruvian restaurant in Chicago, a colleague of mine received a similar email thanking her for her visit and offering her a special booking link for the future. Use it, the email promised, and she could get a complimentary chocolate mousse on a future visit. This was not some professional food writer exclusive, but seemingly an offer sent to anyone. Another colleague received a similarly fleshed-out yet clearly automated email after a meal at LA’s Lucia. It also offers a “direct booking link,” though it just goes to the restaurant’s main Resy page. The automation appears to be a feature of SevenRooms, through which Lucia also offers reservations. As with the manager dropping a business card at the table of guests who’d seemed to have an especially good time, the point of all this is to build regulars. But while he encourages his managers to give their cards out, “I personally hate business cards,” says Cedric Nicaise of the NYC restaurant the Noortwyck. Often, they end up in the trash, and he thinks many people don’t actually end up using them, especially when they’ve had a good experience over a bad one that needs to be made right. For this reason, Nicaise has employed an AI-powered platform called Loyalist, which integrates with every interface on which a restaurant might find itself — reservations platforms, review platforms, event systems, and point-of-sale systems — and creates a single place through which he and his team can manage guest relationships, doing targeted follow-up. While the examples I’ve listed above tend to focus on getting first-time diners to become second-time diners, Loyalist allows the Noortwyck to get hyper-specific. “If someone came for dinner and they were super nice, then we [can] reach out [via email]. But we also get alerts if it’s someone’s like, third visit in a short period of time, or if they give us a really positive review on Google,” Nicaise explains. “The system prompts us to be able to send them an email, and so it’s using technology to further personal connections.” For Nicaise, the benefit of Loyalist is that it allows the restaurant’s staff to direct their energy and use it efficiently. It’s not sending an email blast about a new special or a menu change, but a way of showing appreciation and dedicated interest. The platform can, for example, prompt the Noortwyck’s staff that someone bought a cool bottle of wine and therefore might appreciate a personalized note about it. Or, through the platform, managers can identify which guests they met on a given night, then be prompted to send personalized emails to those guests after. Instead of simply casting the broadest net and seeing who it catches, “we want to make sure that people who are [the most] inclined to come back can come back,” Nicaise says. As the great newsletter boom of the past few years would prove, inboxes are valuable territory. Still, even with all the competition there, an email promises more direct access to potential guests than something as free-range as social media. (It’s perhaps for this reason that Sunn’s has opted for that potentially less crowded field of the iMessage inbox with its additional text line.) “The cost of acquiring a new diner is becoming higher than ever,” according to Maggie Tang, who started Loyalist after working in restaurants including Eleven Madison Park. With so many restaurants and the infinite scroll of social media, “someone’s trying to grab a diner’s attention at all times, and restaurants constantly want to fill seats, so I think restaurants are starting to focus more on how to retain existing diners.” According to Tang, these personalized follow-up emails can also nudge diners who haven’t come back in a while, and on average, she says, 15 percent of guests who receive those book a reservation within 30 days of getting that email. As much as some restaurants want to be showy occasion spots, many are orienting themselves now around repeatability. Restaurants need regulars; emails, with their technology-enabled veneer of “this manager was just thinking about you,” might help them meet the moment. The trick at some hard-to-get-into restaurants, I’ve been told, is to make a reservation with the host upon leaving your first meal there. They have access to the books, and the idea is that you’ve earned some goodwill by having already dined. But, if you’re shy or you forget, maybe a personalized email rewarding you for patronage will pop up in your inbox sometime after.

item.title: NASA images show crater on the moon caused by SpaceX Falcon 9 crash
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.85
NASA images show crater on the moon caused by SpaceX Falcon 9 crash They were taken by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. In the early hours of August 5, the upper stage of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket crashed into the lunar surface. Now, NASA has released a series of images captured by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) from August 11 to 12, showing a new crater on the moon caused by the wandering rocket. To capture the images, NASA engineers had to tilt the spacecraft sideways so its cameras would point downward as it passed 60 miles above the crater. Specifically, they used LRO's Narrow-Angle Camera, which can see features on the lunar surface as small as three feet wide. It wasn't an easy feat, as the spacecraft flew from pole to pole every two hours at a speed of 1 mile per second, while the Moon rotated on its axis underneath. NASA had to wait for the LRO and the crash site to align, and that took six days. The agency did, however, release before-and-after photos, which you can see on the official site. Meanwhile, the photos above show the crash site from different angles. The darker streak radiating out of the crater is made of older materials from near the surface: Dust and rocks whose colors and components have already been altered by years of exposure to solar winds and cosmic rays. The lighter materials near the rim came from deeper underground. Independent astronomer Bill Grey first drew attention to a rocket on a collision course with the Moon in April. He used orbit-computing software to figure out where and when the rocket was crashing. Grey and his colleagues also used a physics simulator to analyze the data, predicting that the upper stage wouldn't make much of an impact. The rocket was 39 feet long and 13 feet wide, weighing around 4,000 kilograms. It slammed into the Moon at 5,400 mph and, based on NASA's calculations, created a crater 60 feet wide and 12 feet deep. The Falcon 9 rocket in this crash came from the January 15, 2025 Blue Ghost mission, which carried two lunar landers to orbit. It used most of its fuel bringing the landers to their intended orbit, so it couldn't make its way back to Earth. Gravity and solar activity brought it to the Moon instead.

item.title: How to check your iPhone's battery health and cycle count
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.68
How to check your iPhone's battery health and cycle count You'll be glad to know if you're buying used. When you buy a new iPhone, you expect it to last. However, all rechargeable batteries are consumable components that chemically degrade over time. As a battery degrades, it can hold less charge, which ultimately affects your device's daily use. Apple provides built-in tools that help you monitor cycle count — the number of full discharges and recharges it has undergone — and overall battery health. Understanding these metrics is essential for knowing if the batter is working as expected, when it might be time for a replacement or for better understanding the condition of a used iPhone before you buy it. Checking your iPhone's battery health is a pretty simple process. To get started, open the Settings app on your iPhone, tap Battery and look for the Battery Health section. On some older models, such as the iPhone 13, this section is called Battery Health & Charging. This screen will show you an estimate of your iPhone's battery capacity relative to when it was new, along with other useful information. What the health numbers actually mean The Maximum Capacity percentage gives you a better idea of the overall condition of your iPhone's battery. According to Apple, a typical battery is designed to retain up to 80 percent of its capacity when operating under normal conditions. For the iPhone 15 and later models, this estimate is based on 1,000 full charge cycles. For older models, the estimate is that the battery will last up to 500 cycles before degrading significantly. When the battery health drops below 80 percent, your iPhone may still work, but you'll likely notice a significant decrease in battery life. In some cases, iOS may even enable additional performance management features to prevent the iPhone from shutting down unexpectedly due to a severely degraded battery. In that case, you'll see a warning below the Peak Performance Capability section. If you don't see anything, it likely means your iPhone hasn't had any battery issues and is still running at full performance. To help preserve your iPhone's battery health, you can enable the Optimized Battery Charging option in the battery settings. When enabled, this feature learns your daily routine and when you typically charge your iPhone, so that it temporarily pauses charging at 80 percent and only completes the charge to 100 percent around the time you need to use your iPhone again. On the iPhone 15 and later, you can also set a maximum charge limit for your device, which also helps preserve battery health for longer. How to check your cycle count and why it matters If you have an iPhone 15 or newer, Apple provides an easy way to check the cycle count directly in the Settings app. Go to Battery > Battery Health, and scroll down to find your cycle count. If you're using an older model, Apple doesn't provide battery cycle statistics natively. This means you'll have to rely on third-party alternatives, such as the popular Mac app coconutBattery, to check your iPhone's battery cycle count. Knowing your device's battery cycle count can be helpful for understanding its long-term lifespan, as well as how heavily you've been using your device. iPhone 15 models and later are rated to retain good battery health for up to 1,000 full charge cycles before experiencing battery issues, while older models are rated for up to 500 cycles. For reference, 1,000 cycles works out to two or three years' use in under real-world conditions. Keep in mind that one cycle represents expending 100 percent of your battery's current capacity, though not necessarily all at once. For example, if you used 50 percent of your battery, recharged your device and then used another 50 percent afterward, that counts as one complete charge cycle. Reaching these numbers doesn't mean your iPhone's battery will automatically fail, but it does mean its capacity will typically be lower, so you may notice shorter battery life. If your iPhone's battery health is below 80 percent or if it has reached 1,000 charge cycles, you should consider replacing the battery to keep your phone running smoothly. To do so, your best option is to contact Apple Support to arrange for a replacement.

item.title: Google is trying to solve contrails with AI
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.47
Google is trying to solve contrails with AI Operation Blue Skies, which also involves the UK government, will subtly reroute flights to test contrail avoidance. Google and the UK government are collaborating on a project to test whether airplanes can avoid creating contrails. The project, called Operation Blue Skies, will conduct the trial over Shanwick airspace, which sits above the northeastern Atlantic Ocean. Contrails are the long white streaks in the sky left by jet engines. Most often created in cold, humid air, they form when water vapor condenses and freezes around aircraft exhaust. Unfortunately for the climate, they can trap heat radiating from the Earth, thus warming the atmosphere. Researchers estimate that they contribute to about one-third of aviation's total climate impact. (Contrails, whose effects have been measured by scientists, aren't to be confused with mythical chemtrails, whose "effects" have been spouted by your conspiracy-obsessed uncle on Facebook.) Operation Blue Skies will last 30 months and make small flight-path adjustments to a limited number of flights while still keeping them within normal operations. The trials will take place over the next two winters. Air traffic controllers will use forecasts to pinpoint atmospheric regions where vertical adjustments of up to 2,000 feet could help reduce contrail formation. Of the 10,000 flights expected to cross the region during each year's trial period, only about one to five percent will be rerouted. Previous research and smaller trials suggest that AI forecasts can identify atmospheric areas where flights are most likely to create warming contrails. Google will provide AI-powered forecasting models to identify these regions and use satellite imagery and machine learning to help measure the results. The company says it's participating on a pro bono basis, contributing £1.4 million ($1.9 million). The Associated Press reports that the UK government will provide over half of the project's £5 million ($6.8 million) budget. Meanwhile, NATS, the UK's air navigation provider, will handle the operational side. Contrails.org, the Met Office, Imperial College London and the University of Cambridge are also involved.

item.title: Framework's cheapest laptop just got a major spec bump
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.30
Framework's cheapest laptop just got a major spec bump The Framework Laptop 12 now ships with Intel's Core Series 3 chips and other hardware upgrades. After introducing a new high-end model of its 13-inch laptop, Framework is turning its attention to its colorful and compact sibling. The newly updated Framework Laptop 12 features Intel's latest Core Series 3 chips and an optional backlit keyboard and fingerprint reader, meaningful hardware upgrades to the charming but expensive first model. Framework leaned on efficiency improvements the Intel Core Ultra Series 3 brought to its Framework Laptop 13 Pro, and the company says the entry-level, non-Ultra chips bring similar benefits to the Framework Laptop 12. Pre-built versions of the new laptop features either a Core 3, Core 5 or Core 7 chip, with 8GB of RAM, 16GB of RAM or 32GB of RAM, respectively. Framework says the Laptop 12 has improved battery life as a result of its new chip, and specifically notes the Core 5 model demonstrated 70 percent better battery life while streaming Netflix when compared to the Core i5 version of the original Laptop 12. Starting at 8GB of memory isn't ideal, but it's possibly a reflection of the RAMaggedon issues all computer makers are dealing with. Speaking of, you can equip the Laptop 12 with up to 48GB of RAM if you're happy paying $659 for that upgrade. Using the latest Intel chip brings along other perks, too, like support for Thunderbolt 4 on two of the Laptop 12's four hot-swappable Expansion Cards, and faster DDR5 RAM. The 12.2-inch display hasn't been improved, but the Laptop 12 can be configured to include a backlit keyboard and a fingerprint reader. You'll have the most flexibility via Framework's DIY option, but the pre-built Core 5 and Core 7 models running Linux feature both upgrades by default. Like the Laptop 13 Pro, the Laptop 12 is yet another of Framework's computers that can come pre-installed with Linux. The company says over 80 percent of original Laptop 12 owners are running Linux, so it's decided to offer the new model pre-installed with Fedora, with Windows 11 available as a $100 upgrade. Framework says the new Laptop 12 hardware has also been seeded to other Linux distros so support will be ready when the laptop ships. The Framework Laptop 12 starts at $699 for a pre-built Linux configuration in green or $549 for a DIY version in black, gray, light purple, pink, or green. Framework is collecting pre-orders now and plans to start shipping the new laptop in October.

item.title: Apple has new in-app transaction commission rates for EU devs
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.15
Apple has new in-app transaction commission rates for EU devs It’s the latest change based on legal challenges under the Digital Markets Act. Apple has laid out its new business terms for apps that will be distributed in the European Union. The new policies, which take effect starting October 1, will see the company's heavily debated Core Technology Fee replaced with a new Core Technology Commission that will be applied to in-app purchases. There are several different permutations of commission rates based on how the app accepts a transaction. Devs that participate in the App Store Small Business Program, the Mini Apps Partner Program and the Video Partner Program will be offered discounted rates under each branch of the terms. "The majority of developers" using Apple In-App Purchase tech on apps distributed on the App Store apps will be charged a 15 percent fee, the company wrote. For devs outside those programs, the commission will be 26 percent. App Store apps using alternative tools for payment processing will be charged a 20 percent fee, while for App Store apps that link out of the app to complete purchases, the fee will be 15 percent. Program members using either of those paths will have commission rates of 10 percent. Any apps that are distributed outside Apple's App Store will have a flat fee of 5 percent as their commission. Apple has been involved in a convoluted, years-long legal battles over how it will conform to Europe's Digital Markets Act (DMA). Most recently, the company took a loss in its fight to avoid the more tightly policed "gatekeeper" status under the DMA. It may also be hauled into court on country-specific charges around potentially anti-competitive practices, most recently in Germany. There has been some movement in the US to loosen sideloading and alternative payment systems restrictions. Apple is also looking for US court support for taking a cut of 5 to 15 percent for transactions on third-party payments.

item.title: Warren Spector, founding father of immersive sims, has retired from game development
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 4.96
Warren Spector, founding father of immersive sims, has retired from game development Spector was the creator behind Deus Ex. The creator of Deus Ex, the action role-playing game franchise originally developed by Ion Storm, has announced his retirement. In a LinkedIn post, Warren Spector said he was a month away from his 44th year as a developer and had worked on tabletop games, 17 digital games, ran small and large teams and helped people with their careers. Now, his age and health are catching up with him, and it was time to "write some books, do a lot of reading, do some lecturing, maybe do some consulting." Spector also said that there are still three games he would like to make, but that the business has changed and it's not as fun for him anymore. While he admitted that he tried to retire in the past but changed his tune, he said he thinks he means it this time. He is typically regarded as a founding father of immersive sim games, characterized by giving players the freedom to solve problems in a variety of ways. On Deus Ex, wherein you play an anti-terrorism agent in a dystopian cyberpunk setting, Spector also served as director and producer. He worked on several Ultima titles as producer and writer, as well as on Disney's Epic Mickey for the Wii as director. His latest game was Thick As Thieves, a stealth-action heist game, released just a few months ago. He also worked on System Shock 3, but Tencent took over that project and its status remains unclear.

item.title: What's the difference between Android's Qi2 And Qi2.2 wireless charging?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 4.72
What's the difference between Android's Qi2 And Qi2.2 wireless charging? There are some key distinctions that make a big difference. We live in a wireless world, so understanding the different standards at play can help you to maximize the performance of your gadgets and your chargers. For most devices, the wireless charging standard you'll be using is Qi2. The latest iteration of this is Qi2 25W, also commonly called Qi2.2. It was announced last summer that the new speed would be supported by both iPhones and select Android smartphones. Although Google was slow to adopt Qi2, we're now starting to see Qi2 25W listed as a feature for the next generation of Android phones, including the Pixel 11 lineup announced recently. So does it matter which version your device supports? There are a couple key distinctions that make Qi2.2 a worthwhile upgrade. More power, more speed The difference between Qi2 and Qi2.2 charging comes down to power. Qi2 25W offers 25 watts of power delivery when it's charging a compatible device. Qi2 is capped at 15 watts, so the new standard offers a substantial boost to power. In practice, that means your device will charge faster if it's using Qi2 25W. With Qi2, your gadgets could take between 50 and 80 minutes to reach 50 percent battery from zero. Qi2 25W, on the other hand, will get you to half battery in about half an hour. Considering wireless charging has traditionally been less efficient than wired, that's a welcome improvement. An additional benefit to Qi2.2 is improved thermal protection. So if you've ever noticed your phone getting pretty toasty while it's on a wireless pad, the upgrade will be a good one. Even if you can't feel the difference, it might subtly help to extend your phone's lifespan, because the lower peak temperature while charging can help your battery last longer. All told, Qi2 25W offers a solid improvement over its predecessor, so reap the rewards if your hardware supports this latest power option.

item.title: Meta's app for creating generative AI minigames is now available in the US
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 4.14
Meta's app for creating generative AI minigames is now available in the US It's called Pocket and is described as a "platform for making and sharing gizmos." Meta's little vibe-coding app Pocket has now arrived in the US after a brief testing phase in Brazil. The app lets people generate minigames, called gizmos, via prompts. The games get published to a scrollable feed, bringing in a social media component. Users can save gizmos to a favorites list and repost gizmos to their feed. These games make full use of the capabilities available in modern smartphones. They can respond to both touch and tilt and can include photos and even songs. Once saved to a profile, other people can remix them into unique creations. They are called gizmos instead of minigames for a couple of probable reasons. First of all, they aren't just games. The marketing advertises simple experiences like a canvas to paint on. Also, Meta hired nearly the entire team behind an app called, well, Gizmo. This led to the app shutting down. Gizmo was basically the same thing as Pocket and even used similar nomenclature (referring to the creations as gizmos). In any event, Pocket is available right now and it's free. It could be worth a download and a couple of minutes before getting bored. This is just the latest AI-forward move that Meta has made. Last year, the company launched a feature for the Meta AI app called Vibes that's basically a feed for AI slop. Facebook also recently introduced the ability to tweak profile photos with AI-powered animations.

item.title: 14 ways to eat a peach
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 5.19
14 ways to eat a peach Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Chefs love peaches. They represent peak summer season (at their ripest from around June to the end of August), and they’re also incredibly versatile – ideal in savoury and sweet dishes. At Café Cecilia, the Hackney restaurant run by chef Max Rocha that turns five this August, peaches have been on the menu from the start, featuring frequently at this time of year. Begin with a peach bellini (a purée mixed with champagne), follow with a panzanella made with Vesuvio tomatoes, bread and peaches, and then try a main of grilled pork, peaches and borlotti beans. For dessert, he serves a roasted peach and basil ice cream sundae layered with meringue and toasted cubes of brown butter cake. “I don’t normally use fruit in savoury dishes,” says Rocha, “but peaches complement grilled meats so well. We pair them with pork coppa steak (from the shoulder), which is really fatty. You want fattiness with peaches. Use yellow or flat peaches, so long as they’re not too hard.” (See full recipe below.) The classic Italian pairing is with soft cheese – ricotta, mozzarella or burrata – often with other salty or herby additions. In her new book La Trattoria (Ebury Press, £30), Dara Klein of Tiella in east London shares a recipe for mozzarella, peaches and anchovies dressed with red wine vinegar, lemon juice, extra virgin olive oil, dried oregano and finely sliced shallots. Serve with fresh ciabatta “to mop up the juices”. At Burro in Covent Garden, Conor Gadd offers a dish inspired by the peach-glazed hams his mother used to serve with boiled Irish potatoes when he was a boy: “I roast white and yellow peaches with dried chilli, fennel seed and a splash of white wine, which brings out the acidity. Then serve them with prosciutto. So many fruits go to mush when you cook them, whereas peaches hold their shape and texture really well. When my chefs ask me how to cook them, I say imagine biting into them and your teeth searching for resistance but never actually finding it.” Sometimes underripe peaches are best. “They have a crunchiness that makes them ideal in my labneh recipe,” says Palestinian chef Fadi Kattan, who arranges skin-on halves on labneh with roasted red onions, a generous pour of olive oil and a dusting of za’atar and sesame seeds. Around Bethlehem, where Kattan is from, green chickpeas, green cherries and green almonds are often consumed. “Recently I tried green peaches,” says Kattan. “Cut in half, sprinkled with Dead Sea salt and eaten as a snack; the crunch is fantastic.” When peaches are too ripe, poaching is a great way to salvage them. Kattan cooks his in pomegranate juice infused with lavender or verbena. “It’s a bit of a grandmother’s trick. The juice gives the fruit a nice colour and the little imperfections are enhanced rather than disguised.” He eats them with mouhalabieh, a milk pudding made by simmering milk, sugar and cornstarch. You can also reduce the liquor, add lime juice and fizzy water, and enjoy as a drink. Gadd suggests poaching peaches in rosé wine with sugar, water and vanilla, then freezing the liquor. “When you scrape the ice with a fork, it produces a beautiful granita, which you can serve with the poached fruit and a dollop of yoghurt,” he says. If your fresh peaches are less than par: “Put them in caramel or butter with brown sugar in an upside-down cake,” says pastry chef Nicola Lamb. “And if the peach is perfect, just eat it. Don’t try and make a cake because the fruit leaks while it cooks so you get a gummy texture. If you do, make the cake separately with flavours that complement peaches like almond, jasmine or rosemary, then cut up the fruit and serve it alongside.” Max Rocha’s grilled pork coppa steak with grilled peaches and fresh borlotti beans Serves two - Combine the olive oil, garlic, rosemary, lemon peel, salt and pepper and rub over the pork steaks. Leave to marinate for at least one hour in the refrigerator. Take out 30 minutes before cooking. - Place the borlotti beans in a saucepan, cover with cold water then add the olive oil, whole chilli, sage and garlic. Bring to a simmer and cook for 20-25 minutes. Once cooked, remove from heat and add a pinch of fine salt. Allow a couple of minutes for the beans to absorb the seasoning, then taste and add more if needed. - Halve the peach and remove the stone, then brush the halves with olive oil. Grill them cut-side down on a grill pan (or barbecue) for three minutes on both sides. The oil helps prevent the peach from sticking to the pan. Once grilled, place the peaches in a bowl with some olive oil and the picked basil and thyme. Leave to marinate until you’re ready to serve. - Grill the pork steaks over a high heat on a grill pan for three to four minutes per side. Place in a 150C oven on an ovenproof tray for five minutes, or until the internal temperature is 64 degrees. Allow to rest with a glug of olive oil on top to create some resting juices. - To serve, carve the pork steaks into strips and plate. Spoon on the warm borlotti beans with a slotted spoon. Place half a grilled peach on each plate and finish with a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil, flaky sea salt, black pepper and a few fresh basil leaves. Finish with some of the resting juices from the pork. Comments

item.title: What Makes Someone A ‘Touron’? Travel Experts Share 11 National Park Mistakes To Avoid
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.79
A "touron" may sound like just another internet insult, but the term is now used for travelers who ignore rules, take unnecessary risks or damage the places they came to see. Social media now makes these mistakes especially visible, yet this behavior is not new. Nor are the consequences, which range from fines and serious injuries to damaged ecosystems, endangered wildlife and extra pressure on park rangers and rescue teams. What Is A 'Touron’? A “touron” is a blend of tourist and moron, generally used for a visitor whose careless, disrespectful or dangerous behavior puts themselves, other people, wildlife or a destination at risk. One of the earliest articles that used the term appeared in The Washington Post on Sept. 20, 1987, which defined a “touron” as “a tourist, usually an annoying one.” Social media has since given the term a much larger audience, such as Tourons of National Parks, an Instagram account dedicated to collecting videos of questionable visitor behavior. The Biggest Mistakes That Turn Visitors Into Tourons Visitors could earn the “touron” label by ignoring the basic rules that protect people and parks. Recent cases show how quickly seemingly thoughtless decisions can escalate. In 2026, a Yellowstone visitor received five days in jail after walking across fragile hydrothermal features at Mammoth Hot Springs, leaving damaging footprints behind. San Francisco Gate also reported that Yosemite visitors are leaving fresh graffiti and stickers around popular trails. A case from Pictured Rocks this year involved four visitors who carved into sandstone cliffs and collected more than 100 pounds of rocks. So, I interviewed 10 experts on the biggest mistakes visitors make in U.S. national parks. I also asked about their consequences and how travelers can explore these protected spaces more responsibly. 1. Getting Too Close To Wildlife Wild animals in national parks may appear calm, but approaching them can quickly become dangerous. Getting too close can provoke an attack, disrupt natural behavior and put both the visitor and the animal at risk. "Wildlife is one of the many reasons people visit national parks, but they are best appreciated from a safe distance," says Mike Reynolds, chief program officer at the National Park Foundation and a former acting director of the National Park Service (NPS), in an email interview. "Wildlife reacts to human behavior as well and the more we respect their natural habitat, the more we help parks manage them for the future," he adds. 2. Feeding Wildlife Feeding wildlife or allowing animals access to human food can teach them to associate people with an easy meal. That can change their natural behavior, increase the risk of dangerous encounters and, in some cases, ultimately result in an animal being relocated or euthanized. "Visitors also need to understand that interfering with wildlife can be detrimental to the animal. There have been quite a few stories recently about bears becoming too used to people and it causes parks to relocate them, or even euthanize them," says John Bowers, director of marketing and sales at Visit Jackson Hole, in an email interview. 3. Leaving Marked Trails And Boardwalks Stepping off a designated trail or boardwalk can damage vegetation, accelerate erosion and create unofficial paths that other visitors begin following. In places such as Yellowstone, leaving a boardwalk can also expose visitors to unstable ground and dangerously hot geothermal features. Jason Frye, author of Moon Great Smoky Mountains National Park, says shortcuts and "pirate" trails can affect an ecosystem for years, disturbing nesting wildlife, destroying habitat or even interfering with scientific research. "Once they’re established, they seem to draw unknowing hikers like a beacon," he adds in an email interview. At Yellowstone, Todd Walton, director of sales and marketing at Yellowstone National Park Lodges, is even more direct in his email to me: “We see people getting off established trails and boardwalks — which is a very bad idea, especially in thermal areas where the ground is very fragile and unstable. Not to mention potentially over 180 degrees, so it would cause massive burns and likely kill someone if they fell in.” 4. Ignoring Signs, Barriers And Closures Signs, railings and closures are not suggestions. They warn visitors about hazards that may not be obvious and, in some cases, protect fragile park resources. Ignoring them can result in serious injury or death while also putting rangers and rescuers at risk. Bill Wade, executive director of the Association of National Park Rangers, says one of the biggest mistakes visitors make is that they "either don’t read or they ignore flyers, signs and barriers warning them of risks and hazards.” He points to incidents such as visitors entering swift currents near the top of Nevada Fall in Yosemite and being swept over the edge, or crossing railings at Grand Canyon overlooks for a better photo and losing their balance. 5. Risking Safety For The Perfect Photo A photo is not worth crossing a barrier, approaching wildlife or stepping into a restricted area. While social media can encourage visitors to prioritize getting the shot, their behavior increases the risk of accidents and could damage the places they came to photograph. "There is often an illusion of control, a false sense of familiarity created by television and social media, and an increasing desire to capture the perfect photograph rather than fully experience the place," says Jesús Parrilla, founder of Experiential Hospitality Group, in an email interview. Those choices can also force rescue teams into unnecessary danger and divert park resources from conservation and maintenance. 6. Arriving Unprepared Visitors can get into trouble without breaking a single park rule if they underestimate the weather, terrain, distance or their own physical ability. Setting out without enough water, appropriate clothing or a map can turn an ordinary hike into an emergency. "Before heading out, research your park destination, check current advisories, and plan for the activities you want to enjoy. Because conditions vary dramatically by elevation, location, and season, always check the weather forecast, pack appropriate gear, carry more water than you think you need, and know your physical limits," Reynolds says. Walton also warns against relying solely on phones because cell service in national parks can be unreliable. Preventable rescues consume staff time and park resources that could otherwise support visitors, conservation and maintenance. 7. Leaving Trash Behind One discarded wrapper may seem insignificant, but millions of visitors making similarly small choices can create a much larger problem. Trash can harm wildlife, diminish the experience for other visitors and leave park staff dealing with damage that could easily have been prevented. Kevin Jackson, co-founder and CEO of EXP Journeys, says visitors sometimes behave as though they are the only person in the park: leaving trash because it is "just one wrapper,” without recognizing how often other people make the same decision. "Even something as simple as tossing away an apple core or banana peel isn’t as harmless as it looks,” says Leigh Barnes, president of North America at Intrepid Travel, in an email interview. “Food scraps can attract wildlife, spread pests or disease, and disrupt the natural balance of an ecosystem," he explains. 8. Taking Rocks, Flowers Or Other “Souvenirs” Pocketing one rock or picking one wildflower can feel inconsequential. But when thousands of visitors do the same thing year after year, the cumulative effect can physically change the landscape people traveled there to experience. Frye warns, “If there are 1,000 visitors on that trail that day and every one of them picks one bloom, then you don't have a meadow of wildflowers to enjoy tomorrow.” "The same goes for taking home a shell or an interesting-looking rock," says Barnes. "One souvenir might not seem like much, but when thousands of visitors do the same thing year after year, it starts to change the landscape people came to experience in the first place." 9. Driving As If Park Roads Are Ordinary Roads Speeding, driving off designated roads or simply treating park roads like ordinary highways can endanger wildlife, damage protected landscapes and leave visitors stranded in remote terrain. National park roads often pass directly through wildlife habitat, where conditions demand more caution than a typical road trip. Walton also lists "driving too fast" among the common mistakes visitors make. The consequences can extend well beyond a speeding ticket. In Death Valley National Park, a driver who went off the legal roadway and became stuck in mud apparently used a historic salt-tram tower as a winch anchor, as reported by the National Park Service. The attempt toppled the 113-year-old structure and pulled its concrete footings from the ground. 10. Hiking A Trail When It Is Too Wet Using a wet trail can cause more damage than many hikers realize. Footsteps create ruts. Visitors walk around puddles and the trail gradually widens, increasing erosion and potentially forcing park crews to undertake extensive repairs or close the route. "When soil is saturated, every footprint becomes a rut that channels water. That is how a 24-inch trail becomes 6 feet wide," says Ryan McLaughlin, founder of trail-condition platform Loam, in an email interview. He warns that beyond forecasts, checking existing conditions is equally important. "Rain three days ago matters more than sun today," he explains. He encourages everyone to do a simple test first: “If you sink in, or the ground sticks to your boots, turn around and pick something else.” 11. Geotagging Fragile Locations Sharing the precise location of a fragile viewpoint, trail or natural feature can suddenly send large numbers of visitors somewhere that may not be equipped for them. The resulting crowds can damage landscapes, disturb wildlife and strain park infrastructure and nearby communities. "A single post can encourage thousands of people to seek out the same viewpoint, placing pressure on fragile landscapes, park infrastructure, wildlife and nearby communities," says Clare Tobin, CEO of Wild Frontiers, in an email interview. She suggests considering whether a location can handle increased visitation before tagging it precisely. "Not every discovery needs to be pinpointed online," she adds. How To Be A Better National Park Visitor Being a good national park visitor means arriving prepared, following park-specific rules, giving wildlife space and leaving the landscape as you found it. Small choices such as staying on trail, carrying trash and knowing when to turn around help protect both visitors and the places they came to experience. "The best visitors arrive prepared, curious and humble," says Parrilla. “Rather than asking, 'What can I do here?' ask, 'How does this place work?'” In short, here are a few ways to be a good park visitor: - Plan before you go. Research the park, current advisories, weather, trail conditions and the activities you plan to do. - Bring enough food and water. Pack appropriate clothing, map and supplies. - Know your physical limits. Choose a trail that fits your capabilities. - Stay on designated trails and boardwalks. Respect closures, barriers and signs even when a shortcut or photo opportunity looks tempting. - Give wildlife plenty of space. Never feed, touch or deliberately approach wild animals. - Pack out what you bring in. Food scraps count as trash, too. - Leave rocks, flowers and other natural or cultural features where you find them. - Be prepared to change your plans. Weather, trail conditions, wildlife activity or your own limits may mean choosing another route or activity. - Ask a ranger. Visitor centers are valuable sources of current information about trails, hazards and changing conditions. Some of these guidelines can also apply to other nature settings. For example, if you’re visiting California state parks or Colorado state parks also plan ahead and respect nature. Why Responsible Tourism Matters Now More Than Ever Responsible tourism means recognizing that visiting a national park comes with a responsibility to protect its wildlife, landscapes and communities. How one visitor behaves may seem inconsequential, but repeated across millions of visits, those decisions will have a wider impact and not only on the ecosystems, but on park staff and infrastructure. "Because the parks belong to all of us, and that means we each bear a responsibility to ensure the next visitors enjoy it to its fullest," says Frye. Responsible behavior also matters because protecting parks requires significant resources. The National Park Service’s FY2025 operating budget was about $3.1 billion, while recreation fees were expected to bring in roughly $366 million. Preventable rescues, damaged trails and vandalized resources require staff time and money. "Sometimes stewardship is simply knowing when to stop, step back and give a place room to be wild," said Bowers. National parks are wild places, not backdrops. Prepare before you arrive, follow signs, stay on trails, keep your distance from wildlife and leave what you find. Responsible travel protects visitors, animals, park resources and the opportunity for future generations to experience these places on their own terms. Frye frames it as a shared responsibility: "If the national parks are 'America's best idea,' then shouldn't we, as Americans, do everything we can to ensure the parks live up to this ideal?"

item.title: Why Some Business Leaders Are Rethinking The ROI Of Private Aviation
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.15
For decades, private aviation has largely been viewed as a luxury: a way to skip security lines, avoid crowded terminals, and fly on your own schedule. But according to executives and industry leaders, that's no longer the only—or even the primary—conversation. "In many ways, I think the market is becoming more sophisticated in how it evaluates private aviation," says Matt Wild, president of Jet OUT, a private aviation company offering charter, co-lease and fractional co-ownership programs. "Today, more business leaders are evaluating travel through the lens of productivity, opportunity cost, and operational efficiency." For some business leaders, the most expensive part of business travel isn't the airfare—it's everything that happens because of it. Overnight stays. Missed meetings. Delayed decisions. Hours lost to layovers and airline schedules that don't align with business priorities. That doesn't mean private aviation is the right answer for every executive—or even most of them. In many cases, commercial airlines remain the most practical and economical option. But for companies whose leaders regularly travel between multiple markets, facilities or client meetings, the equation becomes more complicated than simply comparing ticket prices. Instead, they're weighing a broader set of variables: How many people are traveling? Can the trip be completed in a single day? How much executive time will be lost to commercial schedules? And does the value created by being in the right place at the right time outweigh the added cost of flying privately? The result isn't a wholesale shift away from commercial aviation. Rather, it's a growing recognition that different travel needs call for different solutions—from commercial airlines and on-demand charter to jet cards and fractional ownership. Understanding where each option fits requires looking beyond the cost of the flight itself and asking a more fundamental business question: At what point does paying more to travel actually cost less? Why the cheapest ticket isn't always the cheapest option For many companies, commercial airlines remain the most practical and economical way to travel. Extensive route networks, competitive fares and frequent service between major hubs make them an obvious choice for routine business trips. The equation changes, however, when business travel becomes more complex. Executives overseeing operations in multiple states, meeting with clients in smaller markets or visiting several facilities in a single trip often find themselves working around airline schedules rather than their own. A day that includes a connection, rental car and overnight stay can quickly become two days away from the office. Justin Crabbe, founder and CEO of private aviation platform Jettly, says that's changing the conversation he has with business travelers. Rather than focusing solely on the cost of a flight, many are looking more closely at the cost of the time surrounding it. More than 60% of the roughly 80,000 trip requests Jettly processes each month are business-related, according to Crabbe, noting that the strongest demand comes from industries including private equity, law, manufacturing, healthcare, technology and professional services. He says these travelers increasingly prioritize reliability, schedule flexibility and access to destinations that aren't always well served by commercial airlines. Wild sees a similar pattern among Jet OUT's customers. While they come from a wide range of industries, he says they tend to share one common characteristic: complexity. Their businesses don't operate on airline schedules, and many are juggling multiple facilities, projects, customers and employees across different markets. As a result, travel becomes less about getting from one airport to another and more about maximizing the time spent where they can have the greatest impact. "The challenge isn't transportation," Wild says. "The challenge is throughput." For some business leaders, the issue isn't whether commercial aviation works—it's whether it keeps pace with the way their businesses operate. Choosing the right private aviation model For executives who decide commercial travel no longer fits the way they do business, buying an aircraft outright is rarely the next step. On-demand charter is often the simplest entry point, allowing travelers to book flights as needed without a long-term commitment. Jet cards provide prepaid flight hours and more predictable pricing for those who fly regularly. Fractional ownership allows customers to purchase a share of an aircraft, giving them access to private aviation without the cost and responsibility of owning an entire plane. Whole aircraft ownership, meanwhile, is generally reserved for organizations with the highest annual flight activity. "The best solution depends far more on utilization patterns than income alone," Crabbe says. "Most clients don't begin by asking which ownership model they want. They begin by asking how often they fly, how much flexibility they need and whether predictable pricing is important." That's also the philosophy behind Jet OUT's approach. Rather than focusing on a single ownership model, the company offers charter service, Co-Lease and Co-Ownership programs, allowing customers to choose an option that aligns with how frequently they travel and how much long-term commitment they want to make. Wild says many customers begin with charter or Co-Lease before deciding whether fractional ownership makes sense for their business. Just as importantly, Wild says private aviation isn't the right solution for everyone. Companies with infrequent travel needs—or executives whose trips are concentrated between major airline hubs with flexible schedules—may still find commercial airlines or occasional charter flights to be the most practical and cost-effective choice. The goal, he says, is matching the travel model to the customer's actual needs rather than steering every traveler toward ownership. One executive's calculation For Jerry Jendusa, founder of BREAKTHRU Multifamily, the decision to fly privately wasn't driven by luxury—it was driven by the value of his time. "I view time as capital," Jendusa says. “The question is not only what the ticket costs, it is what return we get when several decision-makers can travel together, work privately, making the meeting, and get home the same day. Used well, the aircraft becomes an office in the sky.” Before joining Jet OUT, Jendusa evaluated commercial travel, charter flights and other private aviation providers, ultimately concluding that fractional ownership best fit the way his company travels. A recent trip illustrates that calculation. Jendusa used Jet OUT to fly with investors and colleagues to Lexington, Kentucky, for a scientific advisory board meeting. “We kept the relationship-building and working session going on board, moved the group efficiently, and completed the trip in a schedule that would have been very difficult commercially,” he says. For Jendusa, the return on investment isn't measured by the aircraft itself. It's measured by what the trip makes possible. "For us, private aviation is not a luxury headline," Jendusa says. "It's a way to protect time, keep confidential work moving, serve people in person, and get back home after the work is done. Do the math, honestly. Look at the number of people traveling, time saved, overnight stays avoided — with six to eight people on board, it can compare to business-class travel while delivering a much higher level of productivity.”

item.title: The Best ‘Workcation’ Destinations Around The World, Per New HolaFly Data
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.39
Remote workers and location-independent business owners have the luxury of being able to work from wherever—but that luxury can fall by a few stars when things like reliable Wi-Fi or access to coworking spaces fall short. New research from travel eSIM provider Holafly has ranked the best workcation destinations around the world by looking at things like Wi-Fi broadband speeds, hotel prices, access to WeWork coworking spaces, and average summer temperatures. These are the five cities that came out on top according to the data: Paris, France The capital of France earned the top spot as the best workcation destination thanks to its balance between work-friendly infrastructure and quality of life. It earned 9.7 out of 10 for walkability and boasts broadband speeds of 240.67 Mbps, which makes it easy to stay connected. It also boasts the maximum score of 15 for access to nature and has plenty of coworking spaces, too. Bangkok, Thailand Bangkok earned second place on the list thanks to its fast internet, warm climate, and relatively affordable accommodations. The city boasts one of the fastest broadband speeds among the top five on the list at 317.03 Mbps, while hotels average around $32 per night according to the study. London, United Kingdom Despite having the highest-priced accommodations in the top five, London still ranked number three overall thanks to its excellent walkability score and access to nature. It has broadband speeds of 158.25 Mbps and coworking spaces easily accessible for travelers who want to work away from the hotel or apartment rental. Hong Kong Hong Kong came in fourth place, boasting the fastest broadband speed of the top five at 355.55 Mbps. It also has the maximum nature-access score, a 9.0 walkability score, and access to plenty of coworking spaces, including WeWork. Guangzhou, China Guangzhou earns fifth place thanks to its combination of fast internet, affordable accommodations, and access to nature. It has broadband speeds of 237.91 Mbps, a perfect score for nature access, and average hotel costs sitting at around $45 per night.

item.title: 4 Manila Spas Where Heritage Meets High-Tech
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.36
Wellness in Manila is becoming more layered. Across the city’s spas, treatments are moving beyond the familiar massages toward a broader approach to restoration, one that can encompass traditional healing practices, personalized skincare, digital wellness tools and holistic programs designed around physical and mental well-being. Rather than following a single formula, established properties are driving this evolution in different ways. At some, centuries-old Filipino healing traditions remain central. At others, customization, technology and wellness resources allow guests to shape their experience around individual needs. The Retreat Spa at Okada Manila At Forbes Travel Guide Five-Star Retreat Spa at Okada Manila, Filipino healing customs also remain part of the spa experience. Indayog ng Duyan is a hilot-inspired therapy using warmed banana leaves soaked in virgin coconut oil. The leaves help the therapist identify areas of concern while the treatment focuses on restoring balance and encouraging the body to heal naturally. Okada Manila’s foot spa and reflexology center, Sole Retreat, provides an array of services that use deep pressure, rubbing techniques and acupressure. Areas of pain are treated as signs of nerve-ending sensitivity, which is expected to diminish over a series of treatments. Nüwa Spa At Five-Star Nüwa Spa, personalization has long been part of the philosophy. The first Five-Star spa in the Philippines, Nüwa Spa has held the distinction since 2020, while Nüwa Manila at City of Dreams has received Five-Star recognition since 2018. Its treatments take inspiration from Nüwa, the goddess in ancient Chinese mythology who restored the sky using five-colored stones. The story reflects a principle of Chinese medicine centered on achieving equilibrium through nature, which the spa incorporates into treatments designed around a guest’s constitution, emotions, the changing seasons and the flow of chi. Therapies also draw from Ayurveda, reiki and other Asian healing practices. That emphasis on personalization extends to skincare. Nüwa Spa offers facial and body treatments using products from French luxury skincare brand Biologique Recherche, whose methodology begins with an individual skin analysis. The guest’s condition informs a tailored regimen. The approximately 7,000-square-foot spa includes twin-bed suites for couples and comfortable single treatment rooms, along with a serene lounge, vitality pool, steam room, sauna and relaxation area. Even its massage beds reflect a more considered tack to comfort, with heated surfaces and an ergonomic design.
The Fairmont Spa Time-honored Filipino healing takes a more prominent role at Four-Star Fairmont Makati’s spa, where the signature Traditional Hilot Foot and Body Massage interprets local wellness heritage for a contemporary urban setting. The 90-minute ritual combines therapeutic massage with antioxidant banana leaf strips infused with warm coconut oil. Traditional acupressure and a dagdagay wooden stick are used on the soles of the feet to help release tension, encourage relaxation and support a deeper mind-body connection. The treatment is designed to harmonize the body’s natural energies, providing a distinctly Filipino approach to restoration and recovery. Fairmont Makati’s Mango Passion Fruit Tropical Saltmousse Scrub and Massage takes a more sensory route. A saltmousse scrub exfoliates and protects the skin before a hydration-focused massage using essential oils infused with geranium and orange. Together, the treatments reflect the spa’s emphasis on combining local traditions and holistic rituals to support relaxation, recovery and overall well-being. The Peninsula Spa Five-Star Peninsula Manila expands wellness beyond the treatment room through Life Lived Best, The Peninsula Hotels’ global wellness and sustainability platform. Built around three pillars (physical fitness, mental health and nutrition), the program guides the hotel’s spa and wellness initiatives, including yoga classes, spa treatments, personal training sessions and the Naturally Peninsula plant-based dining program. Technology plays a practical role through Peninsula’s Wellness Portal, which allows hotel guests to access wellness resources from their personal devices. They can request in-room fitness accessories, follow guided workout videos, listen to audio meditation sessions, explore spa recommendations and view Naturally Peninsula menu selections throughout their stay. The experience can be tailored further through PenChat, The Peninsula Manila’s 24-hour digital concierge service. Patrons can use their preferred messaging app to connect with hotel staff and access wellness concierge support from chefs, spa managers and fitness professionals. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: Top Under-The-Radar U.S. Golf Destinations
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.95
Destination golf travel is enjoying a moment, to say the least. There can be fierce competition, and even wait lists just to book trips, at some of the top golf resorts in the country. Popular bucket list spots like Bandon Dunes (Oregon), Pinehurst Resort (North Carolina), Pebble Beach (California), Sand Valley and Kohler (Wisconsin), Streamsong (Florida), and Big Cedar (Missouri) are all seemingly getting bigger and better. And new golf course development is at its highest levels in more than 15 years, according to the National Golf Foundation, momentum spurred in part by record or near record levels of golf travel. Among the new public golf getaways that have recently debuted, still building out or coming soon are Rodeo Dunes (Colorado), Wild Spring Dunes (Texas), Old Shores (Florida), and Candyroot Lodge (South Carolina). But there are some resorts and regions that – while likely well-known to those itinerant and well-traveled golfers – are still flying a bit under the radar from a national perspective. And given that one great course doesn’t make a destination, the lineup below includes multiple courses across one property or area rather than simply one-off hidden gems. Western Nebraska This one tends to surprise some people, but the Sandhills region in Nebraska is one of the most unspoiled and unsung places for golf in the entire country, with a season that generally runs from April 1 to the end of October. The Uber private Sand Hills Golf Club in many ways gave rise to destination golf, inspiring Mike Keiser to create Bandon Dunes on a remote stretch of Oregon coast even though many people, at the time, thought it would fail. While Sand Hills and CapRock Ranch are private, places like The Prairie Club, Dismal River, and Wild Horse boast absolutely phenomenal courses. Driving sparsely populated roads from one to the next, with a sea of rolling grassy dunes interrupted only by the occasional windmill and watering holes for cattle, golfers will invariably see hundreds of spots that would seemingly make a perfect setting for a golf hole. The Prairie Club is home to two 18-hole championship courses – both with a par of 73 – with the Dunes Course designed by Tom Lehman and Chris Brands, and the Pines Course by Graham Marsh. There’s also the 10-hole Horse Course, crafted by Gil Hanse and Geoff Shackelford, that has no real set tee boxes, making for a choose-your-own-short-course adventure. There’s peaceful and premium lodging, from the Lodge to the Guesthouse, Bunkhouse and Cabins on a property that gets extended late-day sunlight during the summer months given that it almost hits the Mountain Time Zone. Dismal River offers stay and play packages at a club that combines championship golf – including courses from Tom Doak and Jack Nicklaus – with guided hunting. The two courses, the White and Red, are defined by the dunes and influenced by the ever-changing wind conditions that can yield a different experience each round. The rustic cabins and lodge are designed for multiday stays, allowing for an immersive reset in the Sandhills, whether playing golf or pursuing other outdoor activities. Not far from North Platte Regional Airport is Wild Horse, which features a highly rated championship course designed by Dave Axland and Dan Proctor in addition to a new short course called The Pony that free to play for juniors, members and on-site lodging guests. Southwest Utah This picturesque region, best known for its natural beauty and parks like Zion, Snow Canyon and Red Cliffs, continues to quietly emerge as a golf mecca. It was just over 60 years ago now that the City of St. George developed the nine-hole course of Dixie Red Hills along a stretch of sandstone cliffs, part of an effort to draw in tourism and transform the region from more than just a gas station stop in the desert. Today, the area is home to some of the most visually stunning courses in the game. And if Dixie Red Hills introduced golf to the St. George/Zion area back in the 1960s, Black Desert Resort and Sand Hollow are introducing the region to the rest of the country. Black Desert was Tom Weiskopf’s final course design, a showstopper of a layout that cuts through black lava fields and is backed by red rocks and mountains. The massive resort, with a 600-acre campus in an otherworldly setting, landed both PGA Tour and LPGA events immediately. Sand Hollow, meanwhile, is among the most photogenic courses in the country, particularly a string of holes on the back nine that play along the edges of steep cliffs. Nearby, UTV riders bounce across the hills at Sand Hollow State Park. Courses like Copper Rock and The Ledges with their dramatic surrounds add to the depth of golf in the area. Michigan’s Upper Peninsula While Northern Michigan is rightfully celebrated, with terrific destinations such as Forest Dunes, Arcadia Bluffs, and multiple Boyne properties, the upper peninsula has some less heralded great golf. Island Resort & Casino has two strong courses in Sweetgrass and Sage Run and recently had a soft opening of its new 9-hole layout (Cedar) to meet heightened demand at one of the largest golf, casino and entertainment destinations in the Midwest. With template green complexes inspired by places like National Golf Links on Long Island and Prestwick in Scotland, it’s an offering that adds to the appeal of the stay and play offerings at the resort. The star of the U.P. might very well be Greywalls, a Mike DeVries design that takes advantage of the wilder and more geologically dramatic terrain of the region. The routing jags through granite outcroppings, with an abundance of exposed rock throughout that includes sheer gray walls – hence the course name – that frame fairways and greens. Timber Stone at Pine Mountain Resort is yet another layout that masterfully incorporates the landscape of the Northwoods. Pacific Northwest While this region could encompass a wide range, in this case it’s specific to Eastern Washington and the nearby Couer d’Alene region in Idaho. Gamble Sands has been gaining attention since fully opening its second 18-hole course this year, a spectacular addition (Scarecrow) that helps transition the property from what’s been primarily a regional escape. While embracing the same dynamic terrain and former farmland high above the Columbia River, Scarecrow is a bit more intimate and strategic than the sprawling Sands Course. The property also boasts one of the game’s great short courses in the 14-hole Quicksands par 3 course, not to mention what is arguably the best putting course in the world of destination golf. The Cascade putting course, also designed by David McLay Kidd, is a 100,000 square-foot roller coaster of a layout that sits directly behind the inn and has majestic long-range views of the river below and mountains in the distance. A couple hours away into Idaho is Lake Couer d’Alene and a lush, forested region that couldn’t be more different than the high plains in Eastern Washington. It’s a combination that makes for an epic golf trip. The Couer d’Alene Golf Resort features one of the game’s most iconic holes with its floating green and accompanying boat ride, while nearby Circling Raven is one of the finest casino courses in the country. Central Oregon / Bend There are dozens of public golf courses in the Bend area that take full advantage of the scenic Cascade Mountain views and as many as 300 days of sunshine per year. Three of those courses are regular fixtures in Top 100 lists, including Crosswater at the Sunriver Resort, a layout that crisscrosses the Deschutes and Little Deschutes rivers multiple times and first put Central Oregon on the golf map. Sunriver has been selected to host four USGA championships from 2027 through 2036, including the 2031 U.S. Mid-Amateur at Crosswater and Sunriver’s Meadow course. There’s also Pronghorn at Juniper Preserve, a golf and wellness resort which features a public Jack Nicklaus Signature design among its two 18-hole courses in the juniper forest of Central Oregon. And at the Tetherow Resort, a 700-acre property 20 minutes from Mt. Bachelor, David McLay Kidd’s Scottish-links-inspired layout is a contrast to some of its desert style neighbors. Other gems in the area include 36 holes at Black Butte Ranch, Aspen Lakes and Brasada Canyons. Ocean City, Maryland With other spots concentrated in the Midwest and further west, it seems appropriate to touch on a region that counts about 4 1/2 million golfers within a 250-mile radius along the Eastern seaboard but gets understandably overshadowed by places a bit further south – from Pinehurst, Myrtle Beach and Hilton Head in the Carolinas to historic resorts in neighboring Virginia. But Ocean City, Maryland, provides value, variety and accessibility, with courses from celebrated designers that boast bay views or play through maritime forests. There’s also no lack of accomodations, with 11,000 hotel rooms in the area. Among the 10 courses in Ocean City are The Links at Lighthouse Sound, which features picturesque holes that run along Assawoman Bay and boasts the longest cart bridge in the U.S. at nearly 1,500 feet. There are also the two courses at GlenRiddle – a former thoroughbred training facility – that are named after Triple Crown winning horses Man O’War and War Admiral, two more at Ocean City Golf Club, and other popular public facilities such as Eagle’s Landing, Nutters Crossing and Rum Pointe.

item.title: The New €1 House Program In Naro, Sicily
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.95
A new town in Sicily has launched a one-euro house program. The town of Naro, in the province of Agrigento in southwestern Sicily, is now accepting applications from potential buyers and sellers interested in joining the program to buy or sell a house for one euro. For buyers, the homes must be used either as a main residence, a second home, a guest house or for a commercial activity or headquarters. It is open to foreign nationals, such as Americans, as well as commercial companies and foundations. Naro Joins Many Other One Euro House Programs The one-euro house scheme is an urban regeneration program that makes headlines every time another municipality comes online. Most are in Italy, but there are some in France and Spain. One of the first programs can be traced back to England. In 2015, a project was launched in Liverpool to offer dilapidated and derelict houses for just £1, provided that they were converted into proper homes. In many cases, it took tens of thousands of pounds to renovate the properties. It is an increasingly successful attempt to arrest the decline of aging, dwindling populations, particularly as houses have emptied while people have headed to larger cities in search of work. Buyers are obviously attracted to living in authentic villages and towns. Think stone buildings, cobbled streets, small arches and medieval courtyards. The price tag, which is real, albeit symbolic, represents just the first step in a promise you are giving the municipality to invest your time and money. In return, local regions can revitalize and move into the twenty-first century with new residents. The town of Mussomeli, in Sicily, about a one-hour drive from Naro, was nearly abandoned a decade ago. According to The Times, its one-euro program has turned the provincial town around—even former residents are returning. Issues around poor quality of life (garbage, access, and culture) have been transformed by new EU funding, improved public transport connections to Sicily’s capital, Palermo, and the recruitment of new healthcare professionals from Argentina. To-date, 600 houses have been sold to foreigners, with 180 of those for €1. The town is now home to 18 different nationalities. New life has brought cafes, guesthouses, and visitors. In Italy, the U.K.’s Independent newspaper found that renovation costs are still comparatively low, ranging from €20,000–50,000 ($23,000 to $58,000), depending on the property's size and condition. Realtors say potential applicants should consider spending €1,000 per square meter (roughly €100 per square foot) on renovations. In France, the French National Housing Association (ANAH) estimated that the cost of many of these €1 homes would be about €80,000 ($93,000) for a house of around 100 square meters (1,076 square feet). In addition to the one euro, there are legal fees, registration and land registry taxes, and buyers would have to prove they have the financial means and detailed renovation plans for the buildings in question. According to Idealista, the work must be insured or backed by a bank, and a clause requires it to be completed within a specified time frame. This latter point makes sense, as the goal is to renovate the villages and towns, not to pass empty, dilapidated homes into new hands, only to have them remain empty. Naro is a twenty-minute drive to the nearest beach and about an hour to the main southern coastline. It is a wine-growing area and has a strong agricultural community and heritage. How Americans Can Live In Italy For Americans who want to live in Italy, buying property does not, by itself, grant the right to reside there. U.S. citizens may visit Italy and the wider Schengen area for up to 90 days in any rolling 180-day period without a visa, but they need an appropriate long-stay visa and residence permit to remain longer.
