item.title: What the Cockroach Movement Says About the Indian Economy
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.04
What the Cockroach Movement Says About the Indian Economy Young college graduates are struggling to find jobs. When India’s chief justice referred to unemployed youth in India as cockroaches earlier this year, that became the rallying cry for a new political movement called the Cockroach Janta Party. Before long, young Indians discontent with the country’s education system and its labor market were marching on parliament—and being met with harsh police crackdowns and internet shutdowns. Ultimately, the government backed down, resulting in the Indian education minister’s resignation. But the difficulties faced by India’s young people remain—as does the new movement claiming to represent their interests. What exactly is going on with the Indian economy? Why is its education system struggling? And how will advances in artificial intelligence affect employment levels? When India’s chief justice referred to unemployed youth in India as cockroaches earlier this year, that became the rallying cry for a new political movement called the Cockroach Janta Party. Before long, young Indians discontent with the country’s education system and its labor market were marching on parliament—and being met with harsh police crackdowns and internet shutdowns. Ultimately, the government backed down, resulting in the Indian education minister’s resignation. But the difficulties faced by India’s young people remain—as does the new movement claiming to represent their interests. What exactly is going on with the Indian economy? Why is its education system struggling? And how will advances in artificial intelligence affect employment levels? Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter. Cameron Abadi: Are India’s labor market problems directly related to Prime Minister [Narendra] Modi’s overall developmental-state economic strategy? Adam Tooze: The first thing to understand is the scale: There are 367 million people in India between 15 and 29. That’s most of the population of Europe, just in young people. That just explodes the conventional frameworks of Western understanding. The kind of desperation that you feel from this protest, the sense of panic and generational pressure on young people in the big Asian economies, is like nothing we know in the West. And so, yes, this is really a huge challenge to any development program, and Modi’s in particular. It has produced growth, but it has not produced structural change. And without structural change, it has not produced the jobs that will absorb the increasingly gigantic flow of graduates from India’s education system. And that’s the core of the problem, which is that there is measured GDP growth, which is undeniable, and anyone who’s visited India can see it, it’s there. The infrastructure has changed. And for the top segment of Indian society, the resulting affluence is remarkable and easily approaching and exceeding, in many cases, developed economy norms. And then there is this huge part of Indian society and the Indian economy which has simply not experienced that same kind of growth. So where most of the job growth is in India is in agriculture. India added 83 million jobs since the pandemic—that’s half the American labor force—lifting employment from 490 million to 572 million with gains for both men and women. But half of those are in farming. And above all, that’s where women are working. If you look at the structure of the Indian labor market, the share of people in formal employment with regular contracts is—it rose from 18 percent in 2012 to 23 percent in 2025. Which means that 75-plus percent of the Indian population is basically in informality, either in literally casualized work or in something that’s closer to formalized but still radically precarious self-employment. So, this is the central problem that is being voiced and articulated in these protests. And I think you’re right to say that this is surely just the beginning of a rolling process of negotiation. Because this isn’t China. This isn’t a one-party regime with a repressive police state and no freedom of expression. It is by no means a liberal paradise. But the power of insurgent mobilization in India is absolutely real. CA: At the heart of this movement is a discontent with Indian education and a sense that it’s not functioning well. Is it true that India’s education system is struggling—how does it compare with, say, China’s? AT: India’s education system has many incredibly strong points. It has notable centers of technology, like the Indian Institute of Technology in Delhi and its counterparts in the other great cities of India. It has liberal arts colleges, which provide a constant pipeline of absolutely brilliant humanities students. India produces top-class talent across all the disciplines, great engineers, great historians, the whole works. And over the last 30 to 40 years, the other thing to say is there’s been huge transformation. And so the number of universities has exploded from 1,600 accredited institutions in 1991 to 70,000 today, with huge jumps especially in the 2000s. And there has undoubtedly been a story of widening access. And on the other hand, there is, as it were, the dark side, which is that India’s top university, the Indian Institute of Technology in Delhi, at least by the conventional university rankings, ranks at 118th in the global rankings—by comparison with China, which increasingly dominates the top 10. And from conversation with friends in India, what really struck me most was their deep, deep concern about elementary education in India. Because the basic human capital formation of any society is done not really at the top end of the education system, where in the end, brilliant people, often coming from well-resourced households, are going to prevail and charge their way through. But what you really want is to build the biggest possible pipe, the largest possible entry to the funnel. And that’s where India on comparative statistics has fallen down. And this was evident already in the early 1980s, when you compare India and China when the World Bank first got into China. Because their standard of what a poor country looked like was India, and then they discovered post-Maoist China, which actually had near-comprehensive literacy, and they hadn’t seen anything like it. So in India, really, again, there’s huge change. The Right to Education Act of 2009 has now firmly established that there must be schools in every village, that there is a requirement that kids attend school. So within the last 20 years, there has been this move toward comprehensive enrollment. The basic logic of state-building, of building a national society is happening in India on a dramatic scale. But when you look at the results, when you test for what kids are actually learning in those thousands, tens of thousands, presumably hundreds of thousands of village schools, the outcomes are unsurprisingly poor. The teachers are underpaid, the teachers don’t show up. And crucially, of course, there’s very little cultural capital in the households, and particularly with mothers, many of whom are from older generations who are illiterate and therefore find it very hard to support their kids’ education. And it’s at the elementary level that my much better-informed colleagues in India say that’s really where the issue is deepest. By the time they’re at university, they have very high levels of literacy compared to the hundreds of millions of kids coming out of badly funded rural schools, which just really don’t have the wherewithal. And so that I think is the gap that is worth focusing on. CA: India seems to have made a choice to specialize in IT services—but is that now being disrupted by AI? And if so, does India have alternatives—can it pivot to becoming a global manufacturer at this point? AT: AI is potentially a lethal threat. And according to some of the more alarmist surveys—in India it’s something like 130 million jobs, virtually the entire routine white-collar sector is potentially at risk, which would be devastating for an economy which has not principally gone down the manufacturing route. The manufacturing story is the central question, right here, right now. So between 11 percent and 13 percent of Indian employment is in manufacturing, which is the sort of level you’d expect in a highly developed economy having gone through industrialization and come out the other side. And so the central question for India is why is it not doing a Bangladesh? Why is it not doing a Vietnam? Why is there not a huge concentration proportional to the size of the Indian population of low-wage, low-cost manufacturing in India? And there are moments where Indians point the finger at China and say, “It’s all your fault, you’ve undervalued your exchange rate to do industrial policy.” And then they flip to a more introspective mode, and they realize, “Well, why would you expect it to have worked out in India given the multiple obstacles there are to rapid, small-scale capitalist development in India since independence?” Including the License Raj, the notoriously dense network of regulation, the incredibly high wages and security that are offered to public servants, which create a kind of crowding-out effect. And again, it’s important to see past the headlines. There’s the Apple story, and it’s huge. And many of us were skeptics, including myself. This is the idea that, you know, Apple was forever fated to do most of its smartphone manufacturing in China and it was probably laughably implausible that they could establish a supply chain in India. And by importing a lot of money and an awful lot of Chinese technical talent, they have actually set up now substantial smartphone production lines in India. But it hasn’t spawned a dramatic transformation of a larger scale. And smartphones is one thing. The real question is why is India’s share of garment production smaller than that of Bangladesh? CA: Given then the scale of these labor market problems, it seems only natural to ask how the Indian welfare state is responding. Has Modi overseen, accidentally perhaps, an expansion of India’s welfare state? AT: This is exactly the train of thought that I saw people recapitulating again and again the last time I was in Delhi. Which is, OK, so you’re saying that tech will only employ some people and manufacturing isn’t taking off and agriculture is sort of a dead end in productivity terms, so what are we going to do? Does that mean that our future is the world’s biggest welfare state on a low average income? And the answer seems to be yes. And what’s interesting is this is written into the Indian constitution. So the Indian constitution is a postwar social-democratic sort of document in parts, and it includes this provision that India is a welfare state and will provide welfare. And what has been very interesting over the course of the last 20 years is to see how that’s changed shape. Because from the 2000s onward, India became the ground zero for an experiment in a sort of jobs-guarantee program, which was linked to the idea that every poor rural family ought to have the guarantee of some minimum employment on public works programs. I think the promise was 100 days a year, which would secure basic family income by way of public employment of one member of the family. And this became one of the truly iconic elements of the Indian welfare state. Hugely contested on both sides. Modi’s people hated it. And what we’ve seen since the 2010s is a shift away from that model, which has culminated this year. People may not follow this story, but over the winter of ’25, ’26, the Modi government mounted a concerted attack on this program, massively scaling it back. So what are they putting in its place? And that in itself is super interesting, because what they’re putting in its place is on the one hand the iconic Modi kind of Trump style. It’s like, Modi delivers you a toilet. So there was this anti-public-defecation campaign, which was to build public toilets all over India. Huge, obviously transformative development in providing people with dignified and sanitary provisions. Another one was clean cooking. So, Modi is going to provide you with clean gas cooking so you can avoid charcoal and all of the pollution that results from that. So these sort of charismatic items of consumption that the Modi administration is delivering on the one hand. And food supplies also. So increasingly access to free or cheap grain as a right, established in law. So all of this is saying, again, development is real, right? India will no longer tolerate a situation of absolute starvation-style poverty. Which in the ’70s was still omnipresent, and it’s really striking that India has exited that stage quite concertedly. And then on the other hand, this other element of the last 15 years, which is truly innovative and you’ve got to see it to believe it, which is that practically everyone is equipped with some form of smartphone or some form of cellphone. And once you’re in the system, it’s literally a digital money technology, the likes of which very few Western societies have. Because regional governments in India, national governments can ping money to the population directly. You’re feeling hungry? Here’s some extra money for chapatis or whatever. There’s literally a direct channel. It’s not the ridiculous printing presses of checks that the Americans have to go through, or like the German administration, which can’t even operate a digital system for the whole population. It’s truly a remarkably innovative system. And so then there’s a series of experiments going on about whether or not the most effective mechanism is a kind of drip, drip, drip welfare provision, which just provides basic income every month, or if you’re better off doing lump-sum allocations where you give a household or a village enough money to buy capital equipment, to pay off debts, to actually solve a fundamental problem. It’s really a laboratory of experimentation in low-income welfare. And it’s something that’s hugely underrated in the global story. Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Colby’s ‘Flexible Realism’ Won’t Work in the Indo-Pacific
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.03
Colby’s ‘Flexible Realism’ Won’t Work in the Indo-Pacific Washington’s new strategy is little more than a euphemism for unpredictability. Elbridge Colby, the influential but polarizing U.S. undersecretary of defense for policy, just completed a tour of Southeast Asia where he visited Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Thailand. His primary goal was clearly to clarify and promote the Trump administration’s new global defense strategy, underpinned by what it calls “flexible realism,” with U.S. allies and partners in the Indo-Pacific. In a public speech in Manila, he reiterated the turn in U.S. alliance politics, much of which appears to carry his handwriting. Washington seeks “partners, not protectorates,” to increase burden-sharing while continuing to bolster deterrence by denial against China. Colby also highlighted that, unlike the Biden administration’s Indo-Pacific strategy, the Trump administration prioritizes shared interests over shared values, thus enabling the U.S. to significantly widen the aperture of security cooperation across the entire region. Finally, Colby talked of maintaining a favorable balance of power with China in the Indo-Pacific rather than preserving American primacy—a stark departure from previous administrations, including President Donald Trump’s first, which sought to keep the United States as the predominant global power. Elbridge Colby, the influential but polarizing U.S. undersecretary of defense for policy, just completed a tour of Southeast Asia where he visited Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Thailand. His primary goal was clearly to clarify and promote the Trump administration’s new global defense strategy, underpinned by what it calls “flexible realism,” with U.S. allies and partners in the Indo-Pacific. In a public speech in Manila, he reiterated the turn in U.S. alliance politics, much of which appears to carry his handwriting. Washington seeks “partners, not protectorates,” to increase burden-sharing while continuing to bolster deterrence by denial against China. Colby also highlighted that, unlike the Biden administration’s Indo-Pacific strategy, the Trump administration prioritizes shared interests over shared values, thus enabling the U.S. to significantly widen the aperture of security cooperation across the entire region. Finally, Colby talked of maintaining a favorable balance of power with China in the Indo-Pacific rather than preserving American primacy—a stark departure from previous administrations, including President Donald Trump’s first, which sought to keep the United States as the predominant global power. Colby is half-correct. Washington should certainly want to enlist as many partners as possible to counter Beijing, whether democratic or authoritarian. Engaging more with Cambodia, for instance, is geostrategically advantageous to the United States because doing so challenges China within its own backyard. But Colby and the administration are also losing sight of the bigger picture. What looks like strategic flexibility from Washington risks looking like strategic unpredictability for the Indo-Pacific, ultimately making U.S. allies and partners less, rather than more, willing to balance China. From my routine discussions with interlocutors representing key U.S. allies and partners throughout the Indo-Pacific, the common theme is that they all seek a sustained and predictable U.S. commitment to the region—basically the opposite of Trump’s post on Truth Social this week that suddenly downgraded routine U.S.-South Korea military drills because North Korea was offended. Washington’s friends do not want a strategy based on pure transactionalism, which the Trump administration has turned into a synonym for unpredictability. Colby himself has described flexible realism as “contextual” because the appropriate U.S. response “depends on the situation”—likely a function of whether the boss changes his mind. For better or worse, a longer-lasting commitment is typically premised on shared values or at least a few shared principles, such as maintaining the rules-based order (a term forbidden in the Trump White House). Without this common understanding, the U.S. network of allies and partners has no glue keeping it together, which risks a quick unraveling if conditions change and Washington’s help is no longer required. Another problem is that Colby and the administration are demanding substantially higher defense spending from U.S. allies and partners to satisfy Washington’s new burden-sharing requirements. One of the challenges is that many nations, like the Philippines, simply will not be able to meet expectations of dramatically higher spending. Even wealthier states, such as Japan, are struggling mightily to reach only 2 percent of GDP on defense. Complicating matters further is the fact that Colby, during his speech in Manila, reportedly never once uttered the word “China”—even while describing a defense strategy whose deterrence-by-denial concept is overwhelmingly designed around the Chinese military challenge. The omission comes as Trump prioritizes improving his personal relationship with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, in hopes of striking some sort of “deal.” How can Washington reasonably expect allies to spend dramatically more against a threat that Washington itself appears increasingly reluctant to identify? They should not, and probably will not, until they receive some reassurances. And so far, Washington has not exactly reassured. Australia is a case in point. The country signed the AUKUS security pact with Britain and the United States under the Biden administration in 2021 and recently endured a review of the deal led by Colby. Trump assured Canberra that it would be “full steam ahead.” However, in a virtual press conference Colby held during his Southeast Asia trip, he declined to guarantee that Australia would actually receive its first Virginia-class submarine on schedule in 2032. The episode underscores an uncomfortable asymmetry in flexible realism: Washington demands greater commitments and sacrifices from its allies while reserving the right to reconsider its own commitments at any moment. Because flexible realism prioritizes burden-sharing and fewer U.S. commitments, it is also becoming clearer that the Trump administration is concentrating ever scarcer U.S. military resources on the first island chain at the expense of sustained strategic attention to the Indian Ocean region. Colby believes that the United States should no longer spread its resources too thinly. He has long been a vocal opponent to U.S. military aid to Ukraine amid Russia’s invasion, and he will be well aware of reported munitions shortages and the redeployment of missile defenses and other systems to the Middle East to fight the Iran war. Although the first Trump administration’s Indo-Pacific concept deliberately broadened Washington’s strategic aperture westward—forcing Beijing to account for New Delhi and the Indian Ocean even while confronting challenges to its east—flexible realism increasingly concentrates scarce U.S. military resources on deterrence by denial along the first island chain. Prioritizing the first island chain militarily is understandable. But what flexible realism means in practice is that India will have to step up and do more on its own. Indeed, when Colby testified to Congress in March, he noted that “allies and partners will have to adapt and take more of a leading role in security in these regions. In South Asia, it will mean India.” The danger is that reducing attention to South Asia and the Indian Ocean could weaken India’s hand precisely when the United States should be strengthening it. Rather than forcing Beijing to divide its attention between its eastern and western flanks, Washington’s narrower strategic focus could allow China to concentrate more heavily on the very first island chain that Colby considers paramount. Ironically, Colby himself recognized this advantage before he joined the administration, arguing in 2022 that a strong India could force China to confront a “major second-front problem.” Flexible realism now risks relieving Beijing of precisely that problem. Finally, flexible realism suffers from an even more fundamental problem: It treats what is ultimately a geopolitical competition with China primarily as a military one. Washington’s allies and partners want more than just security collaboration—they want diplomatic and economic support as well. On the economic side in particular, Trump’s trade tariffs have angered and frustrated U.S. friends to the point that they are considering other options, including even closer trade and investment ties to China. Vietnam is a good example. In April of last year, it signed dozens of new economic agreements with Beijing amid Trump’s trade war. India, meanwhile, signed “the mother of all trade deals” with the European Union—a deal that had languished for years—in part to reduce its vulnerability to U.S. trade pressure. In the end, Colby and the Trump administration’s flexible realism could indeed widen the U.S. network of allies and partners aimed at deterring China, and that would be a good thing. But over the longer term, it will also probably destabilize these same relationships in the process, inadvertently granting Beijing newfound advantages to undermine deterrence. Flexible realism—if it is more than just a euphemism for Washington’s new unpredictability—is a solution in search of a problem America never had. Derek Grossman is a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Southern California, the founder and chief analyst of Indo-Pacific Solutions, a former analyst at the Rand Corp., and a former daily intelligence briefer to the U.S. assistant secretary of defense for Asian and Pacific security affairs. item.title: Pro-Ject Just Made Its Entry-Level Turntable Even Better for New Vinyl Listeners
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.38
Last year, Pro-Ject introduced the E1.2, a new entry-level turntable designed to deliver audiophile-grade sound at an accessible price. The company said it was designed with the same ethos as its first-ever turntable, the Pro-Ject 1, released in 1991. Priced at $399, the Pro-Ject E1.2 is a fully manual, belt-drive turntable with no modern features. It has no built-in phono stage; it needs to be paired with an external phono preamp or an integrated amplifier with one. It also lacks Bluetooth streaming or USB connectivity. Basically, the E1.2 is a turntable designed for budget-conscious audiophiles who want to build a traditional vinyl hi-fi system without any shortcuts. Pro-Ject E1.2 BT and Phono However, as spotted by What Hi-Fi?, Pro-Ject has now introduced the E1.2 in two new configurations: the E1.2 BT and the E1.2 Phono. The Pro-Ject E1.2 BT adds a Bluetooth transmitter (with support aptX HD and aptX Adaptive), allowing it to stream vinyl to wireless speakers or headphones. While the E1.2 Phono adds a switchable phono preamplifier, so you can hook the turntable directly to a set of powered speakers.

item.title: 3 Important Changes Coming to Your Current Apple Watch
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.14
watchOS 27 is set to be released in just a couple of weeks. And with it, some important changes and new features are coming to your current Apple Watch. We’ve been trialing them thanks to the public beta for a little over a month. Here’s what you need to know. Meet the Dynamic App Grid The biggest change in watchOS 27 is a new display that appears every time you use your Apple Watch. Apple is calling it the Dynamic App Grid. To date, when you’ve wanted to open an app, you’ve pressed the Apple Watch’s Digital Crown and then navigated to it via the List View or Grid View. But that can be a bit tedious. When you use your Apple Watch running watchOS 27, you’re first greeted with the Dynamic App Grid, which gives you quick access to your most frequently used apps. There’s also an icon at the bottom to access the app honeycomb or scrolladex (the Grid View or List View, respectively). Basically, it makes it easier and faster to get the apps you use most often.

item.title: Vosteed Upgrades Its Fan-Favorite Marten 330 EDC Knife with Specialty Carbon Fiber
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.06
Since its launch in 2024, the Vosteed Marten has remained among the brand’s best-selling offerings. And its larger version, the 330, helps close the gap for people who want something a bit beefier. This silhouette’s popularity seems unlikely to change with two stunning new carbon fiber versions added to the Vosteed Marten 330 lineup: Neon Topo and Copper. Lovely layers Classic versions of the Marten 330 come with aluminum handle scales. However, the model has utilized carbon fiber before as well. That said, these new editions are a far cry from what the Marten has seen before, even with that same material. Previously, the carbon fiber handle option was classic woven carbon fiber in a black colorway.

item.title: These Japanese Jeans Blend Three Dying Techniques for a Distinct Denim
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.03
These Japanese Jeans Blend Three Dying Techniques for a Distinct Denim ONI Denim’s “Greencast” emphasizes the green tones in natural Japanese indigo jeans. Plus, a retro computer accessory updated, an unstoppable ATV and more. ONI Denim’s Greencast jean layers authentic indigo rope-dyeing with sulfur dye pigments to produce a blue-green hue that fades toward vintage turquoise and seafoam over time. The 15-ounce Japanese-milled denim is woven with undyed weft yarns for a beige-white undertone, then given a one-wash rinse to soften the feel and streamline sizing. It is available in four fits and comes with a hemmed 34-inch inseam. The A+ is Ploopy’s most capable open-source trackball yet. It’s an evolution of the beloved Adept with eight buttons (up from six), two programmable knobs for high-resolution scrolling and a detachable wrist rest. Running on the Pixart PMW-3360 sensor at a 1,000Hz polling rate, the device uses Omron D2LS-21 switches and introduces gestures, layers and on-device configuration via QMK and VIA. Ambidextrous and fully 3D-printable, it’s built for power users who want deep customization without leaving the trackball. Can-Am’s Defender Prerunner concept is a race-support machine built for chasing hardcore events like King of the Hammers. Accordingly, it adopts a 6×6 configuration and rides on beefy 35-inch tires. Moreover, it pairs four Sparco seats in the cabin with a trophy-truck-inspired LinQ bed at the rear to create a package that’s performance-ready yet also highly utilitarian. Boulder, Colorado’s Mosaic Cycles built the GT-1 i55 32 from scratch around 32-inch wheels: not as an afterthought, but as a purpose-built gravel race platform. The double-butted titanium frame pairs with a carbon fork from Zero Components (a Mosaic-born brand), fully integrated cable routing and MTB-spec boost axle standards (110x15mm front, 148x12mm rear) to extract every performance advantage the larger wheel diameter offers. Compact 440-445mm chainstays and an offset seat tube keep handling sharp, up to 55mm of tire clearance handles the gnarliest gravel, and it’s all configured to the individual rider through Mosaic’s Made-to-Order program. Paka’s Original Hoodie is among its undisputed best-sellers, but this new take slims it down and refines it significantly. While the original is 15.5 ounces, this lightweight follow-up shaves it down to just 11.3 ounces. Yet, it’s still crafted from a robust, cozy blend of 65 percent Royal Alpaca and 35 percent recycled nylon, making it breathable, temperature-regulating, odor-resistant and much more. It could be your next favorite travel hoodie and shoulder season wear.

item.title: Timberland Turns Its Classic Work Boot into a Bona Fide Birkenstock Competitor
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.81
What do you get when you chop the timeless Timberland 6-Inch Boot in half? As it turns out, a clog. The brand’s latest release, the Heritage Clog, is a genuine Birkenstock competitor, bridging the gap between rugged boot sensibility and the easygoing convenience of an everyday clog. Available on the brand’s European channels for now, the Heritage clog ditches the top half of the well-known boot but keeps its robust outsole and materials, resulting in a capable clog with familiar good looks. The low-cut, backless upper is designed with Timberland’s premium leather, plus a 50 percent recycled Rebotl fabric liner, as well as new comfort-focused features including an EVA foam midsole, anti-fatigue removable footbed and heel shank. The funky silhouette revives the brand’s archival “Cement Gray” colorway that first appeared in the ’90s, giving it an extra dose of heritage style.

item.title: Timex’s New Luxury Brand Debuts Its First High-End Accessory
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.61
The clearest sign that Timex’s modern renaissance is for real is the launch and success of Timex Atelier. Timex’s first luxury brand debuted to equal parts fanfare and skepticism in September 2025, but the skeptics have been silenced by the nascent sub-brand’s ability to quickly and repeatedly sell out its stock of $1,000+ sports watches. With a diver, GMT and a pair of chronographs under its belt already, Timex Atelier continues its busy first year with the launch of its first standalone accessory: the Timex Atelier NBR Synthetic Rubber Strap. The new strap should be familiar to anyone who has perused Timex Atelier’s catalog, as it’s the same strap that’s available as an option on the Marine M1a and GMT24 M1a for anyone who doesn’t want the bracelet. However, today marks the first time Timex is offering the strap as a standalone item, meaning if you buy one of the watches on the bracelet, you can now add the strap without having to buy a second watch. The strap is a legitimate luxury rubber strap. Its 20mm lug width is molded to perfectly fit the case of the Marine M1a and GMT24 M1a (which use the same case), meaning there are no unsightly gaps.

item.title: Toyota’s New Limited-Run Corolla Caps Off Six Decades of History
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.60
Just a few months ago, my colleague Chris Chin reported on Toyota’s anniversary efforts to ring in six decades of the Corolla nameplate. At the time, the resulting special edition was solely destined for Taiwan and other South Asian markets. At the time, he noted that whether the US would receive a similar commemorative treatment had yet to be determined. He didn’t get his hopes up, given how much other forbidden Toyota fruit remains off-limits to the American market. Thankfully, Toyota is in fact bringing its celebrations here, too. The automaker just confirmed a 60th Anniversary Special Edition for the US market, and it offers limited availability at a mainstream price point. Anniversary visual exclusives That’s because, if nothing else, Toyota’s 60th Anniversary Corolla will be rare. According to the announcement, just 2,500 examples are allocated for the United States for the 2027 model year.

item.title: This Adventure-Ready Travel Trailer Aims for a Versatile Sleep Under $30k
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.59
While many compact camper trailers make for pretty approachable investments compared to full-on RV or van conversions, those touting any semblance of off-road capability can come with quite a premium. For instance, even Airstream’s smallest Basecamp model starts around $50,000. Likewise, options from competitors such as Stockman can easily take you close to $80,000 or more. With this in mind, a new Oregon-based startup called Motsmann Engineering is entering the small-trailer scene to field a squaredrop that promises rugged capabilities under $30,000. Along with a durable, all-weather construction, it promises a wealth of options to make it your own. Motsmann’s trail-ready squaredrop It’s called the Outranger, and it’s a squaredrop-style composite camper trailer intended to be a modern take on the classic teardrop. Motsmann wanted something small and affordable that was actually ready to leave the pavement. In practice, this means that it adopts a molded composite construction with an aluminum frame and a galvanized steel chassis. As a result, Motsmann says buyers have nothing to worry about when it comes to rusting, rotting or swelling.

item.title: Carhartt WIP Just Gave Its Iconic Active Jacket a Heritage Denim Makeover
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.51
Introduced in 1997 and based on the heavy-duty Carhartt Active Jac dating back to 1975, Carhartt WIP’s OG Active Jacket remains immediately recognizable, despite nearly three decades of seasonal materials, washes and special editions. For Fall/Winter 2026, the brand has updated the timeless outerwear staple with a heritage-minded material that gives the well-loved silhouette a contemporary edge. The OG Active Jacket (Winter) in Blue (Stone Washed) trades standard canvas for 13.5-ounce, 100 percent cotton “Smith” denim, giving the boxy, loose-fitting jacket a substantial feel and a perfectly broken-in appearance. A striped blanket lining and diamond-quilted, nylon-lined sleeves provide warmth for colder-weather wear. Rib-knit trims cinch the jacket at the cuffs and hem, giving it a bomber-jacket feel, while an adjustable hood adds versatility. A kangaroo pocket and interior chest pocket provide storage, and triple-stitched construction reinforces the jacket’s workwear roots. Available now in stone-washed blue denim, the winter-ready OG Active Jacket will also arrive in a black denim variant later this season, extending Carhartt WIP’s long-running silhouette into another rugged, understated colorway.

item.title: Vero Engineering Evolves Its Acclaimed, Affordable Avid EDC Knife with a Strong New Blade
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.51
In 2025, Vero Engineering took home a major accolade from Blade Show Atlanta: Imported Folding Knife of the Year. The knife that brought the award home was the Avid 1. Now, a year later, that same knife is in its third iteration. Better still, the Vero Engineering Avid 3 marks a new frontier, adding a new blade shape to one of the brand’s most approachable and affordable silhouettes. Avid engineering Those familiar with Vero Engineering likely won’t be surprised to hear about Avid’s pedigree. After all, the Joseph Vero-helmed brand has consistently produced exceptional EDC knives and fixed blades since its inception in 2018, earning a well-deserved cult following. What Vero has not been known for, however, is affordability. Unfortunately, the brand’s penchant for high-end engineering and materials means most of its offerings come at a premium.

item.title: Technics Reimagines a Turntable Icon to Celebrate 55 Years of Japanese Hi-Fi Supremacy
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.48
The Technics SL-1200 is a turntable icon. Originally released in late 1972, it was a direct-drive turntable that DJs came to love for its reliable speed and stability, and for its strength in both playback and mixing. Plus, since it was built like a tank, it was robust enough to survive the wildest of nightclub nights and music festivals. Fast forward to the present and Technics makes a modern version of the classic SL-1200, named the SL-1200MK7. Released in 2021, the SL-1200MK7 has been updated with modern improvements, such as an iron-coreless direct-drive motor, digital pitch control and a lighter chassis (which helps make it more affordable). The Technics SL-1200MK7 currently sells for $1,300. Now, to celebrate the 55th anniversary of the original SL-1200’s release, Technics is introducing a special edition model: the Technics SL-1200 (55th Anniversary Edition). Celebrating an icon According to the Japanese hi-fi brand, the model “pays tribute to a turntable lineage that has helped define DJ culture, shaped the evolution of club performance, and become one of the most recognizable instruments in modern music history.”

item.title: Ka-Bar’s Tactical, Affordable New EPT Reimagines the Ideal Form for an EDC Knife
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.31
While it’s not the biggest trend in the marketplace, we have been seeing more and more knives that don’t depend on, you know, foldability to crack into your daily loadout. Fixed blades making the case for EDC include Benchmade’s Dacian, CRKT’s Nessmuk and Böker’s Li’l Friend Micro. Now classic American brand Ka-Bar is getting in on the action, following up its funkily shaped George Roscoe with an ex-Force Recon Marine’s new design. Meet the EDC-able new Elishewitz Pocket Tool, or EPT for short. Fix it up Like those other knives I just mentioned, this one recognizes a long-overlooked reality: when it comes to EDC, it’s less about foldability than it is about overall size and carryability.

item.title: Huckberry and Timex’s Vintage Ironman Watch Drops to an All-Time Low of $90
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.31
As my colleague Brad Lanphear pointed out when he first wrote about this watch, Timex literally invented the sports watch when it dropped the first Ironman collaboration in the mid-80s. But that wasn’t the end of the story; the brand kept improving and iterating. Some might say 1999 marked the collaboration’s magnum opus with the launch of the Flix. Well, in 2025, that watch was faithfully revived as the Huckberry x Timex Ironman Flix. And now, its price has been slashed back to an all-time low. A Flix of the wrist The Flix is so significant that, even today, triathletes, particularly purists and the nostalgic, still use genuine vintage models during races, though mostly as backups. And while it can’t quite match the capabilities of modern GPS smartwatches, it remains an impressively capable throwback option. Along with classic timekeeping capabilities, the watch features interval and countdown timers, three customizable alarms, two available time zones, a 100-lap chronograph with memory recall and much more. And that’s all housed in a durable, lightweight resin case with a bold digital display and a soft polyurethane strap. And since it’s meant for triathlons, it is also rated for depths of up to 100 meters.

item.title: Airstream Is Linking Up with Your Favorite Ferrari Designer to Rework Its Iconic Trailers
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.17
As much as Airstream stands apart today because of a unique enduring legacy, it clearly recognizes the value of teamwork. From the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation to Tommy Bahama, the brand hasn’t been afraid to collaborate, and it’s yielded a variety of results. All the same, I’d like to think that Airstream’s new partnership with Pininfarina promises something more. The Turin design house is responsible for some of the most stunning Ferraris ever built, and both brands have a lengthy history that’s closing in on 100 years. Airstream’s next step Now, at this stage, Airstream and Pininfarina haven’t offered up more than a confirmation that something is coming, well, eventually. The timeline places the project around Airstream’s forthcoming centenary in 2031, but the brands haven’t revealed any sketches or even a concrete idea of what’s planned. All the same, it amounts to an exciting prospect. In the announcement video, Airstream CEO Bob Wheeler describes the goal as both a “next step” and a “conscious and careful evolution.”

item.title: Sonos Just Gave Its iPhone App a Highly-Requested New Ability
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.12
Sonos has been in the news quite a bit recently. Just last month, the multi-room speaker giant rolled out a big app update that introduced a new look and several long-awaited features. And, in the past week, Bloomberg has reported that Sonos is gearing up to introduce two new products: a new “Ultra” pair of headphones and a new and improved version of the Beam (Gen 2), Sonos’s most entry-level Dolby Atmos soundbar, which was released in fall 2021. Now, ahead of those potential new launches, Sonos has rolled out another new update that brings support for a fan-favorite iPhone feature: Live Activities. Sonos now supports iPhone’s Live Activities Introduced in 2022 with iOS 16, Live Activities is a feature that gives you quick access to real-time information right from your Lock Screen. No need to unlock your iPhone or open an app. When you are using your iPhone, Live Activities appear in the Dynamic Island, too.

item.title: Noah Redesigns the Classic Coach’s Jacket with Elevated Materials
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.09
The humble coach’s jacket dates back to the 1960s, when the nylon shell design became a staple of athletic departments throughout America. It was eventually adopted by everyone from concert security companies to surf and skate brands. Defined by a drawstring waist, pointed collar, snap placket, elastic cuffs and dual welted hand pockets, its simplicity and affordability made it incredibly popular. But the New York City-based clothing label Noah reimagined the American classic as an elevated jacket that can see you through the winter. Debuting with the first drop of Noah’s Autumn/Winter ’26 collection, the Campus Jacket sticks to the well-established coach’s jacket blueprint. However, the familiar nylon shell, often seen with a thin synthetic lining, is replaced by pure wool melton lined with a plaid twill. The collar is lined with a 100-percent cotton, medium-wale corduroy, much like a barn coat. It is paired with a snap throat latch, as you’d find on most Barbour jackets.

item.title: New Balance Reimagines Its Archival Trail Runner as a Minimalist Mary Jane
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.09
The majority of New Balance sneakers tend to follow a familiar, if continually refreshed, formula: understated color palettes paired with textured, multi-material uppers and traditional sneaker design. The TDS MT2 eschews that approach almost completely, resulting in a trail shoe-meets-Mary Jane sneaker that looks unlike anything else in the brand’s current lineup. Trail meets trend For those not yet in the know, TDS (Tokyo Design Studio) is New Balance’s Japan-based experimental arm, where the brand pushes further from its mainstream catalog, reinterpreting performance shapes through a fashion-forward lens. The new MT2 is the studio’s take on the Minimus family, which New Balance describes as a “fashion-forward exploration” of the natural-movement range.

item.title: IKEA’s New 22-Piece Collection Is Full of Affordable Collector’s Items
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.08
For most shoppers, Ikea is synonymous with flat-pack furniture that’s functional and cheap. However, it also has an audience in high-design circles. Vintage chairs, lamps and other homewares from the big, blue retailer can go for the thousands in today’s secondary market. In 2022, a 1950s armchair called the Cavelli sold for the equivalent of $20,000 at auction in Sweden. Of course, not all IKEA items are destined for a similar fate. But the 22 pieces that make up its new Konstrunda collection have as good a chance as anything in the current catalog. Affordable, accessible, evocative Arriving in September, Konstrunda culls together seven renowned designers for limited-edition drop of what IKEA describes as “affordable art objects.”

item.title: Porsche’s New Limited-Run 911 Honors the World’s Most Notorious Car Proving Ground
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.06
Nowadays, Germany’s Nürburgring Nordschleife is regarded as one of the most formidable race tracks in the world, the ultimate proving ground for performance cars. That reputation did not materialize overnight. Arguably more impressive than the Green Hell’s reputation is its endurance, as 2027 marks the circuit’s 100th anniversary. To celebrate the occasion, Porsche has announced a limited-run 911 GT3 100 Jahre Nürburgring that’s packed with exclusive visual touches. Add to that a low production count and some matching wrist hardware, and it has all the hallmarks of a future collector’s car for performance enthusiasts and brand purists alike. Porsche honors the “Green Hell” The foundation is the standard 992-generation GT3, complete with its 4.0-liter flat-six. Porsche isn’t making any mechanical changes to the engine, but the aesthetic treatment alone is worth appreciating.

item.title: Aer and Pack Hacker’s Elusive “Ultimate Travel Companion” Sling Bag Finally Returns
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.03
Earlier this year, San Francisco-based Aer and Pack Hacker came together to craft a city-going sling. It far exceeded both brands’ expectations, as shown by how quickly it sold out. Now, the brands have gone to great lengths to bring that bag, the Aer x Pack Hacker Ultra Sling, for a second time. And with any luck, those who missed out the first time will be able to get one this go-around … but there is a slight catch. Lighten up As a consistent producer of EDC and travel bags, Aer is no stranger to sling bags. In fact, if you’re familiar enough with them, you might get the impression that this bag seems a lot like the brand’s existing Day Sling 3 Ultra (or its follow-up, the Day Sling 4 Ultra). While they share some similarities, they are distinct bags. Most notably, their capacities differ. The Day Sling 3 Ultra is a 3.0-liter bag (and the 4 is a 2.5-liter bag), while the Ultra Sling is a much sleeker 2.0-liter bag. That makes it a bit more maneuverable, quicker, and more compact.

item.title: Lamborghini’s 1,050-HP Revuelto SV Is Its Most Powerful Production Car Ever
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.02
Lamborghini’s 1,050-HP Revuelto SV Is Its Most Powerful Production Car Ever Limited to just 1,963 units, the V12 hypercar boasts a 2.4-second sprint. Plus, Formawerx’s new Porsche key, Bruichladdich’s 25th-anniversary single malt and more. If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more Welcome to “Today in Gear,” your daily snapshot of the most important releases in style, watches, tech, motoring, fitness, home and the outdoors. Lamborghini Revuelto SV The Revuelto SV is the most powerful and fastest production Lamborghini ever built, pushing the marque’s V12 hybrid system to a total of 1,050 horsepower and 1,051 lb-ft of torque. On the road, this means it can sprint from 0 to 62 mph in 2.4 seconds before topping out at more than 214 mph. With a lap time of 1:41.6 set by Lamborghini factory driver Marco Mapelli, the Revuelto SV became the fastest production car ever recorded at the Hockenheimring. It’s limited to just 1,963 units, adding touches like a new Pilota driving mode, motorsport-derived adjustable passive dampers, CCM-R Plus carbon-ceramic brakes and bespoke Bridgestone Potenza Race R tires. Brooks’ latest addition to its best-selling Ghost franchise combines performance tech with an approachable $150 price tag, making it more appealing than ever for daily training. The road-running shoe features two key technologies: SpringRamp forefoot technology that drives forward momentum at push-off, and a nitrogen-infused DNA HYPE midsole foam (a PEBA and EVA blend) tuned for a lively, cushioned ride. A lightweight warp knit upper locks the foot down without sacrificing breathability, making the Ghost Amp a strong daily trainer for runners who want a little more snap underfoot. The fourth entry in Bruichladdich’s iconic Still Series, Greener Still is a 25th Anniversary limited release that shifts focus from cask to field. Distilled from three barley varieties — Bere, Biodynamic and Organic — and matured for 15 years exclusively in first-fill bourbon barrels on Islay, it delivers soft florals, ripe orchard fruit and a velvety finish with vanilla and coastal notes. It’s bottled at 51.6% ABV in this sleek matte green container. Formawerx has finally added another entry to its exceptional high-end catalog of custom automobile keys, and this one is special. The Legends 997 is designed as a companion piece to the 2005-2012 Porsche 911, 997.1 and 997.2. For those not in the know, that makes this a key for the last “true analog” 911. Machined from stainless steel to a 0.15 micron finish, the precision of this key is unmatched. Furthermore, each receives a white-glove, full transfer of the existing OEM key components, along with precision duplication of the original key blade. Shinola’s Detrola Color Theory Cool turns the dial into a canvas: pink and blue triangles dance across the face in a pattern that nods to mid-century American art, with a mint green second hand and C1 lume-tipped gray hands finishing the picture. The 41mm case pairs a stainless steel core with co-molded cream TR90 resin for a watch that’s lighter than it looks, while a clear exhibition caseback lets you glimpse the Ronda Argonite 705 quartz movement at work. Like its orange-heavy Color Theory Warm counterpart, this watch is designed and assembled in Detroit. Analogue has collaborated with Supreme to release a limited edition of its Pocket. The handheld console works just like the standard Pocket, and is capable of natively playing Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridges. But this edition comes in two new finishes: one in Supreme’s signature glossy red and one in 24-karat gold. Naturally, each these special-edition consoles is expected to be more expensive than the standard Pocket, which goes for $240 and now comes in many different finishes. At the time of writing, pricing has not yet been announced.

item.title: Long-Term Travel and the Accounts That Stop Recognizing You
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 7.15
Four months into a trip through South America, a long-term traveler can suddenly find their bank has flagged them as fraud. There may be no warning. The card is declined at the counter, the app refuses to open, and the only option is a phone number that does not accept calls from outside the account's country. Long-term travelers often encounter this problem, which is rarely triggered by the transaction alone. The connection also has a part. Banks and payment processors review factors like location, network reputation, and connection type when assessing a login. A ProxyWing ISP proxy provider uses IP addresses registered to internet service providers rather than data-center IPs, which helps explain why different connections may be classified differently. Why Unfamiliar Connections Can Trigger Account Lockouts What Actually Trips the Alarm It is seldom the amount you spent. It is the shape of the session. - Speed of movement matters. A login from Peru eleven hours after one from Colombia is fine, but eleven minutes is not. - The reputation of the network matters. Hundreds of people share hostel and cafe Wi-Fi, and if any have done something suspicious, the address carries that history. - Connection type. Traffic that looks like it comes from a data center rather than a home or a phone gets scored much more harshly, which is why certain VPNs make things worse rather than better. - Doing something unusual at the same time. Changing an address or adding a payee from an unfamiliar country is what turns a flag into a lock. The Two-Factor Problem Nobody Plans For Losing a phone at home is inconvenient. Losing it in month five of a trip can lock you out of everything at once because the phone is usually the second factor for the bank, the email that lets you reset the bank, and the authenticator app that protects the email. The chain matters. If your recovery codes are stored in the email account that needs the authenticator on the lost phone, you have a loop with no way in. This is the most common way travelers get genuinely stuck rather than merely inconvenienced, and it takes about fifteen minutes to prevent. - Print the recovery codes for your email plus primary bank on paper, carried separately from the phone. - Add a second authenticator device if any of your accounts allow it. An old phone without a SIM works fine and can be kept at the bottom of the bag. - Check whether your bank's two-factor works over SMS only. If it does, a local SIM will break it, so you need to know before you swap the card rather than after. What To Do Before You Leave The single most useful thing is boring. Set up a second account at a different bank, fund it, and carry the card separately. Everything else on this list is optional, but that one is not. - Register a travel notice if your bank still offers one. Many have quietly dropped them. - Make sure your phone number on the account is one you can actually receive calls on abroad, not just texts. - Download the offline recovery codes for anything that uses an authenticator app. - Take a photograph of the back of your cards, cropped so the number is not fully visible, and store it somewhere you can reach without your phone. - Tell one person at home which banks you use. If you end up needing someone to receive a letter or make a domestic call on your behalf, this saves a day. How Different Connections Get Treated | Connection you are using | How a bank tends to score it | Practical result | | Local SIM with mobile data | Low risk, looks like an ordinary phone | Usually fine | | HotelWi-Fii | Medium, shared but stable | Occasional extra verification | | Hostel or cafeWi-Fii | Higher, heavily shared | Verification, sometimes a lock | | Commercial VPN | High, recognized as a data center range | Frequently blocked outright | | Residential connection at home | Lowest | The baseline everything else is measured against | | AirportWi-Fii | High, transient and shared | Avoid logging into banking entirely | | Tethering from your own phone | Same as the phone itself | The best option on the road | The general pattern is similar across many banks: the closer a connection looks to an ordinary home line, the less friction a traveler is likely to encounter. The closer your connection looks to an ordinary home line, the less friction you get. This is also why the free VPN people install for privacy tends to be the thing that locks them out. Which Accounts Survive Travel Better Not all banks handle this equally; the difference is structural rather than customer service. Banks built around mobile apps cope better because their fraud models assume people move. Older institutions with branch-based verification cope worst because their recovery path assumes you can walk into a building. The pragmatic setup most long-term travelers use is one app-based account for daily spending, one traditional account holding most of the money and rarely touched, and a card from a third provider kept separate from the wallet. It sounds excessive until the first lockout. If You Are Already Locked Out Do not keep retrying. Repeated failed attempts push the account further into lockdown and make the eventual phone call longer. Find a dependable connection, ideally mobile data on a local SIM, and use the in-app message system if available. It is slower but works from anywhere. If you do have to call, use a voice-over-internet service that presents a number in your home country. Many bank fraud lines will not accept an international caller ID at all, and this is the difference between resolving it today and resolving it next week. FAQ Will telling my bank I am traveling prevent this? It helps for the first few weeks and then stops mattering. Most travel notices expire after thirty days, and many banks have removed them entirely in favor of automatic detection. Is a VPN a good idea for online banking abroad? Generally no. It protects the connection, but it makes you look less like yourself, and banks weigh that heavily. Use mobile data instead. Why does my card work in shops but the app will not open? Different systems score card payments and app logins. The card transaction has a physical terminal behind it, which is strong evidence you are there. The app login has only the connection. How long does a lock usually take to lift? If you can complete identity verification, minutes. If it needs a phone call to a domestic number, expect days. This is the main argument for the second card. Does using the same connection every day help? Yes, more than most people expect. Staying somewhere for a fortnight and using the same Wi-Fi builds a pattern the bank recognizes, which is why lockouts cluster in the weeks when you are moving fastest. This article was published in partnership with ProxyWing.

item.title: How To Choose the Right Dive Center in Koh Tao
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 7.03
What's the difference between the dive centers in Koh Tao, Thailand? They all seem the same. With over 80 dive centers on one small island, Koh Tao is one of the most competitive and confusing places in the world to get certified. In fact, every dive center in Koh Tao offers similar-looking courses, making it hard to tell what actually separates one from another. A cheaper course might seem like a great deal, but you may end up in a larger group with less personal attention. Two dive centers can offer the same certification, but the quality of instruction, safety standards, and overall experience can differ greatly. It can be difficult to choose a quality dive center absent prior experience. Here are the eight factors that actually separate one dive center from another. 8 Things to Consider When Choosing a Dive Center in Koh Tao 1. Start With the Course That Fits Your Goals Koh Tao offers diving courses for every type of traveler. Before you choose a dive center, think about what you want to achieve underwater. Here are the types of courses that most dive centers offer. Try Dive Try Dive offers a beginner-friendly scuba experience. It does not require certification. This course is ideal if you are curious about scuba diving but aren't ready to commit to a certification course. Open Water Course (4 days, No Experience Needed) The RAID Open Water Course is an entry-level scuba certification that qualifies you to descend up to 18 meters. This course includes theory lessons, one pool session, and four ocean dives. Advanced Explorer 30 Course This course expands your diving skills and certifies you to 30 meters. It includes four day dives and one night dive with a focus on buoyancy, navigation, and deeper diving techniques. Master Rescue Course (4 days) Master Rescue Course requires you to have an Explorer or Advanced certification plus valid First Aid and Oxygen Administration certifications. This course develops rescue techniques, oxygen administration, and diver safety awareness. Divemaster Course (Approximately 2 Months) Divemaster course requires you to have First Aid, Oxygen Administration, and Rescue certifications. This course develops leadership skills through theory lessons, pool sessions, unlimited ocean diving, and real-life training assisting instructors. Deep 40 and Nitrox specialty certifications are also required before completing the course if you do not already have them. 2. Don't Choose Based on Price Alone A common story in Koh Tao is a diver books the cheapest course and ends up in a group of 8-10 with one instructor. The diver spends more time waiting than learning. By the time they realize the mistake, they have already paid. Here is why you should not choose a dive center based on price alone: - Some budget centers reduce the price of the course by taking more students per instructor. - Scuba diving calls for patience and confidence. The right course includes proper guidance, explanations, and an instructor who supports you. - Some low-cost options focus on completing the course quickly. A quality dive center makes sure you understand the skills before moving on. 3. Choose a Great Instructor First When choosing a quality dive center, consider the instructor's experience. A great instructor can impact your experience more than the certification agency or course price. Here is how to choose a great instructor. Read Reviews About the Specific Instructors When checking reviews, look out for: - Patience and teaching style. - Clear explanations. - Making beginners feel comfortable. - Professionalism and safety awareness. Look for Experience and Qualifications Consider: - How long they have been teaching. - Their diving experience. - Their ability to teach beginners. - Whether they are active and knowledgeable about local dive sites. Choose Someone Who Makes You Comfortable Many first-time divers feel nervous before going underwater. Look for instructors who: - Listen to your concerns. - Answer your questions. - Avoid rushing you. - Help you build confidence step by step. Ask Who Will Teach Your Course Some dive centers advertise qualified instructors but assign you to someone else. Before booking, ask: - Who will be my instructor? - How many students will they teach? - Can I meet or speak with them before starting? 4. Ask About Student-to-Instructor Ratios Group size affects your training more than most beginners realize. This is why: - With fewer students, the instructor has more time to observe your skills, answer questions, and provide individual feedback. - Smaller groups make it easier for instructors to slow down when needed and correct concerns before they become big problems. Before booking, consider asking a few questions such as: - How many students will be in my group? - How many instructors will be teaching? - Are groups smaller for beginners? - Will the same instructor teach me throughout the course? 5. Check the Quality of the Equipment A reputable dive center should routinely inspect, service, and replace equipment. Here are things to consider: Ask About How Often Equipment Is Serviced Before booking, ask how frequently they inspect and service important gear like: - Regulators - BCDs (Buoyancy Control Devices) - Dive computers - Tanks These pieces of gear reduce most problems underwater. Check the Condition of Rental Gear Before starting your course, take a look at: - Masks that fit properly and do not show cracks. - Regulators that are clean and well maintained. - BCDs that inflate and deflate smoothly. - Wetsuits that are free of excessive damage. - Fins and straps that are in good condition. Look for Clean and Organized Equipment Areas A well-managed dive center keeps its gear storage clean and organized. Proper storage, drying, and maintenance show it takes care of its equipment. 6. Look for Strong Safety Standards Safety should not be an afterthought. Here is what to look for: They Explain Safety Procedures Clearly Check things such as: - How to use your equipment. - Underwater communication signals. - Emergency procedures. - What to do if you feel uncomfortable during a dive. Ask About Instructor Supervision Your instructor should actively monitor students throughout the course and dives. Look for: - Instructors who stay close to beginners underwater. - Clear demonstrations of skills prior to diving. - Regular checks to confirm everyone feels comfortable. Check if They Follow Proper Training Procedures Quality training usually includes: - Classroom theory - Confined water practice - Skill demonstrations - Open water training dives - Final skill assessments 7. Choose a Center That Answers Your Questions A good dive center should make you feel knowledgeable and comfortable before booking. Here are things to consider. Pay Attention to How Quickly They Respond Look for: - Helpful answers. - Clear information about the courses and schedules. - Staff who take time to understand your needs. Ask About Course Details For example, you can ask: - How long does the course take? - What's included in the price? - How many dives are included? - What does the daily schedule look like? - How does the certification process work? Visit or Message More Than One Dive Center Compare a few options before deciding based on these factors: - Response quality - Friendliness - Transparency - Attention to detail 8. Choose a Center That Teaches in Your Language The final tip is to choose a dive center that teaches in a language that you are comfortable with. Many dive centers in Koh Tao offer instruction in several languages, such as: - English - Spanish - French - German Before booking, check if the course is taught in a language you are comfortable with. Also check if the course materials are available in that language. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) 1. Are all dive centers in Koh Tao certified? Reputable dive centers generally operate through recognized training agencies such as RAID, PADI, or SSI. Before booking, confirm the center's agency affiliation and review its instructor qualifications, safety procedures, equipment standards, and recent customer feedback. 2. What questions should I ask before booking a dive course? You can ask questions related to certification, costs, schedule, logistics, gear, and health. 3. How do I know if a dive center is safe? Look for affiliation with a recognized training agency such as RAID, PADI, or SSI. Ask about instructor qualifications, group sizes, emergency procedures, equipment maintenance, and medical screening. They should verify any certification you possess when your selected course or dive requires prior certification. 4. Are online reviews reliable when choosing a dive center? Yes, reviews can be helpful in choosing a dive center. Here is what you need to focus on: - Look for recurring safety complaints, broken equipment, or overcrowded groups. - See how the shop replies to negative feedback to judge their professionalism and accountability. - Look at candid photos. 5. What is the difference between a dive shop and a dive center? A dive shop focuses on retail sales and gear servicing, while a dive center provides professional training courses. If you're planning a longer island stay, explore these other things to do in Koh Tao between your diving sessions. Conclusion You can choose a quality dive center in Koh Tao by considering these tips: - Your goals for the course. - The instructor's experience and teaching style. - Student-to-instructor ratio. - Equipment quality and maintenance. - Safety standards and training procedures. - How responsive and transparent the center is. - Whether they teach in your language. Take time to message a couple of centers and ask questions directly. This article was published in partnership with La Bombona Diving.

item.title: Thinking About Staying Longer in Portugal? Here's How To Explore the Country Like a Local
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.66
A quick trip to Portugal can deliver postcard views, tiled streets, and remarkable meals. Staying for several weeks offers something different: time to notice the rhythm behind the attractions. You can spot familiar faces at the market and take a day trip without rushing, and living like a local means traveling more slowly, following local routines, and leaving room for ordinary experiences. Choose a Base That Fits Your Trip Lisbon and Porto are convenient starting points, especially for first-time visitors who want strong public transportation and many services. They are not the only choices. Coimbra offers a compact historic center and a large student population, while Braga combines city life with easy access to northern Portugal. Travelers looking for nature and outdoor activities without the largest tourist crowds can also consider Portugal's Minho region, including destinations such as Viana do Castelo and Ponte de Lima. Coastal places such as Cascais and Ericeira suit travelers who want the ocean nearby, although prices and crowds can rise during the summer. Tavira provides a quieter Algarve base with rail connections to other towns along the region's eastern coast. Before booking, look beyond the nightly rate. Check if the neighborhood has a supermarket, laundry, pharmacy, and reliable transportation within walking distance. Confirm the kitchen and workspace if you plan to cook or work remotely. A cheaper place on the outskirts can lose appeal if every outing requires a long commute. Portugal's accommodation landscape keeps developing in cities and regional destinations; the Mercan Group is among the companies involved in hospitality projects in the country. Use Public Transportation-But Know Its Limits Portugal is relatively easy to explore without driving, especially along the Lisbon-Coimbra-Porto corridor. Comboios de Portugal, or CP, operates urban, regional, Intercidades, and Alfa Pendular trains. Long-distance buses fill gaps in the rail network. Lisbon and Porto have their own metro, bus, tram, and suburban rail services. For a longer stay, compare single fares with local rechargeable cards or monthly passes. The best option depends on the city and zones you cross. Check current rules rather than relying on advice for another destination. Buy popular intercity journeys in advance when schedules matter, especially around holidays and summer weekends. A car can be useful for rural villages, hiking trails, beaches, and parts of the interior where service is infrequent. Instead of renting one for the entire stay, consider combining public transportation with a short rental for a specific road trip. This can reduce costs while preserving flexibility. Build a Budget Around Everyday Life The habits that make a long stay enjoyable can also make it more affordable. Shop at a neighborhood market or supermarket, cook some meals, and look for a prato do dia-a daily special-at small restaurants. Standing at the counter for an espresso is often cheaper than sitting in a tourist-facing café in a famous square. The goal is not to avoid every popular place but to balance special experiences with regular days. Groceries: Choose markets and supermarkets near your accommodation instead of relying on convenience shops near attractions. Dining: Balance restaurants in major visitor zones with tascas and neighborhood restaurants serving a prato do dia. Coffee: Try local pastelarias for a bica and something from the pastry case, rather than treating every coffee as a destination experience. Create a Routine Without Closing Yourself Off A temporary routine helps a new place feel manageable. Choose a regular grocery store, café, walking route, or weekly market. Learn a few useful phrases: bom dia (good morning), por favor (please), and obrigado or obrigada (thank you), depending on how the speaker identifies. Even when a conversation goes on in English, beginning politely with Portuguese shows respect. At the same time, avoid confusing routine with isolation. Attend a neighborhood festival, visit a city market, or join a group connected to a genuine interest. Be considerate in residential buildings and remember that homes, shops, and public spaces are part of someone else's everyday life-not scenery arranged for visitors. Leave Space for Unplanned Portugal Long stays become memorable in the gaps between headline attractions. Read in a public garden, watch the light change from a miradouro, or take a regional train to a town you might otherwise skip. Plan around the weather instead of forcing every excursion onto a fixed calendar. Northern Portugal is particularly rewarding for spontaneous exploration, with adventure travel in the Minho region ranging from hiking and cycling to surfing and visits to lesser-known towns. Slow travel also permits you to revisit places. Returning to the same viewpoint or restaurant can reveal more than rushing through another checklist. The strongest memories may come from learning how a neighborhood changes between Monday morning and Saturday evening. Understand What "Staying Longer" Allows Do not assume that a rental agreement or remote job automatically gives you permission to remain in Portugal. Entry and stay requirements depend on your nationality, the purpose of the visit, and the total time involved. Check current information from the appropriate Portuguese authorities before booking a stay that approaches or exceeds your permitted period. Travel insurance, access to healthcare, tax questions, and remote-work rules also deserve attention when a trip extends past a normal vacation. Travel Slowly, Decide Carefully Spending several weeks in Portugal can deepen a trip without requiring permanent plans. Choose a practical base, mix public transportation with occasional car rental, establish a respectful routine, and give yourself time to experience the country beyond its best-known sights. For some travelers, that experience eventually leads to questions about employment, immigration, investment, or a more permanent move. Information about those longer-term possibilities is available through the Mercan Group of Companies. Whatever direction you take, use an extended stay to learn how daily life actually feels before making a major commitment. This story was published in partnership with the Mercan Group.

item.title: The Post-Travel Blues: Why Coming Home Can Feel Harder Than Leaving
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.84
The suitcase is still open on the floor. There is laundry to wash, food to buy, and an inbox that seems louder than it did before the trip. Instead of feeling refreshed, you feel flat, restless, or tearful. People often call this the post-travel blues, while online it may be described as post-vacation depression. The phrase captures a real emotional slump but is not a formal diagnosis. Earlier studies found vacation-related well-being improvements could fade after people returned home and resumed work. However, a 2025 meta-analysis suggests those benefits may last longer than previously thought.1, 2 The useful distinction is whether the mood begins to ease as ordinary life settles, or remains persistent and disruptive across daily life. Understanding the difference between sadness and depression can add context without turning a difficult homecoming into a self-diagnosis. Why Re-Entry Can Feel So Abrupt Travel changes the structure of a day. There may be more novelty, movement, shared time, or freedom from routine duties. Even a difficult trip creates momentum: catch the train, find the hostel, reach the trail. Home replaces that motion with familiar rooms and unfinished chores. The return also brings practical pressures. Laundry, groceries, expenses, work messages, and family needs may arrive while sleep is still off. Jet lag or late nights leave you tired and less focused, making the contrast sharper. Sometimes the sadness is simply about an experience ending. That does not make you ungrateful, and it does not prove that life at home is wrong. How the Slump May Show Up A return-home low varies, but people often describe: - Feeling flat, irritable, restless, or unusually tearful - Low energy or trouble concentrating - Sleep timing that remains out of step - Strong nostalgia and little interest in normal plans - Dread about work, chores, or familiar responsibilities None of these signs identifies a disorder on its own. They can occur with travel fatigue, disrupted sleep, stress, ordinary sadness, or a mental health condition. The pattern matters more than a single symptom, especially whether it eases and how much it affects daily life. A Measured Return, Not an Instant Reset A re-entry plan is not treatment or a test of resilience. Its purpose is to reduce avoidable friction while you observe what happens next. - Familiar time cues help. Returning to usual meal and sleep times, where practical, gives the day structure while jet lag settles. - A smaller landing list. Urgent tasks can be separated from those that can wait. One grocery run and one work priority create a more realistic first pass. - Create a place for the trip. Printing a photo, cooking a meal you discovered, or recording a few memories lets the experience remain part of your life. - Choose one local point of interest. A walk, favorite lunch, or connection through peer support puts something concrete on the calendar without demanding another major adventure. Online replay can add another layer. Experimental research found that exposure to certain forms of social comparison on Instagram can reduce momentary well-being.3 A separate randomized trial found that taking a one-week break from social media boosted well-being and reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety.4 Neither study focused specifically on people returning from travel, so the findings do not prove that scrolling causes post-travel blues. Still, when revisiting idealized trips intensifies comparison or worsens your mood, taking a temporary break may be reasonable. The goal is a workable landing, not a perfect first day. When the Low Mood Deserves More Attention Depression is not simply a stronger form of disappointment. Clinicians consider the combination, persistence, and impact of symptoms.
