Reasons to seek assessment include: - Low mood or loss of interest on most days, without signs of easing - Marked changes in sleep, appetite, concentration, or energy - Work, relationships, or basic self-care becoming difficult to maintain - Persistent hopelessness, worthlessness, or a sense that you cannot cope - Thoughts of self-harm, suicide, or not wanting to be alive These signs do not confirm a diagnosis. A primary care clinician or licensed mental health professional can consider travel disruption alongside your health history, previous mood patterns, and current pressures, then discuss suitable support. You do not need the right label before starting that conversation. Safety concerns change the priority. Set this article aside and use immediate support rather than waiting for the mood to pass. Making Room for the Landing An emotional dip after travel can coexist alongside appreciation for the trip. The balanced response is neither to dramatize nor dismiss it. Reduce immediate friction, restore familiar rhythms, and watch your mood's direction. Persistent or disruptive symptoms deserve support. Homecoming is part of travel too, and sometimes it needs a landing period. Safety Disclaimer If low mood becomes severe or you have thoughts of self-harm or suicide, seek immediate support. In the United States, call or text 988 or visit 988lifeline.org. Outside the United States, contact your local crisis service or emergency number. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services now. Sources 1. Ryan S. Grant, Beth E. Buchanan, and Kristen M. Shockley. (2025). I Need a Vacation: A Meta-Analysis of Vacation and Employee Well-Being. Journal of Applied Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/apl0001262 2. Jessica de Bloom, Sabine Geurts, and Michiel Kompier. (2012). Effects of Short Vacations, Vacation Activities and Experiences on Employee Health and Well-Being. Stress and Health. https://doi.org/10.1002/smi.1434 3. Phillip Ozimek, Gabriel Brandenberg, Elke Rohmann, and Hans-Werner Bierhoff. (2023). The Impact of Social Comparisons More Related to Ability vs. More Related to Opinion on Well-Being: An Instagram Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs13100850 4. Jeffrey Lambert, George Barnstable, Eleanor Minter, Jemima Cooper, and Desmond McEwan. (2022). Taking a One-Week Break from Social Media Improves Well-Being, Depression, and Anxiety: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking. https://doi.org/10.1089/cyber.2021.0324 This story is provided in partnership with Modern Recovery Services.

item.title: How To See Venice's Lagoon Side Without Wasting Money
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.59
Venice can make budget travelers feel like they're doing something wrong. Follow the signs, and you'll end up where the crowds are thickest and prices highest. A quick visit can make the city feel like a beautiful obstacle course instead of a place worth slowing down for. The good news is Venice changes when you stop chasing landmarks. Public boats, quieter islands, early strolls, and patience can open a calmer side of the city while helping you spend with more purpose. Stay Long Enough for Venice To Change Pace Many travelers meet Venice at its busiest. They arrive by train, follow the flow toward Rialto and San Marco, grab an overpriced lunch near a landmark, and leave wondering why the city felt stressful. That version of Venice exists, but it's also the most crowded and compressed one. Spend the night, and the mood shifts. Early morning brings empty bridges, delivery boats, quiet canals, and café counters filled with locals. Evening softens the city again after day-trippers leave and the main squares stop feeling like transit hubs. The same logic behind traveling slowly to reduce transport costs works inside Venice. Fewer rushed moves usually imply fewer wasted fares, better days, and more time for the lagoon side of the city to come into focus. Staying overnight doesn't mean you need a hotel beside the Grand Canal. Mestre, Marghera, Lido, and less central parts of Venice can keep costs lower while giving you access to the hours when the city feels most rewarding. For budget travelers, that extra time is often a better investment than another rushed paid attraction. Staying overnight within the Municipality of Venice may also save money on applicable 2026 dates: registered overnight guests are exempt from the city's €5 advance or €10 late-booking access fee, although they must obtain an exemption QR code. Use the Vaporetto Like a Budget Sightseeing Tool The vaporetto is Venice's public water bus, but it can feel like part of the experience rather than simple transport. One ride along the Grand Canal gives you palaces, busy docks, church domes, delivery boats, and water-level views before you decide where a paid experience is actually worth the money. The key is to plan your rides instead of hopping on and off without purpose. Group longer trips together, consider which routes help you avoid backtracking, and check whether a pass makes sense for the day. If you're staying outside the historic center or heading to the islands, a pass can quickly become the better deal. At current prices, a standard vaporetto ticket costs €9.50 (about $11) and is valid for 75 minutes, while a 24-hour pass costs €25 (about $29). That means the day pass starts saving money on your third separate ride. Its validity begins with the first validation, and airport services are not included. Public boats also help you understand Venice as one connected place rather than a small historic center surrounded by water. UNESCO recognizes Venice and its lagoon as a single World Heritage property. Some rides are worth taking slowly, especially early in the morning or near sunset, when the light changes on the water and the decks feel less crowded. For the price of public transport, you get one of Venice's best views. Let the Lagoon Shape Your Route The easiest mistake in Venice is getting stuck between the train station, Rialto, and San Marco. That route is famous for a reason, but it's also where the city feels most crowded, expensive, and rushed. Step away, and Venice opens up through smaller canals, working boats, residential corners, and views that move with the tide. This is where the lagoon side of Venice becomes the real advantage. A quiet ride toward Giudecca, Murano, Burano, Lido, or San Giorgio Maggiore can make the city feel wider and calmer, giving you a clearer sense of where your time and money are worth spending. For travelers who want greater context than a self-guided vaporetto ride provides, Fernwayer's Lagoon Stories of Venice explores the lagoon with a local guide, connecting islands such as Sant'Erasmo and Lazzaretto Nuovo to the area's fishing, agricultural, and maritime history. Travelers interested in Venetian light and lagoon stories can treat this experience as one planned splurge in an otherwise low-cost itinerary. Letting the lagoon shape your route also helps you spend more intentionally. Instead of paying for every major attraction, choose one area or island cluster, save your budget for experiences that add real context, and give yourself time to wander. Venice becomes less about covering ground and more about noticing what changes when crowds thin, water widens, and the city stops asking you to hurry. Pick Islands That Match Your Travel Style The lagoon has plenty of easy side trips, but trying to visit every island in one day can turn a good plan into a checklist. Pick the island that fits the kind of day you want, then give it enough time to feel different from the historic center. Murano works well if you're curious about glassmaking and want a short ride from Venice. Burano is brighter and farther out, with colorful homes, lace shops, and quieter lanes once you step away from the busiest photo spots. Lido gives you beaches, bikes, and a break from tight streets. San Giorgio Maggiore is close, simple, and worth considering when you want a wide view back toward the city without committing to a long trip. The budget move is to group island stops with the same transport pass instead of buying separate rides across multiple days. Choose one main island, add a nearby stop if timing fits, and leave room for the slow parts: waiting at docks, watching boats come in, and realizing the ride itself is part of why the lagoon matters. Eat and Wander Away From the Main Tourist Flow Food gets easier when you stop eating beside landmarks. Around San Marco and the busiest bridges, prices climb quickly, and menus often feel built for people who won't be back tomorrow. Walk ten or fifteen minutes into Cannaregio, Castello, or quieter parts of Dorsoduro, and the same budget usually stretches further. Cicchetti bars are a good place to start. Order a few small bites, stand with a drink, and move on when you're ready instead of committing to an entire sit-down meal every time you're hungry. Bakeries, market stalls, and simple pasta spots can keep the day affordable without changing every meal into a hunt for the cheapest option. Wandering helps here as much as planning. Some of the best budget choices in Venice appear when you're between stops, away from streets where everyone is holding the same map. Follow quieter canals, pause where locals are ordering, and let lunch become part of the route rather than a break from it. Choose One Theme Instead of Chasing Every Landmark Venice punishes rushed itineraries. The more sights you stack into one day, the more time you lose in crowds, queues, and backtracking. A better plan is to choose one theme for the day and let the city emerge around it. If you like art, build the day around one museum and a few churches instead of racing between every major collection. If photography is your focus, start early and follow the light across bridges, canals, and open waterfronts. Food lovers should leave time for markets, cicchetti, and neighborhood bars instead of booking every hour around attractions. Fernwayer's Venice experiences focus on craft traditions, island routes, photography walks, and quieter corners, which suits a slower day better than a packed checklist. A theme keeps your spending under control because it cuts out impulse tickets and unnecessary transport. It also makes Venice feel more personal. Instead of leaving with the same list as everyone else, you leave with a version of the city that suits the way you actually like to travel. A Slower Venice Costs Less Than You Think Venice gets expensive when you force it into a rushed schedule. Quick lunches, repeated boat rides, impulse tickets, and crowded shortcuts add up fast. Slow down, and it becomes easier to tell which costs are worth it. Give yourself fewer targets. Group your transport. Stay away from the busiest dining streets. Let the lagoon do some of the work. A public boat ride, a quiet island walk, or an early morning canal can stay with you longer than another paid stop squeezed into a full day. The best budget strategy in Venice is patience. Spend less energy chasing the city, and your money goes further toward the moments which make Venice feel larger, calmer, and more generous than the version most day-trippers see. This article was published in partnership with Fernwayer LLC.

item.title: Visiting the UAE as an Independent Traveler: The Visa Guide
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 4.82
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is one of those places that rewards going it alone. Skip the packaged tour, and you can watch the sun come up over the Hajar Mountains, sleep out in the Liwa dunes, haggle your way through a Deira souk, and still make it back to a hostel bunk in the city by midnight. The country makes independent travel easy in almost every way but one: the visa. Sort that before you fly, and everything else falls into place. Here is what a solo, self-organized traveler needs to know. First, Do You Even Need a Visa? Maybe not. It comes down entirely to your passport, and travelers split into three groups. Some nationalities get visa-free entry and walk through immigration. Others get a visa on arrival, stamped at the airport for a fee. Everyone else has to arrange an e-visa before they fly. That third group is bigger than most expect, and this is where independent travelers get caught. You cannot always sort it at the airport. The only way to be certain is to check whether your nationality needs a visa before booking any flight. Do it early. It changes how you plan the whole trip. Which Visa Fits an Independent Trip? If you need to apply, the choices are simple: Tourist visit visas come in 14-, 30-, and 60-day versions, each single- or multiple-entry. There is also a 96-hour transit visa for long layovers. For a proper trip, the 30-day is the workhorse. Going for longer, or planning to base yourself in Dubai and explore slowly? The 60-day earns its keep. Only choose multiple entry if you plan to duck out and back, like a side trip into Oman and return over the border. Most people overbuy here. Match the visa to the trip you are actually taking, not the one you are daydreaming about. What To Sort Before You Apply The paperwork is light, but border officers do check it. Have these ready for yourself and anyone traveling with you, since everything is per person: - A passport valid for at least six months from your arrival date. - A clear passport-style photo on a plain background. - A confirmed onward or return ticket. - Proof of where you are staying, even if it is just the first hostel booking. - Enough funds to cover your stay, and valid travel insurance. That last one is no longer optional. More on why in a second. The 2026 Rules That Catch Travelers Off-Guard The UAE tightened its entry rules in 2026, and a few of the changes bite independent travelers specifically, because we are the ones improvising as we go. First, travel insurance covering your whole stay is now expected, not optional. Buy it before you land, not after. Second, and this is the big one: the overstay grace period is gone. Overstay your visa now, and you are fined AED 50 a day ($13.60) from day one, with no warning or buffer. For anyone used to extending a trip on a whim, that is a genuine mindset shift. Set a reminder for your exit date and treat it as fixed. The friendlier change: most visit visas can now be extended online through the ICP portal twice, adding 30 days each time, without leaving the country. Thus flexibility still exists. You have to arrange it properly instead of winging it. How To Apply When Nobody Is Sponsoring You Here is the part that confuses first-timers. You do not need a UAE resident to sponsor you, and you do not need a travel agency. A tourist visa is something you arrange yourself, directly. The process is quick. Pick your duration, upload your passport page and photo, pay, and wait for the e-visa to arrive in your inbox, usually within one to three working days. You can do it through your airline, an official portal, or a licensed visa platform such as GOVR, where you apply for a UAE tourist visa online and track the approval. Whichever route you pick, apply a week or two in advance. Leaving it until the night before is the habit that turns a smooth trip into a stressful one. Once You Are Through the Gate Arrival is painless. Many travelers clear passport control at a smart gate in under a minute, but keep your onward ticket and first accommodation address handy in case an officer asks. Then the real trip starts. This is where going independent pays off. The skyline gets the headlines, but the UAE is small, and the good stuff is close. You can be among the red dunes of the desert within an hour of the city or scrambling through wadis in the Hajar Mountains by lunch. Sort the visa, respect your exit date, and the rest of the country opens up on your terms. Getting around solo is easy on the wallet if you skip taxis. Grab a Nol card at any metro station; it covers trains and most buses across Dubai. Intercity coaches link the emirates for a few dirhams, and for the mountains or desert you can usually split a car with other travelers from your hostel. For inexpensive meals, try the casual restaurants in Karama and Deira. A full plate costs less than a coffee back home. None of it needs a guide or fixed plan. That freedom is the whole reason to come independent in the first place. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need a visa to visit the UAE? It depends on your nationality. Some passport holders enter visa-free, some get a visa on arrival, and the rest must arrange an e-visa before flying. Check your own status before booking, because you cannot always fix it at the airport. Can I get a UAE visa on arrival? Some nationalities can, others cannot. If you are in the visa-on-arrival group, you pay and get stamped in. If you are not, you must apply online in advance. There is no universal rule, so confirm for your passport specifically. Do I really need travel insurance now? Yes. As of 2026, valid insurance covering your full stay is expected for UAE visits. Buy it before you arrive, not after, and make sure the coverage dates span your whole trip, including any extension you might add later.? Can I apply for a UAE visa without a sponsor? Yes. A tourist visit visa needs no local sponsor and no travel agency. You apply yourself directly, through an airline, an official portal, or a licensed platform, then receive the e-visa by email, usually within one to three working days. What happens if I overstay? You pay. Since 2026, the grace period is gone, and overstaying triggers a fine of AED 50 per day from the first day. If you want longer, extend your visit visa online before it expires rather than letting it lapse. How long can I stay, and can I extend? Tourist visas run 14, 30, or 60 days depending on what you buy. Most can be extended twice, 30 days at a time, through the ICP portal without leaving the country, so a 60-day visa can stretch a good deal further if you plan. This story is provided in partnership with GOVR.

item.title: Coming Home After Vacation Is the Worst. Here's the Fix
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 4.44
Coming home after vacation is tough, even before you walk into stale air, an empty fridge, and that one strange smell from the trash can. Within an hour, your luggage is all over the floor, and suddenly you have three loads of laundry to do. Coming home feels gloomy because the fun ends suddenly and chores pile up fast. The solution is not to fake happiness about being back, but to make your return easier, quicker, and less overwhelming. Prepare the Welcome Before You Leave You have more control over your return than you might realize. Before you leave, empty the bins, get rid of perishable food, run the dishwasher, and change the sheets. Coming home to clean sheets after a long trip is a small thing that makes a big difference. Put a simple meal in the freezer and make sure you have something ready for breakfast. Keeping shelf-stable milk, coffee, eggs, bread, or your favorite cereal on hand can save you from a stressful and costly food run on your first morning back. Don't try to do a deep clean while you're searching for passports. Just take care of anything that might smell, block important spaces, or need your attention right away. Make the Bed the Destination Your first night back ought to feel like a reward. Fresh sheets, good pillows, and bedding that makes coming home a treat can turn your own bed from a sign that your trip is over into the best appointment in the house. Before you leave, tidy up your bedroom. Close the drawers, clear laundry off the chair, and set out clean pajamas where you can find them. That way, if you get home late, you can shower, dim the lights, and get straight into bed without any hassle. Hotel rooms feel relaxing partly because there's no clutter and no reminder of unfinished chores. You don't need a perfectly empty room at home, but you do need a clear path to your bed. Protect the First Evening Use the first few hours after you get home as a buffer, not as extra work time. Unless something is wet, valuable, or alive, you can leave most of your suitcase for tomorrow. Just take out your medication and toiletries, plug in your devices, and put dirty clothes together. Eat something simple, drink some water, and try not to check every email you missed. It's fine to scan for emergencies quickly, but going through your whole inbox late at night makes it feel like your holiday ended the moment you got home. Suppose you come home with a night to spare before going back to work. It might not be as fun as another night on vacation, but it stops the trip's good memories from being overshadowed by an early alarm. Unpack by Triage, Not by Guilt You don't have to unpack your suitcase all at once. Sort everything into four groups: laundry, bathroom items, items for drawers or your wardrobe, and items that can wait. Start a load of laundry, put away your toiletries, and put the suitcase away once it's empty. This removes most of the visual clutter right away. You can deal with souvenirs, receipts, and all those extra cables later. If unpacking usually drags on for days, set a 20-minute timer. A quick, focused burst is easier than spending the whole day slowly sorting things out. Use Light and Meals To Find Home Time Again After a long trip or a major time-zone change, your body might not feel like it's morning. Try to get outside soon after you wake up, even if the weather makes you want to stay in bed. Daylight and regular mealtimes can help you get back to your usual routine. Don't try to fix jet lag by sleeping all day. If you're really tired, take a short nap earlier in the day, then aim for a normal bedtime. You might not sleep perfectly on the first night, but sticking to a routine helps more than forcing yourself to sleep. Plan a Deliberately Gentle First Day Your first day back doesn't have to be super productive. Pick three helpful things to do, like buying groceries, finishing laundry, or going for a walk. Everything else can wait. Plan one thing you enjoy at home, like ordering your favorite takeout, taking a long bath, watching a saved show, or grabbing coffee from your local spot. The transition from holiday to normal life feels easier when you give yourself something nice right away, rather than waiting until all the chores are done. Keep One Part of the Holiday Just because your suitcase is put away doesn't mean the trip has to disappear. Make the breakfast you enjoyed, print a photo, use the perfume you bought, or go for an evening walk-just for fun, not as a chore. You don't have to turn your rainy kitchen into a Mediterranean terrace. Instead, think about what made your holiday feel special. Maybe you read before bed, ate without screens, or spent more time outside. You can keep at least one of those habits going at home. A Better Homecoming Changes the Whole Trip When you know you'll come home to clean sheets, food, and a peaceful first evening, leaving for home feels less sad. You're not coming back to a punishment-you're just moving from one comfortable place to another. Before your next trip, take 30 minutes to set up a warm welcome for yourself. When you get back, put off non-urgent tasks, get your sleep back on track, and focus on making home feel nice before worrying about being productive. Your holiday has to end, but it doesn't have to end with you standing in a dark kitchen looking for milk that went bad days ago. This article was published in partnership with Simba Sleep Limited.

item.title: 13 Best Things To Do in the Presidio, San Francisco
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 4.27
San Francisco's Presidio is much more than a place to photograph the Golden Gate Bridge. Once a U.S. Army post, the Presidio has transformed into a national park site where wooded trails wind past historic buildings, museums, and beaches. Even though you're technically still in San Francisco, there are moments when the city noise fades, and you find yourself surrounded by quiet groves or looking out over the bay. My first experience in this part of San Francisco came on an earlier trip, when I visited Battery Godfrey and the Golden Gate Bridge Welcome Center. Like many first-time visitors, I was primarily interested in seeing the bridge. It wasn't until a recent visit with my partner, Kel, that I began appreciating the Presidio as a destination in its own right. We spent two nights at the Inn at the Presidio and used the historic hotel as a base for exploring the park. During our stay, we wandered along one of San Francisco's oldest trails, viewed early sketches of Mickey Mouse, tracked down Yoda outside Lucasfilm, grazed our way through a lineup of food trucks, and kept returning to the Golden Gate Bridge, each time from a new angle and under different light. Here are some of the best things to do in the Presidio, based on my visits. Presidio Attractions 1. Take in the Views From Presidio Tunnel Tops I'd suggest starting at the Presidio Tunnel Tops. It's a natural jumping-off point for exploring the park. Opened in 2022, the 14-acre public space was constructed above the Presidio Parkway tunnels. Its gardens, lawns, overlooks, picnic areas, and walking paths reconnect the Main Post with the Crissy Field waterfront. From up here, you get a wide sweep of San Francisco Bay with the Golden Gate Bridge front and center. If you turn around, the city skyline peeks through in the distance, reminding you just how close you are to downtown. Tunnel Tops is free and open every day. Beyond the views, you'll find picnic tables scattered across the lawns, food vendors set up near the paths, and a nature playground where kids can burn off some energy. 2. Eat Lunch From the Presidio Food Trucks We rolled into the Presidio on a sunny Sunday afternoon. We immediately noticed families spread out on blankets across the Main Parade Lawn, kids playing, and the smell of grilled food drifting through the air. Rather than settle on just one food truck, we made a meal out of sampling a little bit of everything: - Kothay chicken dumplings from Momolicious - A barbecue pork bun from Bao Bao Express - A cheeseburger crowned with pork belly from the Curveball Slider Truck - Sweet Vietnamese coffee from Treats by the Bay If I had to pick a favorite, the Kothay chicken dumplings would win: savory, hot, and gone in seconds. Presidio Pop Up brings a rotating selection of food trucks, carts, and tents to areas around the Main Parade Lawn and Tunnel Tops. The schedule and vendors change, so check the official Presidio website before your visit. 3. Visit the Walt Disney Family Museum The Walt Disney Family Museum occupies a historic brick building overlooking the Main Parade Lawn. Its galleries trace Walt Disney's life from his childhood and early attempts to become a cartoonist through the growth of his studio, advances in animation, and the creation of Disneyland. One of the most fascinating artifacts we saw was the earliest known drawing of Mickey Mouse, dating from 1928. The museum also explores the failures, financial difficulties, and creative risks behind Disney's eventual success. We spent about 90 minutes inside, although committed Disney fans could easily stay longer. Even if you are not a devoted fan, the museum delivers an interesting look at creativity, entrepreneurship, and the development of American entertainment. Buying a timed ticket in advance is advised. 4. Walk Lovers' Lane Lovers' Lane is the kind of trail that makes you slow down. It's one of the oldest in the Presidio, and there's a charm to the way it winds through the trees. This short, 0.6-mile path dates back to the 1800s, when soldiers used it as a shortcut to visit loved ones. Now, it leads you through a mix of eucalyptus, cypress, and pine, with the occasional peek at old Presidio homes tucked behind the trees. There's a brick footbridge from the 1880s that is one of the trail's most photogenic features. Near the trail, look for Wood Line, an outdoor installation by artist Andy Goldsworthy. Fallen eucalyptus trunks form a winding, 1,200-foot-long line through the forest. The walk takes approximately 30 minutes, but connecting trails make it easy to extend your time in this part of the park. 5. Find the Yoda Fountain at Lucasfilm Star Wars fans should make a detour to see the Yoda Fountain outside Lucasfilm's San Francisco headquarters. The small bronze statue sits above a fountain near the entrance to One Letterman, formerly known as the Letterman Digital Arts Center. It has become a popular photo stop for visiting fans. During our visit, we were also able to enter the public lobby, where we found additional Star Wars memorabilia on display. Because Lucasfilm is an active office rather than a conventional tourist attraction, lobby access and hours may change. You can still see the outdoor Yoda Fountain if the lobby is closed. 6. Explore the Park at One Letterman After visiting Yoda, take some time to walk around the landscaped grounds surrounding One Letterman. You'll find curving paths, open lawns, and a small pond with a fountain here. If you wander a bit, you'll spot glimpses of the bay and the Palace of Fine Arts through the trees. The grounds also create a convenient walking connection between Lucasfilm and the eastern edge of the Presidio. 7. Walk Around the Palace of Fine Arts The Palace of Fine Arts is not technically inside the Presidio, but it sits just beyond its eastern boundary and is easy to add to your visit. Originally built for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition, the landmark is known for its monumental rotunda, sweeping colonnades, and reflecting lagoon. We walked over after Lucasfilm, circling the lagoon at a slow pace. Up close, the Palace's size is even more impressive, and I found myself stopping often to take photos from different angles. If you are already exploring the eastern Presidio, there is little reason not to continue to the Palace of Fine Arts. 8. Stop at Inspiration Point Most overlooks in the Presidio aim you straight at the Golden Gate Bridge, but Inspiration Point gives you a fresh angle on the park. From up here, you look out over the Presidio's forest canopy and Tennessee Hollow, with the bay stretching beyond. On a clear day, you might spot the Palace of Fine Arts, Alcatraz, and Angel Island all in one sweep. The overlook is also connected to the Ecology Trail. That 1.4-mile route passes through grasslands, eucalyptus trees, and a small redwood grove before ending near the Main Post. Even if you do not hike the trail, Inspiration Point is worth a quick stop for one of the Presidio's most distinctive views. 9. Compare the Presidio's Golden Gate Bridge Views One thing I like about exploring the Presidio is how the Golden Gate Bridge keeps reappearing, each time from a new angle. Instead of choosing a single "best" view, visit whichever of these locations fit your route. Baker Beach Baker Beach gives you that postcard view of the bridge, rising up beyond the sand and surf. We stopped for a few photos, but you could easily spend longer here, walking the shoreline or settling down for an evening picnic. Be aware that the northern end of Baker Beach is traditionally clothing-optional. Fort Point National Historic Site Fort Point is right under the southern end of the Golden Gate Bridge, so close you can hear the traffic rumble overhead. The unusual perspective makes the bridge look even more immense. When the historic fort is open, visitors may also explore its brick corridors and learn about its role in protecting San Francisco Bay. Check the National Park Service website for current opening days and hours. Admission is free. Battery Godfrey I visited Battery Godfrey during an earlier trip to San Francisco. The former coastal defense battery sits on the bluffs west of the Golden Gate Bridge. From up here, you get a wide-open view of the bridge, the Pacific, and the Marin Headlands. If you're curious, you can follow the California Coastal Trail to explore more of the nearby old batteries. Golden Gate Bridge Welcome Center The Golden Gate Bridge Welcome Center is a useful stop for first-time visitors. It has exhibits about the bridge, a gift shop, and access to nearby overlooks and walking paths. Visitors who want to walk onto the bridge can begin from this area. Presidio Tunnel Tops Tunnel Tops isn't the closest spot to the bridge, but it's where I'd go for a picnic or a relaxed afternoon. The lawns, gardens, food stalls, and bay views make this a place to hang out, not just snap a photo and move on. 10. Have Lunch at Colibri Mexican Bistro Colibri Mexican Bistro is located at the historic Presidio Officers' Club, a short walk from the Inn at the Presidio. Lunch started with a La Doña tequila cocktail for me and a Cactus Bloom (no alcohol) for Kel. We shared guacamole, chips, and a lineup of salsas. The yellow mango salsa was my favorite. We kept going: butternut squash soup, grilled corn the way you find it on the streets in Mexico, rich mole poblano, and a mango cheesecake crème brûlée to finish. Colibri's location makes it a convenient lunch stop when exploring Lovers' Lane, the Main Post, or the Walt Disney Family Museum. 11. Plan Dinner at Dalida Dalida ended up being one of the meals I still think about from our San Francisco trip. The restaurant serves Eastern Mediterranean food from a historic building facing the Main Parade Lawn. Its menu is designed for sharing, making it easy to sample several dishes. We started with the Breaking Bread appetizer (warm pita, bright spreads, olives, and pickles) then moved on to arayes kebab, lamb-filled manti, and saffron tahdig rice. Dessert was a chocolate hazelnut tart and roasted barley ice cream, both worth saving room for. Dalida is popular, so making a dinner reservation in advance is a good idea. 12. Stay Inside the Presidio You can always visit the Presidio as a day trip, but staying overnight inside the park changes the pace. We spent two nights at the Inn at the Presidio, which occupies a restored Georgian Revival building originally constructed in 1903 for unmarried Army officers. From the inn, we could walk to Lovers' Lane, Colibri, Dalida, the Main Parade Lawn, and the Walt Disney Family Museum. Presidio Tunnel Tops and Lucasfilm were also within walking distance. Having a room in the park meant we could wander at our own speed, duck back for a break, and never feel rushed. If you're curious, I've written a full review of our hosted stay at the Inn at the Presidio on Feastio. 13. Play the Presidio Golf Course We did not play golf during our stay, but golfers may want to reserve a tee time at the Presidio Golf Course. The public 18-hole course, dating back to 1895, runs through groves of eucalyptus and Monterey pine in the park's southern hills. There's also a driving range, pro shop, clubhouse restaurant, and lessons if you want to work on your swing. Advance tee times are recommended. Planning Your Presidio Visit The Presidio is bigger than it looks, and the hills can make a short walk feel longer than you'd expect. I like exploring on foot, but if you're trying to see Baker Beach, Fort Point, and the Main Post in one day, you might want to use a car, rideshare, bike, or the shuttle to save time. The free Presidio GO Shuttle connects the park with downtown San Francisco and operates routes within the Presidio. Several Muni bus routes also serve the area. If you've only got a day, I'd focus on Presidio Tunnel Tops, the Walt Disney Family Museum, Lovers' Lane, Lucasfilm, and at least one spot to see the Golden Gate Bridge. Grab lunch at Colibri or from the food trucks, and end the day with dinner at Dalida. With two days, you can explore at a slower pace and include Baker Beach, Fort Point, Inspiration Point, and the Palace of Fine Arts. The Presidio rewards a little extra time. What I first thought of as just the land around the Golden Gate Bridge turned out to be one of San Francisco's most surprising and varied corners. Where else can you walk a wooded trail, visit a cartoon museum, explore a historic fort, sit down to a memorable meal, and take in a world-famous view-all in a single day? Disclosure: Our stay at the Inn at the Presidio was provided as part of a hosted visit to San Francisco. As always, all opinions and recommendations are my own.

item.title: Can an AI-Powered Scribe Curb Physician Burnout?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 6.15
Share Podcast Can an AI-Powered Scribe Curb Physician Burnout? The use of automated note-taking tools during patient visits holds promise in reducing physicans’ administrative load–but the tradeoffs are complicated. In 2024, Mass General Brigham, the largest health system in Massachusetts, piloted an AI-powered ambient note-taking program among a subset of clinicians to address increasing rates of staff burnout and turnover–largely driven by the administrative burden of clinical documentation in the electronic health records (EHR). The pilot program aimed to test AI tools which used natural language processing to record, transcribe, and summarize physician-patient encounters, reducing time spent on documentation and allowing physicians to focus more on patient care. Early results showed promising reductions in clinician burnout, intention to leave, and increased physician efficiency. But concerns about the technology, including the generation of inaccurate notes with errors or hallucinations, made physicians resistant to learn and adopt it into their workflows. Harvard Business School Associate Professor Susanna Gallani and host Brian Kenny discuss the challenges leadership at the health care organization anticipated as they considered scaling the AI technology responsibly in the case: The AI Scribe: Enhancing Physician Presence and Curbing Burnout at Mass General Brigham. BRIAN KENNY: Welcome to Cold Call, the podcast where we dive deep into the groundbreaking ideas in Harvard Business School case studies with the faculty who wrote them. In healthcare, some of the most important innovations aren’t new drugs or breakthrough devices. They’re new ways of giving clinicians back the one resource they can never make more of, time. As artificial intelligence rapidly finds its way into hospitals and medical practices, leaders face a difficult balancing act. Can technology reduce administrative burdens without creating new risks? Will it strengthen the relationship between physicians and patients or subtly change it? And how should organizations measure success when the benefits extend beyond efficiency to include trust, wellbeing and the quality of care? Today’s case explores a real-world effort to answer those questions inside one of the nation’s leading academic health systems. We’ll examine the organizational challenges that accompany technological change and the difficult trade-offs involved in evaluating investments whose returns are both financial and deeply human. My guest today is Professor Susanna Gallani, and we’ll discuss her case, “The AI Scribe: Enhancing Physician Presence and Curbing Burnout at Mass General Brigham.” I’m your host, Brian Kenny, and you’re listening to Cold Call on the HBR Podcast Network. Susanna Gallani studies performance management systems and explores the interplay between monetary and non-monetary incentives, and you probably study much more than that too, Susanna. Welcome back to Cold Call. SUSANNA GALLANI: Thank you. Thank you for having me. It’s good to be back. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, it’s been a little while, so we’re happy to have you back on the show, and we were just chatting before we rolled tape here, and every conversation these days seems to turn to AI. It’s just top of mind for everybody, to the point maybe of AI fatigue, but there are some real-world implications for the case that you wrote and for how Mass General is trying to use AI to help physicians. So, thanks for writing it. Thanks for being here to talk about it. SUSANNA GALLANI: Sure. My pleasure. BRIAN KENNY: Maybe we just get started by asking you, how did you hear about this? Why did you think this would be an interesting case to write? SUSANNA GALLANI: So there’s a combination of things that are happening in this space. First of all, the case is written with Rob Huckman and Suraj Srinivasan and also an external co-author, Asaf Bitton, who is at Ariadne Labs, and of course the conversation about AI in healthcare is everywhere. Everybody talks about AI in healthcare and what we can do or cannot do with that, and we were looking for our course, “Transforming Healthcare Delivery,” which is a second-year course here in the MBA program. We were looking to introduce more of this AI content in our course, because as you can imagine, the evolution of AI in healthcare is a big transformational drive, and we still don’t know exactly what it’s going to do, but we want to be up with it as it evolves, and so Rob had heard about this implementation, and I had known about that system. MGB, which is the organization that we study in the case, is not the only one that is implementing this technique and this technology. It’s pretty much everywhere right now, but MGB was doing it at a large scale, and of course, it’s a leading academic medical center. So it was interesting for us from a number of perspectives, because it layers up, in addition to the delivery of healthcare, there’s also the training and the research part, and so all of these aspects kind of converge into the problems that we address in the case. BRIAN KENNY: MGB being Mass General Brigham, just for our listeners who aren’t from the Boston area, it’s an enormous enterprise. I don’t know how many physicians they have on there. SUSANNA GALLANI: About 12,000. BRIAN KENNY: Okay. So just enormous. So this is an effort to scale something up in a very significant way, and I think oftentimes, when we think about AI in healthcare, we’re thinking about how it could accelerate cures or treatments of some kind. This, I found to be very interesting, because it was really about how they’re doing their work and how they can do their work more efficiently. Can you talk maybe a little bit about some of the challenges that clinicians face? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. So in a way, I have heard this described as the first innovation in healthcare that is improving care without asking the physicians to do more, and I want to extend this. This is not just physicians, it’s clinicians in general, because there’s nurses and there’s advanced practice providers as well. So this is not just a solution for physicians, narrowly defined, but this is the first time that we’re trying to do more and better in healthcare while taking work off the physician’s plate, the clinician’s plate, which is important, because we know we have a burnout problem. We have a wellbeing problem in healthcare. We have a turnover problem. If you listen to the first Friday of the month job report, healthcare jobs are always at the top of the list in terms of job creation, because there’s so much churn, and in addition, the needs for healthcare are increasing. Populations are aging. During COVID, we’re still experiencing the tail end of the COVID effect where people didn’t take as good care of themselves as they should have or they would have in other times. So there’s a lot of demand of physician’s time. In addition to that, we see that physicians don’t want to be physicians anymore, because it’s becoming a job that is away from their calling and it doesn’t let them really engage with the patients in the way that they would want, which is where this technology comes in, because it’s a way for them to really free themselves up from the monitor or the computer while they are sitting with the patient and really focus on the conversation like you and I are doing with each other. Imagine that as I’m saying these things, you were typing up things on your computer. It would feel very unnatural to me to be talking to you, and the same thing is in the office visit, and think about the experience of a patient. I always say healthcare is one of the most human experience we can have, and having the physician look into your eyes or listening, actively listening to what you’re saying and engaging in your conversation instead of doing a lot of what we do in the classroom, which is absorb what you just said and just transfer it to another medium helps a lot in the relationship with the patient. BRIAN KENNY: I hadn’t really thought about it until I read the case, but it occurred to me that my doctor does take a lot of notes while we’re having meetings, and that seems to me like a fairly recent thing, and I think it’s part of the administrative tasks of doctors have increased exponentially. We’ve got all these systems, the information needs to be in there. They’re trying to get better at sharing information across platforms so that your dermatologist can see what your primary care physician is doing and so on, but it reminds me a little bit of education. In elementary education, my wife is a teacher and the amount of administrative work that she has to do has increased quite a bit over the years. So it just sort of sparked that for me. Maybe you can describe what AI Scribe is and how it works. SUSANNA GALLANI: Yeah. It’s actually very simple as a concept. Obviously very complicated to implement it or to develop it, but basically this is how it works. When you see the doctor, they will probably ask for your permission to record your conversation with them, and it will be through an app on their phone. There’s nothing magical. There’s no invasive technology of any kind. BRIAN KENNY: They just put the phone on the table. SUSANNA GALLANI: Just put the phone on the table, and if you agree to that, that conversation will be recorded, and the recording will be decoded by an AI engine behind the scenes, and it will automatically populate the notes that the doctor would otherwise take during the visit. That’s all it is in a nutshell. Now, this unlocks a number of other things. First of all, there’s billing attached to that. So as the AI decodes what was said in the interaction, they also understand that the AI understands or identifies services that are being provided and can attach a billing code to it. So there’s a revenue generation aspect to it, which, by the way, the doctor would have to do anyway. So it’s not that we’re increasing the billing, not necessarily at least, and this is still a task that the doctor would have to do, and oftentimes, they end up doing after hours, the so-called “pajama time,” which is so dreadful, and it takes physicians away from their family time. BRIAN KENNY: So is it agentic in the sense that it just does it automatically? It takes agency? SUSANNA GALLANI: So the agentic part is what happens after with the data. At the moment, the core of this technology is just simply recording, transcribing, and interpreting in a way, in a way that you can create billing codes. The other thing is prescriptions. So if there is a drug that is being discussed in the interaction, the AI identifies that drug and puts it as a possibility for the prescription that the doctor might want to sign off. Now importantly, none of this is set in stone until the doctor actually signs the notes. So there’s still a requirement for the physician to go through the note and make sure that everything has been done correctly and approve it, otherwise the process is not complete. Shortly after, one of the main safety measures of this technology is that the recording is completely deleted. BRIAN KENNY: Okay, but the notes exist. The notes remain. SUSANNA GALLANI: The notes remain in the EHR of the organization that implements… BRIAN KENNY: Who was it at Mass General Brigham that decided they should try to do this? Were they trying to solve a particular problem or were they just aware? Was it the burnout that you mentioned? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. Predominantly that was the driving force. In fact, they actually stated very clearly in one of our interviews that that was exactly the reason. The main reason why they wanted to try this technology was to reduce the burnout among their clinicians. BRIAN KENNY: What were the sort of organizational challenges that they had as they tried to implement this? How was it received by the physicians? SUSANNA GALLANI: Variation as you can imagine. So initially they piloted with about 800 people that were self-selected, and so that went quite well. Although it did spark some controversy and some concerns. There are concerns on all sides. The physician, for example, sometimes is uncomfortable because they have to actually say more things out loud. BRIAN KENNY: Interesting. SUSANNA GALLANI: Because the AI will not transcribe something that it doesn’t hear. So it’s important that the physician kind of verbalizes their thinking, the drugs that we just mentioned. So if I don’t say, “I’m thinking about prescribing you whatever milligrams of this particular drug,” the AI has no idea that you’re thinking that. So in order for it to do the work for you, you have to actually verbalize actively during the visit, which is very different. BRIAN KENNY: Could be better for the patient, though, because you’re hearing a lot more than you might otherwise hear. SUSANNA GALLANI: It could, to the extent that the physician uses accessible language, and that’s one of the barriers that now the patient might actually be sitting next to somebody who’s speaking gibberish from what they can understand, because they are using technical terms and classification of stages of disease and things that might be obscure or maybe somewhat terrifying for the patient that doesn’t understand what’s being said. The other pushback was, “Well, when I read this note, this is not how I would write the note.” So there’s a level of comfort and acceptance and identity that is kind of missing when the note is automatically generated by a machine, and these notes are there to be read later on, and so if the physician doesn’t recognize their code, for lack of a better term, they resist to that. Say, “Well, this is not the information I would want to have in the note. Of course, you can imagine some physicians said there’s too much information, because the fact that Mrs. Jones recently lost her husband and feels lonely might be very significant for the primary care physician or for somebody in behavioral health, but maybe for the surgeon that is doing their appendectomy, is not important. So how do we tailor the amount of additional information that is non-clinical in nature? There’s variation in how much people desire to have in the note. So there’s a number of those additional challenges, and plus there’s change. There’s change and there’s trust that needs to happen. So the physician also doesn’t know what this information is going to do, and so there’s a little bit of resistance upfront. From the patient’s perspective, the most prominent type of challenge is accepting that that conversation is being recorded. So where is my data going? What is this data going to be used for? Is it still my data? Do I feel comfortable speaking to you naturally when I know it’s being recorded? BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, yeah, and I could see, with all the rules and regulations that we have in place to protect people’s information and identity, I could certainly understand that being a concern. There also might be the cynics out there who say that the hospitals are only doing this because it’s in their best self-interest from a legal perspective or a productivity perspective. Were there certain things that Mass General was sort of measuring as they went through this process? Sort of key metrics that they had in mind? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. They measured productivity for sure. That was one, but mostly what they were most interested in was their burnout measures, and during this pilot program, they actually noticed a significant drop in burnout. BRIAN KENNY: Really? SUSANNA GALLANI: People that had embraced this technology felt that they had more time for themselves, that they didn’t feel they had to be on their electronic medical records the whole time during the visit, that they could engage with the patient, but also their family time was freer and more under their control. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. SUSANNA GALLANI: So they definitely noticed an improvement there. BRIAN KENNY: Okay, and are they also using it…? A lot of people are doing telehealth visits now. That’s a way that people are seeing their doctors without having to go in person. Do they still use the technology even in a telehealth type? SUSANNA GALLANI: That was not in the case, but it would be very difficult for me to imagine that that doesn’t happen, because it’s even easier. We have recordings of our Zoom meetings, so why wouldn’t we use this in a telehealth situation? BRIAN KENNY: Were the physicians at all… And this may not have come up in the case either, but it makes me wonder if physicians were concerned that it would be used for review purposes or my performance is being gauged by what’s coming out in these notes. SUSANNA GALLANI: So the notes are not technically part of the performance evaluations. They are for the trainees, which is another important piece of the case, but the concern that the physicians voiced with us was, “You are now giving me back time. What are you going to ask me to do with that time?” BRIAN KENNY: Right. There’s the cynical piece I was trying to get out before. SUSANNA GALLANI: That was the cynical piece, exactly, and that is a valid concern, because in the case, we describe one physician remembered when they were given human scribes, but this human scribe had a cost, and so they had to produce more, so see more patients, in order to pay for the human scribe to be assigned to them, and so the same type of concern was underlying this implementation saying, “Yeah, that’s great. Now you’re giving me back time, but how are you going to take that time back in other ways?”, and so if we end up doing this, obviously the purpose of reducing burnout will just go out the window. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. You want to try and create some more life balance for these people who are working crazy hours all the time. You mentioned there were some early adopters, the people who sort of signed up for it voluntarily. What happened when they tried to do a more general rollout of it? Were there people who were refusing to use it? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. First of all, it was voluntary. So nobody is compelled to use it, but there is some sort of an expectation, because the second order effect, one of the second order effects of this technology is that it generates better data, and so imagine anything you want to do with clinical data, whether it’s research, whether it’s improving care, you want to have enough adoption, enough mass, to have that mass of data so that it’s consistent across an organization. That would make sense. Well, when they open it up for a larger group, which they still haven’t rolled it out to everyone, but they’re progressively getting there, one of the largest groups, which is the group that historically has the highest level of burnout is primary care. Once they opened it up to that group, it was opt-in, but for those people that chose to use the license, many of them, a significant amount did not pursue it. So they had the license, they just didn’t do it, and in fact, there was a rule that if you didn’t use it for three months, they would ask you why and potentially take it away, because it has a cost. There is a monthly fee for this license, which is person by person. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. I mean, we’re finding that the human side of AI, the getting people to adopt the tools and to use them, is highly variable. Some people are comfortable doing it. They think, “Oh, this is great. This is going to make my life easier.” Other people are thinking, “This is something new I have to do. I have to learn how to use this and what if it breaks or what if I don’t do it right?” What would you say to people who are listening, who are maybe going through the same kind of a process in their own organization? What are the sorts of things that you have to be thoughtful about as you’re trying to scale up this kind of platform? SUSANNA GALLANI: The first thing is trust. We talked about it. It’s really difficult for people to just embrace this. When this technology changes daily, it is, from a user’s perspective, an enormous black box. You put things into it, and you don’t really know what happens to those things. Things being information, sometimes sensitive, sometimes personal, and so having this expectation that everybody will jump at the opportunity to use it is probably misguided. BRIAN KENNY: Yes. SUSANNA GALLANI: So understanding what do you need to do to make it so that people trust what you’re going to do with that technology. Generally speaking, security of that technology, it is a black box for the leadership too. It’s not that we understand this infinitely well. BRIAN KENNY: We’re all learning. Yeah. SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes, and it’s changing so much that we tend to understand less and less instead of more and more in certain ways of what it does and what it’s capable of doing. So the first thing would be trust. The second thing would be use it to bring up the humanity of the workers and not to replace them, because there’s a huge fear. Now, this is less prominent in healthcare, I will say, than other industries, but we all are thinking about, “Is this thing going to take my job?”. So understanding that that is a concern that people have, even if it is buried in the back of your psychology, but especially if you’re bringing this technology in to help people—make it help people instead of making them afraid of it. BRIAN KENNY: We’ve done a couple of other cases that are similar in nature to this one. One was Pernod, the spirit company, and they were rolling out a platform, an AI platform, to their sales organization, and the benefit that they touted was essentially the same thing, which is, “You don’t need to worry about what’s going on underneath the hood with your customers. We’re giving you an opportunity to really develop a relationship with your customer. We’re giving you information that’s going to be helpful to them and help your relationship with them,” and this is reminding me of that, but even at that, there were a lot of salespeople who felt like it was going to cramp their style and people were going to be understanding their customers better than they were and then they wouldn’t need the salesperson anymore. It sounds like Mass General is really just trying to help these clinicians free them up of some of the tasks that they’ve had to do that are not patient focused, and really give them an opportunity to focus on the patient, which sounds like a win-win. SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. It’s exactly that. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. As we think about this particular case, which is sort of at the intersection of technology operations and management control, are there lessons that you can think of that this could offer more broadly outside of a healthcare setting, let’s say, like we were just talking about, who are considering AI for sort of thought intensive work, knowledge intensive work? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yeah, for sure. The fact that this is happening in healthcare is just the context. It is, as you were mentioning, happening in many other industries. So it’s not specific to healthcare. Obviously in healthcare, there is maybe a specific type of risk because we’re talking about healthcare data or healthcare information, which is a little bit different than maybe your purchasing information, which it still has to be treated with respect and the appropriate safety precautions, but I think healthcare is one level deeper than that. So in terms of generalizable lessons, well, one thing that is clear to me is that we don’t have to jump into this all at once, and especially when we’re not ready. This technology is changing way too fast to make it profitable or valuable if we jump in when we’re not ready, because by the time we get the organization to be ready, then that technology will be obsolete. So one of the things that they are pondering at Mass General Brigham, but I’m sure in other organizations too, is when is the right time to introduce this technology, and for whom? I mentioned the trainees before. So this, again, it’s a problem that we see in other industries as well. I actually had a recent conversation with a legal firm in England that is thinking about introducing AI for their work, but the problem they share with Mass General Brigham is, what are you going to do with the trainees? When you have a junior partner or an associate in a law firm, as well as a resident at Mass General, are you going to teach them to use AI or are you going to be AI independent, should that technology go away or not work? Or what are the opportunities that we’re missing in not training our trainees to use AI, but at the same time, what opportunities are we missing if we train them just to use AI? So either way, you have to consider the pros and cons of either choice. BRIAN KENNY: Right, and we know that one of the ways that AI learns is by consuming mass amounts of information. So it almost seems like when you scale this up, you really do need to get a high percentage of adoption, or you’re not going to get the full benefit of what the AI is capable of doing. It’s not going to learn as much as it could, and not as fast. So it’s pretty complicated to think about all the implications of that. This has been a great conversation, always is when you’re on the show. So thank you for being here. Just one last question would be, if you think about maybe one thing that our listeners should take away from this case, what would it be? SUSANNA GALLANI: I go back to the point I made earlier, which is think about the human that is using the technology, and use the technology to solve a problem that the human has before thinking that it’s just going to be great. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. SUSANNA GALLANI: We have to really be specific of what problem we’re trying to solve, and I think that Mass General Brigham did a great job in really pinpointing what was the purpose of that implementation. It was not just about… Certainly, they’re not unhappy to improve productivity, but the purpose, the driver of the decision was we have to reduce burnout, and that was their priority. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, that’s great. Susanna, thank you for joining me on Cold Call. SUSANNA GALLANI: Thank you. Thank you for having me. BRIAN KENNY: If you enjoy Cold Call, you might like our other podcasts: Climate Rising, Coaching Real Leaders, IdeaCast, Managing the Future of Work, Skydeck, and Think Big, Buy Small. Find them wherever you get your podcasts. If you have any suggestions or just want to say hello, we want to hear from you. Email us at coldcall@hbs.edu. Thanks again for joining us. I’m your host BRIAN KENNY, and you’ve been listening to Cold Call, an official podcast of Harvard Business School and part of the HBR Podcast Network.

item.title: How to Recognize When Your Customers Want You to Act
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.76
Summary. Customer-listening systems have become adept at identifying what customers want and how they feel, but they often miss a third critical signal: when customers expect action. By combining AI with During the past decade, companies have invested heavily in becoming customer centric. Digital platforms now generate continuous streams of reviews, feature requests, support conversations, and community discussions that firms use to identify new ideas, prioritize product changes, and guide the timing of innovation. AI-powered analytics and translation tools allow companies to process feedback from customers around the world at unprecedented scale. Most customer-listening systems today focus on two familiar signals—what customers want, and how they feel—but they often miss a third signal: when customers expect the company to act. That signal, which we call temporal urgency, is most commonly embedded in subtle cues that have to be picked up during customer communications.

item.title: The Hidden Realities of AI Adoption
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.49
Summary. Many organizations have moved beyond asking whether to adopt AI and are now grappling with how to integrate it successfully. Where are the most common points of failure? What barriers are AI adoption is often framed as a technology challenge. But its success depends just as much on how organizations redesign work, build trust, develop talent, and protect the quality of human judgment. In this subscriber-exclusive HBR Virtual Roundtable, experts Kate Niederhoffer and Thomas H. Davenport joined HBR senior editor Tom Stackpole to explore the hidden organizational dynamics shaping how AI is used at work.

item.title: 3 Warning Signs Your Supplier Is in Distress
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.39
Summary. Suppliers to multinational corporations are under growing pressure from tariffs, logistics disruptions, compliance demands, and repeated global shocks, yet many buyers still rely on conventional Suppliers to multinational corporations are under growing strain. Tariffs, logistics disruptions, rising compliance demands, and repeated global shocks have raised the cost of serving large corporate buyers. Recent studies suggest that many large buyers pass at least part of these additional costs down to suppliers rather than sharing the burden. For many suppliers—especially smaller firms and those in developing economies—the problem is not simply that costs are rising. It is that they are often expected to absorb those costs while continuing to meet the same standards for quality, delivery, auditing, and compliance.
