item.title: Why Great Turnarounds Start with Culture, Not Strategy
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.06
Share Podcast Why Great Turnarounds Start with Culture, Not Strategy A conversation with Verizon CEO Dan Schulman on reshaping the telecom giant amid AI disruption. In an era of constant disruption, successful turnarounds require more than a new strategy—they demand a new culture. Dan Schulman, former CEO of PayPal, came out of retirement to tackle the challenge of taking over the helm of Verizon as it entered the AI age. He explains how they needed to put customers—not engineering—at the center of the business, how he reshaped company culture, and what it really took to prepare employees for an AI-native future. He explains why leaders need to embrace change, invest in reskilling, and balance optimism about AI with honesty about the disruption it will bring. ADI IGNATIUS: I’m Adi Ignatius. ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard, and this is the HBR IdeaCast. ADI IGNATIUS: All right, Alison, so you are a top 30 U.S. company in terms of size, but your market share is down, your share price has plummeted and morale is poor. You need to change. What kind of CEO would you want to lead the transformation? ALISON BEARD: Well, I would typically say an outsider for fresh perspectives, new thinking. I’d probably want someone who’s done a big turnaround at another company before. But I did just interview John Stankey of AT&T who oversaw big changes at that company even as an insider. So I’m not sure. ADI IGNATIUS: All right. So today it is the outsider story and it’s in the same industry. My guest today is Dan Schulman, the man who has taken the reins of Verizon, which was in desperate need of a reset. He was not an exec of the company, though he was on the board, and he had led a successful turnaround earlier at PayPal, but he had no interest in the Verizon job when it was first offered to him. ALISON BEARD: So how’s it going? ADI IGNATIUS: Well, it’s still early days, but Schulman decided to focus initially on the company’s culture. He’s trying to reinvigorate what had become a risk averse, inward-looking organization in order to become competitive again. It has the potential to be a case study of how an outsider can come in to lead the turnaround of a once successful company that has lost its way. Here’s the conversation. You’re at Verizon. You turned down the job, as I understand it, twice, maybe more than twice before you agreed to take it. What made you want to get back in the game? DAN SCHULMAN: Well, I turned it down because I was very happily retired. I was living on our ranch in Montana. I wasn’t looking to come back into corporate life. But I was on the board; I was the lead director, we needed to make a change. I felt a keen sense of loyalty to the company, and I felt like the company had a tremendous amount of assets that we could leverage and that there was a real opportunity to take an iconic American company and at least have the shot at turning it around. And so after a lot of discussions with my wife, I agreed reluctantly to go do it, but here I am nine months into the job and I’m loving it. ADI IGNATIUS: At a high level, what was wrong with the company? DAN SCHULMAN: We had been losing market share for five years. We went from having the largest market gap in the industry to having the lowest P/E multiple, which is the market’s way of saying that they don’t really believe in your growth going forward. Our churn rates were going up, our customer satisfaction results were going down. So there’s just a ton of things. And I think inside the company, really importantly, we were willing to be prey. We were willing to gently seed market share to our competitors. We weren’t playing to win. it was obvious we needed to make a change. The company for a long time had relied on its engineering prowess and it’s not enough anymore. And we had put the network at the center of everything that we do, as opposed to the customer. And then I also think culturally, it’s a proud company. It has a lot to be proud of, but that also means that you’re resistant to change. That you look back at what you did and you want to repeat it. And in the era that we live in right now where change is accelerating at an increasingly hard to imagine pace, we were falling behind. When the pace of change external to a company is faster than the change of pace internal, you’re falling behind. And we were falling behind because we were risk averse. We were hierarchical. We love our process. We love to show our work, but really I’m very much, I trust that you’re doing good work, but I want to see the outcomes and I want to know when those outcomes are coming. I think we’re not imagining enough what kind of role can we play in the age of technology, in the age of AI, and looking backwards to previous success we had as opposed to what success we might have in the future. ADI IGNATIUS: So companies talk all the time about wanting to be customer obsessed. For Verizon in particular, which probably a lot of customers view as a utility, they just want it to work. They’re not sure they want a relationship with you, but they want it to work. What does customer obsession mean for you in this context? DAN SCHULMAN: Yeah. I think most people say that they want to put the customer front and center, but it’s not easy to go and do that. Inside the company right now, we don’t say customer centricity or customer obsessed. The initiative we have inside the company is entitled: every customer has a name. It means we treat you as a person, not as an account, not as a line. Almost like if one of my family members had a problem, how would I want the company to treat them? And that is hundreds of things. It’s when you come into the store, how quickly do we start to serve you? Do you understand the plans that we have in front of you? Are they too complex for you to understand? Are we trying to prey on complexity to drive profitability or can we mak e them simple and easy to understand? When you call our customer service centers, do we treat you with respect and empathy? Customers fire companies all the time in quiet ways because they feel disrespected. They feel like there’s got to be a better way than this. It’s too hard to be a part of your company. We have to have a great network. I want us to have the best network in the country. We are part of the critical infrastructure for America and we take that very, very seriously. But it’s not enough to be fully differentiated. We just launched a whole host of new things where we’ve simplified our pricing plans. We’ve put loyalty. So if you’ve been a customer for a long time, we want to reward you for that. We want you to be excited about being a customer every day. We’re moving into an AI world right now and our service is going to be more important than ever, in terms of connectivity, AI advancements, how you use AI, what’s the right way for you to use AI, how you gin up agents in a safe way. We can be a part of that new infrastructure going forward. And that’s an exciting part and a different way of thinking about Verizon going forward in a place where I think we can add a lot more value to customers around security, other things like that. ADI IGNATIUS: Are you essentially accepting lower revenue temporarily to build longer term loyalty? Is that what that means with simplified plans that give people only what they want and need? DAN SCHULMAN: No, I don’t think that being customer-centric means being less than fiscally responsible back to your shareholders. In fact, I think it can be the opposite. What was happening to us before was our churn rate was going up because people were unhappy with us. We were raising prices. We weren’t treating them with the respect they wanted. Plans were confusing to them. The first thing I did when I came in is I said, “We’re not going to raise prices without real value. And we’re going to invest in the customer experience. And we’re going to create a war chest to go and do that. And we’re going to start growing our customers.” Because if you start to grow your customers because churn starts to come down, then actually your revenues start to increase. And if you can be efficient in the way that you do business, your top and bottom line and your customer satisfaction can all move in the same direction. Now that’s not an easy equation to go and do. And you have to be willing to take difficult decisions early on to make that happen. I think if you do the right things, make the difficult decisions, challenge the culture, inspire people to do great things, that you can satisfy customers, you can inspire employees and you can inspire your shareholders at the same time. ADI IGNATIUS: So it’s never easy to come in. I mean, you were on the board, but you essentially came in as an outsider. And even though you’ve had a great track record at PayPal and elsewhere, people are resistant to change. It’s never you just come in and say, “We’re going to do this,” and everybody says, “Hooray.” Talk about the bumps along the way to get the team, the staff, the company excited in these ideas or willing to explore these ideas. DAN SCHULMAN: Well, first of all, you’re exactly right. People are resistant to change, and change is happening at an accelerating rate right now. People who win the lottery, which you have to admit is a good change, right? You’ve just won the lottery, often suffer divorces, lose friends because it’s such a big change in their life. I think as a leader, you need to do three things simultaneously and you need to do them particularly well. The first thing is you need to tell it like it is without sugarcoating it at all. My view is every employee is an adult. They probably already know what’s going on. They’re just waiting for leadership to admit it. My first all-employee meeting, actually every single all-employee meeting, I have no slides. I have no notes. ADI IGNATIUS: I want to come to those meetings. DAN SCHULMAN: Yeah, they’re good. Yeah. I have a cup of coffee in my hand and I basically just talk from the heart, just like this is what I see. And I said, “Look, I know we have a lot to be proud of as a company, but the fact of the matter is we are losing. And I know that’s actually really hard to hear that we’re losing. And that just does not work for me. I know it does not work for you either, but we need to play to win. We need a full scale internal kind of revolution and cultural re-shift where we play to win.” And that’s not a marketing slogan, that’s a way of life inside the company. And I talked about what’s getting in the way of that, what’s happening in our culture to get away from that. On a scale from 1 to 10, this company is traditionally a 2 in terms of being risk averse. I’m a one when it comes to the integrity of our financial results, cybersecurity. I have no tolerance for any risk in that. But trying new things, failing, learning from them, moving forward, I’m probably an 8 or a 9. The company just needs to feel like it can take risks, that it can fail, that it’s okay to go do that. We’re going to learn from it. Everybody wants to play for a winning team. Nobody wants to be on a losing team. So that’s the first thing you need to do. We also need to invest in the customer. We need money to go and do that. I talked about the need to create that war chest, and that was going to result in layoffs. I made the hard decision and it was my decision. I worked with my team on it, but I take the responsibility for it. We laid off 13,000 people in month two. And I was in front of the whole company talking about that, saying that laying off even one person, one person, because it affects their family, their friends, colleagues who have worked for them is painful. But our job is to make sure that we are as efficient as we can be, that we create this war chest. And I said, “We’re going to do this layoff, but we’re going to take most of those dollars.” And we talked about $5 billion of OpEx savings we’re going to do and invest it back in the customer so that we could be a great company going forward, so that we could reclaim our market leadership, become the most trusted company in our industry. And when we started going through that, that would feel great. That it would feel difficult and disruptive at first. But I’m playing for what are we trying to accomplish? What is our vision going forward? Because people need to be inspired as well. ADI IGNATIUS: So what are your employees thinking about? What is it that’s motivating them? What’s the goal? What are they trying to get to? DAN SCHULMAN: I think what they are really motivated about right now is that we are playing to win. That we are trying to be a trusted company, and that they see that we can do that. Early successes are really important in these things because once people start to see success happening, they really rally around that. The first quarter, I came in October, we had been losing subscribers for a long time. We put on something like 650,000 subscribers that first quarter because I was like, “We are going to play to win. We’re going to do what we need to go do. We’ll be fiscally responsible, but we’re going to win.” And our stock went up that day by the most it had gone up in 18 years. Winning is contagious. You have to see that. And I think people also, they were yearning to play for a winning team. Nobody wants to be in a bureaucratic organization. Nobody wants to be in a hierarchical organization. They want to have permission to be their best selves going forward. And we also push them hard. One of my sayings is that every single day matters here. I want to see improvement every single day. And there’s an intensity about that. There’s a saying, heaven and hell are the same place. It’s just heaven for some and hell for others. And for me, working hard, being disruptive in the market, putting customers at the center, being on a winning team, being available anytime to go make these decisions, to me, that’s like heaven. I love that. Some people don’t like that, and that’s okay as well. We are not the company for that right now. And so I think we’re getting the people who are now inspired to be here, who want to make us better, and better, and better. And we have not just kind of defined what reality is and created the vision of where we want to go to, but we have a roadmap on exactly how we’re going to get there. And I think everybody understands that they’re bought in. We have a ton to execute against still, obviously, Adi, but we’re making good progress. I’m really proud of the team. ADI IGNATIUS: You talked about trying to be a truth teller and you’ve cultivated a reputation about being a truth teller about AI. What is the truth about AI in business? DAN SCHULMAN: Truth is a subjective thing often. It’s your set of circumstances, how you see things, and I may see them differently. So I don’t think there’s any absolutes in that. And especially when you’re thinking about the future. What I do try to be is as authentic and honest about how I see the future playing out. AI is going to be a part of our future. And you will be better at your job and you will be better in life if you understand how to use and capture the benefits of AI. So we’ve put in place gigantic training programs, full week-long training programs on using AI for all employees. I’ve also put into place extensive kind of re-skilling programs for employees who might be affected by AI going forward. In other words, they’re displaced by AI. I want to make sure that they have all of the tool sets and access to be successful in whatever their next chapter might be. But I don’t think we should underestimate the impact of AI. And I want to be as honest about that as I possibly can. ADI IGNATIUS: Obviously, we don’t know the future, but maybe what are some of the early use cases that tell you, yeah, we could accelerate here, here, here and be a very different company? DAN SCHULMAN: Well, first of all, I think the value that we offer to consumers is going to be radically shaped by AI. I don’t think we’ll just be a connectivity company going forward, offering wireless and broadband. I think we’ll be a integral part of how consumers use AI. I think we can put a AI fabric over our network. I think we can do things that enable consumers and small businesses to take full advantage of AI in their lives. That could be things like token packages where people buy tokens from us and we’re an orchestration layer on top of the network where we cost optimize the use of those tokens for you. Because as a consumer, there’s certain LLMs that are good for certain jobs, but they may cost more. But you as a consumer may not know that, but we as a network will know that. And so we could cost optimize the use of tokens. And I think that tokens are going to be the coin of the realm. We could offer a safe place in our network because we have 95 million people in the country that use us, where if you want to utilize an agent, you can utilize it in the context of our network. We could provide that secure environment. What we offer going forward could be very different than what we offer today on top of the connectivity. We’ll also be a part of the AI infrastructure in the company. We’ll connect these data centers through dark fiber and lit fiber. We have the capability by retrofitting all of our central offices into edge computing data centers to take inference out to the edge for applications that need low latency like remote surgery or autonomous driving vehicles. It’s a radically different value proposition that adds much more richness to the depth of the relationship that we have with consumers and businesses. I think AI will enable us to be way more productive. We’ll get more things done, but also really importantly, increase our customer satisfaction levels dramatically. ADI IGNATIUS: So what’s the plausible darker scenario? I mean, I feel like tech CEOs all the time are saying things that alarm us about, “We have 500 days until AI will…” Something bad sounds like it’s coming. And obviously job losses are a certainty. Whether net job losses are… I don’t know. But what’s the plausible dark side and how do you think about that? How do you lead with that? DAN SCHULMAN: If you think about the speed that AI is developing, there are going to be all sorts of considerations to think about. I mean, three years ago when these models first came out, they were great, but they couldn’t even do math, right? Remember? They- ADI IGNATIUS: Yeah. DAN SCHULMAN: … couldn’t really multiply. tTe models that we’re using today are the worst models that we will ever use. OpenAI is going to put out four iterations of their model between now and the end of the year. Every one of them will be substantially better. We are on the cusp of what’s called recursive self-learning for these models, which basically means that the models will write themselves, no human intervention. We’re probably 6 to 12 months from that. You’ve got Quantum coming. We’re preparing for Quantum that it comes by 2028. And the way that I think about Quantum is everything times 1,000. And then several years later, you’ve got humanoid robotics behind that. So obviously there are a lot of things that are going to change in our world. I think there is no question in my mind that there is going to be disruption; we don’t know exactly what that’s going to look like ’cause it’s the future. But the way that I think about life in general and the way that I think about things is it’s scenario planning. Like, “Okay, we don’t know exactly, but let’s scenario plan. What could happen?” As I look function by function, I can see disruption in various functions. And the question really is, how do we get ready for that? How do we provide the right re-skilling, the right training? When I did this initial layoff, we put in place a $20 million fund. We’re the first company to go and do that for AI re-skilling and training. I actually don’t think that’s enough, going forward. I think we’re going to double, maybe triple that amount over the next one to two years to make sure that not only are all employees inside Verizon prepared for a future, however that future may play out, but also the communities that we serve. We’ll go into various cities, various small businesses that may not be experts at how to use agentic forms of AI going forward, and help them with that. Because I think as leaders, we have a responsibility to go and do that. If there’s going to be a two to five-year trough where there’s potentially more unemployment, that’s not good for our economy. That’s not good for our country. That’s not good for any of our companies. And so I think all of us who have positions of responsibility, we all need to step up. And I think we can do our part, and will do our part. ADI IGNATIUS: So I want to talk about leadership at a high altitude. You come into a CEO role. It’s different from your first many, many years ago. What did you learn in terms of, “CEO needs to do this, does not need to do this”? What was the wisdom that you accumulated? DAN SCHULMAN: Well, you’re right. There’s no substitute for a lot of years of experience ’cause you go through a lot. You go through ups and downs. What I tell people here, I think, for a leader is, one, you need to be humble. And what I mean by humble is you don’t know it all. And if you do think you’re the smartest person in the room, you’re just in the wrong room. Get out there. There’s too much going on. I mean, it’s just changing so rapidly. We need to be learning all the time. And that means that things that we thought were certain before are probably no longer certain. You need to challenge yourself continually. I have this saying that I never want to stand still, because when you do, you start falling way behind on it. I also think, being authentic, there’s a superpower in that. I never want to talk in corporate speak. I just want to be me, because it’s the easiest thing that I can be. And people see that. It’s approachable. They know that they can talk to me about anything. They know I’m going to be as truthful as I can be about where we’re going. And I’m also very honest to say, “I don’t know what that future is going to be.” And I think people really respect that. I think we need to inspire. And I think we need to admit when we’re wrong and course correct. ADI IGNATIUS: So that can’t be enough, though, to be humble. I mean, there are a lot of humble, authentic people out there. DAN SCHULMAN: Not that many. But- ADI IGNATIUS: Well, okay. I mean, no, I agree, those are great attributes, but there are probably a lot of humble, authentic guys out there. The ability to inspire, I get. But there’s got to be more than just, “I’m just like this at home. What you see is what you get.” I mean, there have to be other skills, attributes, approaches that are key to doing this job successfully. DAN SCHULMAN: Well, I mean, they’re the basics. You’ve got to be able to work at a very intense level. You have to have extremely high expectations, and insist upon them. You need to be able to make very difficult decisions and stand up to them. People need to know that you’re going to lead, you’re going to be uncompromising, that you have an expectation that you’re going to win. I’m a fighter. I’ve done mixed martial arts for like 40 years. And I’ve learned from that to be very cool, calm, collected in very high stress situations. I feel like as a leader, you can never be too up or too down either, because good things are going to happen, that’s great, but they’re going to be followed by difficult things and that’s also okay. You’ll learn from those. I think those are just from my perspective, the basics of leadership. And then I do think those traits on top of those are really important, being humble, being authentic, and being willing to say the same thing that you say internally, publicly. It’s great because you don’t really have to think that much about- ADI IGNATIUS: You got to get your story straight. DAN SCHULMAN: Exactly. What did I say every year or what did I say every year? It’s very consistent. ADI IGNATIUS: So, for Verizon, this is a turnaround. You’ve used that term. DAN SCHULMAN: Yeah. ADI IGNATIUS: When does it end? DAN SCHULMAN: You’d expect me to say this, probably never ends, but that’s not really your question. So, in my view, there’s a three-year plan that we’re under right now. The first year is about admitting the issues that we have, confronting them head on, putting into place a fully comprehensive transformation program. We have 10 work streams. We have 400 initiatives in them. Everyone in the company is engaged in those. I meet every single week on those. I spend hours on every single one of the 10 work streams. We have the leaders of the company involved in all of them. Year two is institutionalizing that. We’re making that transformation right now. Let’s see the results, course correct, solidify. And then year three, we turn into an AI native company. We are part of the AI infrastructure and we’ve transformed who we are as a company. ADI IGNATIUS: So, I guess another way of saying it, what would have to be true for people to say Dan Schulman fundamentally changed Verizon? DAN SCHULMAN: Well, I think you’ll see it in all of our metrics. You’ll see it in our customer satisfaction results. You’ll see it in our churn rate. You’ll see it in our employee satisfaction results. You’ll see it that we are truly AI native. I think to become AI native, the technology is going to be there. There’s no question about it. I mean, I think in two years time, we’re approaching AGI, if not at AGI, two or three years. We’re at quantum by 2030 at the latest. So, I think the technology will be there. I think the most successful companies will have figured out culturally how to adopt to that. I think that is probably the biggest challenge for any company because people can be scared of all of the change. They can be scared of what could AI do to my job, that kind of thing. And so, I think the issue that we will all face is how do we adopt it. And I think again there, in our network teams, when they see what we can do in terms of improving the network by running these things autonomously. When we look at our cyber security and we see how much better we can be than we’ve been in the past. And by the way, I think we’ve been amazing in the past, but we’re living in the time of AI. It’s not good enough for how we’ve been. There’s a lot to be very excited about on the AI front. People talk about is there going to be disruption. There is going to be disruption, but we’ve had a lot of disruption in our lives and humans are amazingly adept at moving through it. People always have tragedy in their life. Somehow they bounce back from that. And I feel like the utilization of AI, how AI native we are as a company, how we’ve been able to adapt it, and what that’s done for all of the constituencies that I serve will be the legacy that I hope to leave. ADI IGNATIUS: Dan, this is a great conversation. Thank you for your time. DAN SCHULMAN: Yeah, Adi, thank you so much. I appreciate it. ADI IGNATIUS: That was Dan Schulman, the CEO of Verizon. Next week, Alison looks at how organizations can create products and services to appeal to both emerging and developing markets. If you found this episode helpful, share it with a colleague and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, please consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter, and unlimited access to HBR Online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to our team, senior producer Mary Dooe and senior production editor Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new episode on Tuesday. I’m Adi Ignatius.

item.title: The Innovation Strategy Most Companies Miss
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.70
Share Podcast The Innovation Strategy Most Companies Miss A conversation with Dartmouth’s Vijay Govindarajan and MIT’s Amos Winter on why designing for emerging markets before developed ones can yield benefits. Companies often build products for wealthy markets first and then try to adapt them for the rest of the world. But according to Dartmouth Tuck professor Vijay Govindarajan and MIT professor Amos Winter, designing for the toughest constraints first—whether that’s affordability, portability, or limited infrastructure—can lead to products that perform better everywhere. They explain how leaders can identify high-impact opportunities, uncover customer needs through deep field research, and design solutions that balance performance with cost. They also discuss why organizational mindset—not technology—is often the biggest obstacle to global innovation, and where AI can (and can’t) accelerate the design process. Together they wrote the book Global by Design: How to Create Innovations That Scale, Travel, and Transform. ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard. ADI IGNATIUS: And I’m Adi Ignatius, and this is the HBR IdeaCast. ALISON BEARD: Adi, today we’re focusing on how to create products and services with widespread global appeal. But let me start with a question for you. If you wanted to make something that would be popular around the world, where would you start? ADI IGNATIUS: Well, I guess the obvious example is look for products and services that are successful in one market and try to adapt them to other ones. ALISON BEARD: Like Coca-Cola and different sizes and levels of sweetness or Nike running shoes with lighter mesh or a more basic iPhone? ADI IGNATIUS: Yeah, I mean they all seem to be doing pretty well. ALISON BEARD: Yes, they are. But our guests today say that a lot of companies actually fail when they try to adapt goods in this way, and there might be more value in taking a different approach. Amos Winter, professor at MIT, and Vijay Govindarajan, professor at Dartmouth’s Tuck School of Business, argue that there’s an advantage to tackling international markets first, using innovation to solve the toughest problems most efficiently there, versus starting with offerings for wealthy markets and then watering them down. Winter and Govindarajan, who goes by Vijay, are authors of the book Global by Design: How to Create Innovations That Scale, Travel, and Transform. Here’s our conversation ALISON BEARD: Why should leaders today take a global perspective on innovation from the very beginning? AMOS WINTER: Well, I think you can look at it from a number of opportunity standpoints. One, business. The greatest economic growth in the world right now is in emerging markets. And so that, in addition to the large populations, creates amazing business opportunities. But I think the other opportunity is from a social perspective. All the most compelling issues facing humanity really present most compellingly in low resource settings; you can make that positive humanitarian impact and make a viable business at the same time. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. VG, you and a few coauthors introduced the idea of reverse innovation about 15 years ago now, I think. How does this work build on that? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I would call it reverse innovation 2.0, because the reverse innovation that I pioneered 15 years ago, it was really looking at it from a business strategy point of view. When I accidentally met Amos, I realized reverse innovation has actually two sides. There is a business strategy side, but then there is an engineering side. And I said, wouldn’t it be nice to bring these two perspectives together? That’s what led to global by design. ALISON BEARD: And you hear the phrase global by design. And the first thought or challenge that comes to my mind is that if you’re trying to design for everyone, for the world, you’re not really designing for anyone. So, how do you address that worry? AMOS WINTER: Well, a big part of making globally attractive solutions is figuring out what core values are shared across many different markets. So, I suspect people don’t worry about iPhones selling everywhere or Coca-Cola selling everywhere. There’s commonalities between different user groups that you can utilize. And then there’s modifications to products that are relatively small that you can make so they best align with different markets to maybe change price point or change feature set. But that core value that’s universally appreciated still persists between markets. ALISON BEARD: And do you think that companies still try to target primarily wealthy markets first and then are unsuccessful in adapting to less developed countries? AMOS WINTER: Yeah, very much so. Part of that is historical in that really all product design for the last 200 or so years has been focused on U.S.-European type markets. Part of that I think is still because of a bit of a stigma in that companies can look at poor countries and think like, “Oh, those are poor people. They can’t afford to buy products,” which isn’t true at all. They’re also consumers. But I would say more and more multinationals are realizing that the big economic gains in the world are happening in emerging markets. But even if you see that opportunity, actually realizing it is challenging because now you’re designing for different population sets than we’ve historically designed for. So, if you’re say an American engineer sitting in Wisconsin, how do you get into the mindset of a mother of five in India? That’s a totally different demographic. And so, a lot of this book also is about expanding the perspective of innovators so you can see these new opportunities and see the requirements they present. And so, you can design effectively for them because you’re better informed about the differences in the markets and what they demand for solutions. VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: If you really look back, innovation always started in rich countries and the reason is rich countries have resources and rich countries have consumers who can afford to buy those innovative products which are premium priced. The reason this is important is there is a dominant logic that develops inside the organization. So, the biggest barrier to reverse innovation is not technology. It’s not that people don’t understand emerging markets are important. It is the dominant logic. Companies are so entrenched in terms of the systems, the structures, the processes, the incentives, the capabilities. It is extremely difficult. It’s like moving the Titanic 180 degrees. That is the real problem. It’s a mindset issue. It’s not a technology issue. ALISON BEARD: And so, while there have been innovators in these emerging markets that have developed solutions for those markets, you’d like to see more cross-pollination? AMOS WINTER: Well, coming back to why this is reverse innovation 2.0 is that emerging markets present new challenges than what we’ve designed for in wealthy markets. And the situation I’m constantly in as an innovator, and I think many multinationals are facing in emerging markets, is that consumers there still demand a certain level of performance in the products that they buy. Nobody wants semi-clean water, nobody wants a semi-functional toilet. There’s baseline performance. But those consumers may not be able to afford to pay for the existing solutions at the price point that’s already in wealthy markets. And so, you’re faced with this conundrum of how do we provide that high performance at a low cost to engage emerging markets? And what’s powerful about this in the reverse part of this is that if you can actively focus on emerging markets first and figure out that high performance, low cost solution, you end up creating something very valuable. Valuable enough to be adopted in emerging markets, but also valuable enough to potentially disrupt wealthy markets by providing just as good or better performance at a much lower price. VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: And I would say there are three forces that are coming together. That’s why it’s also a place for entrepreneurs. The three forces that are coming together is the rich country, the growth has slowed down. The second is in the emerging markets, as you rightly said, there are smart companies which are innovating and they could potentially disrupt multinationals in their own home market. So, the second threat these companies are facing is, hey, we cannot ignore emerging markets because those giants from emerging markets can come and disrupt us. And the third is affordability. Affordability crisis has hit even in a rich country like the U.S. People can’t afford to buy healthcare. They can’t afford to get good education. They can’t afford to buy grocery. So, we need affordable solutions in the U.S. And where best to find them is in poor countries. ALISON BEARD: So, let’s dig into some practical advice. First, how do you recognize global by design opportunities? AMOS WINTER: So, we talk about in the book three merits that you really need to check yourself whether you’re satisfying before you launch into a new initiative. And so, the first of those is what we call problem merit. And that’s a gut check on understanding, are you solving a problem that’s going to impact ideally a large number of people in a meaningful way? And ideally with a business opportunity behind it. So, if you’re successful in making that impact, there’s a viable business to scale and sustain a solution. And that problem merit identification goes beyond just saying, “Oh, people need clean water.” It’s really distilling what are the metrics of performance that must be satisfied for a successful solution. So, it may be volume of water or what contaminants you have to get out or the price point people are willing to pay. Then the second area of merit we have to evaluate is what we call innovation merit. And that’s a gut check on is innovation actually required to solve this problem? Because there’s many problems where you can just give money through philanthropy or maybe just adapt something in a slight way for it to work in a new market. So, you have to convince yourself, does actually something new have to be created to solve this problem? And then the third area of merit we talk about that you have to satisfy is what’s called value merit. And that’s all about aligning value propositions. So, one, people are going to support your work, creating a solution. And two, people are going to support the dissemination of your solution, which typically means people are going to make money by using your product or at least derive value from it and people are going to make money by producing and selling it. We represent it in a Venn diagram. When you look at that Venn diagram and you say, “Hey, I have a compelling problem. It needs innovation. And boy, if I’m successful, it’s going to deliver a lot of value.” That not only shows you have a compelling opportunity in a resource constrained market, but also that you likely have a reverse innovation that’s going to deliver value globally because it creates high performance at low cost. ALISON BEARD: And if you’ve identified a problem that is large and could be tackled in any market where innovation is required and you might be able to create value, how do you then narrow it so that you can focus on something specific enough to design around? AMOS WINTER: There’s a very important concept that we talk about called being a tempered dreamer. And that is all about recognizing your own limitations as an innovator and figuring out the niche where you can make the largest impact. And so, I’ll give you an example. The most inspiring professional meeting I’ve ever had in my life was with a mission director for Gaza and West Bank. I met him in Israel and he said, “Look, we need solutions for farmers to grow better crops, to have water, to have energy. We need that now in order to prevent extremism.” Because if people have these more promising livelihoods by being like a farmer, they’re less likely to join a terrorist group. And this resonated with me very powerfully from a patriotic standpoint. I care about global stability and insecurity in the U.S. I’m not a policymaker, but I do create irrigation technology, desalination technology. And I realized that I can play my part by creating those technologies to help global stability, even though I’m not a government employee. And so, I think innovators have to figure out what skills do they have, what resources do they have, what is tractable to realize in a reasonable amount of time in order to still be creative and ambitious, but narrow down where can I make an impact? ALISON BEARD: VG, do you have an example from the corporate world where you’ve seen leaders or executives identify those three things that we’re talking about, the problem merit, innovation, merit, value merit, but then narrow down the problem in a way that it’s something they can tackle? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: When I went to work for GE Healthcare, I was sent to India. And what we quickly realized was there was almost 60% of Indians who did not have access to healthcare devices that we have in the U.S. So, we found a very huge problem that can be solved, which is how do you give access to high quality medical imaging products to these 60% of Indians? Then we said, “That’s like boiling the washer. That’s so big.” So, we said, “Let us focus on one small s egment within this, which is EKG, the electrocardiogram,” because as it turns out, the bulk of the people who die in India, they’re because of heart attack. So, EKG is a very important thing that is missing. So, we said, how do we create an EKG machine which has got the features of the $20,000 EKG machine we have in the US, but at a price point Indians can afford, which is $400. So, now we have come to a very specific problem which requires innovation to close the gap. We went from big to something that we can actually solve. ALISON BEARD: So, let’s talk about that process of innovation. You talk about three parts, elucidating requirements, designing a solution, and then scaling locally and globally. But there are steps within these phases, so I want to pull them apart and sort of tackle each one at a time. When it comes to elucidating requirements, how should innovators work to understand all of the stakeholders’ needs and goals? So, Amos, in your example, it’s those farmers in Gaza. Vijay, in your example, it’s the doctors trying to do medical testing, heart testing in India. AMOS WINTER: So, it’s always valuable to map out who are all the stakeholders that are going to play a role in the dissemination of your eventual product and understand the power that they have on your success or failure. So, you can usually just do that as a mental exercise and map it out like, oh, the government’s going to subsidize this or there’s a retailer who’s going to do this. And once you map those out, nothing beats going to talk to them. If you can travel and go interact with them and talk with them and build rapport and understand their needs and desires and requirements, you get a much clear insight about what value propositions are going to resonate with them and promote them to adopt your solution. And the big thing about elucidating requirements is figuring out what problem are you actually trying to solve and intentionally putting yourself in a necessity as a mother of invention situation. We talk about this idea of primary and secondary requirements. So, a lot of innovation is very much driven by primary requirements and a lot of academic research is driven by primary requirements as well. So, you want to make the lighter or faster or more efficient gizmo. And a lot of that innovation work forgets that, well, if the gizmo is adopted, it has to be cheap enough and people have to like how it looks and it has to last long enough. So, if you intentionally, as you’re elucidating requirements, try to form as comprehensive a set as possible of the primary and secondary, you put yourself in the best position for success and not missing some of those critical, but maybe hidden secondary requirements too late in the game. VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I think once we decided we wanted to create a value product, what we did was a small portion of our innovation team went and lived in rural India for two months. The mandate I gave the team was don’t focus on the solution. Focus on the problem. Independent of the solution. And when they lived there, they observed the villagers. They talked to the villagers. They did deep ethnographic research and came out with four important requirements. One is affordability. The machine can’t cost more than $400. That’s all they could afford. Second, it has to be portable because there was no hospital, no imaging center in these places. You got to carry the device. Third, it has to work not out of house electricity because most of these villagers didn’t have electricity. And fourth, it should be easy to repair because these villagers didn’t have places where you could go repair them, easy to operate and easy to repair. So, they just came back with those requirements. It is by actually living in rural India. ALISON BEARD: And how long do you spend on this elucidating requirements phase before moving on to actually prototyping and testing solutions? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I think corporations want to move fast, but the same time, do it right. Fast and fail is no good. So, I think this EKG project took us 18 months from beginning to end until we came up with the solution, which was hugely commercially successful. So, the design requirements took us three months. But as Amos said, it’s not a black and white, it’s about we got to get this right because this is the foundation on which everything relies. So, get the requirements right. ALISON BEARD: Okay. So, now to that design phase, could one of you just briefly walk me through an effective structured design process? AMOS WINTER: Yeah. So, your very general design process is first understand the problem you’re trying to solve and generate a list of requirements, then generate multiple ideas for viable solutions. People tend to kind of lock themselves into favorite ideas oftentimes and just think of one really cool one. If you think of a cool idea, force yourself to take a step back and say, “What are some other ways I could solve this?” Then you have to evaluate those ideas and down select to what the most compelling concept is. Then you go into a detailed design phase where usually a concept has multiple parts to it. So, if you’re designing a consumer product, there may be the product, there may be the packaging, there may be marketing. And so, you work out all of those different parts and then you integrate them together into a fully integrated final solution. And so, a lot of times you want to take a mock-up or it might be kind of a kludgy prototype, but it actually works correctly. Take that back to stakeholders. Get a gut check. Is it working before you really polish a product? So, you want to do some testing to know you’re on the right track and then go into a deeper validation where you may do a field pilot or a randomized control trial before you actually go to market. ALISON BEARD: How is AI helping with all of this? AMOS WINTER: I think it’s an incredibly powerful tool in terms of aggregating a lot of information really quickly. I’m finding it amazing as a designer so I can get a whole background on a field of work very, very quickly and understand the lay of the land. What AI is not equipped well-to-do right now is directly solve the type of problems we’re talking about in this book. Because one, a lot of these problems deal with information that’s not formally recorded. And so, you’re dealing with people’s emotions and also math and physics and economics, and you have to integrate those together in an interesting way. Second is I work in physical technologies and AI still has a lot of knowledge gaps around the physical world in nuances around weather or friction or all these little things that we as people perceive. AI doesn’t have the feel of touch and insight in the same way as people do. And then the third is that so much of the work I do personally and that we talk about in this book depends on building rapport and talking face-to-face with stakeholders. And so, when you get to know stakeholders, that can influence how you actually design things because you get insights in how they’re thinking. That relationship building is still so important in the type of design that I do in design for really global products. ALISON BEARD: We’ve been talking a lot about products, but does this global by design process work for services, business models, internal practices as well? AMOS WINTER: Good design is good design no matter the field. So, one example we put in the book is about how McDonald’s figured out how to make hamburgers really quickly and cheaply. And so, before they designed a building and installed the kitchen, they mocked up the layout of the building on a tennis court. And they got a bunch of high school kids who would be their future employees to act out all the actions of filling drinks and flipping burgers. And they were able to figure out the flow of the process without any physical infrastructure. And the same goes with policy. You need to figure out your design requirements before you implement a policy. So, that’s something we really try to bring out is that the principals in the book are relevant across fields. ALISON BEARD: Let’s now talk about scaling. How has the fact that you’ve followed this global by design process made it more likely that you will be successful in adapting your initial product to deliver around the world? Is the idea that if you follow these steps, that shift to scaling locally and globally will be inherently easier? AMOS WINTER: I think it comes down to reducing uncertainty and actively always trying to put yourself in that necessity is the mother of invention situation. Too much innovation is a game of playing darts blindfolded. And I think academia is guilty of this, is that you throw a lot of darts, you hit some bullseyes. But if you take that time and care and effort to aim, you may not hit a bullseye, but you’re much more likely to hit it. And so, that time and care and effort goes into the define your requirements. If you know what problem you’re trying to solve, you’re more likely to solve it. Designing a solution, well, if you go through a diligent process to create something you’re confident in, rather than just conjuring something willy-nilly, it’s more likely to be successful. And if you test it with actual people who would adopt it, then you get good feedback. Going both local and globally, there’s some strategy you can really identify to understand what features are going to be demanded in different markets. What is the core value that translates across markets? How do I correctly segment my products so I’m not cannibalizing? So, that’s foresight, which again is aiming those darts so you don’t fall into an unknown that’s a trap that ends up killing your product. ALISON BEARD: VG, what’s the biggest challenge that you see companies run into when they try to scale? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I think the biggest and the most problematic ones for multinationals is they’re afraid these high performance, low cost solutions will disrupt their premium priced products in the US. Because if you’re going to bring a $400 ECG machine into the US where you are currently selling $20,000 ECG machine, if the $400 start replacing the $20,000, your profit margin disappears. So, this is the biggest worry companies have. The way to overcome this is not to see this as substituting the $20,000 ECG machine, but it is about transforming the whole industry. And you will continue to have market for $20,000 ECG machine. Maybe the market may decline slightly, but the overall industry will expand phenomenally because of this. So, you have to think of this as transforming the space as compared to one-to-one substitution. This is the biggest mindset issue. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. More generally, how should leaders find the most innovative people in their companies to tackle these kinds of projects? AMOS WINTER: I think it comes down to equipping people and giving them the opportunities to think about problems from their own vantage point and creating a culture of asking about that and valuing their input. Because a forklift operator in a warehouse is going to really understand the problems of moving stuff around a warehouse. So, if you create a culture of saying, “Hey Joe, what’s causing you a lot of time and agony? Or do you have an insight of how we could speed things up?” That person’s going to give a lot of great feedback. And so, I see this happen a lot actually in companies around the world in that they try to isolate innovation to a certain group of people. And what can be most toxic is if the innovation has to come top down because you’ll get the business leaders who are amazing, wonderful, smart people, but they’re lacking a lot of context and perspective about problems like on the ground or on the shop floor. So, if you can bring together those perspectives, it makes you much more powerful as an innovator. And I say this in every class I teach too. The most powerful tool a designer has is perspective. ALISON BEARD: How do you do this at an under-resourced company? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I say resources are the biggest impediment to global by design because then you have resources. You substitute resources for thinking. So, you throw money at the problem. In fact, I would say to the CEOs that I work with, give your innovation team less resources. When you give people less money, they actually do out of the box thinking. I would also say it is always very good to put in the innovation team at least a few people. Of course, you want domain experts and so on and so forth, at least a few people who are mavericks. And my definition of mavericks, they satisfy two criteria. One, they always talk about crazy things. Second, they’re an organizational nightmare to manage. Put them on the team because they are more likely to come up with totally out of the box ideas. ALISON BEARD: What would you two like executives to go out and do today, this week, to start thinking in a more global by design way? AMOS WINTER: You know what I love, Alison, is I meet companies all the time that have a sense of opportunity. They see that there’s new markets they could grow into, often emerging markets. They want to do it. And many of these companies want to make a positive social impact too, and they’re just unsure of how to approach that opportunity. So, I guess the advice to executives is I would say dream big about where your business can grow and how you can really harness the collective purchasing power of these massive, rapidly growing markets around the world. And I think maybe the humanitarian side of me would say too, can you do it while making a positive impact in the world? And my answer would be, yeah, absolutely. ALISON BEARD: You’re anticipating my last question, which is in what areas of business or society do you most want to see this thinking applied? You talk about wicked problems and the fact that we have a lot of them. So, what’s your ambition for where we should all be looking? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I say there are three sectors which are absolutely craving for the ideas that we have in the book. Education, healthcare, and energy. These are three foundational sectors on which economies get built, and we need affordable, high quality solutions in all the three. ALISON BEARD: All right, listeners, get started. Amos, Vijay, thank you so much for talking with me today. I’ve learned a lot. AMOS WINTER: Thank you, Alison. VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: Thank you so much. ALISON BEARD: That’s MIT professor Amos Winter and Dartmouth Tuck Professor Vijay Govindarajan. They’re co-authors of the book, Global by Design: How to Create Innovations That Scale, Travel, and Transform. Vijay also has a LinkedIn weekly column on innovation. Next week, Adi will dig into how to build a sustainable long-term career in today’s uncertain world. If you found this episode helpful, please share it with a colleague and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter, and unlimited access to HBR online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to our team, senior producer Mary Dooe, and senior production editor, Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new episode on Tuesday. I’m Alison Beard.
