item.title: Research: How AI Agents Broaden the Scope of Knowledge Work
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.52
Summary. AI agents don’t just speed up knowledge work; they change its nature. In a field study of Perplexity’s conversational assistant and autonomous agent, researchers found that not only You ask two different AI tools the same question—say, to pull together a comprehensive competitive landscape for a new product line. The first comes back in seconds with a tidy summary and a list of links. You read it, open a dozen tabs, copy numbers into a spreadsheet, build the chart, and write the memo yourself. The second comes back twenty-some minutes later with the spreadsheet built, the chart drawn, and a draft memo attached. One handed you information to act on. The other handed you completed work.

item.title: Research: What Physical Retail Stores Deliver in a Digital Economy
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.32
Research: What Physical Retail Stores Deliver in a Digital Economy Summary. As shopping becomes increasingly digital, the role of physical stores is shifting from simply completing transactions to solving customer problems that online channels cannot. Research on One could be forgiven for concluding that the physical store is in terminal decline. Vacant storefronts remaining a common sight on many high streets, and e-commerce continues to capture a growing share of consumer spending. Yet some of retail’s fastest-growing companies are not retreating from physical stores. They are opening them at an accelerating pace.

item.title: What Does AI Talent Look for in an Employer?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.23
Summary. The competition for AI talent remains strong—and expensive. How can companies possibly compete for skilled AI talent when Silicon Valley behemoths are offering salaries and signing packages The tech hiring landscape is in a state of flux. On one hand, companies like Meta have laid off thousands of employees, fueling concerns that artificial intelligence will eliminate many technical jobs. At the same time, many of the world’s largest technology firms are engaged in an intense scramble for AI talent. Despite the recent layoffs, Meta continues to aggressively pursue AI researchers and engineers with compensation packages reportedly worth millions of dollars; Elon Musk is creating an “elite unit” to recruit top AI engineers that reports directly to him; and Amazon recently announced plans to hire thousands of engineering employees and interns in 2026 (including, possibly some of the recently laid off Meta employees). As one AI company department head noted, “If I’m going to spend a billion dollars to build a model, $10 million for an engineer is a relatively low investment.”

item.title: AI Makes Building Easy. Choosing What to Build Is Harder.
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.22
Summary. AI is making it possible for individuals with little technical expertise to build sophisticated products, raising questions about whether collaboration is becoming less important. Observations AI tools are powerful enough to make solo-founding increasingly viable, and allow innovators with no technical skills to create functional products. The solo builder concept is playing out not only in startups, but also in bigger organizations as AI adoption grows. AI has commoditized execution across the innovation lifecycle: product managers build working prototypes without touching a line of code and developers accelerate software development, testing, documentation, and data manipulation.

item.title: Why Lateral Hires Rarely Become CEO
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.12
Summary. Internal CEO succession candidates are primarily judged on whether they can lead the enterprise. Lateral hires are judged on two dimensions: whether they can lead the enterprise and whether they Boards often hire senior leaders from outside the company to strengthen their CEO succession bench. When internal options appear limited, companies recruit accomplished division presidents, regional CEOs, CFOs, or functional leaders into roles one or two levels below the chief executive.

item.title: Research: How Remote Work Is Narrowing Early-Career Opportunities
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.10
Summary. Remote work is quietly reshaping early-career opportunity. A study that included analysis of 50 million European job postings and experiments with 1,200 hiring managers found that remote roles Imagine that somewhere, a hiring manager faces a decision between two candidates for a remote position. One is a recent graduate: competent, motivated, and full of potential. The other has accumulated five years of experience and can hit the ground running. Not long ago, managers would regularly take a chance on the graduate, confident that the organization could turn raw potential into exceptional performance. The right team, strong mentors, and moments of informal learning can transform a promising newcomer into a high-performing professional.

item.title: Devil's Bridge Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 6.16
Ranked as one of the best hikes in the USA, Devil’s Bridge in Sedona is a must-do. The trail can be crowded, but I’ll also show you a more pleasant route that’s easier to park at. Devil’s Bridge, the largest natural sandstone arch in the Sedona area, is doable by most folks, with only some steep stairs at the end. Here’s how to do it. Distance 4 mi Difficulty Easy Total Climbing 550 ft Time 2–3 hrs GearFitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 0.5L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here. There are two main trailheads for Devil’s Bridge: Dry Creek and Mescal. The hikes are about the same distance, but Mescal has advantages over Dry Creek. The Mescal Trailhead parking lot has about double the spaces of Dry Creek. Perhaps more importantly, for a pleasant hike, Dry Creek follows a dirt road halfway to Devil’s Bridge, open to vehicles. On the other hand, the first half of the Mescal route is on a regular trail with no vehicles and offers some incredible views along the way.

item.title: Garmin inReach Subscription Cost: Which Plan Is Cheapest
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.96
Garmin inReach Subscription Cost Jump to a section A Garmin inReach subscription is required to use your device, and there’s a lot of variation in what you’ll pay. There are even inReach plans that Garmin doesn’t sell. Here’s how to figure out the best plan for you. | Plan | Best For | Price | |---|---|---| | Enabled | Pay only for what you use | $7.99/mo | | Standard | Sharing your live position with family on every hike | $29.99/mo | | ProteGear | Power users who want maximum flexibility | Pay per day | | Suspended | The cheapest way to keep 24/7 SOS (compatible devices) | ~$8/yr | Info I’ve paid for my own inReach device and subscription since 2014, when I got my first one. I buy all my own gear and don’t take sponsorships, so I’m free to use and recommend what works best. What You Get A Garmin inReach subscription is a monthly service plan, just like a cell phone plan. Two things have to be in place to get connected: an active subscription (these plans) and an inReach device to run it on. No plan means no SOS or messaging, even if you own the hardware. Here’s what a subscription unlocks: - Emergency SOS to the 24/7 Garmin Response center, who coordinate (but don’t perform) the rescue. Included on every plan, and still works when suspended on compatible devices - Two-way text messaging using satellite when you’re beyond cell range - Location tracking that shares a breadcrumb trail over satellite that others can follow on a map - Weather forecasts with hourly and multi-day outlooks, including a marine option - Photo and voice messages over satellite on inReach Plus-enabled devices like the Messenger Plus and Mini 3 Plus - Check-in messages, three preset “I’m OK” type messages you can send for less than a normal message Pricing Levels Pricing on each plan is purely based on how much you use it. The more expensive the plan, the more usage you essentially prepay for. | Plan | Price/mo | Annual | Texts/Weather | Photo/Voice | Live Tracking | Check-ins | Text Overage | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Enabled | $7.99 | $95.88 | $0.50 ea | $1.00 ea | $0.10/pt (10 min+) | $0.10 ea | $0.50/msg | | Essential | $14.99 | $179.88 | 50 | 25 | $0.10/pt (10 min+) | Unlimited | $0.50/msg | | Standard | $29.99 | $359.88 | 150 | 50 | Unlimited (10 min+) | Unlimited | $0.50/msg | | Premium | $49.99 | $599.88 | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited (2 min+) | Unlimited | N/A | - There’s a one-time $39.99 activation fee on all plans, charged on every device, including inReach smartwatches like the Fenix 8 Pro. - A weather forecast counts as one satellite text message. - Incoming messages count too, including replies to your check-ins. - Emoji reactions (tapbacks) to messages in the Garmin Messenger app are billed the same as check-ins: free/unlimited on Essential, Standard, and Premium, and $0.10 each on Enabled. - Messages sent over Wi-Fi or cell through the Garmin Messenger app don’t count against your plan. Only satellite messages do. - Live tracking points always go out over satellite, so they’re always charged, even if your phone has signal. - A group message counts as a single message, but each reply costs a message. - Photo and voice messages only work on inReach Plus-enabled devices like the Messenger Plus, GPSMAP H1i Plus, and Mini 3 Plus. - You can switch between plans at any time for free. You can also keep more than one device active on a single account (a new option since the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro), but each one needs its own activation fee and subscription. - Every plan includes Emergency SOS messaging through Garmin Response. - The plan prices are identical whether you carry a Mini 2, Mini 3, Messenger, or a GPSMAP. Garmin charges for the plan, not the device, so the “Garmin inReach Mini 2 subscription cost” is the same as the Mini 3 or Messenger. - Photo and voice messages only work on inReach Plus-enabled devices, so on an older unit like the Mini 2 those rows simply don’t apply. - Smartwatches with inReach (like the Fenix 8 Pro) add unlimited LTE messaging and calling when you have cell service. Cost Calculator Enter your estimated monthly usage and how many months a year you use the device, and this shows the monthly and annual cost for each plan. Click “Edit Charges” to adjust pricing for your local currency or region. Edit Charges Simply change the numbers here based on your currency. Overages | Plan | Monthly | Annual | |---|---|---| | Enabled | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Essential | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Standard | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Premium | $0.00 | $0.00 | Annual is your monthly cost times the months you use it, assuming you suspend for $0 the rest of the year. Year one adds a one-time $39.99 activation fee on every plan. - Most people: Enabled, about $146 a year. Full SOS, and you only pay for the tracking and messages you actually use. - Track every hike? Standard. Unlimited tracking beats Enabled once you pass about 36 tracking hours a month. - Essential rarely wins. It only makes sense for steady messaging with almost no tracking. Any real tracking, around 25 hours a month, pushes you to Standard. - Premium is niche. It’s only worth it above about 190 messages a month, or if you need 2-minute tracking, like guiding a team or sailing. - Seasonal user? Suspend. Keep SOS on a compatible device for about $8 a year instead of paying all year. Suspending You can suspend your plan for $0 for up to 12 consecutive months, with no reactivation fee. This is the move for seasonal users, and it beats canceling, which wipes your data and charges a fresh $39.99 activation fee to come back. The big deal is SOS. On compatible devices, Emergency SOS keeps working while your plan is suspended, even though messaging, tracking, and weather are off. That means you can carry a working SOS beacon in the off-season for almost nothing. To qualify, it has to be a compatible device, on the latest firmware, and previously on an active plan before you suspend. Not every device supports it, and the list keeps growing, so check Garmin’s current compatible-device list before you count on it. Older units like the original Mini and Explorer don’t qualify. After 12 consecutive months suspended, Garmin automatically moves the device onto the Enabled plan ($7.99/mo) to keep SOS alive. So the real cost of free suspended SOS is one paid month every 13: twelve months free, then the single auto-Enabled month before you suspend again. Call it about $8 a year. Third Party Plans A few partners resell the same Iridium connection with different pricing. ProteGear is the one worth knowing, and its whole angle is pay-per-day instead of per-month. - Pay-per-day. A €49 yearly base, then only the days you’re active, from about €1.50/day (safety) to €6/day (expedition). Flip it on and off yourself for free. - Same safety net. SOS still routes to Garmin Response, and you keep the Garmin Explore account and apps. - Extras Garmin dropped or lacks. Editable preset messages, a dedicated two-way email address, tracking down to 30 seconds, better weather reports, and Wikipedia or Google News over satellite. - The catches. The dashboard and setup are power-user territory and can be confusing, but human support is excellent and responsive. If you’re in Australia or New Zealand, TrackMeNZ is another third party option. inReach Rentals If you only go off-grid occasionally, renting can beat buying a device and paying for a plan. Outfitters will mail you a unit for your trip, usually around $10 to $15 per day with a few-day minimum. The typical flow: - Order online and choose a data plan and insurance. - The device ships to your home or a pickup location. - You get setup instructions by email. - Use it, then mail it back. I don’t have any specific company I recommend. Google “Garmin inReach rentals” and compare options. inReach Professional Garmin’s Professional plans are built for teams, organizations, and families that want one account across multiple devices. - Central management. Run multiple devices under one login, assign them to users, and monitor everyone from a single dashboard. - Best for. Guides, SAR teams, land managers, and anyone coordinating a group in the field. - Pricing. Tiered by how much messaging and tracking your team needs, billed monthly. See Garmin’s Professional plans for current rates. - Off-season. You can suspend Pro devices and still keep SOS on compatible units, so a fleet doesn’t lose emergency coverage when it’s stood down. Rescue Costs Your subscription pays for the SOS service, not the rescue itself. Most rescues are free, but if a private helicopter or air ambulance gets involved it can cost thousands, which is what rescue insurance covers.

item.title: Garmin inReach SOS: How It Works & When to Use It
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.71
Garmin inReach SOS Guide The SOS button is the most important feature on a satellite communicator, and the one people understand the least. It’s not the same as calling 911. An inReach SOS routes to Garmin Response, a 24/7 center that coordinates with local rescue teams and messages with you the whole time. Here’s when to hit it and what to actually expect if you do. When to SOS - Unsure of a safe outcome? Hit it. The best advice I’ve heard, from an LA County search and rescue veteran: if you’re not sure you’ll be okay, press SOS. It’s two-way, so you can describe the situation, lost, stranded, chest pain, and Garmin Response helps you figure out what to do. - Not just for the backcountry. Garmin’s own SOS data is full of vehicle use: cars, boats, motorcycles. Carry it when you drive out of cell range, because a flat or a breakdown can just mean a tow, not a helicopter. - Medical issues and injuries are the top reasons people hit it. A pre-existing condition doesn’t disqualify you. If something feels wrong, ask. - More than half of SOS calls are for someone else. Like calling 911 as a Good Samaritan, hitting SOS for another person doesn’t make you liable. Just know that rescue insurance only covers you, not them. - Don’t abuse it. Being tired or having a sore stomach isn’t an emergency. Use common sense, same as you would with 911. Hitting the Button - There’s a countdown. Once you trigger it, the device counts down before the message goes out, and you can cancel during that window. - Sent one by mistake? Cancel it, don’t power off. Cancel the SOS on the device and reply to Garmin Response so they know you’re okay. Powering off leaves them assuming the worst, and a search may start anyway. - False alarms don’t cost you. Garmin doesn’t charge for an accidental activation you cancel. Cancelling isn’t an embarrassment, it’s the system working. - SOS can stay active on a suspended plan. On compatible devices you keep a working SOS button even with messaging suspended. Details on the subscription page. What Happens When You Hit SOS - A helicopter is not the default. Garmin’s data shows most rescues aren’t helicopters. They’re usually local volunteers organized by a sheriff’s department or park service. - It takes hours to mobilize. Even a helicopter rescue usually takes several hours. Be ready to wait, and carry enough to spend the night: an emergency bivy, extra layers, and food. - Rescue comes in many forms. It might be self-evacuation with guidance, a ground team, a cliff extraction, or just a ranger walking you down. I’ve seen that on Mount Whitney for altitude sickness. About 10% of people handle it themselves. - You stay in contact the whole time. Unlike a one-way PLB, Garmin Response keeps messaging you updates until help arrives. Rescue Costs Triggering SOS is included in every inReach plan, so there’s no charge to hit the button. The rescue itself is a separate question. Most rescues are free, but if a private helicopter or air ambulance gets involved it can run well over $20,000. That’s what rescue insurance is for, and I break down the options on that page.

item.title: Garmin inReach Messenger Review: 28-Day Battery
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.60
Garmin inReach Messenger Review Reviewed August 2026 The inReach with the best battery life, but minimal navigation and heavy reliance on your phone. When the Garmin inReach Messenger first came out, I didn’t know who it was for. No real navigation, marketed toward car campers, and not even a clip or strap to mount it to a pack. After a few months of trail use, I have a clearer answer. It’s a solid inReach if battery life and price are your priorities and you’re comfortable relying on your phone for everything else. If you need backup navigation on the device itself, get the Mini 2 instead. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Video Why It Exists Garmin already has the Mini 2 and the GPSMAP 67i. The Messenger fills a different slot: more affordable (often on sale for $199), designed around phone pairing, exceptional battery life, and intentionally limited onboard navigation. Performance The Messenger uses Iridium, so you get 100% global coverage. I’ve had subscribers send messages from the South Pole. In my testing: - Messages went out faster than my Mini 2, usually within a minute. - Reliability in heavy canopy was better than other devices I’ve tested. - It supports GPS, Galileo, BeiDou, and QZSS, which helps with satellite lock in tough terrain. - You can stow it inside the brain of your pack. Keep it upright and near the top and it works fine without external mounting. A subscription is required for all satellite functionality. See the inReach subscription breakdown, including plans Garmin doesn’t advertise. The App The Messenger has a small screen and buttons for standalone use, but it works best with the Garmin Messenger app. The app handles two-way messaging, location tracking, SOS, weather forecasts, and device settings. A few things to know: - When connected to cellular or Wi-Fi, the app sends messages over data automatically instead of satellite. - You can start and stop breadcrumb tracking, trigger SOS, and pull weather from the app. - The Messenger does not pair with Garmin Explore, so there’s no app-based navigation. Trackback on the device is all you get. - Location sharing always goes over satellite regardless of connectivity. - Even when your phone is on Wi-Fi or cellular, the device still checks for messages via satellite every hour. Turn it off when indoors to avoid battery drain. You can also control the Messenger in a limited way from a Garmin watch. Battery Garmin claims 28 days in 10-minute tracking mode. In my testing: - Averaged 5% drain per day, even in cold weather. - On a 5-day trip with regular check-ins and tracking, I used less than 30% total. It charges via USB-C. Battery life is the strongest argument for this device over the Mini 2. Navigation The Messenger records your location every 10 minutes automatically. If you need to backtrack, you get an arrow pointing toward where you were 10 minutes ago. That’s it. It’s not a replacement for track navigation on a device like the Mini 2, and it’s not the same as location sharing via satellite to your MapShare page. If backup navigation matters as an emergency fallback, this device isn’t the right call. Who It’s For The Messenger makes sense if battery life and price are your top priorities, you always hike with your phone, and you don’t need the device to function as backup navigation. If your phone dies in the backcountry and you need to find your way back, you want a Mini 2 or GPSMAP device with that capability built in. For a specific use case, like thru-hiking where your phone is always on and you want the longest possible satellite battery, the Messenger is a strong option. Comparison | Feature | inReach Messenger | ZOLEO | inReach Mini 2 | |---|---|---|---| | Sale Price | $199 | $149 | $299 | | Messaging | Yes (2-way) | Yes (2-way) | Yes (2-way) | | Navigation | TrackBack only | No | Yes (but no maps) | | Battery Life | Up to 28 days | 200+ hours | Up to 14 days | | Display | Very small screen | No display | Small screen | | Weight | 4.0 oz | 5.3 oz | 3.5 oz | | Satellite Network | Iridium | Iridium | Iridium | | SOS Coverage | Global | Global | Global | | Weather Forecasts | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Reverse Charging | Yes | No | No | | Location Sharing | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Phone Required for Full Use | No | Yes | No |

item.title: Mt Mitchell Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.59
Blue Ridge Mountains, North Carolina Mt Mitchell Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026
Reach the highest peak east of the Mississippi the right way, on foot. The Mt. Mitchell Trail climbs 3,700 feet over 12 miles, earning you what the summit road never will. I’ve hiked this a dozen times over the years. In this guide, I’ll show you everything you need to know to conquer Mt. Mitchell on the trail.
- Distance - 12 mi
- Difficulty - Hard
- Total Climbing - 3700 ft
- Time - 5–7 hrs
Who It's For Strong hikers who can do the climbing. Biggest Risk Extreme weather, including snow or thunderstorms at top. When to Go May-November. Summit much cooler than valley. Snow possible through late spring.
Video I made a video showing you what it’s like to hike the trail so you can be prepared when you do it on your own.
Trailhead
Maps
Directions
Info The summit’s Fraser fir forest has been decimated by the balsam woolly adelgid, an invasive insect. The standing dead trees are a visible reminder of this ecological loss.
Info Mt Mitchell is named for Elisha Mitchell, a professor who fell to his death here in 1857 while trying to verify the mountain’s height. He’s buried at the summit.

item.title: Peekaboo Loop Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.46
The Peekaboo Loop Trail takes you away from the crowds and into some of the most dramatic hoodoo scenery in Bryce Canyon. This scenic, up-and-down loop is a great way to explore the Bryce Amphitheater from below, with fewer people and nonstop views. In this guide, I’ll show you how to hike and get the most out of the Peekaboo Loop. Distance 5.2 mi Difficulty Moderate Total Climbing 1500 ft Time 3–4 hrs WhenSummer can be hot, winter can have snow, check the weather. GearFitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 2L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here. Fees: $20+ Park Entry Fee (or use your America the Beautiful pass) There’s a parking lot at Bryce Point with roughly 30 parking spots. In the summer Bryce Canyon NP usually runs a shuttle bus, and if you’re staying in Bryce Canyon City you can easily take the shuttle here and avoid the hassle. Warning Bring water with you before getting to Bryce Point; there’s no water fill station here. My trail guide follows the Bryce Canyon NP’s recommendation to do the Peekaboo Loop clockwise. Directions Info The Peekaboo is one of the only shared use trails (humans, horses, mules). You can bring your own horse or mule with you, or you can book a ride with the park’s official concessioner. The are also other ‘horse-only’ trails that are closed to humans. Info Once you pass the Wall of Windows, you go from Peekaboo Canyon into Bryce Canyon. Info If you want to connect to the Navajo Loop or Queens Garden Trail, you can do it at the bottom of this climb. See my guide for the Figure 8 Trail for more information. Info Do hoodoos fall down? They sure do, but usually it happens over a period of thousands of years, but given the amount of hoodoos at Bryce, it could really happen whenever. An iconic hoodoo called The Sentinel tumbled between 1980 and 2016.

item.title: inReach Messenger Plus: Photo & Voice Tested
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.44
Garmin inReach Messenger Plus Review Reviewed August 2026 The inReach for phone-first users, with up to 600 hours of battery life against the Mini 3 Plus’s 350. Cumbersome to use without a phone. The first inReach with Iridium Messaging Transport (IMT) that gives you 1,600-character messages, voice notes, and photos. Performance was top-notch, even in dense Redwood canopy. But typing on the device with its small screen and minimal buttons is slow, so plan on using the Garmin Messenger app for almost everything. If you want a device that works well with or without an app, get the Mini 3 Plus How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Video Here’s a video I made using the Messenger Plus out on the trail so you can see how it works in real-world conditions. vs. Messenger Should you upgrade from the original inReach Messenger? Not unless you specifically need images or voice notes. | Feature | Messenger Plus | Messenger | |---|---|---| | Price | $499 | $299 | | Messaging System | Iridium Messaging Transport (IMT) | Short Burst Data (SBD) | | Voice Messages | Yes (via app) | No | | Photo Messages | Yes (via app) | No | | Message Length | Up to 1600 characters | Up to 160 characters | | App Compatibility | Messenger & Explore | Messenger only | | Battery Life | Up to 600 hours | Up to 672 hours | | Subscription Rates | Higher for image/voice | Standard | Features The Messenger Plus is built around Garmin’s switch from Iridium’s older Short Burst Data (SBD) protocol to Iridium Messaging Transport (IMT), which is faster and supports larger payloads. In practice, that enables: - Photo and voice messaging: Record a voice note or send a photo via satellite when paired to a phone. Garmin Response can receive both in an SOS. - 1,600-character messages: The old 160-character limit is gone. Longer messages go through in full when sent to a phone or another Plus device. - Tapbacks and emojis: Standard smartphone messaging tools, no message credit cost for tapbacks. - Garmin Explore compatibility: Unlike the original Messenger, the Plus works with Garmin Explore for offline maps, routes, and waypoints via phone. Speed - Messenger Plus was about 20-30% faster overall, but not dramatically so. - Both devices sent standard messages in under 2 minutes in most conditions. - Photo messages sometimes took 10 minutes or longer in dense forest. The 10+ minute figure was under heavy Redwood tree cover, which is a good stress test for satellite signal. Under normal conditions, open sky or light cover, Garmin specs and other testers put typical photo or voice send time closer to 1-2 minutes. If your trips are mostly above treeline or in open terrain, you’ll see much faster results than my worst-case numbers. Messaging - 1,600-character messages go through in full when sent to a phone or another Plus. Sent to a traditional inReach like a Mini 2 or GPSMAP 67i, they break into 160-character chunks, each counting as a separate message on the receiving end. - Voice messages are useful. Record in the app, it sends as an audio file. The limit is 30 seconds, short enough that some people are caught off guard. Voice notes can’t be sent to older inReach models. - Photos are compressed but clear enough for trail documentation and emergency use. One thing nobody mentions upfront: recipients need the Garmin Messenger app installed to receive photos and voice messages. Standard SMS contacts get text only. If your emergency contacts or family don’t have the app, they won’t receive anything beyond a text message, worth sorting out before you leave the trailhead. Emergency - SOS still routes through Garmin Response, which can now receive voice notes and photos from the Plus. - Being able to send an image of an injury or describe a situation by voice instead of typing is a real upgrade in a serious emergency. Navigation - Connecting to Garmin Explore unlocks offline maps, routes, and waypoints, but the app uses your phone’s GPS rather than the device’s. The Plus has onboard GPS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou, but no multi-band. - Trackback functionality had bugs at launch but has been addressed in firmware. - If navigation matters, this isn’t the device. Use the GPSMAP 67i or pair your phone with an inReach Mini 3. Battery The new Certus protocol can burn more battery depending on how you use it. Garmin offers two modes: - Performance mode maintains a near-constant satellite link for fast back-and-forth messaging. Battery drains fast, especially in heavy cover where the signal is intermittent. - Low power mode checks for messages roughly once an hour, similar to older inReach models. Battery life improves dramatically. Real-world battery was more variable than older inReach devices. Garmin specs performance mode at up to 110 hours with 10-minute tracking and no media, but that’s a light-use baseline. In heavy tree cover using performance mode with several images and messages sent, I was tracking around 22 hours. That’s a stress test, not typical use. In open sky on low power mode with 10-minute location tracking, the battery barely moved over a 5-hour hike. Default to low power mode unless you’re expecting active back-and-forth communication.

item.title: State High Points: Which Ones You Can Actually Hike
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.41
State High Point Hikes Most lists treat all 50 state high points as one bucket list. They’re not. The majority are drive-ups or short walks. A handful are real trail hikes. Seven of them aren’t hikes at all: they require mountaineering, technical climbing, or glacier travel to reach the summit. Technical Peaks These peaks require skills and gear beyond standard hiking. Here’s the best hikeable alternative for each. Alaska Denali (20,310 ft) is obvious. The harder problem is finding any normal-hike alternative in Alaska. Even mid-elevation peaks in the 4,000–7,000 ft range typically have exposed sections I wouldn’t recommend to most hikers. Flattop Mountain (3,510 ft) outside Anchorage is the best option: maintained trail, one short scramble near the top, manageable if you take your time. Washington Mount Rainier (14,411 ft) requires mountaineering year-round. Mount St. Helens (8,363 ft) is the best alternative: forest trail, marked boulder field, steep ash slope to the summit. Open in late summer when snow clears. No technical skills required. Wyoming Gannett Peak (13,810 ft) requires glacier travel and is considered the hardest state high point after Denali. Medicine Bow Peak (12,018 ft) has an official USFS trail (#295) all the way to the summit. Cloud Peak and Fremont Peak are closer in elevation but involve off-trail travel and scrambling I wouldn’t universally recommend. Nevada Boundary Peak (13,147 ft) has a route, but the Forest Service describes it as requiring cross-country navigation. Wheeler Peak (13,065 ft) in Great Basin National Park is only 84 feet lower with a maintained NPS trail. The elevation difference is negligible; the experience difference is not. Montana Granite Peak (12,807 ft) involves exposed Class 4/5 rock climbing and is one of the hardest state high points in the lower 48. Trapper Peak (10,157 ft) in the Bitterroot Mountains has an official USFS trail and is a straightforward, if steep, full day. Idaho Borah Peak’s (12,662 ft) “Chicken Out Ridge” names the problem. Scotchman Peak (7,018 ft) in northern Idaho has an official USFS trail and is called the hardest Class 1 peak in the state. Hyndman, Castle, and Iron Creek Point are higher alternatives but involve scrambling and route-finding I wouldn’t broadly recommend. Oregon Every route to Mount Hood (11,249 ft) requires mountaineering. South Sister (10,358 ft) is the highest non-technical summit in Oregon, hikeable in late summer when snow clears. Loose and gravelly near the top, but no exposure and no route-finding. All 50 - Technical: mountaineering or climbing required; guide links to the recommended alternative above - Hike: non-technical trail, real effort - Walk-up: drive-up available or very short trail | item.title: Best Hiking GPS: Trail Tested
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.23
Best Hiking GPS Your phone does most of what a handheld GPS does, usually with a better screen. But when conditions turn harsh and battery life matters, a purpose-built handheld wins. I’ve tested them all since my Garmin GPS 12 in 1999, and I buy my own units and don’t take sponsorships, so I’m free to recommend what works best. | Option | Best For | |---|---| | GPSMAP 67 | Best all-around hiking GPS. Rugged, accurate, long battery, with inReach built in the 67i model | | GPSMAP 65s | This multi-band GPS is my budget pick, and it runs on AA batteries | | Enduro 3 | If you don't need a big screen, the Enduro does everything a handheld does on your wrist | | Phone + App | Casual hikers in tame conditions who are fine carrying a backup battery | My Picks Best All-Around Garmin GPSMAP 67i - My overall pick. I’ve used it for years on the trail and it’s the most accurate and longest-lasting handheld Garmin makes: multi-band multi-GNSS gets me around 6 feet of accuracy even in canyons and heavy tree cover, and I get about 140 hours of battery with 10-minute inReach tracking and messaging on (200+ in GPS-only mode). The inReach features match the dedicated devices, so you get SOS, two-way messaging, and weather reports in one unit. I’ve tested the newer GPSMAP H1i Plus side by side, and the 67i is the better performer and the better value. ↳ REI ↳ Review Best Budget Garmin GPSMAP 65s - If you want the same multi-band accuracy without the inReach features or the price tag, get the 65s. It runs on two AA batteries that you can swap in the field, and you can also buy rechargeable AA batteries on Amazon. Accuracy is the same as the 67i in my testing. You lose the inReach, the longer internal battery, and USB-C, but it’s smaller and handles the essential navigation functions that you need. ↳ Amazon ↳ Review Best for Vehicle and Trail Garmin Montana 750i - A big touchscreen like a phone with a removable battery, great for a combined vehicle and dashboard setup with inReach built in. It’s too heavy to be my main hiking handheld, but if one device has to do overlanding and the occasional hike, this is it. ↳ Amazon ↳ Review Best on the Wrist Garmin Enduro 3 - The best hiking GPS watch I’ve tested. If you abandon the idea that the form factor has to be handheld, the Enduro 3 does everything my GPSMAP 67 does with the same accuracy. It has offline maps with trail names, offline navigation, and tracking. It also has solar and a battery that lasts weeks. The downside is that you only have a small screen to work with. If you do a lot of navigation on the fly in the field, this isn’t your best choice. But if you just want maps, navigation, tracking, and the ability to reroute in an emergency, this works well. ↳ REI | Amazon ↳ Review Phone As GPS For a casual day hike in good weather, your phone is probably the best hiking GPS you have. The screen is better, the apps are slicker than anything Garmin provides, and you already have it with you. Two apps I recommend: - AllTrails is the best starting point for beginners and for discovery. Huge trail database, user reviews, and simple offline downloads on the paid tier. I use it to find trails I haven’t done before. - Footpath is what I use when I want to draw my own route. Trace a line on the map with your finger, and it snaps to trails and estimates distance and elevation. Nothing else matches it for quick planning. - CalTopo is what I use for more hardcore planning. They have a mobile app but the navigation is basic, although effective if you know how to use it. The weak areas of a phone are battery and durability. Here’s how to address it: - Carry an external battery. Navigation will drain a phone faster than you think. - Put it in a durable case like an Otterbox Defender. A cracked screen in the backcountry is a real problem. - Download your maps before you leave service. Most apps make this easy on paid plans, but you have to remember to do it. Info In harsher conditions, rain, snow, cold, or multi-day trips, I use a handheld or a watch as my primary and use the phone as a backup. What to Look For Here are the key features that a handheld GPS should fulfill. - Give you directions to navigate a route - Have offline maps and routing so that you can do it on the fly - Have buttons that allow you to use the unit when wet, in gloves, etc. - Have a battery life of days not hours - Be durable enough to survive the outdoors, including extreme temperatures - Drop waypoints to mark camps, water sources, or bail-out points - Record your track so you have record of where you went - Customize and view key metrics like elevation, distance, and pace at a glance - Have enhanced accuracy down to 6-9ft, leveraging multiple GNSS systems and multi-band GPS The downside of a handheld GPS is that it’s another piece of gear you have to buy, charge, and update periodically. It’s generally heavier than you’d hope it would be, and the interface for many Garmin units will seem like a step back 20 years from your phone. Today there are dozens of phone apps that can handle navigation. But for me the question becomes is the phone something I can rely on when the conditions get really bad. When I’m in the backcountry I prefer to save my phone for “phone things” and use a GPS to do the heavy lifting on navigation, including any changes to plans. When you’re tired, wet, and need to get directions, the old clunky interface of a handheld GPS is much easier to use than hunting and pecking on a slick app interface on your phone. Testing Criteria I buy every GPS myself and navigate with it on real hikes before it earns a spot here. I test accuracy against known tracks in hard conditions (canyons, heavy tree cover), battery life against the spec sheet, and whether I can run the whole interface with wet hands or gloves. If a unit isn’t a meaningful upgrade in accuracy, battery, or reliability, it doesn’t make my picks, and I update this page as devices and firmware change. Here are the units I tested that didn’t make the cut. | Device | Why I Didn’t Choose It | |---|---| | GPSMAP H1i Plus | Adds a camera and mic over inReach, but accuracy and screen brightness fell behind the 67i in my testing. | | GPSMAP 66sr | Still accurate multi-band, but the 65s does essentially the same thing for less money. | | eTrex Touch | Solid hardware and accuracy, but the battery claims fall apart on trail. | | eTrex 32x | Still works as a bare-bones AA trail GPS, but the 65s is worth the step up. | Maps If you have an older Garmin handheld that takes “add maps” or you want alternate coverage on a newer one, you can load free OpenStreetMap topo maps onto it. - Download your region from GMapTool, then install using the free Garmin MapInstall and MapManager apps. Connect your GPS unit and use MapInstall to send the maps to the device. Works on Mac and Windows. Check your unit’s spec page on Garmin.com to confirm it supports added maps before you start. - For worldwide maps, check this site. - To connect to newer devices that run on MTP mode, use OpenMTP. You can also create custom maps for your GPS using CalTopo. Using Your GPS Accuracy - Turn on multi-GNSS if you have the option. GPS is the USA’s satellite system, but there are others: GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU), BeiDou (China), QZSS (Japan), IRNSS (India). They all work on the same principles. The more signals your receiver can pick from, the better the fix. If battery doesn’t matter, turn them all on. If battery matters, run GPS-only. In my experience, GPS alone works well in the US. Galileo has also been reliable. - Get a multi-band receiver if you’re buying new. This is the biggest accuracy upgrade in years. Multi-band receivers pick up both the old public GPS signal and newer civil bands from modern satellites. In practice, that means better performance in canyons, slot canyons, and urban corridors where older single-band units lose the signal. The GPSMAP 65s, 67i, Fenix 8, and Enduro 3 are all multi-band. Some newer phones are too. - Do a GPS soak at the trailhead. When you get out of your car, power on your GPS and set it on top of the car for 2-5 minutes while you lace up and pack. Let it lock onto satellites before you start recording. You’ll get a cleaner track from the first step. Just don’t drive off with it up there. - Sync your device before you leave. Your GPS downloads an almanac file (Garmin calls it EPO) that tells it where the satellites are going to be. It gets this over satellite during use, but it’s faster over WiFi. Open Garmin Connect or Garmin Explore on your phone before the trip to update the almanac and firmware. - Enable WAAS or EGNOS if your device has it. These are correction signals that account for satellite drift and atmospheric distortion. They’ll improve accuracy at a small battery cost. If battery matters, turn them off. - Check the satellite screen. On a Garmin handheld, there’s a satellite page that shows a sky map of every signal you’re receiving. The center is directly overhead, the edge is the horizon, and there’s a 45-degree line in between. Ideally, you want satellites on all four compass points at or above that 45-degree line. If they’re all clustered together, your fix will be weaker. - Live with environmental limits. Canyons, thick canopy, and even solar weather can interfere with GPS. There’s a space weather report that shows how disturbed the ionosphere is. If accuracy really matters, get to higher ground with an open view of the sky. When the sky is blocked, no GPS is going to save you. Battery and Recording - Turn off smart recording for the most accurate track. On Garmin, smart recording drops track points based on movement detection, which can create big gaps. I set my recording to “every second” instead. Just remember to pause the unit when you stop, or you’ll get dozens of overlapping points from a device that thinks it’s moving. Unpaused, 10 feet of GPS noise over a minute stopped can add 600 feet of phantom distance. - Tracks are just the distances between points. If you and a friend record the same hike with different settings, your totals won’t match. More points, more chances for noise. Fewer points, more chances for shortcutting corners. Neither is wrong, they’re just different recording strategies. - Clean up your tracks after. Load the GPX into Basecamp, Garmin Connect, or CalTopo and delete any obvious outlier points. A single dropped signal can add hundreds of feet of distance. A minute of cleanup gets you a much more accurate record. - Kill what you’re not using to save battery. Bluetooth, WiFi, notifications, map shading, and the backlight all draw power. On a multi-day trip, turn off anything you don’t need. If your handheld takes AAs, lithium AAs last noticeably longer than alkaline. GPX Files - A GPX file is a plain text file that stores geographic data, specifically routes, tracks, and waypoints. It is the universal standard used to save your recorded activities, load trail plans onto a GPS device, or share navigation data with others. - Tracks are breadcrumb trails, routes are a series of waypoints that your device will calculate the path between. - Modern Garmin devices use something called a Course, which is a combination of a route and track. Course points are waypoints along your route. Navigation - Plan on a real screen. The best planning happens on a computer with CalTopo or the Footpath/AllTrails web app. Export the GPX, then sync or drag it onto your device. The mobile apps are fine, but nothing beats a big monitor for a complex route. - Carry it with the antenna up. On a handheld, clip it to a pack strap with a carabiner, antenna pointing at the sky. A unit buried in a pocket or stuffed in a pack fights for signal and burns battery doing it. - Drop waypoints at decision points. When you hit a tricky junction, a water source, or a campsite, take 10 seconds to mark a waypoint. On the way back, or if you get turned around, those marks can save you. - Use waypoint averaging for a precise fix. If you really need an accurate location, marking a cache, a trailhead, or a water source for future trips, use waypoint averaging. The GPS takes multiple readings over time and averages them for a much tighter position than a single drop. - Elevation is approximate. GPS elevation can be off by hundreds of feet. If your device has a barometric altimeter, use it and calibrate it from a known elevation at the trailhead. Treat all elevation numbers as a ballpark, not a measurement. General - How much accuracy do you actually need? Survey-grade GPS units get you centimeter precision and cost thousands. Follow the tips above and a consumer unit will get you 8-12 feet. That’s plenty for navigation, recording, and finding your way home. Unless you’re competing on Strava segments or doing real survey work, you don’t need more. - Sync apps before you leave the house. An app update can log you out, and if that happens off-grid, you’re stuck. Open every app paired with your GPS the night before and make sure it’s signed in and synced. - Know the difference between GPS and satellite messaging. A GPS is a receiver, it doesn’t broadcast anything. You can put it next to your head and nothing happens. A satellite communicator (like an inReach) actually transmits to a satellite. They’re different tools that often live in the same box. Here’s my sat comm guide if you want one device that does both. And of course, always bring a paper map as backup.

item.title: RECCO Reflector Review: What It Is & Does It Work
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.16
RECCO Reflector Review Reviewed August 2026 Cheap, weightless insurance for being found, but only where rescue teams have detectors, and never instead of a satellite communicator. A RECCO reflector is a battery-free radar tag that makes you searchable to equipped rescue teams when you can’t call for help. After two years with one on my pack and talking to the SAR professionals who train with the detectors: if teams in your area carry them, it’s worth the $40. If they don’t, skip it. Either way, your primary is a satellite communicator; this is the passive backup that answers when every battery is dead. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Video What I learned in the two years since recommending the RECCO: what SAR teams told me, the documented rescues, and where it falls short. How It Works Crack one open and you’d find two foil antennas connected by a diode. No battery, no electronics, no registration. It’s a harmonic reflector, not an RFID tag. - The detector does the work. Rescuers carry a handheld detector, or fly a helicopter-mounted one, that broadcasts a specific radar frequency (917 MHz). - The reflector answers. When the signal hits the reflector, the diode doubles the frequency and bounces it back (1834 MHz). The detector hears that answer as a distinct chirp, so rescuers know it’s a RECCO and not a random piece of metal. - Closer means louder. The stronger the chirp, the closer the searcher is to you. The helicopter detector sweeps about a 300-foot swath and can clear roughly a square kilometer every six minutes. - False hits happen. Detectors sometimes get weak reflections off phones, radios, and other electronics, even powered off. A real reflector returns a much stronger, cleaner signal, and any ping still gives searchers a clue. Rescue Record Has RECCO found anyone? The question that matters, in three parts. - Documented live saves exist, all in avalanches. A skier in Spain was located alive under the snow in 2015, the first case published in medical literature. Another was found alive under 3.2 meters of snow in Switzerland in 2019. RECCO’s own count is 17 live saves through 2019, mostly in Europe, none in the US. - Recoveries are more common. Most confirmed finds are body recoveries, including climber Marc-André Leclerc (from the film The Alpinist) in Alaska in 2018, where rescuers who worked the search say RECCO was essential to locating him. That’s worth something on its own: it ends a search and gives a family an answer. - No documented live save of a lost hiker yet. The technology doesn’t care whether you’re alive, a reflector answers either way. The record is thin on summer rescues because few hikers carry reflectors and detector coverage is still growing. Every SAR professional I’ve talked to says the same thing: the tool works, the bottleneck is people carrying it. Coverage A reflector is only useful where someone has a detector. Check before you buy. - Check the coverage map. RECCO publishes a map of every team and resort with detectors that you can filter by handheld and helicopter units. If nobody near your trails has one, skip it. - US helicopter coverage is small but growing. Eleven US agencies fly the SAR helicopter detector as of mid-2026, including LA County Sheriff (the only one in California) and a new unit covering the Sierra out of Reno. Hundreds of ski patrols and SAR teams carry handhelds. - One reflector works everywhere. Detector frequencies vary slightly by country, but the same reflector answers all of them, US and Europe alike. Carrying It - You might already own one. RECCO has been sewn into ski jackets, pants, and helmets for over a decade, and it’s now showing up in backpacks and even trail runners. Check your gear for the logo before buying anything. - Old reflectors don’t expire. There’s no battery to die and nothing to wear out. A reflector in a 2012 jacket works like a new one. - Placement matters. Anything between the reflector and the detector weakens the signal, including your body, which is mostly water. High on your pack keeps it clear if you’re face down. The other school of thought puts it on your person (a belt loop) in case you’re separated from your pack. Or carry one in each spot. Be Searchable The reflector is one layer in a system. If you can’t hit SOS (heart attack, stroke, rockfall), these are the layers that get you found: - Leave a plan. Send someone your route link and a turnaround time. Searchers start where your plan says, not from the whole mountain. - Note your RECCO in your emergency details. Add “carrying RECCO reflector” to your inReach or PLB emergency notes and tell whoever holds your trip plan. SAR can only deploy a detector if they know to look for one. - Turn on tracking. inReach breadcrumbs give rescuers a trail to your last known point. - The RECCO is the last line of defense. A PLB’s homing beacon and your phone are useless after a few days of battery drain. The reflector still answers. From the comments: if everyone carries one, how do rescuers know who’s lost? They don’t scan the whole planet. They grid a defined search area for a missing person, and any return in that area gets checked. More reflectors make the tool stronger, not weaker. Worth $40? The materials inside are worth maybe $2, and yes, you could technically build one. What you’re paying for is a tested, sealed unit that’s part of a system rescue teams train on, and RECCO reinvests a portion of reflector sales into putting detectors in SAR hands, which is the only way coverage grows. For me the math is simple: a few grams and $40 for a chance of being found when nothing else on my pack works, and at worst, a faster answer for my family. I’m still carrying mine. If you hike where teams have detectors, it’s cheap insurance. If you don’t, spend the money elsewhere, and check the full gear list for where I’d put it instead.

item.title: Guadalupe Peak Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.13
Guadalupe Peak Hike Updated & Reviewed August 2026 With 3,000 ft of steep climbing, it’s not a beginner hike, and weather can make you turn around. At 8,751 feet, Guadalupe Peak is the highest point in Texas and one of the most rewarding hikes in the USA. You’ll climb the Guadalupe Peak Trail, starting in desert scrub and finishing above the clouds on an incredible summit ridge. It’s a tough but doable hike, and in this guide I’ll show you how to hike it safely yourself. - Distance - 8.4 mi - Difficulty - Hard - Total Climbing - 3000 ft - Time - 4–8 hrs Video I made a video of what it’s like to do the hike so that you can watch it and be prepared when you do it yourself. Trailhead Info Trailhead Address: Pine Springs Trailhead, Salt Flat, TX 79847. There is a fee to enter the park or use your National Parks Pass. Guadalupe Peak is remote. - There is no gas station between El Paso and the park, or Carlsbad and the park. - Bring all the food you need with you. - You can refill with water at the Visitor Center or at the campground by the trailhead. - Guadalupe Mountains National Park is situated right on the edge of two time zones (Mountain and Central Standard Time), and the time on your phone could be incorrect. Parking can be a big challenge for this hike. The main lot has about 44 spaces, but they can fill up quickly. Your best bet is to arrive at sunrise for the hike and you’re generally assured to get a spot. As the morning progresses it can get tougher and tougher, and often after 730am the parking lot can be full. If the lot is full, you’ll have to park at the Visitor Center (also not a big lot) and walk up from there. I’d say if you’re going to come all the way here to do the hike, get here around sunrise. Camping There’s a small backcountry campground about a mile below the summit, accessible only by hiking up the Guadalupe Peak Trail. It has a few tent pads and no water, so you’ll need to carry everything you need, including extra water for the night and descent. Camping here gives you a head start for sunrise or sunset at the summit, but be prepared for strong winds and cold temperatures, even in warmer months. Permits are required and available at the Pine Springs Visitor Center or on Recreation.gov in advance. Info After the first mile or so of climbing, the trail enters the Guadalupe Mountains Wilderness, and from there all human waste and toilet paper must be carried out. Bring a WAG Bag in case you have to “take care of business.” Maps | Resource | What It’s For | |---|---| | CalTopo Map | Interactive map for planning and printing | | GPX Download | Put my route on your GPS | | AllTrails recent reports | What other hikers are seeing now | | Trailhead Weather | Forecast at the trailhead, including wind | | Summit Wind Forecast | Elevation-specific wind speed near the top | | Park Alerts & Conditions | Current closures and hazard notices | Directions Mile 0 - 1.5: The Big Effort The first 1.5 miles is the hardest part for many hikers. It’s steep, rocky, and doesn’t offer many spots to catch your breath. Info The El Capitan Trail goes to a viewpoint below it. There is no official trail to the top of El Capitan. Mile 1.5-3.3: The Breather After the initial tough climb, the grade eases and you traverse a north-facing slope where the cooler temperatures allow for evergreens like Douglas Fir and Ponderosa Pines. Mile 3.4-4.2: The Last Push The last mile to the summit is steep and tough, especially if you’re not used to the altitude. Take your time and take breaks. Miles 4.2-8.4: The Descent The 4.2-mile descent is harder than most hikers expect. Focusing on footing the whole way down on steep, rocky terrain is tiring, and the constant downhill impact hits the knees. Trekking poles help a lot on this stretch.

item.title: The Wave Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.94
The Wave Hike Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Hiking to The Wave in Arizona can be overwhelming. There are permits, a remote location, and off-trail hiking. I’ll show you how to hike it safely and easily in this guide. Despite all the hassle, the Wave is spectacular and worth it. - Distance - 6.5 mi - Difficulty - Moderate - Total Climbing - 1000 ft - Time - 4–6 hrs Video Here’s a video I shot on the trails outlining what you need to look for and what the experience is like so you’re prepared when you get there yourself. Permits | Lottery Type | Details | |---|---| | 4-Month Advance Lottery | Rolling 4-month lottery, apply 4 months in advance of your desired date. 48 people allowed per day. BLM mails you the permit and info packet. No briefing or in-person pickup needed. | | 2-day Lottery | Applied through the Recreation.gov app, must be geofenced within the Page and Kanab area (won’t work from the Grand Canyon). 16 people per day. If you win, pick up your permit the next day in Page or Kanab and attend a safety briefing there. | Choosing the right time to do the hike is important. | Season | Notes | |---|---| | Spring and Fall | Peak seasons, cooler temperatures and decent weather. Advance lottery success rate is about 2%. | | Winter | Great time to go, lottery success rate jumps to around 10%. Snow and rain can make the drive to the trailhead impassable. | | Summer | Temperatures can be deadly, people have died from heat-related issues. Leave very early, even before dawn, to beat the heat, and don’t risk it if it’s too hot. Also monsoon season, when flash floods can occur. | You can also do a guided tour with an outfitter to The Wave, but know that you still need to obtain a permit on your own. Read the directions in this guide before you book. I do a lot of guides and this hike isn’t very doable without a guide service. Trailhead The Wave doesn’t fit nicely into any type of National Park or Forest. It’s located in Coyote Buttes North, which is part of the Paria Canyon-Vermilion Cliffs Wilderness, which is also part of the Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, which is not managed by the Park Service, but rather the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). Confusing? Yup… | Destination | Drive Time | |---|---| | Zion National Park | 2 hours | | Grand Canyon South Rim | 3 hours | | Las Vegas | 4 hours | | Phoenix | 5 hours | When planning your trip to The Wave, staying in Page, AZ or Kanab, UT makes the most sense. Both towns have plenty of lodging and food options, with Page having more and a Walmart. There are also two primitive campgrounds, Stateline Campground and White House Campground, which require driving down dirt and sand roads to reach. They are remote and don’t have any supplies or facilities nearby. The condition of the road to the trailhead can vary. Generally in dry conditions, it’s pretty tame. After rain or snow the mud can be extremely slippery, almost like ice. I’ve seen low-clearance cars at the trailhead over the years, so it is doable. But if you’re traveling here and renting, I highly recommend opting for a 4-wheel drive vehicle like a Jeep. It will take any anxiety about the drive out of the equation. Maps | Resource | What It’s For | |---|---| | CalTopo Map | Interactive map for planning and printing | | GPX Download | Put my route on your GPS | | AllTrails recent reports | What other hikers are seeing now | | Trailhead Weather | Extreme heat check, no shade or water | | BLM Permits & Alerts | Lottery odds, closures, road status | - The BLM will give you a printed guide with the landmarks along the hike. It’s helpful to bring this. - Some sections are on rock, and some sections are in the sand. You can follow the footsteps in the sand, but the rock is much harder. - I use my phone GPS with AllTrails Pro to make sure I’m in the right place. - I’ve seen some other guides recommend that you use offline Google Maps, but the trail line isn’t the same as the actual trail. - There are lots of other places to explore along the hike. I’ve included them in the map and GPX file below. Notes - Most of the rock you see on the hike is called Navajo Sandstone. Millions of years of wind and water shaped the rock. Oxidation of all the minerals created the colors. - The sandstone is fragile. Leave no trace. Take all your trash out, leave everything else as is. - How did The Wave get so popular? It was first featured in a German nature documentary in 1996 called Faszination Natur, which led European tourists on a hunt to surface the location. When Instagram exploded in the early 2010s, the spot became overrun, leading to the implementation of the permit system you see today.

item.title: Mt LeConte Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.70
Great Smoky Mountains National Park Mt LeConte Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026
The hike to Mount LeConte from the Alum Cave Trail is considered the marquis trail in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. It’s a challenging hike but very doable by most folks. The trail is beautiful, easy to follow, and offers lots to see along the way.
- Distance - 11.2–12 mi
- Difficulty - Hard
- Total Climbing - 3050–3100 ft
- Time - 6–8 hrs
Who It's For Strong hikers who can handle all the climbing. Biggest Risk Lightning on exposed summit ridge. Turn back if afternoon storms develop, weather escalates fast. When to Go April-November. Winter can bring snow and ice.
Video Here’s a video I shot of what it’s like to hike the trail and what you can expect if you do it yourself.
Trailhead
Notes
- According to the USGS, Mt LeConte is named after Joseph Le Conte (1823-1901), a geologist and early conservationist. Le Conte was a co-founder of the Sierra Club with John Muir in 1892. He was such a popular guy that after he died in 1901, he became the namesake for Le Conte Glacier, Le Conte Canyon, Le Conte Divide, Le Conte Falls, Le Conte Mountain, and Le Conte Lodge. - But some people say it’s named after Joseph’s older brother, John, who helped measure the mountain’s elevation. - These mountains formed around 480 million years ago, making them some of the oldest in the world. The rounded peaks you see today are the result of 200 million years of erosion. Maps
Directions
Info The arch came into being as the softer rock underneath the harder rock was worn away by the cycle of freezing and thawing.
Info Alum Cave Bluffs is a vast overhanging cliff, named for the alum deposits found here in the 1800s.
Tip For a better viewpoint, continue straight past the summit on the short downhill.
Tip You can avoid the spur to Cliff Top and just go straight down.

item.title: Limestone Canyon and The Sinks Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.69
Limestone Canyon Regional Park is an incredibly beautiful area to hike, but it’s also home to a famous area called ‘The Sinks,’ also known as ’the little Grand Canyon of Orange County.’ Limestone Canyon is not always open to the public, but this easy trail guide will show you how to visit and see The Sinks for yourself. Distance 9 mi Difficulty Moderate Total Climbing 850 ft Time 3–4 hrs GearFitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 1L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here. Limestone Canyon Regional Park is located in Orange County, CA, in the foothills of the Santa Ana Mountains.Before visiting Limestone Canyon Regional Park, you must register for an open event. Go to “Activities” and filter by “Limestone Canyon Nature Preserve” Find a match for the day that you want to visit. There are two types of hikes. Open hikes allow you to pick any open trails you’d like and hike freely. Docent-led hikes are traditional group hikes led by an expert. These hikes are great because you’ll usually get a guided tour along the way. Note that the hikes have difficulty ratings; you should find one that matches your level. Hikes can have different starting areas. The website has a downloadable map of the current trails and starting areas. Maps If you go on a general open day, I recommend hiking to The Sinks, aka the Mini-Grand Canyon, the main attraction. This guide has directions for that hike. There are many more trails and you could include others to choose your own adventure as well.

item.title: South Kaibab Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.65
South Kaibab Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026 The South Kaibab Trail is a must‑do Grand Canyon hike with big views from start to finish. Follow the ridge to iconic spots like Ooh Aah Point, Cedar Ridge, and Skeleton Point, each offering a different perspective of the canyon. The NPS recommends Skeleton Point as the farthest turnaround for most day hikers, and there’s no water anywhere on the trail, so start early and come prepared. In this guide, I’ll show you exactly how to hike each section the easy way. - Distance - 1.8–6 mi - Difficulty - Moderate - Total Climbing - 600–2200 ft - Time - 1–5 hrs Info Kaibab is a word of Southern Paiute origin meaning “mountain lying down,” aka inverted mountain. Video I shot a video outlining what the trail looks like and what you can expect when you do this yourself. Dangers Overall the South Kaibab Trail is safe. I’ve seen people of all shapes, sizes, ages, and fitness levels do these hikes. The trail is well-maintained, easy to follow, consistently about 4 feet wide, and has wider sections for passing. But you still need to be mindful of a few things. - When people get into trouble on the South Kaibab Trail, it’s usually because of the heat. The trail is totally exposed with no shade, so in hot weather it can be brutal. Even in the shade, summer temperatures often exceed 100F (38C). Check the weather and park alerts regarding the heat. - The hike back up is much harder than going down. Many first-time Grand Canyon hikers overcommit on the easy downhill and pay for it on the climb out. A good rule of thumb: expect the hike up to take about twice as long as the hike down. - Snow and ice can linger on the upper sections in winter, especially in the morning. Be prepared for slippery, frozen sections near the rim, so bring microspikes. - Outside of the trailhead and Colorado River, there is no water anywhere on the South Kaibab Trail. You have to carry all the water you need, and in summer that can mean several liters per person. - The trail is generally wide enough to hike comfortably and pass other hikers. But people have also died after getting too close to the edge (taking pictures). Be conservative. - Mules also use the trail, so be ready to step aside in safe areas when they pass. Trailhead The road to the South Kaibab Trailhead (Yaki Point Road) is closed to vehicles. Here’s what I would recommend. - Take the free Orange shuttle bus from the Visitor Center. This is by far the easiest way to get back and forth to the trail. If you want to get an early start, take the Hiker’s Express Shuttle, which is set up for long distance hikers but can be used by anyone. Getting an early start is a smart way to beat the crowds and see the sunrise in the canyon. - You can also walk from the Visitor Center along the wide and easy Rim Trail. It’s about 2.2 miles and takes most folks around 40-60 minutes. - There’s a very small parking lot along Desert View Drive, not intended for hikers but rather as a turn-off for drivers. From here you can walk about 0.5 miles to the Rim Trail and then to the South Kaibab trailhead. Maps | Resource | What It’s For | |---|---| | CalTopo Map | Interactive map for planning and printing | | GPX Download | Put my route on your GPS | | AllTrails recent reports | What other hikers are seeing now | | Rim Weather | Trailhead forecast | | Inner Canyon Weather | How much hotter it gets below the rim | | Key Hiking Messages | Water status, heat risk, trail conditions | Directions Trailhead to Ooh Ahh Point Info The South Kaibab Trail was built by engineers in 1924-25 to create a smooth and direct route down to the river. It has been described as “a trail in a hurry to get to the river.” Info At the bottom of the canyon, the layers date back 1.84 BILLION years! To put that in perspective, the Earth is 4.543 billion years old. Info If this is your final destination, turn around and hike back from here. Ooh Ahh Point to Cedar Ridge Info While Cedar Ridge seems open and a great place to camp, no camping is allowed along the South Kaibab Trail. If this is your final destination, turn around and hike back from here. Cedar Ridge to Skeleton Point Info The South Kaibab Trail is part of the Arizona Trail (AZT), which stretches about 800 miles from Mexico to Utah.

item.title: HMD OffGrid Review: Satellite SOS Without a Garmin
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.62
HMD OffGrid Review Reviewed August 2026 Not a Garmin inReach replacement, but a smart lightweight backup if you mostly hike in North America. I’ve been using the HMD OffGrid since it came out. No global coverage, no navigation, no weather, and it needs your phone for most functionality. Coverage is in select areas of North America, Canada, Europe, and Australia/New Zealand; if you need true worldwide coverage, this is not it. But as a supplement to a satellite-enabled phone, it’s a solid buy. Messaging is fast, battery is good for its size, and SOS coverage is bundled into every plan. At $6.66/month on the Freedom plan, that’s hard to beat. If you mostly hike in the lower 48 and want a backup you can clip to your pack and forget about until you need it, the HMD OffGrid makes sense. For a full comparison with Garmin and other options, see my best satellite communicator picks. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Video Features - No screen. It’s designed to be used with your smartphone (iOS or Android). If your phone dies, your options are limited to the physical SOS button. It does work when your phone is in airplane mode. - Messaging, SOS, and location breadcrumb sharing are the core features. - Uses GEO satellites via Skylo instead of Iridium LEO. In practice: faster messaging, slightly more directional sensitivity. - SOS coverage is included in every plan. If you’re billed for a rescue, Overwatch & Rescue covers it directly. - Battery life is acceptable for a 60g device: good for long day hikes and weekend trips. - IP68-rated. No durability issues over many miles in rain and rough conditions. Messaging Pair the device with the HMD OffGrid app via Bluetooth to access full messaging. The app is free and works without a device, so friends and family can receive messages without owning one. A few things to know: - Available on Android and iOS. - Your phone number is your user ID. - The app automatically sends via WiFi or cellular when available, saving satellite usage. You can force satellite-only if needed, and it defaults to satellite in airplane mode. - If the recipient doesn’t have the HMD OffGrid app, they get an SMS asking them to download it (free) to reply. - The app shows message status: sent, sent via satellite, and read confirmations. - Currently text-only. HMD has demoed voice notes over satellite, but as of now that feature isn’t available, and I wouldn’t buy this assuming it will ship. Reliability The HMD OffGrid uses geostationary satellites (GEO) through the Skylo network, fixed at around 22,000 miles above the equator. That’s different from Garmin inReach, which uses Iridium’s low-earth orbit (LEO) network where dozens of satellites pass overhead each hour. GEO has tradeoffs. Messages often go out faster since you’re connecting to the same stationary satellite repeatedly. But the farther north you go, Alaska, northern Canada, Scandinavia, the lower the satellite angle, which makes connections harder. In my experience it’s connected the majority of the time, though it’s more directionally sensitive than other communicators. One of the GEO providers used is ViaSat, the same network behind in-flight internet on commercial airlines. SOS SOS is fully bundled into every HMD OffGrid plan, which is one of its strongest selling points. Unlike Garmin, where you either accept the risk or add separate insurance, HMD bundles Overwatch & Rescue emergency assistance into every plan, which in many common scenarios can cover coordination and certain rescue costs. How it works: - Trigger SOS from the physical button on the device or from the app. - The alert goes to Overwatch & Rescue, a 24/7 response center staffed by former military, law enforcement, paramedics, and first responders. - They build a full response case file, contact your emergency contacts, coordinate with local agencies, and stay involved until you’re safe. - Any rescue-related costs, like private evacuation or transport fees, are covered directly. You send the bill, they handle it. No reimbursement process. You can also use the SOS button for a Good Samaritan call, triggering help for someone else in trouble. No liability, no penalty. Tracking Tracking works like other communicators: set a ping interval, and the app creates a breadcrumb trail you can share. If there’s no satellite connection, the device buffers track points and sends them when signal returns. Positioning uses an internal chipset with GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, and BeiDou. Battery It’s a small device at 60g, so battery is shorter than a full inReach. With location sharing and a few messages per day: around 2% drain per hour, projecting to about 50 hours. With lighter use it drops to around 1% per hour, getting you closer to 100 hours. Plans Two plans. Run the math for your usage before choosing. | Plan | Annual Cost | Per Month | Activation Fee | Messages/Year | |---|---|---|---|---| | Freedom | $79.99 | $6.66 | $19.99 | 350 | | Unlimited | $139.99 | $11.66 | $9.99 | Unlimited | Unlimited live tracking is an optional add-on at $4.99/month. SOS/Overwatch & Rescue is included in both plans. Freedom is $79.99/year with up to 350 messages; Unlimited is $14.99/month or $139.99/year with unlimited messages. If you were going to buy rescue insurance separately anyway, the Freedom plan at $6.66/month covers it and gives you messaging too.
