item.title: Love Sideloading on Android? Watch Out for This Upcoming Rule Change
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.57
Android is changing the way sideloading works on your smartphone or tablet, and the first major step is now rolling out to devices. First announced last August, the changes are designed to make it harder for casual users to mistakenly download malware. The first part of the change is gradually rolling out now to devices. Announced in a Reddit post, Google called this its "first version of the advanced flow," restricting users from downloading apps from unverified developers. The advanced flow is intentionally more difficult to use on the first try and is designed to discourage users from downloading apps from untrustworthy sources. It won't affect any apps from developers who have registered with Google, regardless of where you downloaded the software. After the changes roll out, to continue sideloading an app from an unverified developer, you’ll need to wait 24 hours after enabling an option in your phone's settings and restarting your device. If you choose to do this once, you can use an option to avoid having to repeat the steps later. Google’s logic is that this better protects the average user from downloading dangerous software from bad actors, while allowing power users and developers to continue sideloading onto their devices. The new scheme begins on Sept. 30 for users in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand, with a planned global expansion to all app installations at some point in 2027. Google has yet to suggest what time of year to expect the changes. How to Continue Sideloading Apps Once Advanced Flow Is Active To keep access after this new option is enabled, you will need to make a change in the Developer Options on your device. This feature is gradually rolling out, so you may not find it available immediately. You have always needed Developer Mode enabled to sideload apps, and you can turn it on by heading to Settings > About Phone and tapping Build Number seven times. Once available, head to Developer Options, select Apps from unverified developers, then turn on Allow apps from unverified developers. You’ll be asked to enter your screen lock and confirm that you’re not being prompted by someone else to make a change to your phone. The biggest roadblock is that you will then have to restart your device and wait 24 hours before you can begin downloading apps from unverified developers. After a day has passed, head back to the Settings and choose to allow apps for either seven days or indefinitely. If you are sideloading regularly, choose indefinitely, as you’ll have to wait another 24 hours if you download any more unverified software after the initial week is up. Once activated, you will continue to see a warning about apps as you install them, but you can override them to download without restrictions. item.title: Claude Can Now Send Gmail Messages, Sometimes on Your Behalf
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.19
Anthropic’s Claude now has more control over Gmail, allowing its AI to send emails on your behalf. The Claude connector for Google Workspace has been available for over a year to help you manage your Google accounts, but this is the first time it can send an AI-generated message. The tool now lets you enter a prompt to ask Claude to draft, reply to, or forward emails, and you can choose whether to confirm approval of the task before sending or let Claude send without a final check. By default, you'll be asked to approve all messages, with Anthropic saying those on Team and Enterprise plans will see "owners decide whether members can allow these actions to run without asking each time.” The feature is now available for everyone on paid Claude plans of all tiers. The upgrade also improves file management in its Google Drive integration by enabling prompts to share, move, or delete files across your cloud storage. Anthropic says it will, by default, ask for approval before each of these actions, much like it does when sending emails. Anthropic confirms it can’t do everything with Gmail, saying current limitations mean you can’t access attachments directly through the Workspace connector tool. It also says it may struggle to load a large inbox or interact with particularly complex Gmail filters. Claude also can't extract images embedded in Drive files, instead focusing its AI tools on text. The tool also gives you access to your Google Calendar, although there are no changes to the service in this latest update. You can continue to view, create, update, and manage events, as well as set up recurring meetings or manage attendees. Claude’s Cowork agentic tools are also now available across all mobile and web interfaces if you have a paid account. Anthropic confirmed the rollout finished on Aug. 18, allowing you to ask Cowork to start a task and then pick up the results on another logged-in device later. It means you can now run a task on your computer and access the results on your smartphone or another less powerful device. item.title: Firefox Just Proved AI Browser Features Don't Have to Suck (or Spy on You)
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.98
Firefox has embraced AI more slowly than other browser giants, such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge, which quickly went all in on AI, from agents to omnipresent assistants. However, the situation is changing, as the latest Firefox update brings a new type of Smart Window browser tabs, AI-powered tab grouping, and visual previews of your browsing history. After meeting with the company about these features and trying them out for myself, I’m a big fan of Firefox's vision for AI browsers. Here's what you need to know. What Firefox’s New AI Upgrade Does—and How to Get It As mentioned, Firefox is gaining an AI-powered system for grouping similar tabs, Smart Window tabs that allow you to directly prompt your AI model of choice, and visual previews of your browsing history to help you pick up where you left off. Mozilla also announced a partnership with Exa to help power the Smart Window feature. As of this writing, these new features are available only in English to users in Canada and the US. Somewhat confusingly, you can't access them by simply updating your browser or enabling them in the settings. After you update your browser, you must go through Smart Window’s onboarding process here. Smart Window: An AI Assistant That Stays Out of Your Way The experience with Smart Window in Firefox is about the same as with an AI chatbot or any other AI web browser that lets you prompt an assistant directly. You can ask questions, change models, and share tabs with it, all of which work as expected. For example, I asked Smart Window in Fast mode for the top restaurants in my area, and it gave me a reasonable list, along with articles I could read for further recommendations. Then, when I shared one of those articles back to Smart Window as a tab, it had no trouble understanding the page and picking out the restaurant recommendations. Just keep in mind that the quality of responses depends on the model you use. If you’re using Fast mode, which runs on Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, you shouldn't expect the deepest answers. Smart Window doesn't support the newest, most advanced models by default, but it performs just fine for casual queries. The latest AI models often don't offer dramatic improvements for simple tasks, after all. Tab Grouping: Simple, Effective, and Surprisingly Useful The Tab Grouping feature also works as advertised. During testing, I ran another Google search for restaurants in my area and opened several tabs. Then, when I clicked Firefox’s Organize Tabs button, it quickly sorted all my restaurant-related tabs into a group. The feature also gives tab groups a name: In my case, it was the name of the town in which the restaurants were located. Microsoft Edge’s similar Organize Tabs function works just as effectively, for comparison. Visual History Previews: A Smarter Way to Track Down Old Tabs Firefox’s visual previews work reliably, but the results ultimately depend on what pages you visit and if there’s a preview attached to the site in question. The AI component here isn't the previews themselves; rather, it's finding the relevant entries in your history and highlighting them for you. When I opened Smart Window and asked Firefox to show me the restaurants I had looked at earlier, it displayed tiles with images of the sites I had visited. However, sometimes you get a tile with an image that’s just a Google logo or something similar, depending on what you ask for and your browsing history. Why Mozilla’s "User-First" Philosophy Beat Chrome's Bloat None of these features is exciting enough to convince a Chrome loyalist or heavy Edge user to switch to Firefox, but I'm far more excited about how they play into Mozilla’s larger vision for AI in Firefox. Whereas Google and Microsoft shove their AI tools into just about every product and service possible, Firefox still lets you opt in to its AI features or easily block all related features and pop-ups. Meanwhile, if I want to remove the Gemini button in Gmail, I have to look up a guide on how to do that. You can also disable individual features in Firefox, too. For example, if you like the idea of the Smart Window but aren’t interested in tab groups, you can stick with just the former. When I spoke with Ajit Varma, head of Firefox, about these features, he acknowledged that “some people are really leaned into AI, and some people are more skeptical." Mozilla’s approach is to “create something that is easy for the people who really want to experiment with new things and easy to turn off for those who don't.” User choice extends to model availability, too. By default, Firefox supports Exa, Gemini, GPT, and Qwen, but you can connect other models, too, including local ones. According to Mozilla, building not a closed AI stack but an open AI ecosystem aligns with the company’s belief that “the web is strongest when it encourages technology competition and variety.” Mozilla’s approach is to “create something that is easy for the people who really want to experiment with new things and easy to turn off for those who don't.”
Beyond user choice, privacy is another core focus for AI in Firefox. Accordingly, Mozilla doesn’t keep your chats, sell your data, or train its models with your data. It processes only a limited amount of technical information. Where possible, Firefox relies on local models, such as for tab grouping, that don’t require a server. Smart Window tabs also store memories on your local machine, and you retain control over what they remember. During my conversation with Varma, what struck me most was how in tune Mozilla seems to be with what users want. Varma followed the rise of AI agents in web browsers aimed at automating the browsing experience, but his takeaway from talking to users was that “a lot of people don't necessarily want an agent to do everything. They actually want to look at the restaurants they might want to book. They actually want to, you know, potentially read documents.” Considering my unimpressive experiences with AI agents and OpenAI shutting down its agent-focused Atlas browser after less than a year, this all tracks with my experience. In my experience, when Google adds a new Gemini feature to Chrome or its search engine, it's usually something I put up with rather than something I actually want (to say nothing of Google’s obsession with vacuuming up every byte of my data). Meanwhile, Mozilla is taking the time to introduce features that you might actually want, giving you a choice, and protecting your data. This is a vision for AI browser features that I can support. The Verdict: Firefox Proves AI Can Be Helpful Without Being Intrusive I’m not a huge fan of AI features in web browsers, since I can get most of what I want out by clicking a bookmark and loading up a chatbot’s website. That said, I can genuinely imagine using common-sense features like easily grouping tabs or sorting through my history more quickly. More importantly, Mozilla’s approach to adding AI features to Firefox makes me much more willing to try them than the ones in Chrome. About Our Expert I’ve been writing about consumer technology and video games for over a decade at a variety of publications, including Destructoid, GamesRadar+, Lifewire, PCGamesN, Trusted Reviews, and What Hi-Fi?, among many others. At PCMag, I review AI and productivity software—everything from chatbots to to-do list apps. In my free time, I’m likely cooking something, playing a game, or tinkering with my computer.

item.title: Googlebook Launch Event Confirmed, Set for Sept. 15 in NYC
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.54
Google is hosting a launch event dedicated to its new Googlebook laptop range in New York City on Sept. 15, according to Chrome Unboxed. The website received an invite, though Google has yet to make a public announcement, which may mean it's designed for press, without a livestream. Designed to unify its ChromeOS and Android platforms into a more functional, laptop-first operating system, Googlebooks will be more powerful than Chromebooks and built from the ground up to be AI-native. Google suggests its new operating system could be used to create custom widgets on the fly. We've had a few hints of different Googlebook designs from partners over the past few months, but this event will give attendees hands on time with a range of partner devices. Although Google doesn't name them, it's likely that previously announced partners like Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo will be among them. Google will also reportedly hold a keynote to formally introduce the new brand and its intent, as well as the software platform, including the operating system. Journalists will also reportedly be able to photograph, film, and benchmark the laptops in person, so we may get some real performance and efficiency data from the event. The main website for the Googlebook still lists an "Autumn 2026" release window, so a September reveal followed by an October release may make sense. It would also align the laptops for sale during the holiday season. Confirmed features for the new range so far include a "magic pointer" that lets you have Gemini AI interact with anything on screen, a way to run phone apps natively on a laptop, easy file and data transitions between devices, and the return of the iconic Glowbar. We still don't know what Googlebook devices will cost, but judging by the prices of most 2026 laptops, they won't be cheap. These likely won't be $300 Qualcomm Snapdragon C laptops, but they could use Intel Wildcat Lake chips. They're unlikely to target the multi-thousand-dollar market either, at least not with the base versions. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: American Airlines Will Add Seatback Screens to Narrowbody Jets
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.53
In 2028, American Airlines will upgrade many of its smaller Airbus and Boeing jets, adding 4K screens with Bluetooth audio to seatbacks for passengers' enjoyment. The move marks a reversal for the Fort Worth, Texas, carrier, which in early 2017 decided to stop ordering screens on new single-aisle mainline planes and to remove displays already installed or on order for those aircraft while keeping screens on widebody jets. AA’s thinking at the time: Everybody will bring their own device, so we can save on display weight and instead provide Wi-Fi fast enough to stream Netflix, plus our own onboard streaming. That assumption aged poorly as AA’s competitor Delta Air Lines made seatback screens based on cheaper, lighter hardware part of its standard experience. In 2021, United Airlines announced its own commitment to audio-video-on-demand (AVOD), including Bluetooth support, on narrowbody jets. Since then, both Delta and United have increasingly made onboard tech part of their pitch to passengers. AA’s change, which it announced Tuesday, comes with more than the promise of screens with higher resolution than the average laptop (sizes go unmentioned) that welcome Bluetooth headphones. The airline is also committed to providing USB-C power at every seat. The airline's press release further touts personalization, including TV and movie recommendations and flight maps that feature “destination information and real-time flight insights.” But not all existing narrowbody Airbus and Boeing airframes will get upgraded, spokesperson Andrea Koos clarifies in an email. Out of the airline’s current 1,045-plane mainline fleet, all 132 Airbus A319s, 310 domestic-configuration A321s in two versions, and 303 Boeing 737-800s and 103 737 Max 8s are in line for upgrades. But 48 older Airbus A320s with planned retirements won’t get any, while 12 new internationally configured A321XLRs already have seatback screens. The smaller regional jets built by Bombardier in Canada and Embraer in Brazil—593 aircraft that fly shorter routes operated by AA subsidiaries and partners—also aren’t part of this screen expansion. Koos says AA hasn’t yet picked a company to add this tech, but suggests the ability to monetize a passenger’s attention (already a priority at United) would matter. “Beyond meeting today's needs, we are looking for a partner with a modern, scalable platform that can evolve alongside technology advancements, enabling continuous enhancements to the customer experience while creating incremental revenue opportunities for American,” she writes in an email. The airline’s news on Tuesday also includes putting more first-class seats in these aircraft and expanding the number of extra-legroom Main Cabin Extra seats, which AA says would push the percentage of seats with more personal space on narrowbody departures from 25% to about 40%. Last year, American announced plans to install free Starlink Wi-Fi on a subset of its planes, joining such domestic carriers as Alaska Airlines and its Hawaiian Airlines subsidiary, Frontier (where Starlink apparently won’t be free), Southwest, and United in adopting SpaceX’s satellite broadband. Delta and JetBlue Airways will switch to Amazon Leo, another low-Earth-orbit satellite service that has seen its own flight delays after one of its primary launch vehicles, Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, exploded and destroyed its sole launch pad in Florida. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 Review: Oh, Snap! Elite CPU Speed at a Heavy Price
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.49
Lenovo's high-end Yoga laptops are widely appreciated for their style, comfort, and performance, and the company’s latest, the Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11, is a stunner with speed to back it up. Starting at $1,499.99 ($1,999.99 as tested), the Yoga Slim 7x gives a similarly configured 13-inch Apple MacBook Air, our Editors' Choice pick for Mac laptops, one heck of a fight. The Yoga's Snapdragon CPU also sprints faster than a comparable Intel Core Ultra Series 3 laptop, like the Dell XPS 14 2026, our current Editors' Choice ultraportable laptop pick, and the laptop lasts longer than both on a charge. This year's Yoga Slim 7x has its shortcomings, however, such as limited ports, weaker graphics performance, and a higher price compared with the aforementioned award-winning laptops. If you're dead set on a faster, longer-lasting laptop, the Slim 7x will deliver, albeit only with apps coded directly for Arm processors. The Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 starts at $1,499.99 (on sale by Lenovo for $899.99, at times, during this review) and features a six-core/six-thread Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus (X2P-42-100) processor with a Qualcomm Adreno X2-45 integrated graphics processor (IGP), 16GB of LPDDR5x memory running at 9,523 megatransfers per second (MT/s), and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 solid-state drive. The screen is a 14-inch 1,920-by-1,200-pixel (1200p) OLED touch display with HDR500, 100% DCI-P3 color coverage, and a 60Hz refresh rate. The specific review configuration I tested is available at Best Buy for $1,999.99, with an 18-core (six Performance plus 12 Prime cores) Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite (X2E-88-100) CPU with a faster Qualcomm Adreno X2-90 IGP, 32GB of RAM, a 1TB SSD, and the same 14-inch 1200p display as the starting configuration. It’s worth noting that this Asus Zenbook A14 on sale at Best Buy has almost identical specs to the Yoga Slim 7x reviewed here, just with 16GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD, for $650 less. I don’t know if the extra RAM and storage in the Slim 7x are worth $650 for you, but I don’t think this is reasonable, and so it takes some of the shine off this laptop for me. This Zenbook A14 laptop is also often found for just $999, to further the point. You can also configure the laptop somewhat on Lenovo’s website, with the priciest build using a slightly less powerful 12-core (six Performance plus six Prime cores) X2-80-100 CPU, 32GB of RAM, a 2TB SSD, and an upgraded 14-inch 120Hz OLED touch display with 2,880-by-1,800-pixel resolution, HDR1000, and 100% DCI-P3 color coverage. This setup will run you $2,309.99 at list price, but Lenovo sells it for $2,194.49 on sale at publishing time. The Lenovo Yoga line rarely looks anything less than gorgeous, and the Yoga Slim 7x delivers with a sleek, ultra-thin (0.55-inch), and feather-light (2.58-pound) aluminum chassis in a deep Cosmic Blue. You'll notice a subdued Lenovo logo on the lid and a similarly slight Yoga branding on the right wrist rest below the keyboard. Cool white backlighting beneath the keys brings quality of life while adding a bit of aesthetic appeal. I feel some stiffness in the hinges, which makes the lid a bit of a challenge to open one-handed, but the slight webcam bulge along the top of the display helps your grip in this regard. The Yoga Slim 7x includes an OLED display even on the base configuration, and that screen is gorgeous to watch. The visuals are crisp, even at 1200p, and the HDR500 and DCI-P3 color coverage make the display pop when watching movies. The 60Hz refresh is more than functional for most needs, though many laptops at this price have landed on 120Hz as the standard. The screen's peak brightness goes up to 400 nits without HDR, with 600 nits peak brightness with HDR, and it supports Dolby Vision. The audio, meanwhile, is fantastic for a laptop this thin. You won’t hear deep bass or anything desk-shaking out of the speakers here, but you'll find two top-firing 2W speakers in addition to the two 2W woofers on the underside of the chassis, so the audio is fuller than most laptops in this size bracket. Lenovo included Dolby Atmos support to further improve the audio. Anecdotally, I can tell you that running the battery test on this laptop required me to put it on a shelf in the front hallway closet in my apartment, since the volume at 100% was loud enough that I could hear it from several rooms away through two closed doors. I love a Lenovo laptop keyboard, and the Yoga’s keys don't disappoint. They're comfortable enough to type on for hours-long writing sessions, with deep enough travel and quick response. The keyboard backlighting is configurable through the Lenovo Advantage app, with Auto, Low, High, and Off settings. The buttonless touchpad has a smooth glass surface and is comfortable to use, with only the slightest bit of flex at the bottom corners. It’s responsive enough that you won't long for a haptic alternative, and it’s spacious enough for everyday work. It also supports multitouch gestures. Lenovo's webcam is a 9.2MP IR cam with better-than-4K video and picture resolution (2400p). Though it’s limited to 30-frame-per-second (fps) recording for all other resolutions, the sensor can record at 60fps at 1080p. You'll find no physical privacy shutter here, but Lenovo included an E-Shutter switch on the side of the laptop that cuts off power to the webcam, which is better than nothing. You won't find many ports on the Slim 7x. You might chalk that up to its slimness, were it not for other laptops at this size including more options. The laptop houses three 40Gbps USB4 ports, two on the left and one on the right, and all three support DisplayPort 1.4 and up to 65W power delivery. Lenovo didn't include a 3.5mm audio jack, so if you want to listen to music or watch movies without disturbing those around you, you’ll either need an adapter or Bluetooth-connected headphones. On the bright side, Lenovo included Wi-Fi 7 connectivity, as well as Bluetooth 5.4. To see how the Yoga Slim 7x’s overall performance and speed measures up to the competition across specific tasks, we've gathered several competing ultraportable laptops together to see how they all match up. First up is the recent $2,932 Framework Laptop 13 Pro we tested, followed by the Asus Zenbook A14 ($1,349.99 as tested; $1,999.99 similarly configured). To round things out, we included our Editors' Choice picks for ultraportables: our $2,199.99 Dell XPS 14 review configuration, and the 13-inch MacBook Air ($1,599 as tested; $1,999 similarly configured). Our first group of tests represents workloads such as content creation, office productivity, and raw CPU speeds. Our go-to overall productivity and storage test, PCMark 10, is not yet Snapdragon-compatible, so we focused on core-stressing tests and media tasks. The three primary tests presented below are CPU-centric or processor-intensive. Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the transcoding freeware HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Additionally, we have encountered issues with Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators Adobe Photoshop 25 test on systems with Qualcomm Arm processors, so we’ve skipped it here until we resolve our problems with the test. These tests are where the Slim 7x stood out, outperforming its Intel x86 rivals as well as the MacBook Air in multi-core performance, which is essential for multitasking and overall system responsiveness. The Yoga also defeated the x86 competitors in single-core speed, which is important for single-app and basic task responsiveness. Its Snapdragon chip only landed within 75% of the Apple M5’s single-core Cinebench 2024 result, however. Surprisingly, it put up the best HandBrake time on the list, finishing the 1080p video transcoding task nearly 90 seconds faster than the M5. However, this performance advantage falls away if you run apps through Windows 11 Prism x86 emulation. Apps developed for x86 processors, like Intel and AMD, can’t run directly on an Arm-based processor like the Snapdragon X2 Elite, so Windows Prism converts an app’s existing x86 code into Arm-compatible code on the fly so it runs on Arm chips, though this impacts performance. In Cinebench, for instance, running the x86 version of the benchmark on the Zenbook results in about 44% lower multi-core performance and about 41% lower single-core performance compared with the version designed for the Arm CPU architecture. Most popular apps nowadays have Arm versions of their software, so this shouldn’t be too much of an issue; you just need to make sure you’re downloading the right version to get the most out of this laptop. A shrinking number of Windows apps simply will not work on an Arm system, or will run so poorly through emulation that it’s not worth the hassle. We challenge all systems’ graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. Graphics performance is where the Slim 7x struggled, falling behind its Intel and Apple rivals in some tests, with Wild Life showing an especially poor result against the Arc B390 GPU in the Intel chips. The Yoga's Snapdragon also reported noticeably lower ray-tracing speed than both Intel and Apple chips in Solar Bay. These workloads represent advanced creative work and gaming, so the results aren't a deal-breaker for this laptop, since that's not really what this device is going for. If you want the capability to play PC games or work in 3D creative apps, however, the MacBook Air or the latest XPS 14 will perform much better in either regard. We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with display brightness at 50% and audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. To gauge display performance, we also use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). In this case, Qualcomm Snapdragon's renowned efficiency came through with a clear win against Intel-based Windows laptops, lasting 28 hours and 48 minutes against its nearest Intel-based rival, the Framework Laptop 13 Pro. The Yoga's result was even more impressive than the XPS 14's and MacBook Air's times. The Yoga Slim 7x display, meanwhile, cleared 100% of the sRGB color gamut (common for web content) and covered 98% of both the Adobe RGB and DCI-P3 color gamuts, which are important for still media and video work, respectively. This is much better than the Framework while essentially tying XPS 14 and Zenbook screens. The MacBook Air’s display, meanwhile, covers about 11% less of the Adobe gamut than the Yoga’s, while effectively tying on sRGB and DCI-P3 coverage. For brightness, the Slim 7x is the second dimmest display on the list, with a max non-HDR brightness of 397 nits, which is slightly lower than the Dell laptop. The MacBook Air's brightness is noticeably higher, and the Framework's 796 nits max brightness is in another realm entirely. Final Thoughts Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 is an excellent showcase for the new Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite chips, especially in terms of battery life and CPU performance. It doesn’t hurt that the Yoga is one of the better-looking laptops out there, ready to easily accompany you on your college commute or around the office. Its graphics performance is less impressive, but since the most important workload for a GPU at this level, gaming, isn’t practical on a device like this (where Arm's app-compatibility issues still hurt most), it’s not a deal-breaker. For everyday productivity tasks, the Slim 7x is outstanding, even if it does come in at a higher price than it should for the parts inside. Look to the MacBook Air and Dell XPS 14 for a slightly more premium treatment at a similar price, as they still hold on to our Editors' Choice awards for that reason. But watch for price fluctuations: Lenovo's selling prices seldom stand still, and you could catch a slick bargain if you're alert.
About Our Expert John (he/him) is a programmer, gamer, activist, and Brooklyn College alum currently living in Brooklyn, New York. Named by the CTA as a CES 2020 Media Trailblazer for his science and technology reporting, John specializes in all areas of computer science, including industry news, hardware reviews, and PC gaming. He's also well-versed in general science writing and the social impact of the tech industry. John has a Bachelor’s degree in English and a Master’s degree in Computer Science. You can usually find him on Bluesky, where you’ll get his hot takes on stuff, as well as his reposts of content that is almost as good as the worst stuff you used to be able to find on Vine. Beyond PC gaming, he spends his evenings building digital circuits, multiboxing Linux kernels, and coding shell scripts.

item.title: Framework Refreshes 12-Inch Laptop, Uses Linux To Hit $699 Price
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.39
Upgradable laptop maker Framework is refreshing its budget 12-inch notebook with some user-requested features and a surprising focus on Linux, rather than Windows. On Tuesday, the San Francisco company debuted the new Framework Laptop 12 over a year after the product first arrived to address the entry-level and education market. The new version starts at $699, a $100 price cut from the first-gen model, making it a potential rival to Apple’s MacBook Neo, but expect a compromise on the laptop's RAM. The biggest change is the Intel Core Series 3 “Wildcat Lake” processors, which promise to increase the laptop’s battery life, a much-requested improvement that owners of the first-gen model asked for. In the company's early testing of the Laptop 12 with Intel's Core 5 320 chip, "we’re seeing a 70% increase in Netflix 4k streaming battery life over the Core i5-1334U in the original Framework Laptop 12,” the company wrote in a blog post. The 12.2-inch laptop also adds a backlit keyboard and a fingerprint reader in the power button, two other requested features. That said, the backlit keyboard and fingerprint reader are absent in the $699 base model, and only available when configured with Intel’s higher-end Core 5 320 and Core 7 350 processors. Other enhancements include Wi-Fi 7 and support for Thunderbolt 4 over the two rear Expansion Card slots, "enabling you to plug in high-speed peripherals like eGPU’s or two 4k 60Hz displays," the company says. We’ll be curious to see how the Laptop 12 stacks up against Apple’s MacBook Neo and Dell’s new XPS 13, which both start at $699. The $699 XPS 13 also uses a Core 5 320 chip, features 8GB of RAM, and is so far the “budget Windows ultraportable to beat,” according to our review. In contrast, Framework's $699 Laptop 12 uses a lower tier processor in the Core 3 304. Still, the laptop promises to excel at repairability and upgradability since it features an easy-to-access modular design Framework is already accepting pre-orders, but the first batches won’t ship until October. Although the “pre-built” base model starts at $699, it only features 8GB of RAM, which is low, especially on the Windows OS. To get 16GB of RAM, you’ll need to buy the Core 5 320 model, which costs $400 more at $1,099. But on the plus side, it includes the fingerprint reader and backlit keyboard. Meanwhile, the Core 7 350 model is going for $1,399. The laptops can also ship with the Linux distribution Fedora, which is open source and free. To get Windows 11, you’ll need to pay an extra $100, which might explain the price cut from the first-gen model. On why it's pushing Linux, Framework noted: “Almost 80% of Framework Laptop 12 owners are running Linux across a range of distros. This was a clear signal to us that we should push even further on Linux ease of use.” The Framework Laptop 12 will also be sold through "DIY editions" that start at $549, featuring the Intel Core 3 304 processor. The DIY editions expand the color options from merely a greenish "sage" to five other color ways. However, the DIY models don't come with RAM or storage unless you pay to add them. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: ChatGPT’s newest feature is like Windows Recall without screenshots
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 6.06
In summary: - PCWorld reports that OpenAI has launched a ChatGPT feature called Computer History, currently available only on Mac, which tracks desktop activity to create a searchable timeline of user actions. - Unlike Windows Recall, the feature avoids constant screenshots, instead logging activity more discreetly, with users able to manually enable it and exclude specific apps or websites. - The feature is expected to reach users in the European Economic Area within coming weeks. ChatGPT’s desktop app now includes a new feature called “Computer History,” which was announced via social media post by Ari Weinstein, a Codex product manager at OpenAI. Computer History allows ChatGPT to track your computer activity, creating a timeline of your actions that can then be used by ChatGPT and Codex. It’s similar to Microsoft’s Windows Recall feature, which also tracks your activity history, except Computer History doesn’t take screenshots. In a demonstration video, OpenAI showed Computer History being used to do things like find the most recently used documents on the computer, check whether they were shared via Slack, and summarize what the computer user did in the morning. Computer History must be manually enabled before it starts tracking, and the user can decide whether to exclude certain apps and websites from it. It’s also possible to delete entries from Computer History. The feature is currently only available in the Mac version of the ChatGPT app. It’s not yet available in the European Economic Area (EEA), but OpenAI says the feature will be coming to the EEA in the coming weeks. It’s not yet known when it will be available in the Windows app.

item.title: Firefox 154 fixes 58 security bugs, adds Nvidia GeForce Now streaming
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 6.03
The newest major release of Firefox 154 for Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android brings a number of usability improvements, such as game streaming with Nvidia GeForce Now, faster video skipping, and new optional app icons, as well as nearly 60 security vulnerabilities fixed. Updates are also available for the ESR versions. The next major version of Firefox 155 is scheduled for September 1st. With it, Mozilla is switching—like Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge—to a fortnightly release cycle for its major versions. What’s new in Firefox 154? For Windows users, Firefox 154 now offers game streaming via Nvidia GeForce Now, which can save on the cost of expensive hardware. Also limited to Windows for now is the option to choose a different app icon for Firefox, as is already available on Android and iOS. (macOS and Linux are set to follow later.) Options include the old Firefox icons from 2004 and 2017, a rainbow-style icon (“Pride”), and bonus icons. On all platforms, skipping to a different part of a video should now be faster. And while the translation feature for web pages previously relied on information provided by the website itself regarding the language used, Firefox now performs its own language detection. This means that content from iframes is now also translated. If you add websites to the exception list for deleting cookies and website content, they are no longer automatically excluded from tracking protection. The free built-in VPN, introduced with Firefox 149, continues to offer a selection of virtual locations—temporarily extended to 28 countries until the end of August—with unlimited data. The free VPN is currently available to Firefox users in the US, Canada, the UK, France, and Germany. In addition, the free VPN can now also be used in Firefox for Android (rolling out gradually) with iOS to follow soon. Security updates in Firefox 154 In the security report for Firefox 154, Mozilla lists 58 resolved security vulnerabilities, 54 of which were discovered and reported by external security researchers. Mozilla classifies 17 of these vulnerabilities as high risk. A further 30 vulnerabilities are classified as medium risk, with the remainder classified as low risk. The last four entries in the security report (CVE-2026-74987 to CVE-2026-74990) summarize an unspecified number of internally discovered security vulnerabilities, most of which are classified as high risk, resulting from programming errors in memory management. The vulnerabilities are grouped according to which program versions are affected. Firefox ESR browser updates In addition to Firefox 154.0, the ESR releases 153.1.0, 140.14.0, and 115.39.0 are also available. However, the latter are only available for Windows 7 and 8.1, and macOS 10.12 to 10.14. In the ESR versions, Mozilla has fixed those of the above-mentioned vulnerabilities that are present in the code of those older browser generations. That amounts to more than 52 security vulnerabilities fixed in Firefox 153.1.0, at least 31 in Firefox 140.14, and at least 13 in Firefox 115.39. Firefox ESR 140 will be replaced by Firefox ESR 153 in October.

item.title: You can run multiple monitors off one DisplayPort cable. Here’s how
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.30
Many PC users assume that every monitor requires its own cable to connect to the computer. However, DisplayPort offers another solution. Thanks to Multi Stream Transport (MST for short), several monitors can be connected via a single DisplayPort port. This allows you to set up a multi-monitor configuration without having to run multiple cables from the PC to the screens. Ivanky First and foremost, your graphics card must support MST. However, this feature was introduced with DisplayPort 1.2 and has been available on numerous systems since around 2013. If in doubt, it’s worth checking the device’s technical specifications. It’s equally important to have at least one monitor with a DisplayPort output. This is usually labelled “DP Out.” Kabeldirekt The monitor displays part of the video signal itself and passes the remaining data stream on to the next screen. The final monitor in this chain only requires a standard DisplayPort input. The setup is simple: Connect the PC’s DisplayPort output to the first monitor. From its DisplayPort output, run another cable to the next monitor. This so-called “daisy chain” can then be extended to include further monitors as required. Next, enable the MST function in the first monitor’s settings menu. Windows will then automatically recognize the additional displays. You can arrange them accordingly in the Windows display settings. If monitors do not have a DisplayPort output, an MST hub can be used instead. Foundry This device connects to the computer’s DisplayPort or USB-C port and distributes the video signal across multiple outputs. This technology is particularly handy for laptops, as many models only have a single video port. With MST, you can still run a multi-monitor setup while significantly simplifying cable management.

item.title: Geekom mini PCs were vulnerable to malware. Here’s how to check yours
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.13
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Geekom mini PCs, including the A7, A8, AE7, and AE8 series, were compromised after attackers injected backdoors into drivers hosted on an outdated support page, enabling spying and password theft. - Only users who downloaded drivers through unofficial search engine results are affected, while the current official Geekom website remains safe. - Affected users should disconnect from the network, run antivirus scans, change passwords, and consider a factory reset. Detailed instructions are provided below. A few days ago, Tom’s Hardware and Videocardz reported on a Geekom incident affecting several of the manufacturer’s mini PCs. Attackers were able to inject malware onto several devices via a tampered driver—one that was hosted on an official Geekom support page, which, according to the company, had already been taken offline. Geekom confirmed the incident and explained that, although the outdated website had been replaced by a new one, it could still be found via search engines. The attackers exploited this to insert a backdoor into the driver package, enabling them to install malware on Geekom mini PCs. According to the latest details, the following models were vulnerable: - Geekom A7 - Geekom A8 - Geekom AE7 - Geekom AE8 - Geekom AX7 Pro - Geekom AX8 Pro Important: You are only at risk of malware on your Geekom mini PC if you manually searched for a driver for one of these vulnerable models and downloaded it from the outdated Geekom site. Geekom’s official driver packages on their current site did not include malware. This incident is problematic because many users are likely to search for new driver packages using terms like “[device name] driver update” and download from the first result that appears on the search page. Using this malware, attackers were able to gain extensive permissions on affected Geekom systems, spy on personal data, and steal passwords. You should act quickly if you were affected. Here’s what you can do If you own one of the vulnerable devices, you should launch your antivirus software right away and run a thorough malware scan. (If you don’t have one, check out our picks for the best Windows antivirus software.) You can also use the Windows Device Manager to check when drivers were downloaded and installed for which devices. If you suspect malware, you should disconnect your PC from the network and factory reset it. Ideally, you’ll have backed up your data beforehand using a backup tool. (Again, if you don’t have one, protect yourself going forward with one of the best Windows backup software.) Learn more about how to factory reset a Windows 11 PC. After the reset, you should change all the passwords you used on the affected device. As a general rule: Never install updates or drivers from unknown or untrusted sources. In this case, although it was an official manufacturer’s website, it was only accessible via a Google search. Instead of searching, it’s always safer to directly visit a manufacturer’s website and navigate to their support pages for drivers.

item.title: Microsoft is killing this 25-year-old Windows tool. Your scripts might break
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.04
With the latest Windows 11 preview update (KB5120998), Microsoft is finally bidding farewell to a tool that has been part of the operating system since Windows XP: the Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line (WMIC). It’s being removed from Windows 11 in an upcoming patch, and it’ll affect both Windows 11 versions 24H2 and 25H2. The announcement comes via Microsoft’s official release notes for KB512098, meant for Release Preview Builds 26100.9267 and 26200.9267. The removal is set to be incorporated into the regular Windows versions when the update gets its wider release. Microsoft already classified WMIC as deprecated back in 2024. Since then, the company has been phasing the tool out, with new Windows 11 installations already excluding WMIC. But with this preview update, even existing Windows PCs will no longer have WMIC at all. What exactly is being phased out? WMIC is a command-line utility that can be used to retrieve system information and automate administrative tasks. Administrators and power users could, for example, use it to retrieve hardware data, BIOS information, or run processes via commands. With this update, Microsoft is removing the wmic.exe executable file. The underlying Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), however, remains fully intact and will continue to be supported. For most home users, the change is unlikely to have any immediate impact. Most Windows users have probably never used WMIC. These scripts may be affected Problems are most likely to arise where older management and automation scripts still rely directly on WMIC. After installing the update, such commands will no longer work. The following may be affected: - Batch files containing wmic commands - PowerShell scripts that launch WMIC as an external utility - Login and startup scripts - Scheduled tasks - Inventory and monitoring scripts - Older installation and deployment packages Anyone using such commands and scripts should review them and, where appropriate, switch to modern alternatives. Microsoft suggests using PowerShell as a replacement. It provides access to the same WMI data and is considered even more powerful and better suited to modern automation. Part of a larger Windows update The removal of WMIC is just one of several changes in update KB5120998. In this update, Microsoft is also trialing the return of a freely positionable taskbar. Users should once again be able to place it at the top, bottom, left, or right edge of the screen. In addition, the Start menu is gaining new resizing options, Windows Search is being revamped, and Microsoft is integrating additional security features such as “Administrator Protection.” With the end of WMIC, Windows is thus bidding farewell to yet another tool from the Windows XP era. For most users, the change will go unnoticed; however, anyone still using older administration or automation scripts should check and fix compatibility soon.

item.title: Hackers want your nudes. Here’s how to keep your privates, private
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.82
Sexploitation isn’t a new concept. Long before the internet, people blackmailed others over sexually explicit photos or videos. But this week, the US Federal Bureau of Investigation released a fresh warning around hackers and sexortion—an alert aimed at both adults and children. In its public service announcement, the FBI says sexual exploitation actors have been breaking into “social media and personal accounts” to download any saved explicit content. The stolen images and video then gets spread to criminal forums and marketplaces, often with personal details like name, email, phone number, social media username, and date of birth also shared. Victims usually don’t immediately know their accounts were compromised. Instead, they may only realize the hack after receiving a demand for money or additional explicit material. Or if other forms of harassment or attack begin. So, how do you prevent sextortion from hackers? The same as preventing any unauthorized access to your accounts. Be careful about what you click and protect your accounts with good login habits: - Use unique, strong passwords and PIN codes for all accounts - Ignore messages that threaten account lockout unless you reply with a verification code - Change your password by logging into a site directly, then going to your settings. Don’t click a link in an email unless you just directly requested a password reset - Switch to passkeys whenever possible These tips protect you from credential stuffing attacks and phishing attempts. A verification code request? A hacker can initiate a password reset for an account that generates a real verification code. Share that info with the bad actor and boom—now they can change your password and take over. Email messages with password reset links? Might be a hacker impersonating the real service, hoping to steal your login details either directly or through stealing authentication cookies or tokens. My advice? Use passkeys often you can. This form of login is naturally more protected against credential stuffing and phishing attempts. Every passkey is unique and tied to a specific device (e.g., security hardware key) or service (Microsoft account, Google account, independent password manager). Hackers can’t exploit a passkey in the same ways as a password. If you’re stuck with passwords, make them complex and unique, and also enable two-factor authentication wherever possible. You can offload all the work to a password manager—it’s actually the better way to be lazy about passwords.

item.title: Xfinity routers can now sense movement in your home, without cameras
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.22
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Comcast has launched WiFi Motion, a feature that turns existing Xfinity routers into motion sensors using standard Wi-Fi signal interference. - The technology is integrated into the Xfinity Shield security option and is available free to customers through the Xfinity app, with no cameras or video recording involved. - While convenient, data privacy concerns remain regarding how movement information may be shared with third parties. Comcast, the largest residential internet service provider in the US, is introducing a new feature called “WiFi Motion” that enables physical motion detection using nothing but Wi-Fi signals. By monitoring signal interference, WiFi Motion can accurately detect and track people and objects in and through physical space. The technology behind WiFi Motion is still relatively new—we reported on Wi-Fi body fingerprinting last year—and has thus far mostly been theory and proofs of concept. Now, the theory is being put into practice. In the Xfinity app, users will be able to enable or disable the “Xfinity Shield” option, according to Comcast’s official announcement. All connected routers and other network devices can then use WiFi Motion together to monitor the home and protect against intruders. The service is free for Comcast customers and doesn’t require any additional cameras or sensors. However, the disadvantage compared to conventional home surveillance systems is that WiFi Motion doesn’t provide a clear image of the environment. Users can’t take photos or record videos, so in the event of a break-in, it’s not possible to identify faces or other visual characteristics. Nevertheless, Wi-Fi-based surveillance is becoming increasingly attractive, especially among businesses. Alongside Comcast, other companies like Linksy, Wiz, and Philips Hue have also launched similar services. However, the technology still needs time to develop in order to become more accurate and less prone to errors. Of course, there are privacy concerns, too. TechCrunch, for example, warns against using WiFi Motion in one’s own home without due care. In its terms and conditions, Comcast reserves the right to pass on data to third parties without informing users beforehand. This data could, for example, be used by governments for legal proceedings and more.

item.title: NASA Images Confirm Moon Crater Made by SpaceX Rocket
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 6.59
The atmosphere-less Moon is frequently bombarded by meteors, asteroids, and comets, and now it can add another item to that list: SpaceX rockets. After news that one of the company’s Falcon 9 rockets had crash-landed on the Moon on August 5 after being discarded in space by the Elon Musk-owned company, researchers and space agencies were in a race to capture images of the landing site. The first photos to emerge were taken by the Danuri lunar orbiter, operated by the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA), which flew over the site shortly after impact. But NASA wanted its own photos, and on August 11 and August 12 the space agency’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) captured a series of images of the new crater. NASA engineers tilted the spacecraft so its cameras would point toward the crater each time LRO passed above the crater; the LRO flies roughly 60 miles above the Moon while traveling one mile per second. The orbiter circles the Moon from pole to pole every two hours, while the Moon slowly rotates underneath it. To photograph a specific spot, the spacecraft must wait until that location turns into view, which took six days in this case. As well as being in the right spot, NASA also had to time the camera shutter just right: if it was released 10 seconds too early, it would miss by 10 miles. NASA scientists believe that the crater is about 6 feet wide and less than 10 feet deep, based on the length of its shadow. The Falcon 9 made its crash landing after spending more than a year in an unstable orbit. The rocket launched in January 2025 and completed its mission to deliver lunar landers. For more than a year afterward, the gravity of Earth, the Moon, and the Sun gradually altered its trajectory until it eventually struck the lunar surface. The almost 46-foot-long and 8,800-pound Falcon 9 upper stage impacted the Moon near the Einstein crater, named for physicist Albert Einstein. The crater is located toward the edge of the side of the Moon visible from Earth.

item.title: Camera-Equipped AirPods Shown In Action in macOS Beta
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 5.83
Earlier this month, Apple insider Mark Gurman at Bloomberg said that new AirPods with cameras could be coming this year. The evidence is mounting. Gurman noted that the new AirPods were referenced in iOS 27 beta code, but now a new macOS Tahoe 26.7 beta does more than reference AirPods, it actually shows them in action with an instructional reference video. As MacRumors reports, the macOS release candidate includes video showing a demo of AirPods that work alongside Apple’s Visual Intelligence feature. Here is your first look at AirPods with Cameras in action using Visual Intelligence. This video file came from macOS 26.7 RC pic.twitter.com/yo7RI4MCeu — Aaron (@aaronp613) August 18, 2026 As MacRumors says and PetaPixel has written before, camera-equipped AirPods will capture visual information that works alongside Apple Intelligence and Siri. The AirPods can see the world around the wearer, and the wearer can then ask questions about it. In the demo video above, the wearer holds up a book and the AirPods record visual information about the book’s cover. Camera-equipped AirPods will likely exist solely to work alongside Apple Intelligence. “Taking a photo from someone’s ear is not what anyone wants — and that’s not what these new AirPods will do,” PetaPixel‘s Matt Growcoot wrote earlier this month. “Instead of recording photos or videos, the AirPods will capture low-resolution images of the world around the user, powering contextual artificial intelligence via Siri.” Per a follow-up story on MacRumors, the camera-equipped AirPods are “likely to be part of the AirPods Pro lineup rather than separate ‘AirPods Ultra.'” The situation with the camera-equipped AirPods has been rather confusing, with multiple codenamed products seemingly being very similar to one another. It has long been rumored that Apple is working on smart glasses as well, which presumably would work alongside AirPods, camera-equipped and standard alike. Smart glasses have become very popular in recent years, both for recording content from a first-person perspective and also for working alongside AI to deliver information about the wearer’s surroundings. Apple is expected to hold its annual iPhone launch event next month, during which the company could unveil the long-rumored AirPods with a camera. Image creditsApple. Header photo created using an asset licensed via Depositphotos.com. Affiliate Disclosure PetaPixel articles may include affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through one.

item.title: You Can Play Doom On a 16-Year-Old Canon DSLR
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 5.21
It’s possible to run the pioneering 1993 first-person shooter video game Doom on just about anything, even cameras. By using Magic Lantern software on a Canon EOS 550D from 2010, also known as the EOS Rebel T2i and EOS Kiss X4, photographers can install a custom build of Doom on their APS-C cameras. Bas Lichtjaar has shared the Doom module they built for Magic Lantern on Github, detailing how it works and how to install it. As Lichtjaar notes, the release is still experimental and is not intended for use on any other cameras at this time, so photographers should proceed with caution. However, as the video above shows, it definitely works, and photographers can control the famous space marine, or “Doomguy,” using the 550D’s four directional function buttons. The Menu button brings up the in-game menu, and the central “Set” button can fire the weapon. The Canon EOS 550D has a built-in speaker, albeit a poor one, which Lichtjaar uses to play Doom‘s 8-bit effects. The game also runs natively using the 550D’s entire 720×480-pixel display. It even includes save files and a secret cheat code menu. Importantly, running Doom on the DSLR through Magic Lantern doesn’t prevent it from being used as a regular camera. The old DSLR has an 18-megapixel APS-C image sensor and nine autofocus points. Magic Lantern can actually do a lot to enhance the camera’s performance beyond letting users play a classic FPS video game on it. For example, Magic Lantern expands the ISO range from 100-12,800 to 100-24,000. It also adds RAW video recording, an intervalometer, zebras, focus stacking, focus peaking, RAW RGB histograms, an electronic shutter function, and much more. The complete installation guide for Doom is available on Github. The Magic Lantern builds for the Canon EOS 550D are available on Magic Lantern’s website. Speaking of Magic Lantern, it’s nice to see the name again after the company made its glorious return just over a year ago following a lengthy hiatus. For photographers with older Canon DSLR cameras they’re willing to tinker with, it’s great to have Magic Lantern available again. Image creditsHeader photo by Bas Lichtjaar Affiliate Disclosure PetaPixel articles may include affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through one.

item.title: World’s First Flying Pocket Camera Quickly Raised Over $230,000 on Indiegogo
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 5.17
When HoverAir announced the world’s first flying pocket camera, the Versa, late last month, it did so with relatively few details. Now the unique new camera has fully launched on Indiegogo, bringing with it a wealth of new information. With 59 days left in the campaign, HoverAir has already raised over $230,000 at the time of writing. The Versa’s primary selling point is that it looks and behaves like a relatively straightforward content creator gimbal camera, like a DJI Osmo or Insta360 Luna. It has a gimbal camera on top, a small display, and a few on-device controls. However, what sets the Versa apart is that users can attach wings directly to its sides; inside these wings are four propellers that turn the Versa into a self-flying drone that tracks the user. HoverAir is no stranger to self-flying drones, as that is what the company is best known for. It even has a water-friendly model, the Aqua, the world’s first waterborne self-flying drone. The HoverAir Versa is the company’s first foray into a content creator-style pocket camera, though it admittedly serves a very similar target audience to the company’s other products. Like HoverAir’s other cameras, the Versa is built around simplicity and ease of use. “Change from handheld mode to flying in seconds,” HoverAir promises. “Slide down the sliding cover, attach Versa to the Flight Kit, unfold the wings, and take off.” The Versa’s “cinema-quality” 3-axis gimbal camera features a Type 1/1.3 image sensor and promises “17.5 stops of dynamic range.” It’s quite a lofty promise. It utilizes AI to improve image quality, particularly in low-light situations, promising cleaner video. It remains to be seen whether this AI noise reduction delivers natural-looking results or ends up overly smooth, a common issue on cameras with relatively small image sensors like this. The camera can record full Open Gate video with its 4:3 image sensor, making it easier for users to crop videos for a wide variety of social media applications, including 16:9 for YouTube or 9:16 for Instagram. When used handheld, the built-in lens has a 19mm equivalent focal length. When in aircraft mode, it is slightly wider, equivalent to a 16mm lens on a full-frame camera. The lens has an f/2 aperture and can focus as close as 0.1 meters (3.9 inches). HoverAir notes that the standard ISO range is 100-12,800, although with AI Night Enhancement enabled, the maximum ISO is 25,600. The HoverAir Versa captures 12-megapixel still photos in JPEG only and 4Kp60 video. HDR and H-Log video recording modes are limited to 4Kp30. The camera’s Dolly Zoom mode is also limited to 4Kp30, but the Spin (“Inception”) Mode shot is available at 4Kp60. Versa uses AI to frame and track subjects automatically. It can also orbit a scene and rebuild it using 3D Gaussian Splatting, creating a 3D model of a space that can be shared as an interactive 3D file. As for its flying specs, the HoverAir Versa can fly up to 36 kilometers per hour (22 miles per hour) and can fly up to 15 meters (49.2 feet) above the ground. It’s not a traditional drone in any real sense, as it is designed to record people on the ground. Pricing and Availability The HoverAir Versa is available to back now on Indiegogo, starting at $449 for the Pocket-Only version and $629 for the FlyMore Combo with the Flight Kit, extra battery, charger, and protective accessories. There’s also the Creator Combo for $799. This includes ND filters, a case, a suction cup mount, and a compact tripod. Some of these prices are only available for the first 48 hours of the campaign, which ends at 12 PM EDT (9 AM PDT) on August 20. HoverAir expects mass production to begin next month ahead of an October delivery. Complete details are available on Indiegogo.
