item.title: 10 things most people don't realize are making their home smell bad
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.98
10 things most people don't realize are making their home smell bad These are the real reasons your house smells bad, from washing machine gaskets to water heaters nobody thinks to check Most bad smells at home don't come from the places people blame first. The trash can and the litter box take the blame constantly. Cleaning them rarely fixes the problem. The actual source is usually something mechanical, something wet, or something nobody thinks to open. A rubber gasket. A drain that hasn't carried water in weeks. A filter basket tucked under a dishwasher's spray arm. These are the reasons your house smells bad even right after a thorough cleaning. Part of the problem is a real, well-documented phenomenon called olfactory adaptation, or nose blindness. The brain stops registering a smell that is constantly present. The people who live in a home are often the last to notice its odor. A guest walking in for the first time catches it right away. That means the fixes that actually work are rarely about spraying air freshener over a smell that has already been noticed. They are about finding the specific object or system producing it in the first place. Most stubborn household odors trace back to one of two conditions. Either trapped moisture is letting mold, mildew, or bacteria grow, or organic material, such as food, water, or skin oils, is sitting somewhere it can decompose undisturbed. Both conditions hide well. A washing machine gasket looks clean from the front. A dishwasher filter sits where nobody looks. A dry drain trap gives no visible sign of trouble until sewer gas starts leaking through it. This list covers 10 specific sources that produce or trap odor in ordinary homes. Each one was chosen because it's easy to overlook and straightforward to fix once identified. None of them require professional deodorizing or specialized equipment. Most take a few minutes with tools already sitting in a kitchen or bathroom cabinet. What they have in common is that they operate out of sight, behind an appliance, under a sink, or inside a machine. That's exactly why they keep producing odor long after every visible surface in the house has already been wiped down. The rubber gasket in a front-loading washing machine The rubber door seal on a front-loading washing machine is one of the most common sources of a musty smell in an entire house, not just the laundry room. Water, detergent residue, and fabric softener collect in the folds of the gasket after every cycle. If the door gets closed right after a wash, that moisture never fully dries out. Mold and mildew grow fast in a damp, dark, sealed space like that. Washing machines often sit in small utility rooms or closets with limited airflow. Odor from the gasket can travel through vents and hallways well beyond the laundry area itself. Many people switch to a more heavily scented detergent to compensate. That only covers the smell for a while and does nothing to address the mold underneath it. Wiping the folds of the gasket dry after each load solves most of this within about a week. Leaving the washer door open between cycles helps just as much. For a machine that already smells musty, pull back each fold of the rubber seal and check underneath. That usually reveals a visible ring of black or gray mildew that a quick wipe-down misses entirely. A monthly hot-water cycle, run empty with either a washing machine cleaning tablet or a cup of distilled white vinegar, helps too. It clears out residue that ordinary wash cycles leave behind in the drum and pump. Front-loading machines are more prone to this than top-loading machines. The door has to seal tightly to keep water from leaking out during a horizontal spin cycle, and that same seal traps humidity inside once the cycle ends. Some newer models include a dedicated tub-clean or self-clean cycle for this exact issue. It only helps if someone actually runs it on a regular basis instead of leaving it as an unused button on the control panel. Checking the owner's manual for the manufacturer's recommended frequency, often once a month, keeps the gasket from turning back into a hidden odor source after it has been cleaned. A dirty filter basket inside the dishwasher Credit: Castorly Stock / Pexels Most dishwashers built since the early 2010s have a removable filter at the bottom of the tub instead of a garbage disposal-style grinder. That filter is the reason a dishwasher can smell like spoiled food even when every dish inside it looks clean. Food particles, grease, and small bits of paper or bone collect in the filter basket with every cycle. Unlike older models, this filter does not clean itself. The filter sits below the bottom spray arm, so it stays out of view during normal use. That's often the first sign anything is wrong. Some manufacturers describe the smell as similar to a wet dish rag left in a closed container, which is essentially what has been sitting there. The smell tends to get stronger during the dry cycle, when heat activates bacteria in the trapped food debris. Most filter baskets twist or lift out by hand, without any tools. Manufacturer instructions typically recommend rinsing the filter under running water every one to two weeks, depending on how often the dishwasher runs. A soft brush or old toothbrush clears out grease that a rinse alone leaves behind, especially in the fine mesh screen above the coarser filter piece. Soaking the filter in warm water with a small amount of dish soap for 10 to 15 minutes loosens buildup that has hardened over several weeks. Skipping this step does more than cause odor. A clogged filter reduces water pressure at the spray arms, so dishes come out less clean even as the machine keeps running its full cycle. Checking the filter once a month, and rinsing it immediately if food particles are visible, keeps both the smell and the machine's performance from declining at the same time. Some dishwasher models list a recommended cleaning interval directly in the settings menu or owner's manual. Running an empty cycle with a dishwasher-specific cleaning tablet once a month helps clear residue from the spray arms and interior walls that a filter rinse alone won't reach. The splash guard and grinding chamber of a garbage disposal Credit: SHVETS production / Pexels A garbage disposal traps food waste under its rubber splash guard and around its grinding chamber long after visible scraps have washed down the drain. That trapped material is usually the real source of a persistent kitchen sink smell. Running water after grinding food clears what's directly in the flow path. Grease and small particles still cling to surfaces the water never fully reaches. The rubber splash guard, the flexible flap at the top of the disposal opening, is a common culprit. Its underside rarely gets touched during normal dishwashing. Bacteria multiply in the residue that collects there, producing a smell that seems to come from the drain in general rather than from one identifiable part. Flipping the splash guard up to check underneath it, something most people never do, often reveals the source immediately. A simple cleaning method works well for most units. Drop several ice cubes into the disposal along with a half cup of coarse salt, then run cold water while switching the disposal on for about 30 seconds. The ice knocks loose buildup on the grinding components while the salt provides mild abrasion. Following that with a few thin lemon or lime slices ground through the disposal leaves a fresher scent without relying on a chemical cleaner. Disposals should be run with cold water rather than hot. Cold water keeps grease and fat solid enough to grind and flush away, rather than melting it into a coating on internal parts. Running the disposal briefly at the end of every use, even after washing dishes by hand, prevents buildup that leads to a stronger, harder-to-remove odor. Cleaning the disposal doesn't need to happen every day. Skipping it for more than a couple of weeks lets buildup settle into a smell that's harder to remove. A quick rinse and a five-second run right after a meal that generates scraps keeps grease and food particles from settling into the grinding chamber. That takes far less effort than tackling an odor that has already set in. A clogged refrigerator drip pan Credit: Lucie Liz / Pexels Refrigerators with automatic defrost cycles route the water from that process into a drip pan, usually located underneath the unit or behind a bottom access panel. A musty smell coming from a refrigerator that looks clean inside almost always traces back to that pan. Standing water sitting in a warm spot near the compressor creates close to ideal conditions for mold and bacteria. The drip pan fills gradually every time the refrigerator runs its automatic defrost cycle, which happens several times a day in most modern units. Under normal conditions, the water is meant to evaporate on its own from heat given off by the nearby compressor. If the pan cracks, sits at a slight angle, or simply never gets checked, water and debris can accumulate for months. The pan is rarely visible without pulling the refrigerator away from the wall or removing a front kick panel. Locating the pan usually requires checking the appliance's manual, since placement varies by brand and model. It is typically accessible by removing a toe grille at the base of the unit or a panel near the compressor in back. Sliding the pan out, washing it with warm water and dish soap, and drying it completely before sliding it back into place clears out mold and residue. This is worth doing roughly twice a year, or sooner if a musty smell is noticeable near the floor by the refrigerator. A refrigerator drip pan is easy to overlook because nothing about daily use draws attention to it. The odor it produces often gets blamed on food inside the refrigerator instead. Checking the pan before assuming spoiled food is the cause saves time and usually solves the smell on the first try. Older refrigerators tend to have pans that are easier to reach than newer built-in models, where the pan may sit behind panels designed to stay sealed. If a refrigerator is still under warranty, checking with the manufacturer before removing any panels avoids voiding coverage over a simple cleaning task. A dirty air conditioner coil and condensate line Credit: Canva Images An air conditioning system that smells musty when it turns on is almost always dealing with mold on the evaporator coil or a clog in the condensate drain line. Because the system pushes air through every room in the house, that smell doesn't stay confined to one place. The coil sits inside the indoor air handler and stays cold and wet during normal operation. That makes it an easy place for mold to establish itself if airflow or drainage isn't working correctly. The condensate line carries the water the system removes from the air during cooling out to the exterior of the house. Dust, algae, and debris narrow that line over time. When it clogs completely, water can back up into the drain pan or, in more serious cases, overflow into the surrounding ductwork or ceiling. A sour or musty smell right when the system starts a cooling cycle is one of the clearest early signs the line needs attention. Replacing the air filter every one to three months keeps dust from accumulating on the coil in the first place. The right interval depends on the filter type and whether pets are in the home. That's the single easiest way to prevent this issue. Pouring a cup of distilled white vinegar down the condensate drain access point, typically a capped PVC pipe near the indoor unit, keeps algae from building up inside the line. A musty smell that shows up specifically when the system first kicks on, rather than persisting throughout the day, points toward the coil or drain line. It's a different signal than a general air quality issue elsewhere in the house. A licensed HVAC technician can inspect and clean the coil directly during a routine service visit. Most manufacturers recommend scheduling that visit once a year, regardless of whether an odor has appeared yet. Reusable grocery bags that never get washed Credit: Canva Images Reusable grocery bags carry raw meat packaging, unwashed produce, and spilled liquids trip after trip, and most owners never wash them. The fabric absorbs bacteria and odor the same way a kitchen towel does. Left folded in a car trunk or kitchen closet between shopping trips, that residue keeps developing in a warm, enclosed space. The smell from a dirty reusable bag often gets misidentified as coming from the pantry or the refrigerator. The bag itself gets tucked away rather than left out where it would be an obvious suspect. Canvas and cotton bags soak up moisture and odor more readily than the woven polypropylene bags common at grocery checkouts. Both types still need regular cleaning. Most cotton and canvas reusable bags can go directly into a washing machine on a warm cycle. Tumble drying on low heat afterward works too, the same way any other kitchen linen would be washed. Polypropylene bags, the stiffer woven type, typically shouldn't go in a dryer, since heat can warp the material. They can be hand-washed with warm water and dish soap, then air-dried fully before folding them away again. Keeping raw meat in a separate bag from produce and pantry items cuts down on how often deep cleaning is needed. Cross-contamination is the main reason these bags develop a smell faster than expected. Washing reusable bags roughly every two weeks keeps them from becoming a hidden odor source. The same goes for washing one immediately after it carries raw meat or a leaking container. Insulated or thermal tote bags used for frozen and refrigerated groceries need the same attention. Condensation inside them creates the same damp conditions that let bacteria multiply. Wiping the interior lining with warm water and a small amount of mild dish soap takes care of most residue. Leaving the bag open to air dry completely afterward keeps it from developing a musty smell of its own between shopping trips. A dry P-trap in a rarely used drain Credit: Caleb Wright / Unsplash A U-shaped section of pipe called a P-trap sits under every sink, shower, and floor drain. Its job is to hold a small amount of water that blocks sewer gas from rising back up into the house. When that water evaporates from lack of use, the smell that comes through is often mistaken for a sewage leak rather than a simple dry trap. Guest bathrooms, basement floor drains, and laundry room sinks are the most common places this happens, since they can go weeks without water passing through them. Floor drains in garages and utility rooms are especially prone to drying out, since they're built to handle an occasional spill rather than regular daily use. The trapped water in a P-trap evaporates gradually even without any leak or plumbing failure, especially in a dry climate or a room with limited humidity. Once the trap runs dry, there is nothing left to block the connection between the house and the sewer line or septic system. The smell of sewer gas travels straight up through the drain opening and into the room. Running water down a rarely used drain for about 30 seconds once every one to two weeks keeps the trap full and blocks the odor before it starts. Some drains go unused for extended periods, such as a floor drain in an unfinished basement. For those, adding a small amount of mineral oil on top of the water after refilling the trap slows evaporation further. That prevents the water underneath from drying out as quickly. This is one of the few odor sources on this list that isn't caused by dirt, mold, or bacteria at all. It's a mechanical gap that opens up simply from a drain not being used. That makes it easy to rule out other causes first, rather than wasting time cleaning a fixture that was never actually dirty to begin with. A humidifier or dehumidifier tank Credit: Canva Images The water reservoir inside a humidifier or dehumidifier grows mold and bacteria within days if it isn't cleaned regularly. Running either machine then pushes that contamination directly into the air of whatever room it sits in. A humidifier sprays or diffuses the water straight into the room. A dehumidifier's collection bucket sits full of water pulled from the air, giving mold the same damp, standing conditions it needs to grow. Manufacturers generally recommend emptying and rinsing a humidifier's tank daily, plus a deeper clean with water and white vinegar once a week. Many households run the same tank of water for several days in a row without emptying it. A dehumidifier's collection bucket needs similar attention. Standing water left in the bucket after the unit shuts off gives mold and mildew a foothold in a spot most people only check when it needs emptying. A musty or slightly sour smell coming specifically from the direction of either appliance, rather than from the room generally, is the clearest sign the tank needs cleaning. Some humidifier models include a demineralization cartridge or filter that also needs regular replacement. Mineral buildup on the filter can trap moisture and bacteria the same way the tank does. Both appliances are easy to overlook as odor sources because people associate them with improving air quality rather than degrading it. The smell often gets blamed on something else in the room first. Checking the tank or bucket before assuming the problem lies elsewhere usually identifies the source within a minute or two. Portable humidifiers used only in certain seasons are particularly prone to this if they're stored with water still inside the tank between uses. A closed, damp tank left in a closet for months gives mold far more time to establish itself than a tank used and refilled daily. Emptying, rinsing, and fully drying the tank before long-term storage keeps that problem from developing before the machine is even turned on again. Standing water under houseplants Credit: cottonbro studio / Pexels Water left sitting in a plant's saucer for more than a day or two creates a damp, low-oxygen environment. Anaerobic bacteria and root rot thrive there and produce a distinctly sour or musty smell. That smell often gets mistaken for general mustiness in the room rather than traced back to a specific plant. Overwatering is the most common cause, since most saucers are sized to catch drainage rather than hold a reservoir of water long-term. Soil that stays soggy for extended periods starves plant roots of oxygen. The roots that die off in that environment begin to decompose while still in the pot. Standing water plus decaying organic matter is what produces the odor. It also attracts fungus gnats, small flies that breed specifically in overly wet potting soil. Emptying any water left in a saucer within an hour or two of watering, rather than letting the plant sit in it, is the simplest fix. It prevents the problem before it starts. Checking that a pot has proper drainage holes in the first place matters just as much. A decorative pot without drainage forces excess water to collect at the bottom of the soil with nowhere to go. A plant that has already developed a sour smell from its soil usually needs to come out of its pot so the roots can be inspected. Soft, dark, or mushy roots indicate rot that has already set in. Trimming those sections away before repotting in fresh, well-draining soil is often enough to save the plant while eliminating the smell at its source. Succulents and cacti are especially sensitive to this problem. Their native growing conditions involve infrequent watering and fast-draining soil, so standing water beneath them causes root rot faster than it would in a plant adapted to consistently moist conditions. Self-watering pots, which separate a water reservoir from the soil with a wicking system, avoid the issue by design. That only works if the reservoir itself gets emptied and rinsed out periodically rather than simply topped off indefinitely. The anode rod inside a water heater Credit: Alex Tyson / Unsplash Most storage tank water heaters contain a sacrificial anode rod, usually made of magnesium or aluminum. It's designed to corrode in place of the tank itself. In certain water conditions, that rod reacts with naturally occurring sulfate-reducing bacteria to produce hydrogen sulfide gas. The result smells like rotten eggs coming straight out of the hot water tap. This is more common with well water than with municipal water, since well water more often contains the bacteria involved in the reaction. The smell typically shows up only in hot water, not cold. That's a useful way to confirm the water heater is the source rather than a drain or sewer line elsewhere in the house. A water heater that has sat unused for an extended period, such as during a vacation, often develops the smell more quickly. The water inside simply has more time to react with the rod. Replacing a magnesium anode rod with an aluminum-zinc alloy rod usually reduces or eliminates the reaction. The zinc component interferes with the bacteria's ability to produce the sulfur compound. In some cases, flushing the tank and raising the thermostat temperature to around 140 degrees Fahrenheit for several hours kills off the bacteria directly. This should be done carefully, given the scalding risk at that temperature. A plumber can also install a powered anode rod, which uses an electrical current instead of a sacrificial metal to protect the tank. That avoids the chemical reaction entirely. The anode rod sits inside the tank and is never visible during normal use. Most homeowners never learn it exists until a rotten egg smell in the hot water forces them to look into the cause. Some water heaters come equipped with two anode rods rather than one. In those units, only the rod that's actively reacting with the bacteria typically needs replacing, while the second rod can usually stay in place. A plumber, or a model number lookup on the manufacturer's site, can confirm how many rods a specific unit has before any parts get ordered.

item.title: 15 things every parent should know before their kid goes to college
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.52
15 things every parent should know before their kid goes to college What parents should know before their kid goes to college, from FERPA and FAFSA deadlines to health insurance and dorm room coverage The paperwork that gets a teenager into college looks nothing like the paperwork that governs their life once they're actually there. Somewhere between the acceptance letter and move-in day, a legal switch flips. The same child whose school records, medical information and financial aid file a parent could once access without asking now controls all of it alone. Turning 18 does that, regardless of who is still paying the tuition bill. Most families spend the summer before college focused on dorm shopping lists and orientation schedules. They skip the handful of legal, financial and medical steps that actually determine whether a parent can help if something goes wrong during freshman year. This is not a packing list. It is the practical, occasionally bureaucratic layer of preparation that a school orientation session tends to rush through. Most of it gets squeezed into the 15 minutes between the financial aid presentation and the campus tour. Some of it is legal: who can see grades, who can talk to a doctor, who has authority to act if a student is incapacitated. Some of it is financial: how a family actually pays for four years, and how a young adult starts building credit before signing a first apartment lease. Some of it is procedural: how billing, housing and campus safety work once a student is no longer a minor living under one roof. None of it requires a lawyer or a financial planner to understand. Almost all of it needs to happen before move-in day, not after an emergency makes it urgent. What parents should know before their kid goes to college has less to do with extra-long twin sheets and more to do with 15 specific, low-drama tasks. These are forms to sign, accounts to set up, conversations to have while everyone is still calm and sitting at the kitchen table. Below are the 15 that matter most, organized roughly in the order a family will need them. The list starts with the legal fine print of turning 18 and ends with the roommate conflict that a parent will not be the one to solve. FERPA privacy law limits what colleges can tell you after your child turns 18 Credit: Canva Images The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, or FERPA, transfers control of a student's education records from parent to student. This happens the moment that student turns 18 or enrolls in any postsecondary program, whichever comes first. That is true even if a parent is covering the full cost of tuition. In practice, this means a college registrar cannot confirm grades, class attendance, disciplinary status or academic standing to a parent by default. That holds even over the phone, once a student is enrolled. The law does carve out one exception. A school may, but is not required to, share education records with a parent if the student is claimed as a dependent for federal tax purposes. That exception is permissive, not automatic. Individual colleges set their own policy on whether they actually use it. The more reliable path is consent. Most colleges have their own FERPA release or consent form, separate from the federal statute itself. A student can sign it to formally authorize the school to discuss specified information with a named parent or guardian. These forms typically let a student choose exactly what to share: academic records, financial aid status, housing information or all of the above. Some schools call this a "FERPA waiver." Others build it into a general parent or guardian access portal tied to the student's account. The practical move for a family is to ask about this form during orientation, before the semester starts, rather than discovering the policy exists during a crisis. A student who is reluctant to sign a blanket release can still agree to a narrower one, covering only emergencies or only financial matters, for example. Colleges vary in how they administer this. The office to contact is usually the registrar or the dean of students, not general admissions. It is worth saying plainly to a college-bound 18-year-old that this is not a trust issue. It is simply how the law is written. The same privacy protection will apply to that student's own employer, landlord and future creditors for the rest of their adult life. Learning to manage it now, while the stakes are still relatively low, is part of the transition itself. Set up a health care proxy and power of attorney before they leave Credit: Scott Graham / Unsplash A health care proxy, sometimes called a medical power of attorney, names a specific person authorized to make medical decisions on a patient's behalf. It applies if that patient becomes unable to make decisions personally. A separate document, a durable power of attorney, does the same thing for financial and legal matters, such as accessing a bank account or handling a lease. Neither exists automatically for an adult child, even a parent who has managed every doctor's appointment and bank account for 18 years. This distinction surprises many families. A parent assumes that if their 18-year-old is seriously injured or hospitalized, they will simply be allowed to make decisions, the way they always have. Legally, that assumption is wrong. Once a child turns 18, a parent has no more automatic authority over that child's medical treatment or finances than a stranger has. That changes only once the appropriate document is signed and on file. These forms are inexpensive and simple to execute. The exact requirements, including notarization and witness rules, vary by state. A student will likely spend the school year in a different state from where the family lives. It is worth checking the requirements of the state where the college is located, not just the family's home state. Some hospitals will look for a document that follows their own state's format. A number of states offer free, downloadable health care proxy forms through their department of health website. Some colleges distribute these forms directly to incoming students as part of orientation materials, occasionally alongside the HIPAA authorization described earlier. It is common, and efficient, to complete both the health care proxy and the HIPAA release in the same sitting. They cover related but distinct situations: one grants the right to receive information, the other grants the right to act on it. For most 18-year-olds heading to college in good health, these documents will sit unused in a drawer for four years. That is the intended outcome. The purpose is not to anticipate disaster but to remove one layer of legal uncertainty from a difficult situation. Without it, a family may discover they have no formal standing to help when it matters most. File the FAFSA every year, not just senior year of high school Credit: Canva Images The Free Application for Federal Student Aid, known as the FAFSA, must be submitted every academic year a student wants to be considered for federal aid. It is not a one-time step during the college application process. Families sometimes complete it once as high school seniors and assume it carries forward automatically. It does not. The form determines eligibility for federal grants, federal student loans and work-study. Most colleges also use it to award their own institutional grants and scholarships, along with many state aid programs. Skipping it in sophomore or junior year, even for a family that did not qualify for aid as freshmen, can mean missing aid that becomes available later. A change in household income, a second child enrolling in college, or updated federal aid formulas can all shift eligibility from one year to the next. Federal law requires the FAFSA for each academic year to launch no later than October 1 of the prior calendar year. Families should plan to file as close to that opening as their financial documents allow. A portion of aid at many schools is awarded on a first-come, first-served basis until funds run out. Filing early does not lock in a worse outcome. It simply ensures a student's application is reviewed before need-based funds are exhausted at that particular school. Both the student and at least one contributing parent need their own account on the federal student aid website to complete the form. Both parties provide separate consent and sign separately. Setting these accounts up in advance of the FAFSA's opening, rather than waiting until filing day, avoids a common bottleneck. The FAFSA also generates a Student Aid Index, the number colleges use to calculate a family's expected contribution toward the cost of attendance. This figure can shift meaningfully year to year based on income, family size and the number of siblings enrolled in college at the same time. That is exactly why refiling annually, rather than assuming last year's result still applies, protects a family from leaving aid on the table. Confirm your child's meningitis vaccine status before move-in day Credit: Canva Images Meningococcal disease spreads more easily in group living situations like dormitories. That is why many colleges require documentation of meningitis vaccination before a student can move into campus housing. Two separate vaccines are involved, and they are not interchangeable, so it is worth understanding both before assuming the requirement is already satisfied. The MenACWY vaccine protects against four strains of meningococcal bacteria. The CDC recommends it for all adolescents, typically as a first dose at age 11 or 12 with a booster at age 16. A student who received that first dose before turning 16 needs the booster to be considered up to date. A student who received their only dose at 16 or older generally does not need an additional booster. Many colleges specifically require proof of a dose received within five years of enrollment for students living in residence halls. The second vaccine, MenB, protects against a different strain not covered by MenACWY, and it is handled differently. The CDC recommends it through shared clinical decision-making between a patient and their doctor, generally for those between ages 16 and 18. It is not treated as a routine, universal requirement. Some colleges require MenB in addition to MenACWY, particularly in states or campuses that have experienced past outbreaks. Others leave it as a personal decision between the family and their physician. Requirements differ by state and by individual college. The reliable way to confirm what is actually needed is to check the specific documentation requirements published by the college's student health center. Do not rely on a general assumption based on a sibling's experience at a different school or an outdated pediatrician's note. Scheduling a pre-college physical several weeks before move-in, rather than the week before, leaves time to get any needed doses. It also leaves time to have paperwork properly signed and submitted through the health portal most colleges use to track compliance. Decide whether your child stays on your health insurance or gets a student plan Credit: Marek Studzinski / Unsplash Under the Affordable Care Act, a young adult can remain on a parent's health insurance plan until age 26. This holds regardless of student status, marital status or financial independence. That makes staying on a family plan the default option for most college students, but it is not automatically the right one for every situation. The relevant question is not eligibility, since virtually every college student qualifies to stay on a parent's plan. The relevant question is network coverage in the location where the student will actually be living for nine months of the year. A family health plan built around doctors and hospitals near home may have thin or nonexistent in-network coverage in a college town several states away. That gap can turn a routine urgent care visit into an unexpectedly expensive out-of-network bill. Most four-year colleges offer their own student health insurance plan, sometimes called a SHIP, as an alternative or supplement. These plans are typically priced for a healthy young adult population. They are often designed to work seamlessly with the campus health center, nearby urgent care clinics, and referral networks the school already has in place. Some colleges automatically enroll and bill every student for the SHIP unless the family formally submits a waiver proving comparable coverage already exists. Checking for this waiver deadline, usually in the first few weeks of the semester, matters even for families planning to stay on their existing plan. The practical step, before move-in, is to call the family's insurance provider. Ask specifically whether major hospitals and urgent care centers near the college are in-network, not just whether the plan is technically valid nationwide. A plan that is valid does not guarantee it is useful in an actual emergency near campus. For students attending college in another country, or for graduate and international students, the calculation changes further. A school's international student office is usually the best source for what coverage is actually required. Get renters insurance for your child's dorm room Credit: Canva Images A standard homeowner's or renter's insurance policy covering the family home does not automatically extend full protection to a child's belongings in a dorm room hundreds of miles away. Many policies do offer some coverage for a dependent's property while they are away at school. That coverage is often capped at a fraction of the home policy's total limit, sometimes as low as 10 percent of the policy's personal property coverage. That fraction can fall short of the real replacement value of a laptop, a bicycle, a musical instrument and a dorm room's worth of electronics combined. The first step is a phone call to the family's existing insurance agent. Ask specifically what the policy covers for a college student living away from home, and what the dollar limit is. This single question resolves most of the uncertainty and costs nothing. If the existing coverage seems thin relative to what the student is bringing to campus, a separate renters insurance policy is worth considering. Purchased directly for the student's dorm room or off-campus apartment, it typically costs little. It covers theft, fire and water damage, along with liability if a guest is injured in the room. Off-campus apartments raise a related but separate issue. Most landlords do not carry insurance that protects a tenant's personal belongings, only the physical building itself. A renters policy becomes considerably more important once a student moves out of college-managed housing after freshman year. It is also worth checking whether valuable individual items exceed the per-item limits most standard policies set for a single high-value object. A musical instrument used for a music program or specialized camera equipment are common examples that sometimes require a separate rider to be fully covered. This is a five-minute conversation with an insurance agent that most families skip entirely. Many discover the gap in coverage only after a laptop is stolen from an unlocked dorm room during a fire alarm evacuation. That is one of the most common dorm theft scenarios on record. Set up tuition portal access before the first bill arrives Credit: Julio Lopez / Unsplash Most colleges manage billing through a separate online system from the one used for grades and academic records, commonly called a bursar account or student financial portal. Tuition bills, payment history and tax documents like the 1098-T form all live in this system. FERPA governs access to it just as it governs academic records. A parent generally cannot view or pay a bill through this portal unless the student has specifically granted access. The mechanism for this is usually called authorized user or authorized payer access. It is set up by the student, from inside their own account, by adding a parent's name and email address to a designated payer list. This is a separate process from any general FERPA release the student may have signed for academic records, so completing one does not automatically complete the other. A family that assumes a signed FERPA form covers billing access may discover otherwise when the first bill goes unpaid because no one but the student received the notification. This step is worth completing during the first week on campus, before the first bill is generated, rather than after a payment deadline has already passed. Many schools send billing notifications only to the student's school email address by default. A parent has no visibility into this unless the authorized payer system is set up and the parent has created their own login for the portal. The same portal typically houses the 1098-T tuition statement needed for education tax credits at filing time, along with a running ledger of scholarships, loan disbursements and any outstanding balance. Setting up access early means a parent can review this information directly each semester. That beats relying on a student to forward documents during a busy academic term, when tax paperwork is rarely a priority. Campus counseling centers are free, but sessions are often capped Credit: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash Nearly all colleges provide free or low-cost mental health counseling to enrolled students through a campus counseling center, but the free part typically comes with real limits. Many centers cap the number of individual counseling sessions available per student per semester, commonly somewhere between six and 12 sessions. After that, a student is referred to an outside provider for ongoing care. Demand at these centers tends to spike around midterms and finals. Wait times for an initial appointment can stretch to several weeks during exactly the periods when students are most likely to seek help. Some schools have added same-day crisis appointments or a separate emergency line specifically to handle urgent situations outside the standard appointment queue. It is worth identifying these options in advance rather than during a crisis itself. Because of these caps and wait times, it is useful for a family to research off-campus therapy options in the college's area before the semester begins. This matters most if a student has an existing mental health condition or has worked with a therapist in the past. Many campus counseling centers keep a referral list of local providers who accept the student health insurance plan or offer sliding-scale rates. This list is generally available on request even before a student needs it. Telehealth has also expanded access considerably, letting a student in a college town continue sessions with a therapist based elsewhere. State licensing rules for therapists can restrict this option, though, depending on which state the therapist is licensed in versus where the student is physically located during the session. Confirming this detail with an existing therapist before the semester starts avoids an unwelcome surprise later. A session should not need to be rescheduled or discontinued right after a student has relocated for school. Ask about your college's medical amnesty policy Credit: Dennis Zhang / Unsplash A medical amnesty policy, sometimes called a Good Samaritan policy, is a formal college rule. It waives certain disciplinary consequences for a student who seeks emergency medical help during an alcohol or drug related crisis. This applies whether the student is calling for themselves or for someone else. The intent is straightforward: remove the fear of getting in trouble as a reason a student might hesitate to call for help in a genuine emergency. The specifics vary considerably from school to school. Some policies protect only the person calling for help. Others protect the person needing help as well, and some extend protection to everyone present at the scene. Certain policies limit the exemption to a first occurrence, requiring the student to complete an educational program or meet with a dean afterward even though no formal disciplinary record results. Others place no limit on how many times the policy can be invoked. This information is typically published in the student handbook or code of conduct, usually under a heading related to alcohol and drug policy. It is not always framed prominently or explained during orientation. It is worth a student actually locating and reading the specific policy at their own school. It should not be assumed to work the same way it might at a friend's college, since the differences between schools can be significant. The policy generally applies specifically to alcohol and drug related medical emergencies, not to unrelated conduct violations that might come to light during the same incident. It is not a blanket protection against all disciplinary consequences. It helps to understand this distinction in advance and to discuss it directly with a college-bound student before the first party of the semester. Doing so gives a young adult one less reason to hesitate before calling 911 or campus safety when someone genuinely needs medical attention. Your child has to pick one address for voter registration Credit: Edmond Dantès / Pexels A college student who moves to a different city or state for school has a choice, not an obligation, about where to register to vote. The options are a campus or college-town address, or a permanent home address. They cannot be registered in both places at once. Choosing one over the other can affect which local and state races they are eligible to vote in. School board seats, local ballot measures and state legislative races all differ by address. Registering at a college address means voting in local elections that directly affect the community where a student spends most of the year. Some students find that more relevant to their day-to-day life. Registering at a home address, and voting by absentee or mail ballot from school, keeps a student connected to elections in the place they still consider home. That option also avoids the paperwork of establishing residency in a new state. Deadlines matter more here than most students expect. Voter registration deadlines are set by each state individually. They commonly fall somewhere between 15 and 30 days before an election, though a growing number of states now offer same-day registration. Absentee or mail ballot request deadlines are a separate and usually earlier cutoff from the registration deadline itself. Missing either one is one of the most common reasons a college student ends up unable to vote in an election they intended to participate in. Because these rules are set at the state level and change periodically, the most reliable source of current deadlines is each state's official secretary of state or elections website. Do not rely on a general assumption based on a previous election cycle or a friend's experience in a different state. Encourage a student to check this before the semester starts. Setting a personal reminder ahead of the actual deadline, rather than the election date itself, prevents the scramble that otherwise tends to happen in the final week before an election. Sign up for your college's emergency alert system as a parent Credit: Canva Images Nearly every college operates a campus-wide emergency notification system that sends text messages, emails or app alerts for severe weather, active threats, campus closures and other safety incidents. Students are typically enrolled automatically using their school-issued phone number and email. The system depends on that contact information staying current, which does not always happen if a student changes their phone number or rarely checks their school email. A growing number of schools also offer a separate way for parents or other family members to subscribe directly to a filtered version of these alerts. This is distinct from the general parent newsletters or social media updates most colleges also send. This family-facing alert option is usually opt-in and found through the campus safety or emergency management office's website, rather than the general admissions or parent relations page. It is worth searching specifically rather than assuming it does not exist. This is different from the more routine parent communications a college sends about billing deadlines or family weekend. It is also different from the FERPA-protected records discussed earlier, since safety alerts are treated as general public safety information rather than a student's private education record. Signing up does not give a parent any access to a student's personal data. It simply adds a parent to the distribution list for time-sensitive safety notifications that any member of the public in a genuine emergency might also receive. This system tends to matter more than families expect during the first semester. That is especially true for a student attending school in a region prone to a particular kind of severe weather, or on a campus in a dense urban area. Neither the student nor the parent yet has a strong sense of how the school handles communication during an actual incident. It is worth a few minutes during the first week of the semester to confirm a working phone number and email are on file. Check both the student's own account and any parent subscription option. That beats waiting until the first weather alert reveals the contact information was never updated from an old number. Roommate conflicts go through the RA, not through you Credit: Canva Images Resident advisors, commonly called RAs, are trained student staff members who live in the dorm alongside first-year students. Their job includes managing the day-to-day realities of communal living, including roommate conflicts. Most colleges structure their housing conflict resolution process to start with the RA, then move up to a hall director or residence life staff member if needed. A formal room-change request typically comes only after those earlier steps have been attempted. This structure exists partly because colleges want students to practice resolving interpersonal conflict directly. It is a skill that will matter in shared apartments, workplaces and other group living situations for the rest of their lives. It also exists because housing staff are simply better positioned than a parent hundreds of miles away. They can understand the specific dynamics of a hall, mediate a conversation in person, or move furniture and belongings if a room change is approved. A parent who calls the housing office directly on a student's behalf is often redirected back to the student. This is not because the concern is not taken seriously. Most housing offices require the student themselves to initiate a room-change request or formal complaint. That is partly for the same privacy reasons that govern academic and billing records elsewhere in college life. This can feel frustrating to a parent used to intervening directly during the K-12 years, but it reflects a consistent pattern across nearly every part of the college experience. The more effective role for a parent in a roommate conflict is coaching from a distance. That means helping a student think through what they actually want to say to the RA. It also means rehearsing how to describe the specific behavior that is a problem, rather than making a general complaint about a roommate's personality. It also means encouraging the student to document specific incidents if a pattern is forming that might eventually support a room-change request. This approach tends to produce a faster and more durable resolution than a parent trying to work the college's administrative structure directly. Grades and attendance won't be reported home to you Credit: Canva Images Most K-12 schools give parents a login to a portal tracking every quiz grade, absence and missing assignment in real time. Colleges generally do not provide this kind of ongoing academic monitoring to parents at all. That holds true regardless of who is paying tuition. A student can miss three weeks of a class, fail a midterm or stop attending entirely, and no automated system will notify a parent of any of it. This is a direct extension of the FERPA privacy protections described earlier. It is worth calling out specifically because it is the single biggest structural shift many parents underestimate. In high school, a missed assignment often triggers an email within days. In college, a professor may not follow up with a struggling student at all unless that student proactively reaches out during office hours. Grades typically only become visible to the student themselves through the school's portal, at their discretion, once posted. Academic advising exists at every college, but advisors generally meet with students only a few times a semester, usually around registration periods. They are not monitoring day-to-day performance. Most advisors will not contact a parent regardless of how a student is performing. That is partly because of privacy law, and partly because the student is considered the primary point of contact for their own education from day one. The practical response for a family is to set expectations before the semester starts rather than assume information will surface on its own. Some families ask a student to share a screenshot of grades at the end of each term. Others have a standing conversation partway through the semester specifically about how classes are going, before a single bad exam becomes an unmanageable spiral. Whatever the arrangement, it needs to be an explicit agreement made in advance. No institutional system will fill that gap automatically, and a parent hoping to stay informed by default will generally be left with no information at all.

item.title: Hershey is loading up Halloween bags with popcorn and pretzels as health-conscious eating rises
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.29
The chocolate maker says its Zero Sugar candy business has grown more than 4 times over the past five years as health-conscious eating rises The company said its 2026 Halloween lineup includes more than 20 product additions across chocolate, candy and salty snacks. For the first time, brands including SkinnyPop, Pirate's Booty and LesserEvil will be part of Hershey's seasonal Halloween offering, joining its established chocolate and candy lines. "Certainly, the Lesser Evil brand and our salty snacks brands broadly, Skinny Pop and Pirate's Booty, having a greater presence in Halloween is in response to the (healthy eating) dynamic," Daniel Mohnshine, who serves as Hershey's vice president for demand creation, strategy and innovation, said in comments to Reuters. Mohnshine said chocolate remains the Halloween snack of choice and that the category has shown resilience in the face of GLP-1 weight-loss drug adoption. He also noted, without providing specific numbers, that Halloween-season purchases of smaller chocolate and candy packs were tracking well ahead of the prior year's pace, according to Reuters. Mohnshine said the Zero Sugar segment spanning candy, mints and gum achieved roughly 4.3-fold growth in U.S. dollar terms over the five years ending in 2025. The salty snack additions include individually portioned SkinnyPop popcorn packs in Halloween-themed packaging, Pirate's Booty aged white cheddar puffs in snack-size bags, LesserEvil Pumpkin Spice Popcorn and an assortment of Reese's Dipped Pretzels and Reese's Filled Pretzels, the company said. LesserEvil is appearing in the Halloween lineup for the first time. Hershey's "Unwrapping Halloween" report, produced with data intelligence firm Morning Consult, found that 30% of parents plan to bring their children to trunk-or-treat events this year. The report surveyed 3,026 U.S. adults between July 8 and July 10, 2026. Mohnshine said artificial intelligence has helped accelerate product development timelines. "We've removed about three months from the typical timeframe it takes to go from consumer insight to approved concept," he told Reuters, and said the accelerated pace had driven a 75% expansion of the company's innovation pipeline over the prior nine months. Hershey also pointed to an extended Halloween shopping season as a driver of the broader lineup. Its report found that a significant share of parents — nearly two-thirds — had already stocked up on Halloween candy before summer ended, with half entering what Hershey describes as "Halloween mode" well ahead of October. Hershey raised the upper end of its full-year guidance after second-quarter net sales rose 6.6% to $2.79 billion, with North America Salty Snacks sales climbing 22.9%. The company has pointed to new product introductions and seasonal campaigns as catalysts for its back-half performance. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

item.title: Marvell stock surges after chipmaker hands Google a $12.2 billion stake option in new AI chip deal
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.28
Marvell Technology issued Google $GOOGL a warrant to purchase up to 58.97 million shares of its common stock, valued at as much as $12.2 billion if fully exercised, as part of a new custom semiconductor agreement, the company said. Marvell stock jumped more than 11% in premarket trading on Wednesday.

item.title: Here are the top 9 best rotisserie chickens, according to Consumer Reports
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.21
Here are the top 9 best rotisserie chickens, according to Consumer Reports Store-bought rotisserie chicken can vary in seasoning, texture and sodium. Consumer Reports tested nine brands to find the best-tasting bird Rotisserie chicken offers an easy weeknight dinner solution without turning on the oven, but flavor and sodium content vary widely by store. Seasoning style, moisture level and how much salt ends up in the meat can differ significantly even among birds sold at a similar price. Consumer Reports tested rotisserie chicken from nine grocery chains for taste, texture and nutrition, so shoppers can pick up the best bird for their weeknight dinner. Sam's Club Member's Mark Seasoned Rotisserie Chicken Credit: Sam's Club Priced at $4.98 for a 3-pound bird, or about $1.66 per pound, the Sam's Club Member's Mark Seasoned Rotisserie Chicken uses a paprika rub for color and flavor. Consumer Reports named it the best-tasting chicken of the nine brands tested, describing the meat as very moist and juicy with a deep roasted flavor. CR also noted hints of onion and garlic in the seasoning, along with a bronzed color that suggested even cooking throughout. Testers said this pick surprised some loyal Costco $COST shoppers, since Sam's Club edged out its more famous rival on flavor alone. Costco Kirkland Signature Seasoned Rotisserie Chicken Credit: Costco Matching the Sam's Club price exactly, the Costco $COST Kirkland Signature Seasoned Rotisserie Chicken costs $4.99 for 3 pounds, or about $1.66 per pound. Consumer Reports described it as unusually plump compared with the other chickens tested, with meat that tasted moist and well seasoned. CR found its labeled sodium of 460 milligrams tied with ShopRite, both higher than every other brand tested, though actual samples measured only 112 and 194 milligrams. Testers noted the saltiness varied noticeably between the two samples they checked. Stop & Shop Whole Rotisserie Chicken Credit: Stop & Shop Shriveled skin and a couple of nearly burnt samples didn't stop testers from enjoying the $7.99, 1.75-pound Stop & Shop Whole Rotisserie Chicken. Consumer Reports found the meat itself tasted far better than it looked, rating it very flavorful and tender. CR recorded calorie and fat counts below every other chicken in this test, at 120 calories and 4 grams of fat. Testers also measured its saturated fat at just 1 gram, again below every other brand tested. Walmart Traditional Fully-Cooked Rotisserie Chicken Credit: Walmart Lemon and rosemary notes season the $5.97, 2.25-pound Walmart $WMT Traditional Fully-Cooked Rotisserie Chicken. Consumer Reports found the meat well seasoned and described the texture as moist and tender. CR recorded its calorie and fat counts well above every other chicken in this test, at 250 calories and 19 grams of fat. Testers also measured its saturated fat at 6 grams, again higher than any other brand tested. Wegmans Whole Roasted Chicken, Plain Credit: Wegmans Sea salt is the only seasoning on the $9.99, 2.13-pound Wegmans Whole Roasted Chicken, Plain. Consumer Reports called this plain approach a good choice for purists, since it let the roasted chicken flavor come through clearly. CR found it looked paler than every other chicken in this test, a direct result of skipping the seasoning rubs used elsewhere. Testers recorded its labeled sodium at 440 milligrams, with actual samples measuring 188 and 206 milligrams. Whole Foods Market Classic Rotisserie Chicken Credit: Whole Foods At $8.99 for 1.75 pounds, or about $5.14 per pound, the Whole Foods Market Classic Rotisserie Chicken costs more per pound than every other brand in this test. Consumer Reports found it seasoned with only salt and cracked black pepper, which added some heat to the flavor. CR rated the meat a bit drier than other chickens in this test but said it remained tender with plenty of flavor, and noted it was the only brand tested that wasn't brined. Testers also recorded its protein content at 23 grams, higher than any other brand in this test. BJ's Wellsley Farms Whole Rotisserie Chicken Credit: Wellsley Farms At $4.99 for 3 pounds, or about $1.66 per pound, the BJ's Wellsley Farms Whole Rotisserie Chicken matches the price of both the Sam's Club and Costco $COST picks above. Consumer Reports described the flavor as fairly mild, with meat that ran dry and had a somewhat chewy bite. CR's own sample testing measured its sodium at 82 and 151 milligrams, below every other brand tested despite a labeled sodium content similar to several pricier competitors. Testers listed its brine as containing carrageenan, natural flavors, salt, sodium phosphate and sugar. Hannaford Original Rotisserie Chicken Credit: Hannaford Unlike every other chicken in this test, the $7.99, 1.88-pound Hannaford Original Rotisserie Chicken came from a retailer that didn't provide full nutrition information. Consumer Reports still measured sodium directly from tested samples, recording 102 and 182 milligrams. CR found the meat a bit salty and on the dry side, with an appearance that varied from pale golden to almost burnt across samples. Testers listed its brine as containing carrageenan, salt and sugar. ShopRite Bowl & Basket All-Natural Whole Rotisserie Chicken Credit: ShopRite A wide swing in sodium between samples set apart the $7.99, 2.06-pound ShopRite Bowl & Basket All-Natural Whole Rotisserie Chicken. Consumer Reports found its well-seasoned, roasted flavor stood out, though the texture varied, with two samples turning up slightly dry and chewy. CR found its labeled sodium of 460 milligrams tied with Costco $COST, both higher than every other brand tested. Testers recorded an especially wide gap in actual sodium between the two samples checked, measuring 142 and 322 milligrams.

item.title: The 5 best headphones and their budget alternatives, ranked by Consumer Reports
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.18
The 5 best headphones and their budget alternatives, ranked by Consumer Reports Headphones can sound tinny or fail to block outside noise. Consumer Reports tested five categories to find the best-sounding picks Headphones and earbuds range from budget-friendly basics to premium models built for critical listening, with sound quality varying widely between the two. Noise cancellation, fit and how accurately a pair reproduces bass, midrange and treble can differ dramatically even within the same price tier. Consumer Reports tested headphones and earbuds across five categories, from noise-canceling earbuds to open-back wired models, and identified a budget alternative for each top pick, so shoppers can find great sound at nearly any price. Top pick: Apple AirPods Pro 3 Credit: Apple Priced at $250, the Apple $AAPL AirPods Pro 3 pair an isolating ear-insert design with an ambient sound mode for staying aware of surroundings. Consumer Reports rated its sound quality very good and its active noise reduction excellent. CR found the bass hits deep but runs a bit boomy, while the treble stays extended but can sound slightly sizzly on certain recordings. Testers said the earbuds come with five pairs of ear tips in different sizes and support MagSafe and Qi wireless charging. Budget alternative: Beats Studio Buds+ Credit: Beats by Dre The Beats Studio Buds+ cost about $170 and don't carry the Apple $AAPL name, though Apple owns the Beats brand and sells them in its own stores. Consumer Reports found these true wireless earbuds pair smoothly with an iPhone or other Apple hardware, much like AirPods do. CR pointed to satisfying sound and impressive noise-canceling performance as reasons to consider this pick over the pricier AirPods Pro 3, especially for anyone who doesn't need its hearing-aid-adjacent features. Testers found very little difference in performance between the Studio Buds+ and the previous-generation Studio Buds. Top pick: Sony WF-1000XM6 Credit: Sony Four sets of ear tips in different sizes come with the $300 Sony $SONY WF-1000XM6, along with a carrying case. Consumer Reports scored its overall performance ahead of every other pick in this test, rating sound quality and active noise reduction both excellent. CR found the isolating design provides some muffling of external noise on top of the electronic cancellation, while an ambient mode lets outside sound back in when needed. Testers said it charges via a USB-A to USB-C cable and comes with a quick start guide and aux cable in the box. Budget alternative: Soundcore Space A40 Credit: Soundcore The Soundcore Space A40 is sometimes priced below $50, well under the Sony $SONY WF-1000XM6's $300 price tag. Consumer Reports found it delivered solid sound quality along with top-notch noise reduction in testing, despite the price gap. CR's member surveys placed the Soundcore brand's reliability in the very good range, with owner satisfaction scoring even higher. Testers pointed to this model as proof that strong ANC performance doesn't require spending hundreds of dollars. Top pick: Bose Ultra Open Earbuds Credit: Bose A non-isolating design that leaves the ear canal open defines the $300 Bose Ultra Open Earbuds. Consumer Reports rated its sound quality very good, noting these earbuds don't block external noise and let some of their own sound escape. CR said this design suits people who listen in quiet settings or want to stay aware of what's happening around them. Testers noted it comes with a USB-A to USB-C charging cable and a charging case with a built-in battery. Budget alternative: Sony LinkBuds Credit: Sony The Sony $SONY LinkBuds cost $180, much less than the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds above. Consumer Reports found these earbuds use a doughnut-shaped driver with a hole through the center, producing an ambient-sound effect similar to the Bose model. CR said they're well-suited to activities where staying connected to your surroundings matters. Testers found the earbuds stay in place well, though the most secure fit doesn't always deliver the best sound, so trying before buying or choosing a flexible return policy makes sense. Top pick: Apple AirPods Max 2 Credit: Apple A closed, over-ear design with an ambient sound mode defines the $550 Apple $AAPL AirPods Max 2. Consumer Reports rated its sound quality and active noise reduction both excellent. CR said the closed design muffles outside noise both acoustically and electronically, while also reducing how much sound escapes to bother others nearby. Testers noted it comes with a USB-C charging cable and a smart carrying case, and pointed out that its home/studio-style size won't suit everyone. Budget alternative: Monoprice BT-300ANC Credit: Monoprice For around $55, the Monoprice BT-300ANC offers a low-cost path to wireless noise-canceling sound. Consumer Reports found it sounds better than models costing hundreds more, with noise-canceling performance the company called top-notch. CR rated its closed, over-ear design capable of working with the noise-canceling feature on or off, and it can connect wirelessly or via a cable. Testers said it comes with a detachable audio cable, a USB charging cable and a carrying case, backed by a 12-month warranty. Top pick: Grado RS2x Credit: Grado An open-air, home/studio-style design that doesn't block outside noise defines the $550 Grado RS2x. Consumer Reports scored its overall sound quality ahead of every other pick in this test. CR said this open design suits listening in quiet environments where letting some sound escape isn't a concern, or for anyone who wants to stay aware of their surroundings. Testers noted it comes with a mini-plug-to-quarter-inch-plug adapter and requires being comfortable with its home/studio-style size. Budget alternative: Grado SR125x Credit: Grado The Grado SR125x costs about $175, a fraction of the RS2x's price, and stays within the same open-back Grado lineup. Consumer Reports suggested moving down the Grado lineup as a way to get similar sound characteristics at a lower cost. CR also pointed to the even less expensive Grado SR60 for shoppers who want to spend still less. Testers said anyone who needs a closed-back design that won't leak sound into the room should consider the Audio-Technica ATH-M50x instead.

item.title: Mortgage demand stalls as rates hold near their highest level in a year
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.09
Total mortgage application volume fell 0.4% last week, with purchase applications down 2% and refinance activity rising only slightly According to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index, total mortgage application volume slipped 0.4% from the prior week. The 30-year fixed rate for conforming loan balances at or below $832,750 stayed at 6.77%; associated points edged down to 0.65 from 0.67 — origination fee included — on loans carrying a 20% down payment. Applications to purchase a home dropped 2% for the week and were 3% below the same period a year ago. Refinance applications posted a 2% weekly gain yet still trailed year-ago volume by 18%, a period when borrowing costs were modestly cheaper. "Mortgage rates and applications changed little last week, with just a slight increase in refinances for conventional and VA loans, while FHA refinances were lower," Joel Kan, MBA's vice president and deputy chief economist, said in a statement. "Borrowers with larger loan sizes remain less likely to refinance with rates at these higher levels. The average loan size on refinances continues to shrink, dipping to $282,200 last week, the lowest level since June 2025." Joel Kan also pointed to deteriorating affordability as a factor weighing on purchase activity. "In addition to the economic uncertainty, affordability difficulties have reemerged as a reason for homebuyers to delay purchase decisions given the impact of higher mortgage rates on monthly mortgage payments," he said. A separate Mortgage News Daily survey showed rates ticking up slightly as the new week got underway. The current stretch of elevated rates marks a shift from conditions earlier this summer. As reported by the MBA for the week ending July 3, the 30-year fixed rate stood at 6.58% — nearly 20 basis points below last week's level — though total application volume had already begun softening, falling 2.2% that week. Refinance volume at that point was still running 8% above year-ago levels, a contrast to the 18% year-over-year decline recorded last week. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: Treasury is doubling its long-term bond buybacks to boost market liquidity
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.07
The U.S. Treasury Department announced Wednesday it is increasing the maximum size of its liquidity support buyback operations for longer-dated nominal coupon securities by at least double, from $2 billion per operation to at least $4 billion per operation. The change covers the 10-to-20-year and 20-to-30-year sectors and takes effect September 9, remaining in place through November 4, 2026.

item.title: Estée Lauder's stock pops as profit forecast beats expectations on fragrance demand
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.04
The cosmetics company forecast fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS of $3.10 to $3.35, with the midpoint above analyst estimates Revenue for the fourth quarter reached $3.63 billion, topping the $3.54 billion Wall Street had anticipated, according to Reuters. On an organic basis, net sales grew 5% in the quarter, the company said, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of growth. For the full fiscal year ended June 30, 2026, net sales rose 5% to $15.0 billion. Adjusted diluted earnings per share came in at $2.51, compared with $1.51 in the prior year. Full-year adjusted operating margin expanded 320 basis points to 11.2%. Fragrance was the standout product category, with net sales rising 10% organically for the full year, led by luxury brands Le Labo, TOM FORD, and KILIAN PARIS. Le Labo's Classic Collection and TOM FORD's Private Blend and Signature lines drove the gains, the company said. Fragrance net sales in the fourth quarter also grew 10%. Skin care net sales increased 4% organically for the full year, driven by La Mer, The Ordinary, and Estée Lauder. Makeup net sales were roughly flat for the year, with growth from M·A·C and TOM FORD offset by declines at Bobbi Brown and Too Faced. Mainland China net sales grew 9% organically for the full year, with the company reporting value share gains driven by fragrance, skin care, and makeup. All four geographic regions posted net sales growth for both the quarter and the full year. The company disclosed that tariff refunds generated a $38 million improvement to cost of sales in the fourth quarter, which helped cushion a $102 million full-year gross charge tied to incremental tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. For fiscal 2027, the company affirmed organic net sales growth guidance of 3% to 5% and raised its adjusted operating margin outlook to a range of 12.7% to 13.5%, up from a preliminary outlook of 12.5% to 13.0% issued in May 2026. President and CEO Stéphane de La Faverie said in a statement that the company delivered fiscal 2026 results "ahead of the expectations we had to start the year" and ended with organic sales growth accelerating to 5% in the fourth quarter. The company concluded approvals for the restructuring component of its Profit Recovery and Growth Plan as of June 30, 2026, with total expected gross benefits of $1.2 billion and a net reduction of approximately 10,000 positions, both at the high end of previously communicated ranges. item.title: BioMarin is acquiring Alesta Therapeutics for $275 million to develop a first oral rare bone disease treatment
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.87
BioMarin $BMRN Pharmaceutical announced Tuesday it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Alesta Therapeutics for $275 million upfront, plus up to $215 million in additional payments tied to development and regulatory milestones. The deal gives BioMarin access to ALE1, a small-molecule drug in early-stage trials that could become the first oral therapy for hypophosphatasia The acquisition centers on ALE1, an orally active small molecule being developed to treat hypophosphatasia, or HPP — a rare genetic bone disease caused by mutations in the ALPL gene. HPP can impair bone and tooth mineralization, leading to frequent fractures, early tooth loss, and, in adults, muscle weakness, fatigue, and pain. The company said the condition has been diagnosed in more than 9,000 Americans, though it is thought to be more widespread than current figures reflect. ALE1 is currently in a Phase 1/2a clinical trial evaluating its safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers and adults with HPP. If approved, it would be the first oral treatment for the disease. Current approved therapies for HPP are injectable. "ALE1 is a strong strategic fit for BioMarin, bringing a potential oral alternative to the injectable therapies available today for people living with HPP around the world while meaningfully strengthening our early-stage clinical pipeline," BioMarin President and Chief Executive Officer Alexander Hardy said in a statement. Under the terms of the deal, Alesta will spin out all non-ALE1 assets to a separate entity before the transaction closes. Alesta employees will also transfer to that spinout entity, meaning no Alesta staff will join BioMarin as part of the acquisition. BioMarin said it plans to fund the deal with cash on hand. The transaction has been approved by the boards of both companies and is expected to close in the third quarter of 2026, subject to customary conditions. ALE1 works by inhibiting a target that regulates levels of inorganic pyrophosphate, the metabolite at the center of HPP's disease pathway. By reducing excess pyrophosphate, the drug aims to restore bone and mineral metabolism. Following the close of the transaction, the program will be integrated into BioMarin's Skeletal Conditions Business Unit, the company said. Alesta Chief Executive Officer Ilan Ganot said the acquisition made sense given BioMarin's standing in the rare disease field. "BioMarin's global reach, scale, and proven expertise in rare disease drug development make it an ideal partner to advance ALE1 and realize its potential as a promising treatment for patients with HPP worldwide," Ganot said.
